title: Recognition, Simulation, and Refusal: A Contamination-Aware Study of Classic Psychological Effects in LLM Agents
summary: An LLM producing the response pattern associated with a human psychological effect is not the same claim as the LLM possessing that bias. We present PsyAgentBench, a benchmark that re-runs classic psychology experiments on LLM agents under a factorial design built to separate these: each paradigm is run with the paradigm explicitly labeled in the prompt (named) or framed as a routine task (blind), and on the literal textbook version of the task (canonical) or a structurally matched variant written to reduce lexical and scenario overlap with likely training data (counterfactual), crossed with a persona manipulation. Across five completed paradigms, evaluated on up to three open-weight model families with 41,904 trials released, apparently human-like effects arise through qualitatively different routes rather than one susceptibility: paradigm-label gating with explicit override (Asch conformity, 0 percent blind to 83.3 percent named on gpt-oss-120B), knowledge-dependent signal reliance (anchoring, exactly zero on grounded facts versus near total on invented quantities, a pattern equally consistent with rational use of the only available signal), amplification on novel content under labeling (framing), robust absence (sunk cost), and safety-mediated selection where refusal itself is the primary finding (minimal-group allocation). A one-sentence persona change (agreeableness, framed as an instruction rather than a verified trait manipulation) eliminates, dampens, or reverses these effects depending on which effect it is, arguing against any single response-bias account. We further formalize, and in two cases document empirically, three ways a psychology paradigm can fail to port to LLM agents: persona dominance, population collapse, and safety selection. We argue scalar bias-susceptibility scores obscure this structure and report replication profiles instead.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PsyAgentBench, a benchmark that re-runs classic psychology experiments on LLM agents under different conditions to distinguish between true psychological biases and mere response patterns, showing that human-like effects in LLMs emerge via multiple distinct mechanisms rather than a single bias susceptibility.
AI.motivation: Researchers increasingly test LLMs with tasks from human psychology to claim that models possess human-like cognitive biases, but such claims conflate similar output patterns with underlying mechanisms. There is a need for a principled way to determine whether LLM behaviors in these tasks reflect genuine analogs of human biases, safety filters, prompt framing, or training artifacts, and to understand when and why standard psychology paradigms fail when ported to LLM agents.
AI.method: The authors design PsyAgentBench, a factorial benchmark that re-runs classic psychology paradigms on LLM agents with controlled manipulations: (1) tasks are either explicitly labeled as a known paradigm (named) or presented as ordinary tasks (blind); (2) standard textbook task formulations (canonical) are contrasted with structurally equivalent but lexically and scenariowise altered versions to reduce overlap with training data (counterfactual); and (3) agent persona is manipulated via a brief instruction (e.g., higher agreeableness). They test five paradigms (e.g., Asch conformity, anchoring, framing, sunk cost, minimal-group allocation) across several open-weight LLM families, yielding over 40k trials, and analyze how effects depend on labeling, content novelty, knowledge grounding, and persona prompts. They also formalize three failure modes for porting paradigms to LLMs: persona dominance, population collapse, and safety selection.
AI.result: The experiments show that superficially human-like psychological effects in LLMs arise through divergent mechanisms. For Asch-style conformity, models largely ignore misleading social information in blind settings but strongly conform when the paradigm is explicitly named, revealing label-gated behavior with possible explicit override (e.g., 0% blind vs 83.3% named conformity for one model). Anchoring effects appear only when the anchor is the sole available signal (invented quantities), but vanish for grounded factual questions, suggesting rational reliance on available information rather than a generic anchoring bias. Framing effects are amplified under explicit labeling and on novel content; in contrast, no reliable sunk cost effect is found. Minimal-group allocation is dominated by safety behavior, where refusal to engage with the task becomes the main outcome. A simple persona prompt (e.g., “be more agreeable”) can remove, reduce, or invert observed effects across paradigms, undermining a single unified bias explanation. The authors empirically observe and document instances of persona dominance, population collapse, and safety selection as threats to validly porting human paradigms to LLM agents.
AI.conclusion: LLM results on classic psychology tasks cannot be straightforwardly interpreted as evidence that models possess human-like cognitive biases; similar response patterns can emerge from multiple, qualitatively distinct mechanisms including task labeling, safety policies, content familiarity, and shallow persona instructions. Scalar bias-susceptibility scores oversimplify this complexity, so the authors recommend reporting richer replication profiles that capture when and how effects appear or disappear across conditions. They further caution that many human psychology paradigms may fail to transfer directly to LLMs due to persona dominance, population collapse, and safety-driven refusals, and argue that careful experimental design is needed before drawing cognitive claims about LLMs from such tasks.

title: Memory That Looks Forward: A Zero-Inference Prospective Term for Personal Memory Retrieval
summary: Retrieval over a personal memory store is retrospective: it surfaces what resembles the query, and it is blind to what the user has committed to do. We describe a prospective term for memory retrieval that costs no inference at query time. Commitments are held in an explicit ledger as dated or trigger-conditioned entries; memory items linked to a firing entry receive a salience boost, blended multiplicatively into embedding-based retrieval so that relevance remains sovereign. On a synthetic prospective-memory task set modeled on TriggerBench's published structure (48 blind-authored dialogues, 175 tasks), the term raised recall@5 on the hard stratum from 0.000 to 0.955 at the default blend weight and to 1.000 under a floor variant, with zero false boosts across 53 resolved-commitment tasks. Blind authorship also produced a scope finding: only 17-29% of naturally phrased commitment-trigger pairs defeat embedding similarity, so the term matters on a real minority of cases and must do no harm on the rest, which it does not. We position precomputed commitment linkage as the always-on floor of a layered design whose expansion layer is query-time prospection. Results are preliminary: the evaluation set is author-constructed, and evaluation on TriggerBench proper is committed follow-up work once its data is released.

AI.tldr: They introduce a cheap, prospective retrieval term that boosts items linked to user commitments, greatly improving recall for commitment-triggered tasks without hurting normal retrieval.
AI.motivation: Standard embedding-based retrieval over personal memories is purely retrospective: it returns items similar to the current query and ignores what the user has previously committed to do, so it fails on prospective-memory tasks (remembering to act when a condition holds). The authors want a way to make retrieval sensitive to explicit commitments and their triggers, without expensive reasoning at query time and without degrading regular relevance-based search.
AI.method: They maintain an explicit ledger of commitments, each dated or conditioned on triggers (e.g., events or phrases). Memory items are pre-linked to the commitments they satisfy. At query time, when a commitment entry is considered to be “firing” (e.g., its trigger matches the query context or its date condition holds), the associated memory items receive a multiplicative salience boost that is blended into standard embedding-based similarity scoring. They design a synthetic evaluation set modeled on TriggerBench: 48 blind-authored dialogues containing 175 tasks, including a “hard” stratum where trigger wording differs from the original commitment. They compare recall@5 with and without the prospective term, and also test a “floor variant” of the boosting strategy.
AI.result: On the hard stratum in their synthetic task set, adding the prospective term increased recall@5 from 0.000 with baseline retrieval to 0.955 at the default blend weight and to 1.000 with the floor variant. Across 53 tasks where commitments were actually resolved, there were zero false boosts—no irrelevant items were wrongly promoted. Blind authorship of the dialogues allowed them to estimate scope: only about 17–29% of natural commitment–trigger pairs are badly handled by pure embedding similarity, indicating the prospective term meaningfully helps in a minority of realistic cases while not harming the majority.
AI.conclusion: Precomputing and storing explicit links between commitments and memory items, then using them as a prospective, multiplicative salience term at retrieval time, can dramatically improve performance on commitment-triggered (prospective memory) tasks without corrupting general embedding-based relevance. This mechanism is cheap at query time and well-suited as an always-on “floor layer” in a layered retrieval design, with more sophisticated query-time prospection forming an upper layer. However, their results are preliminary because the evaluation set is author-constructed; validating the approach on the official TriggerBench dataset remains future work pending its release.

title: Summarize, Judge, Refine: Decoupled Content Understanding and Policy Learning for Multimodal Content Moderation
summary: Content moderation systems traditionally entangle multimodal understanding with policy-specific classification, requiring full pipeline retraining for every policy change and suffering from label scarcity since multimedia cannot be meaningfully augmented. We propose Summarize-Judge-Refine (SJR), a two-model architecture that decouples these concerns via a natural language interface: a multimodal Content Model produces structured text summaries, and a text-only Policy Model classifies them against policy definitions. An iterative co-training loop refines the Content Model via GRPO to produce policy-relevant summaries, while text-space augmentation generates adversarial summary variants---an augmentation pathway impossible on raw multimedia---enabling few-shot policy bootstrap. Every decision is grounded in a human-readable summary, providing interpretability as a structural byproduct. On misleading advertisement detection, SJR achieves +23.6\% relative non-misleading F1 over a zero-shot chain-of-thought baseline, outperforming end-to-end SFT, STaR/RFT, and RLFT. Notably, a variant trained on zero real violating examples---with all positive-class data synthetically generated---matches the full-data model within 0.2\% relative on violating F1, demonstrating that new policies can launch without any real violation data.

AI.tldr: Proposes a two-stage ‘Summarize-Judge-Refine’ architecture that uses a multimodal model to summarize content and a text-only model to apply policies, enabling flexible policy updates, data augmentation in text space, and interpretable moderation decisions, with strong empirical gains and even working without real violation examples.
AI.motivation: Content moderation is hard to adapt to changing policies because current systems tie multimodal understanding directly to policy labels, requiring full retraining for each policy change and suffering from limited labeled multimedia data and no good augmentation strategies. The authors want a system that can easily plug in new or updated policies, work well with few labeled examples, and provide interpretable, policy-relevant justifications for decisions.
AI.method: They introduce Summarize-Judge-Refine (SJR), a two-model pipeline: (1) a multimodal Content Model that converts multimedia inputs into structured, human-readable summaries; (2) a text-only Policy Model that classifies these summaries according to policy definitions. They run an iterative co-training loop where the Policy Model’s feedback is used to refine the Content Model with GRPO so that it focuses on policy-relevant details. Additionally, they perform extensive text-space augmentation of summaries, including adversarial variants, to enrich training data and bootstrap new policies from few or even zero real violation examples.
AI.result: On a misleading advertisement detection task, SJR substantially improves performance over a strong zero-shot chain-of-thought baseline, with a 23.6% relative F1 gain on the non-misleading class, and it outperforms alternative training strategies such as end-to-end supervised fine-tuning, STaR/RFT, and RLFT. A striking result is that an SJR variant trained with no real violating examples—using only synthetic positive-class data—achieves almost the same violating-class F1 as the model trained on full real data, with only a 0.2% relative gap.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling content understanding from policy application via a natural language summary interface yields a flexible, data-efficient, and interpretable content moderation system. SJR can rapidly adapt to new policies, leverage rich text-based data augmentation that is impossible at the raw multimedia level, and maintain high performance even when real violation examples are scarce or absent, making it a practical approach for real-world, evolving moderation needs.

title: AI-inferred expressed well-being and collective-action discourse in climate-change campaigns on X
summary: Climate campaigns are often evaluated through attention and mobilization, but less is known about the well-being language that accompanies them. Whether campaign periods alter positive affect and hope, and whether happiness aligns with action language, remains unresolved. We analysed 364,118 public Twitter/X posts from Earth Day, Earth Hour, Global Climate Action Day and World Environment Day in 19 occurrence-years, using 30-day pre-event, event and post-event windows. A versioned weighted lexical model estimated happiness, future-oriented hope, collective capability, distress and action language. Event-period happiness prevalence was 9.02 percentage points higher than the pre-event baseline , whereas paired occurrence contrasts showed a 10.75-point decline in action language, indicating a happiness--action divergence. The happiness estimate remained positive across composition and text-deduplication checks, but was less precise under a 19-cluster wild bootstrap. Happier source posts had lower odds of an observed matched retweet cascade.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes Twitter/X posts during major climate campaign events and finds that happiness expressed in posts increases during events, while action-oriented language decreases, revealing a divergence between positive affect and calls to action.
AI.motivation: To understand not just attention and mobilization during climate campaigns but also the emotional and efficacy-related language surrounding them—specifically whether campaign periods change positive affect and hope, and how happiness relates to action-oriented language and online diffusion.
AI.method: The authors collected 364,118 public Twitter/X posts related to four major climate and environment campaign days across 19 occurrence-years, using 30-day pre-event, event, and post-event windows. They applied a versioned weighted lexical model to estimate levels of happiness, future-oriented hope, collective capability, distress, and action language. They conducted prevalence comparisons across time windows, robustness checks via composition and text-deduplication, and a 19-cluster wild bootstrap for uncertainty, as well as modeling the relationship between happiness in source posts and the odds of retweet cascades.
AI.result: During event periods, happiness language was 9.02 percentage points higher than in the pre-event baseline, while action-oriented language dropped by 10.75 percentage points in paired occurrence contrasts, indicating a divergence between emotional positivity and action framing. The elevated happiness estimate was robust to composition and deduplication checks but became less precise under a 19-cluster wild bootstrap. Additionally, posts with higher happiness levels had lower odds of generating matched retweet cascades.
AI.conclusion: Major climate campaign days are associated with increased expressions of happiness but decreased action-oriented language, suggesting a happiness–action divergence in online discourse. This divergence may limit the mobilizing potential of climate campaigns if positive affect is not aligned with action cues, and happier posts appear less likely to propagate via retweet cascades. The findings highlight the need for campaign strategies that balance positive emotional framing with clear action-oriented messaging to enhance both well-being and mobilization.

title: Didactic knowledge or Clinical Cases? How Data Types Shape Medical Large Language Models
comment: This paper is accepted by NLPCC 2026 oral
summary: Medical large language models are commonly trained on mixtures of didactic data (e.g., textbooks) and clinical data (e.g., patient records), yet how these data types differentially shape model capabilities remains unclear. We address this issue with token-matched experiments that vary the didactic-to-clinical ratio and analyze how data composition affects performance, capability profiles, and error patterns across knowledge-intensive and clinic-oriented tasks. We uncover an asymmetric transfer across task types: clinical data improves clinic-oriented tasks while remaining competitive on knowledge-intensive ones, whereas didactic data mainly improves knowledge-intensive tasks. Error analysis suggests a knowing-doing gap, where improvements in knowledge recall do not reliably generalize to clinical reasoning. We further observe that modest amounts of clinical data yield most of the gains on EHR-grounded tasks, while the optimal mixture ratio varies with the knowledge and clinical reasoning demands of downstream tasks. These findings suggest that medical LLM data curation should be application-driven, with higher proportions of clinical data preferred for reasoning-intensive use cases.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how different mixtures of didactic (textbook) and clinical (patient record) data used to train medical LLMs affect their performance on knowledge-intensive vs. clinic-oriented tasks, finding asymmetric transfer and showing that small amounts of clinical data provide most benefits for clinical reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: Medical LLMs are typically trained on both didactic and clinical data, but it is unclear how each data type contributes to different capabilities such as factual medical knowledge recall versus real-world clinical reasoning. Understanding this can guide data curation strategies for specific medical applications.
AI.method: The authors run token-matched training experiments where they systematically vary the ratio of didactic to clinical data while keeping total tokens constant. They then evaluate the resulting models on a suite of knowledge-intensive and clinic-oriented tasks, analyze performance differences, capability profiles, and error patterns to characterize how data composition impacts outcomes.
AI.result: The study reveals an asymmetric transfer effect: clinical data substantially improves performance on clinic-oriented tasks while remaining competitive on knowledge-focused benchmarks, whereas didactic data predominantly boosts knowledge-intensive tasks with limited benefit to clinical reasoning. Error analysis points to a knowing–doing gap, where gains in knowledge recall fail to reliably translate into improved clinical decision making. They also find diminishing returns for clinical data on EHR-grounded tasks, with modest amounts providing most of the benefits, and that the optimal didactic–clinical mixture depends on each downstream task’s balance of knowledge and reasoning demands.
AI.conclusion: Medical LLM training data should be curated according to the intended application rather than using a fixed didactic–clinical mix. For reasoning-intensive or EHR-grounded use cases, higher proportions of clinical data are preferable, while knowledge-focused applications may benefit more from didactic-heavy mixtures. Overall, aligning data composition with target task characteristics is key to optimizing medical LLM performance.

title: Token Signatures of Code: Comparing Coding Behaviors Across Large Language Models
summary: The evaluation of large language models (LLMs) on coding tasks has primarily focused on performance metrics such as pass@k. As LLMs continue to advance, many models now meet baseline performance requirements, reducing the discriminative power of performance-based evaluation alone. Yet a key question remains largely unexplored: how do LLMs differ in their coding behavior? We propose CLIC (Code Learning for Identification and Comparison), a visual analytics approach that characterizes LLM coding behavior through token-frequency analysis. CLIC represents each code sample as a feature vector of token frequencies and trains an interpretable decision tree to separate two LLMs' code sets. Beyond classification accuracy, we define two new metrics: robustness, which measures whether the two LLMs remain distinguishable as their most-discriminative tokens are progressively removed, and concentration, which measures whether the difference is driven by a few dominant tokens or spread across many. Interpreting numerous pairwise comparisons (across LLM pairs, tasks, and tokenization levels) and tracing the full analytical chain form an inherently multi-scale, hypothesis-driven exploration task. We therefore develop an interactive visual analytics system to navigate the comparison landscape, identify pairs of interest, and drill down into discriminative tokens and their code contexts. Case studies comparing 10 LLMs across 22 Kaggle ML tasks reveal actionable insights for LLM selection and prompt engineering.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CLIC, a visual analytics method to compare how different LLMs write code, going beyond simple accuracy metrics.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of LLMs on coding mostly use performance metrics like pass@k, which are becoming less informative as many models now achieve similar baseline performance. There is a need to understand *how* models differ in their coding behavior, not just how often they succeed, to support better model selection and prompt engineering.
AI.method: The authors propose CLIC (Code Learning for Identification and Comparison), which represents each generated code sample as a token-frequency feature vector and trains an interpretable decision tree classifier to distinguish between code produced by two LLMs. They introduce two new behavior-focused metrics—robustness and concentration—based on progressively removing discriminative tokens. They further build an interactive visual analytics system that supports multi-scale, hypothesis-driven exploration across many model pairs, tasks, and tokenization levels, allowing users to inspect discriminative tokens and their contexts.
AI.result: Using CLIC, the authors compare 10 LLMs across 22 Kaggle ML coding tasks. The system successfully uncovers patterns that distinguish models’ coding styles and behaviors, and the new metrics quantify how strongly and how broadly these differences manifest in token usage. Case studies show that these analyses yield concrete observations about individual models and their relative behaviors.
AI.conclusion: Performance alone (e.g., pass@k) is insufficient to understand LLM coding behavior once many models meet baseline accuracy. CLIC provides a complementary, behavior-oriented evaluation by characterizing and visualizing how models differ in their token usage and coding styles. This helps practitioners make more informed choices about model selection and prompt strategies, and offers a general framework for systematic, interpretable comparison of LLMs on code generation tasks.

title: An Affordable AI-Integrated Smart Cane for Multimodal Mobility Assistance of Visually Impaired Users
summary: Visual impairment affects over 2.2 billion people worldwide, yet conventional white canes cannot detect elevated hazards or provide semantic environmental context. Existing AI-assisted navigation systems typically rely on expensive hardware or cloud connectivity, limiting accessibility in resource-constrained settings. This paper presents an affordable (\$88 USD), fully offline AI-integrated smart cane designed for multimodal mobility assistance on an ultra-low-power Raspberry Pi Zero 2W. The system fuses RGB vision sensing with Time-of-Flight (ToF) distance estimation, pairing an INT8-quantized SSD MobileNet V1 model with distance-aware vibrotactile feedback and real-time audio alerts. To ensure operational robustness on constrained hardware, a multiprocessing architecture isolates sensor acquisition, neural inference, and haptic feedback into independent processes with fail-safe sensing support. Experimental evaluation across indoor mobility scenarios demonstrates a macro-averaged F1-score of 0.82 (precision: 0.85, recall: 0.81), a mean end-to-end latency of 330\,ms, and a peak power draw of 2.8\,W. A preliminary usability study with 12 participants (SUS: 78.5, NASA-TLX) demonstrated positive user perception and enhanced obstacle awareness. The proposed prototype validates the feasibility of deploying privacy-preserving, edge-native assistive intelligence for cost-sensitive mobility assistance.

AI.tldr: An $88 offline AI-powered smart cane using Raspberry Pi Zero 2W fuses RGB and ToF sensing with an efficient SSD MobileNet model to provide real-time vibrotactile and audio feedback, achieving good accuracy, low latency, and positive user feedback for assistive navigation.
AI.motivation: Conventional white canes cannot detect elevated obstacles or provide semantic context, and existing AI navigation systems often depend on costly hardware or cloud connectivity, making them inaccessible in low-resource settings. There is a need for a low-cost, privacy-preserving, fully offline assistive device that enhances mobility and situational awareness for visually impaired users.
AI.method: The authors design a smart cane built around a Raspberry Pi Zero 2W that combines RGB vision and Time-of-Flight distance sensing. They deploy an INT8-quantized SSD MobileNet V1 object detection model, integrating distance-aware vibrotactile feedback and real-time audio alerts. A multiprocessing software architecture separates sensor acquisition, neural inference, and haptic feedback into isolated processes with fail-safe sensing mechanisms. They evaluate performance in indoor mobility scenarios and conduct a preliminary usability study with 12 participants using SUS and NASA-TLX.
AI.result: In indoor navigation experiments, the system achieves a macro-averaged F1-score of 0.82 with precision of 0.85 and recall of 0.81, mean end-to-end latency of 330 ms, and peak power consumption of 2.8 W. The usability study with 12 users yields a SUS score of 78.5 and NASA-TLX results indicating positive perception and improved awareness of obstacles.
AI.conclusion: The prototype demonstrates that it is feasible to deploy an affordable, fully offline, edge-native AI smart cane that preserves privacy while providing effective multimodal mobility assistance in cost-sensitive environments. This validates low-cost embedded AI as a practical solution for enhancing navigation and obstacle awareness for visually impaired individuals.

title: TreeSpark: Calibrated, Load-Adaptive Draft Trees for Semi-Autoregressive Speculative Decoding
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates language-model inference by letting a cheap drafter propose tokens that the target model verifies in parallel. Recent block drafters make drafting nearly free: a single backbone pass emits an entire block of draft tokens. Draft trees promise a further gain -- several alternative continuations verified in one target forward -- but existing constructions rank candidates by per-position marginals that ignore which parent a candidate extends, so on semi-autoregressive drafters wider trees mostly add mis-ranked nodes; and a tree of fixed size ignores how much speculation each decoding round, and each serving load, can support. We introduce TreeSpark, which reads a parent-conditioned distribution from the drafter's existing Markov head at negligible cost, calibrates it into an edge-acceptance estimate, and lets path survival govern everything else: best-first expansion, per-round stopping, and a load-adaptive serving policy. Sampling siblings without replacement, with matching residuals in recursive rejection, keeps decoding lossless at any temperature. Adaptive trees improve on matched fixed budgets at every temperature; against a tuned chain on the same drafter, TreeSpark accepts 15-25% more draft tokens per round and decodes 8-14% faster in single-request wall-clock, and under rising load it gracefully shrinks the tree back to the chain. Code and artifacts: https://github.com/PopSoda2002/TreeSpark

AI.tldr: TreeSpark is an adaptive tree-based speculative decoding method that uses parent-conditioned probabilities to more efficiently select and verify draft tokens, improving acceptance rate and speed over chain-style speculative decoding while remaining lossless.
AI.motivation: Existing speculative decoding methods speed up inference but either use chain-style drafting or fixed-shape draft trees that are poorly ranked and not adaptive to decoding round or system load. Per-position marginal ranking ignores the dependency on parent tokens, so wider trees mainly add low-quality branches, and fixed tree sizes fail to account for how much speculation is actually useful under varying temperatures and serving load. There is a need for a tree-based speculative decoder that both respects the model’s conditional structure and adapts its tree size to runtime and load constraints.
AI.method: TreeSpark reads a parent-conditioned token distribution from the drafter’s Markov head at minimal extra cost, then calibrates these probabilities into estimates of edge-acceptance by the target model. It uses these estimates to perform best-first tree expansion, decide when to stop expanding in each decoding round, and adapt tree size according to serving load. The algorithm samples sibling tokens without replacement and uses residual-matching in recursive rejection sampling to ensure that the decoding process remains exact (lossless) at any temperature. The resulting tree structure is adaptive both to model behavior and to system conditions.
AI.result: Compared to a tuned chain-based speculative decoder using the same drafter, TreeSpark accepts 15–25% more draft tokens per decoding round and yields 8–14% faster single-request wall-clock decoding across temperatures. Adaptive trees consistently outperform fixed-budget tree configurations at all evaluated temperatures. Under increasing system load, TreeSpark automatically shrinks its speculative tree back toward a simple chain, maintaining robustness while still providing speedups when possible.
AI.conclusion: TreeSpark demonstrates that parent-conditioned, adaptively sized draft trees can significantly improve speculative decoding efficiency without sacrificing exactness. By using calibrated edge-acceptance estimates to drive best-first expansion and a load-aware serving policy, it achieves higher token acceptance and faster decoding than chain-based and fixed-tree baselines, and smoothly degrades to chain-style speculation under high load. This makes it a practical, more efficient speculative decoding strategy for real-world language model serving systems.

title: PAANI : On Device Visual Evidence Fusion and Explainable Guidance for River Robot Simulation
comment: 20 pages, 8 figures, 11 tables. Includes system and AI architecture diagrams, model-training results, qualitative evaluations, and Arduino UNO Q deployment measurements. Project code, trained models, ONNX artifacts, logs, and reproducibility documentation are available at https://github.com/immanuelihs/ASV_PAANI
summary: Mobile river monitoring robots must interpret obstacles and water boundaries that geographic waypoints alone cannot describe. On resource constrained platforms, converting imperfect visual predictions into timely and inspectable guidance is a distinct challenge. An object label or steering command does not explain which evidence supports a decision or when that evidence is unreliable. We present PAANI, an on-device perception to guidance architecture that combines a project trained YOLO11n detector and a custom MobileNetV3 Small semantic segmenter with timestamp aligned evidence fusion on Arduino UNO Q. Bounded tracking supplies object persistence, while an explicit corridor policy combines surface labels, accepted detections, urgency and mask uncertainty. Each final advisory exposes its contributing evidence and policy reasons. ROS 2 interfaces connect the local AI pipeline to a separate Gazebo vessel, localization and control testbed. Training uses 10,000 WaterScenes images for four-class detection and 1,127 MaSTr1325 images for segmentation, including 198 segmentation validation images. The selected FP32 ONNX models occupy 14.817 MB. Detector checkpoint test mAP at 0.5 IoU is 0.7388, while the separately evaluated rectangular ONNX export achieves validation mAP at 0.5 IoU of 0.7367. Segmentation ONNX validation mIoU is 0.9750. A five-minute UNO Q recording produced median and 95th percentile pipeline latencies of 467.8 ms and 580.3 ms at a configured 0.5 Hz cadence. The evaluation also identifies black input misclassification and a sampling rate mismatch that prevents the diagnostic apparent motion estimator from collecting sufficient evidence. These results support an inspectable and reusable edge robotics foundation while clearly distinguishing model accuracy and on-board execution from validated on-water collision avoidance.

AI.tldr: The paper presents PAANI, an on-device perception-to-guidance architecture for river-monitoring robots, fusing object detection and semantic segmentation on a constrained Arduino UNO Q platform to produce explainable navigation advisories.
AI.motivation: Geographic waypoints alone cannot capture dynamic obstacles and water boundaries for mobile river robots, and existing perception outputs (e.g., labels or steering commands) lack inspectability and reliability cues, especially on resource-constrained hardware. The authors want a perception system that not only runs on-device but also explains which evidence led to navigation guidance and when that evidence may be unreliable.
AI.method: They design PAANI, an edge robotics pipeline that runs on Arduino UNO Q and fuses a custom-trained YOLO11n object detector with a MobileNetV3 Small semantic segmentation model using timestamp-aligned evidence fusion. The system uses bounded tracking for temporal object persistence and an explicit corridor navigation policy that combines surface labels, accepted detections, urgency, and mask uncertainty to generate navigational advisories. Each advisory is traceable to its evidence and policy logic. They train YOLO on 10,000 WaterScenes images for four-class detection and MobileNetV3 on 1,127 MaSTr1325 images for segmentation, export FP32 ONNX models, and integrate the pipeline with a ROS 2 / Gazebo-based vessel and control simulation testbed. They then profile model accuracy and end-to-end latency, and analyze failure modes like black input misclassification and sampling rate mismatches affecting apparent motion estimation.
AI.result: The YOLO11n detector checkpoint achieves a test mAP@0.5 of 0.7388, and its ONNX export reaches a validation mAP@0.5 of 0.7367. The MobileNetV3 segmentation model reaches an ONNX validation mIoU of 0.9750. The deployed pipeline on Arduino UNO Q, tested over a five-minute recording at a configured 0.5 Hz cadence, exhibits median and 95th percentile end-to-end latencies of 467.8 ms and 580.3 ms, respectively. Evaluation reveals specific issues, such as misclassification on black inputs and a sampling rate mismatch that hinders the diagnostic apparent motion estimator from gathering enough evidence.
AI.conclusion: PAANI demonstrates that it is feasible to deploy an explainable, evidence-linked perception-to-guidance pipeline for river robots on constrained edge hardware, with reasonable accuracy and latency. The architecture cleanly separates model performance from system-level collision-avoidance validation, exposes decision evidence and uncertainty, and identifies concrete limitations (e.g., particular misclassifications and timing mismatches). This positions PAANI as a reusable and inspectable foundation for future on-water collision avoidance research and deployments, rather than as a complete, fully validated safety solution.

title: A framework for recipe data structure with applications for culinary and nutritional insights
comment: Main Text (11 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables); Supplementary Information (6 pages, 5 figures, 1 table)
summary: Cooking is a complex process that transforms raw ingredients into delicious and nutritious dishes, yet the recipes that encode this process remain largely free text; readable by people but not directly computable. Existing recipe collections capture fragments of this information, but no shared representation links a recipe's structured ingredient composition, its geo-cultural provenance, and its nutritional profile within a single queryable schema. We address this representation gap by formalizing a framework for recipe data structure that decomposes each recipe into typed ingredient entities, grounds those entities in a reference nutritional database, and annotates them with geo-cultural and dietary context. We present RecipeDB2, a structured compilation of 128,942 recipes with 35,474 ingredients from 32 regions and 99 countries. Ingredient phrases are parsed into seven culinary attributes using a transformer-based named-entity model; ingredients are linked to the USDA reference tables through a BERT embedding strategy (F1 = 87.90 on a manually adjudicated set of the 200 most frequent ingredients), yielding 148 nutritional parameters per mapped ingredient; a Random Forest classifier propagates 34 ingredient categories across the full vocabulary; and a deterministic, conservative rule set assigns each recipe a dietary style. Through RecipeDB2 (https://cosylab.iiitd.edu.in/recipedb2/), we demonstrate a scalable framework for making recipes computable, turning culinary heritage (long treated as an artistic rather than a quantitative object) into a data-driven analysis.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces RecipeDB2, a large, structured, and queryable database that makes free-text recipes computable by linking ingredients to nutritional, geo-cultural, and dietary information.
AI.motivation: Most recipes exist as unstructured free text, making it hard to computationally analyze relationships between ingredients, nutrition, and geo-cultural traditions. Existing collections only partially capture this information and lack a unified, machine-readable schema that supports integrated queries across composition, provenance, and nutrition.
AI.method: The authors define a formal data framework that decomposes each recipe into typed ingredient entities and associates them with multiple attributes. They parse ingredient phrases into seven culinary attributes using a transformer-based NER model, align ingredients with USDA nutritional tables via BERT embeddings, classify ingredients into categories with a Random Forest model, and assign dietary styles to recipes using a conservative rule set. They then populate this schema with nearly 129k recipes from 99 countries and 32 regions, creating RecipeDB2.
AI.result: RecipeDB2 comprises 128,942 recipes and 35,474 ingredients, each enriched with structured attributes, geo-cultural labels, dietary annotations, and links to USDA nutritional data with 148 parameters per mapped ingredient. The BERT-based mapping achieves an F1 of 87.90 on a curated benchmark of the 200 most frequent ingredients, and ingredient categories are propagated over the full vocabulary using the trained Random Forest classifier.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that large recipe collections can be systematically transformed from unstructured text into a rich, computable representation. RecipeDB2 provides a scalable, generalizable framework for quantitative, data-driven analysis of culinary heritage, enabling integrated studies of ingredients, nutrition, culture, and dietary patterns.

title: Social Influence and the Allocation of Scientific Attention in AI Populations
summary: AI systems are becoming participants in the evaluation and use of scientific research. They encounter citation counts, download statistics and lists of popular articles developed around human readers, but the collective consequences of these signals for artificial readers remain uncertain. This paper adapts the Music Lab design to a market for academic attention. In the first experiment, 1,000 AI agents choose papers from the titles and abstracts of all 114 regular research articles published in the American Economic Review in 2025. The experiment has five independent-choice communities and five social-influence communities, each with 100 sequential agents. Only agents in the social-influence condition observe earlier selections within their community. Agents may select any number of papers. Social-information communities select 17.2 percent fewer papers per agent, concentrate their choices more heavily, and collectively cover 73 papers, compared with 90 independently. Between-community variation is greater under social information. In a second experiment with 200 agents across twenty social communities, randomly assigning papers five initial selections raises their subsequent selection rate by 45.55 percentage points (95% CI: 41.20 to 49.90). Choices have modest correspondence with external citations and little correspondence with download counts. The results show how a simple information rule shapes the volume, breadth and distribution of scientific attention in an artificial population.

AI.tldr: The paper experimentally studies how simple social information rules (seeing others’ choices) affect which scientific papers AI agents choose to read, finding that social influence makes attention more concentrated, reduces the number of papers selected, and amplifies early popularity shocks.
AI.motivation: As AI systems start consuming and using scientific literature, they face human-designed attention signals like citation counts and download statistics. It is unclear how these signals will shape collective AI ‘reading’ behavior and, by extension, the distribution of attention and influence in science. The authors want to understand whether and how simple forms of social information—knowing what others have chosen—change the volume, breadth, and inequality of attention among scientific papers when the ‘readers’ are artificial agents.
AI.method: The authors adapt the classic Music Lab social-influence experiment to a market for academic attention. In Experiment 1, they deploy 1,000 AI agents across 10 communities (five independent-choice, five social-influence), each with 100 sequential agents. Agents choose among 114 AER 2025 research articles based on titles and abstracts; social-influence agents see prior selections in their own community, while independent agents do not. Agents can pick any number of papers. The authors measure how many papers are selected, how concentrated choices are, and how many distinct papers receive attention, plus between-community variation. In Experiment 2, they run 200 agents in 20 social-influence communities and exogenously seed some papers with five initial selections, then estimate the causal effect of this artificial early popularity on subsequent selection rates. They compare agent choices to external citation and download data to gauge alignment with standard impact metrics.
AI.result: In Experiment 1, communities with social information choose 17.2% fewer papers per agent and concentrate their selections more heavily on a smaller subset of articles: they collectively cover 73 distinct papers vs. 90 in independent-choice communities, and exhibit greater between-community variation (path dependence). In Experiment 2, seeding papers with five initial selections increases their subsequent selection rate by 45.55 percentage points (95% CI: 41.20–49.90), indicating strong popularity feedback effects. Across both experiments, agents’ choices show only modest correlation with real-world citation counts and almost no correlation with download statistics.
AI.conclusion: Even very simple social information rules substantially reshape how AI agents allocate attention across scientific papers: social influence reduces exploration, narrows the set of papers that receive attention, increases inequality and path dependence, and makes early popularity shocks highly consequential. Because AI systems increasingly mediate and consume scientific information, these dynamics imply that small design choices in recommendation or visibility rules could meaningfully alter which research is collectively read and potentially used, in ways that only weakly track conventional impact measures like citations or downloads.

title: AdaMem: Adaptive Memory Token Allocation for Soft Compression in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves language models with retrieved evidence, but processing many long passages is costly and can introduce distracting information. Soft compression addresses this challenge by encoding passages as compact sequences of continuous memory embeddings before generation. However, existing methods typically assign each retained passage an identical number of memory embeddings, irrespective of its query-specific relevance. To address this, we propose AdaMem, a relevance-guided soft-compression framework that maps learned passage-relevance estimates to a query-dependent allocation of a fixed memory-token budget. A shared query-conditioned compressor produces both continuous passage memories and relevance scores in a single pass; a deterministic allocation rule assigns more memory tokens to higher-scoring passages and can omit low-scoring ones. Across six open-domain QA benchmarks, AdaMem consistently outperforms OSCAR (the closely matched soft-compression baseline that uses uniform allocation) as well as other soft-compression methods at matched memory budgets. Under standard 16$\times$ compression, AdaMem improves sub-string match by up to 3.2 points (5.5%) over uniform allocation baseline, with an average relative gain of 3.4%; under aggressive 64$\times$ compression the average relative gain grows to 14.6%, with a maximum of 9.8 points (19.7%) on PopQA. AdaMem matches the answer quality of the uncompressed at up to 4$\times$ lower inference latency than full context baseline. AdaMem retains an efficiency profile comparable to the uniform-compression baseline, while achieving up to $4\times$ lower inference latency than full-context inference. Thus, relevance-guided memory allocation is particularly effective when retrieval pools are large and the available memory budget is tight.

AI.tldr: AdaMem is a relevance-guided soft-compression method for RAG that adaptively allocates a fixed memory-token budget across retrieved passages, improving answer quality and latency over uniform soft compression at the same memory cost.
AI.motivation: RAG systems must process many long retrieved passages, which is computationally expensive and can hurt performance when irrelevant text distracts the model. Soft compression helps by encoding passages into compact continuous memories, but current approaches allocate the same number of memory tokens to every passage regardless of how relevant it is to the query. This wastes memory on unhelpful passages and limits how much detail can be stored for highly relevant ones. A query-aware, relevance-sensitive allocation scheme is needed to better use a fixed memory budget and to scale RAG to large retrieval pools under tight latency and context constraints.
AI.method: The paper introduces AdaMem, a soft-compression framework that adaptively distributes a fixed total memory-token budget across retrieved passages based on estimated query-specific relevance. A single, shared query-conditioned compressor takes the query and each passage, and in one forward pass both (1) produces a sequence of continuous memory embeddings (compressed representation) for the passage, and (2) computes a relevance score for that passage with respect to the query. A deterministic allocation rule then maps these relevance scores to an allocation of memory tokens: more tokens for highly relevant passages, fewer or none for low-scoring ones, while keeping the total memory budget fixed. These continuous memories from selected passages are then fed to the generator instead of the full texts. The framework is compared against OSCAR and other soft-compression baselines which use uniform token allocation per passage.
AI.result: Across six open-domain QA benchmarks, AdaMem consistently outperforms OSCAR (a strong uniform-allocation soft-compression baseline) and other soft-compression methods at the same overall memory budget. With 16× compression, AdaMem yields up to a 3.2 absolute point (5.5% relative) improvement in substring match over the uniform baseline, with an average relative gain of 3.4%. Under more aggressive 64× compression, performance gains become larger, with an average relative improvement of 14.6% and up to 9.8 absolute points (19.7%) on the PopQA benchmark. In addition, AdaMem reaches answer quality comparable to using uncompressed full context while achieving up to 4× lower inference latency. Its computational efficiency is similar to the uniform-compression baseline but substantially better than full-context inference.
AI.conclusion: Relevance-guided allocation of continuous memory tokens in soft-compressed RAG leads to better use of a fixed memory budget than uniform allocation across passages. By assigning more representation capacity to highly relevant passages and pruning low-relevance ones, AdaMem improves answer accuracy, especially under tight compression and large retrieval pools, while maintaining or improving efficiency. The approach can match full-context answer quality at significantly lower latency and suggests that adaptive, query-aware memory budgeting is a key ingredient for scalable, efficient retrieval-augmented generation.

title: Learning 3D biophysical cell properties from 2D images and cell-population statistics
summary: Inferring 3D cellular properties from 2D microscopy is difficult when a reference instrument reports only population statistics rather than labels for individual cells. Here we develop a population-supervised framework that maps single 2D red-cell images to latent biophysical quantities and aggregates them to mean corpuscular volume, red-cell distribution width and mean corpuscular haemoglobin. The model combines shared local inference, a biophysically structured decoder for volume and haemoglobin, learned instance weighting and device-specific calibration. We formalise conditions under which aggregate observations identify restricted instance predictors, show why population agreement does not by itself identify single-cell properties or 3D geometry, and derive the dispersion penalty induced by subset mean matching. The development dataset comprises 390 specimens and 1,105 acquisitions across six devices, with reported Pearson correlations of 0.86--0.98 against a Sysmex analyser. The framework provides a testable route from 2D images and population supervision to 3D cellular biophysics without claiming explicit 3D reconstruction.

AI.tldr: They build a learning framework that uses only population-level blood test statistics to infer latent 3D biophysical properties of individual red blood cells from 2D images, achieving high agreement with a reference analyser.
AI.motivation: In routine haematology, clinical analysers report only population-level statistics (e.g., mean corpuscular volume, red-cell distribution width, mean corpuscular haemoglobin) rather than per-cell labels. However, modern microscopy and machine learning operate on individual cell images. There is a gap between what is observable and labelled (population aggregates) and what we wish to infer (single-cell 3D biophysical properties). The authors aim to bridge this gap so that 2D microscopy can be used to infer meaningful, testable 3D cellular properties without requiring explicit 3D imaging or per-cell ground truth from reference instruments.
AI.method: They propose a population-supervised learning framework: a model takes single 2D red blood cell images as input and maps them to latent biophysical quantities (e.g., per-cell volume and haemoglobin content) through a biophysically structured decoder. These single-cell predictions are then aggregated to match population-level haematological indices (mean corpuscular volume, red-cell distribution width, mean corpuscular haemoglobin). The architecture includes shared local inference across cells, explicit biophysical structure in the decoder for volume and haemoglobin, learned instance weighting to account for varying cell importance or quality, and device-specific calibration layers to handle multiple acquisition devices. On the theory side, they formalise identifiability conditions for learning restricted instance-level predictors from aggregate observations, explain why matching population statistics alone does not uniquely determine single-cell properties or full 3D geometries, and derive how subset mean matching induces an effective dispersion penalty on predictions. Empirically, they train and validate on a multi-device dataset of red-cell images linked only to population CBC statistics, evaluating against a Sysmex analyser as reference.
AI.result: On a dataset of 390 specimens and 1,105 acquisitions across six imaging devices, their framework’s aggregate predictions for standard red-cell indices achieve high Pearson correlations (0.86–0.98) with measurements from a Sysmex clinical analyser. They also provide theoretical results that characterise when and how population-level supervision can constrain single-cell predictors and quantify the implicit regularisation (dispersion penalty) introduced by subset mean matching. The framework successfully handles cross-device variation via calibration and instance weighting while remaining consistent with known biophysics of red cells.
AI.conclusion: Population-level supervision from standard haematology analysers can be leveraged to learn meaningful, biophysically structured predictors of single-cell properties from 2D microscopy images, even without explicit 3D reconstructions or per-cell labels. Their framework offers a principled, testable route from 2D image data to 3D-relevant cellular biophysics, supported by both theoretical identifiability analysis and strong empirical agreement with a clinical reference device, and it is adaptable across multiple imaging instruments via calibration mechanisms.

title: Context Poisoning as Extreme-Value Attention Interference in Long-Context Language Models
summary: Large language models can process increasingly long prompts, yet their ability to locate and use decisive evidence may degrade as irrelevant or confusable context is added. We formulate this phenomenon, which we call context poisoning, as extreme-value interference in attention: the decisive-evidence score is upper-bounded, while the maximum score among effective distractors grows with their number. Under a softmax retrieval abstraction, we derive a finite-sample upper bound showing that maintaining a fixed accuracy target above base rate requires the evidence margin to scale as $Ω(\sqrt{\log N})$, where N denotes the effective distractor count rather than necessarily the raw context length. The analysis connects long-context degradation to score aliasing, positional aliasing, and softmax dilution. Controlled experiments show that retrieval accuracy decreases as total context grows in the presence of embedded hard negatives, that the same-format condition produces the largest observed accuracy drop among the tested distractor constructions at fixed context length, and that retrieval gating can improve evidence use while its net benefit depends on preserving evidence recall. These results motivate evidence bottlenecks, alias-resistant representations, retrieve-then-reason architectures, verifier-mediated memory, and contrastive anti-poison training.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how long contexts with many distractors can cause large language models to ignore or misinterpret decisive evidence, a phenomenon called context poisoning.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are given longer prompts, they must sift through more irrelevant or misleading information. Empirically, performance often drops with longer context, but there is limited theoretical understanding of why this happens and how it scales with the number of distractors. The paper aims to formally characterize this degradation and connect it to attention mechanisms, to better guide model and system design for reliable long-context reasoning and retrieval.
AI.method: The authors model attention-based retrieval under a softmax abstraction and formalize context poisoning as an extreme-value problem: the correct evidence has a bounded score, while the maximum score among many distractors grows with their count. They derive a finite-sample upper bound showing how much the evidence–distractor margin must grow to maintain accuracy as the number of effective distractors N increases (Ω(√log N)). They connect this to issues like score aliasing, positional aliasing, and softmax dilution. They also run controlled experiments with LLMs, systematically varying context length and types of distractors (including hard negatives and same-format distractors) and test retrieval gating mechanisms to see how accuracy changes.
AI.result: Theoretically, they show that in a softmax retrieval model, to keep accuracy above base rate as the number of effective distractors N increases, the evidence margin must scale at least as Ω(√log N). This frames long-context failure as an extreme-value interference problem. Empirically, they find: (1) retrieval accuracy reliably drops as context grows when hard negatives are embedded; (2) distractors with the same format as the evidence cause the largest accuracy drop at fixed context length; and (3) retrieval gating can mitigate context poisoning by focusing attention on likely evidence spans, but its net gain depends critically on not losing genuine evidence (i.e., preserving recall).
AI.conclusion: The work concludes that context poisoning is a fundamental challenge for long-context LLMs arising from extreme-value interference in attention. Reliable evidence use at scale requires growing evidence margins or improved mechanisms to resist distractor interference. The authors argue for architectural and training strategies such as evidence bottlenecks, alias-resistant representations, retrieve-then-reason pipelines, verifier-mediated memory, and contrastive anti-poison training to improve robustness to long-context distraction and maintain effective retrieval in large prompts.

title: Goal-driven Variant Categorization
summary: Process discovery rarely yields a single coherent process structure. For analysis, a common step is to cluster process variants based on structural similarity and then assign business meaning to the resulting groups. Since these partitions are not derived from the organization's goals, analysts must manually interpret and consolidate variants into business-meaningful categories. This judgment-intensive step becomes increasingly difficult as the number and complexity of variants grow. In this paper, we propose a goal-driven approach to variant categorization that reverses this workflow. We first author an organization's goal model that predefines the categorization axis. Each variant is transformed into a textual narrative describing its behavior, and a Large Language Model (LLM) interprets it in the context of the goal model and assigns the variant to the most appropriate category. LLM-based semantic reasoning connects low-level process behavior with analyst-defined business goals. We instantiate this approach end-to-end and evaluate it on three public logs differing substantially in scale and behavioral diversity. Goal-model guidance yields partitions that differ from those produced by unguided induction and respond to controlled edits to the declared alternatives, at the cost of authoring a goal model.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a goal-driven, LLM-based method to categorize process variants according to business goals instead of purely structural similarity.
AI.motivation: Existing process discovery methods often produce many structurally different variants that must be clustered and then manually mapped to business-meaningful categories. This mapping is subjective, labor-intensive, and becomes impractical as the number and complexity of variants increases. There is a need for an automated, goal-aligned way to categorize variants that reflects organizational objectives rather than only structural similarity.
AI.method: The authors define a goal-driven workflow: (1) model the organization’s goals to define in advance the dimensions along which variants should be categorized; (2) transform each process variant into a textual narrative describing its execution behavior; (3) use a Large Language Model to interpret each narrative in the context of the goal model and assign the variant to the most appropriate goal-based category. They instantiate this end-to-end pipeline and compare the resulting partitions to unguided clustering approaches using three public event logs of varying size and behavioral diversity. They also test the responsiveness of the categorization to controlled changes in the declared alternatives in the goal model.
AI.result: The goal-driven, LLM-based categorization produces variant partitions that differ from those generated by traditional, unguided structural induction. The partitions are sensitive to controlled edits in the goal model, demonstrating that the approach effectively aligns variant categorization with the declared business goals. However, this comes with the additional cost and effort of authoring a suitable organizational goal model.
AI.conclusion: Embedding an explicit organizational goal model into process variant categorization, combined with LLM-based semantic interpretation of textualized variants, can bridge the gap between low-level process behavior and high-level business goals. This yields categorizations that are more aligned with analyst-defined objectives than unguided, structure-only methods, at the expense of having to define and maintain the goal model.

title: DeepInstructor: An Agentic AI Instructor for Experience-Driven Idea Evaluation
summary: As automated scientific discovery advances, Large Language Models (LLMs) can now generate research ideas at an unprecedented scale, shifting the bottleneck from idea generation to idea evaluation. Existing evaluators mainly rely on parametric LLM knowledge or unstructured retrieval, producing judgments that lack the experience-grounded reasoning used by human instructors. To address this, we propose DeepInstructor, an agentic framework that formulates idea evaluation as reasoning over structured scholarly experience. DeepInstructor constructs an Experience Graph from 58,607 peer reviews and employs a ReAct-based agent to retrieve dimension-specific evidence for traceable evaluation. We further introduce DeepInstruct, a dataset with controlled pairwise comparisons across novelty, significance, and feasibility. Experiments show that DeepInstructor substantially outperforms existing baselines, improving Hit@1 and Hit@2 alignment with human judgments by 24.4% and 29.7%, respectively. Our findings suggest that scientific idea evaluation can be grounded in explicit reasoning over structured scholarly experience

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DeepInstructor, an agent framework that evaluates LLM-generated scientific ideas by explicitly reasoning over structured scholarly experience extracted from peer reviews, leading to much better alignment with human judgments.
AI.motivation: LLMs can generate many research ideas, but evaluating which ones are novel, significant, and feasible is now the key bottleneck. Existing automatic evaluators either depend solely on LLM parametric knowledge or on unstructured retrieval, so they fail to emulate the evidence-based, experience-grounded reasoning that human reviewers and instructors use. The authors want an evaluation system that can systematically leverage accumulated peer-review experience to make more reliable, transparent judgments.
AI.method: The authors build an Experience Graph from 58,607 peer-review reports, organizing scholarly experience in a structured form. On top of this, they design DeepInstructor, an agentic framework using a ReAct-style agent to iteratively retrieve and reason over dimension-specific evidence (for novelty, significance, and feasibility) from the graph. They also construct DeepInstruct, a dataset of controlled pairwise comparisons of scientific ideas along these three dimensions to train and benchmark evaluators.
AI.result: DeepInstructor significantly outperforms existing evaluation baselines on the DeepInstruct benchmark. In particular, it improves alignment with human judgments by 24.4% in Hit@1 and by 29.7% in Hit@2, indicating that its top-ranked (and top-2-ranked) choices much more often match human preferences on novelty, significance, and feasibility.
AI.conclusion: By structuring a large corpus of peer-review reports into an Experience Graph and using an agent to reason over this graph, the paper shows that scientific idea evaluation can be better grounded in explicit, traceable scholarly experience rather than opaque LLM intuition. This approach yields substantially higher agreement with human evaluators, suggesting a promising direction for scaling reliable, transparent evaluation of LLM-generated research ideas.

title: Replication Without Persistence in Hosted LLMs: Measurement Sensitivity in Action-Time Belief Evaluation
summary: Behavioural evaluations of hosted language models can vary because the evaluated service, the measurement instrument, or both differ across runs. We separate three validation questions: whether a prior finding recurs on fresh data under its historical configuration (replication), whether the endpoint changes when the evaluation-and-inference configuration is rebuilt under the same identifier (measurement sensitivity), and whether the finding persists across subsequently tested identifiers under one common instrument (persistence). We study these questions in Regent Chess, a sequential environment in which a hidden, mutable state is recorded exactly, allowing stated beliefs to be scored against ground truth at action time; positive endpoint values mean worse performance than a matched-uniform comparator. The previously reported Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite deficit recurs on fresh games under its historical configuration (+0.0530, 95% CI [+0.0329,+0.0714]). In a back-to-back same-day H/R comparison under the same public identifier, the model-minus-uniform endpoint is 0.0429 lower under the rebuilt configuration (95% CI for the H-minus-R contrast [+0.0182,+0.0667]); all six configuration components vary jointly, so no component is isolated. Under rebuilt R, the prospectively frozen, interleaved same-window 4K comparison reverses sign between Gemini 3.1 and Gemini 3.7, identifiers that differ in release and product tier; additional descriptive and exploratory cells show the same directional pattern. Any additional serving-period contribution remains unresolved (-0.0166, [-0.0483,+0.0157]). Replication, measurement sensitivity, and persistence can therefore yield different conclusions within one evaluation, motivating explicit indexing of hosted-model behavioural claims by tested identifier, serving period, measurement instrument, and inference configuration.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how consistent behavioural evaluations of hosted language models are by separating three validation concepts—replication, measurement sensitivity, and persistence—using a controlled Regent Chess environment, and finds that these three lenses can lead to different conclusions about the same model family.
AI.motivation: Hosted language models are often evaluated behaviourally, but results can change over time because providers silently update models, infrastructure, or configurations. This raises questions about whether observed performance differences are stable, reproducible, and comparable across versions and setups. The authors aim to clarify how to validate behavioural findings when both the models and the evaluation pipelines can change under the same public identifier, which is crucial for scientific reliability, monitoring, and policy decisions that rely on benchmarked performance.
AI.method: The authors conceptually distinguish three kinds of validation: (1) replication—retesting a previously reported effect on new data using the original configuration; (2) measurement sensitivity—assessing how the endpoint changes when the evaluation and inference stack is rebuilt while keeping the same model identifier; and (3) persistence—testing whether a previously observed effect holds for later model identifiers using a common, prospectively frozen instrument. They instantiate this in Regent Chess, a sequential environment with precisely tracked hidden state that lets them score the model’s stated beliefs against ground truth at each action. Performance is measured relative to a matched-uniform baseline; positive differences mean worse model performance. They run controlled comparisons involving Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite and Gemini 3.7 under historical and rebuilt configurations, using confidence intervals and interleaved evaluations to control for time-window effects.
AI.result: The earlier finding that Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite underperforms the uniform baseline is replicated on new data under the historical configuration, with a similar positive endpoint difference (+0.0530, 95% CI [+0.0329,+0.0714]). However, when the evaluation-and-inference configuration is rebuilt under the same public identifier, the model-minus-uniform endpoint shifts downward by 0.0429 (95% CI for the contrast [+0.0182,+0.0667]), showing notable measurement sensitivity. In prospectively frozen, interleaved 4K-window comparisons under the rebuilt setup, the performance difference between Gemini 3.1 and the newer Gemini 3.7 reverses sign, and additional exploratory conditions show the same directional change, indicating that the prior deficit does not persist across identifiers. A possible additional effect due to serving period remains statistically unresolved (-0.0166, 95% CI [-0.0483,+0.0157]).
AI.conclusion: Even within a single evaluation domain and family of hosted models, replication, measurement sensitivity, and persistence can yield different answers about model performance. Behavioural claims about hosted language models are therefore fragile to changes in model identifiers, serving periods, and evaluation configurations. The authors conclude that claims should be explicitly indexed by the tested identifier, the time window of service, and the exact measurement and inference setup, and that future work on evaluation should treat these dimensions as core to the validity and interpretability of behavioural benchmarks.

title: Evaluating Fine-Tuned and Base Language Models in Maternal and Vaccination Healthcare for African Settings
summary: Background: Large language models (LLMs) can improve healthcare information delivery in low-resource settings but may produce inaccurate or culturally inappropriate advice. This study evaluated domain-specific fine-tuning for maternal health and vaccination in Nigeria. Objective: To compare HelpMum's MamaBot-Llama and Vax-Llama with Meta's Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct for accuracy, safety, clarity, contextual appropriateness, and trustworthiness. Methods: We evaluated 200 healthcare questions, 100 each for maternal health and vaccination, across five subdomains per domain. MamaBot-Llama and Vax-Llama were fine-tuned using Low-Rank Adaptation on over 36,000 maternal health and 9,000 vaccination question-answer pairs, respectively. Two Nigerian licensed physicians independently rated responses using a 5-point Likert scale. Paired comparisons used Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Results: Performance varied by domain. MamaBot-Llama significantly outperformed the base model across all criteria, with a 4.9% overall improvement (p < .001), including gains in clinical trustworthiness (+7%) and medical accuracy (+5%). Critical issues decreased by 50%, and clinicians preferred it in 78% of cases. In contrast, Vax-Llama showed a 5.2% overall decline (p < .001), with critical issues increasing by 192% and safety concerns by 400%. Conclusions: Domain-specific fine-tuning can improve healthcare LLM performance when based on high-quality, clinician-curated data, but may also degrade performance when dataset quality is inadequate. Rigorous domain-specific validation is essential before clinical deployment. Physician evaluators provided informed consent, and chatbot logs were anonymized. Keywords: Large language models; Fine-tuning; Maternal health; Vaccination; Healthcare AI; Low-resource settings; Nigeria; Model evaluation; LoRA; Medical accuracy

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates two domain-specific fine-tuned LLMs for maternal health and vaccination in Nigeria against the base Llama-3.1-8B model, finding that fine-tuning can significantly help or harm performance depending on data quality.
AI.motivation: To understand whether domain-specific fine-tuning of LLMs can safely improve healthcare advice in low-resource settings like Nigeria, and to test if such tuning always helps or can sometimes worsen performance, especially in sensitive areas like maternal health and vaccination.
AI.method: The authors fine-tuned two models, MamaBot-Llama and Vax-Llama, using LoRA on 36,000+ maternal health and 9,000+ vaccination Q&A pairs. They then compared these against the base Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on 200 curated questions (100 maternal, 100 vaccination) spanning five subdomains per domain. Two Nigerian physicians independently rated responses on a 5-point Likert scale for accuracy, safety, clarity, contextual appropriateness, and trustworthiness. Statistical comparison used Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for paired responses.
AI.result: MamaBot-Llama significantly outperformed the base model across all evaluation criteria, with about a 4.9% overall improvement, including +7% in clinical trustworthiness and +5% in medical accuracy; critical issues dropped by 50%, and physicians preferred it in 78% of cases. Vax-Llama, however, performed worse than the base model overall by 5.2%, with a 192% increase in critical issues and a 400% rise in safety concerns.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific fine-tuning can substantially improve healthcare LLMs when training data are high-quality and clinician-curated, as shown for maternal health, but can also meaningfully degrade safety and accuracy if dataset quality is inadequate, as seen with vaccination. Therefore, careful dataset curation and rigorous, domain-specific validation are necessary prerequisites before clinical deployment of fine-tuned LLMs.

title: The Wisdom of Artificial Deliberative Crowds
summary: The aggregation of many lay estimates often outperforms individual expert judgment, a phenomenon known as the wisdom of crowds. While this is usually attributed to the independence of estimates, an even stronger effect arises through deliberation: averaging the consensus estimates of small deliberating groups outperforms the classical wisdom of crowds, with individual judgments themselves also becoming more accurate after deliberation. Whether these improvements transfer to large language models deliberating amongst themselves is unknown. Here we adapt a three-stage deliberation paradigm previously used with human participants for use with large language models from three different families, and test it across four domains of increasing real-world stakes: visual numerical estimation (Study 1), peer review of machine-learning papers (Study 2), detection of hidden malicious behavior by an artificial intelligence agent (Study 3), and sports forecasting against a real prediction market (Study 4). Across domains, deliberation reduced collective error beyond passive aggregation of independent responses, and post-deliberation individual judgments retained this collective gain. Notably, the advantage required model diversity: groups composed of clones of a single model did not benefit from deliberating. These results establish machine deliberation as a general-purpose aggregation mechanism, and point to diversity as an active ingredient.

AI.tldr: Paper shows that structured deliberation among diverse large language models (LLMs) produces more accurate judgments than simple averaging of independent answers, and even more than human-style ‘wisdom of crowds’.
AI.motivation: The wisdom-of-crowds effect suggests that aggregating many independent lay judgments can outperform expert individuals, especially when errors cancel out. Recent work shows that allowing small human groups to deliberate before giving a consensus estimate can further improve accuracy, and that individuals themselves become better calibrated after deliberation. It is unknown whether similar benefits arise when LLMs deliberate with one another, and under what conditions (e.g., diversity vs. cloned models). Understanding this could improve AI-assisted decision-making in high-stakes, real-world domains.
AI.method: The authors adapt a three-stage human deliberation paradigm for use with LLMs from three different model families. In each task, models first give independent judgments, then engage in structured, multi-turn deliberation in small groups to reach a consensus, and finally produce revised individual post-deliberation judgments. They test this across four domains with increasing real-world relevance: (1) visual numerical estimation tasks, (2) peer review quality assessment of machine learning papers, (3) detection of hidden malicious behavior in an AI agent, and (4) forecasting sports outcomes against an existing prediction market.
