They compare the accuracy of: (a) simple aggregation of independent LLM responses, (b) consensus outputs from deliberating groups, and (c) post-deliberation individual judgments. They also vary group composition, comparing heterogeneous groups (different model families) to homogeneous groups made of clones of the same model.
AI.result: Across all four domains, LLM deliberation improves performance beyond classical wisdom-of-crowds style aggregation of independent LLM responses. Group consensus estimates after deliberation are more accurate, and the individual model outputs after deliberation also show lasting accuracy gains. However, these gains crucially depend on model diversity: groups composed only of cloned instances of a single model family do not show meaningful benefits from deliberation relative to passive aggregation, indicating that diversity of inductive biases and error patterns is necessary for improvement.
AI.conclusion: Machine deliberation—structured interaction among multiple, diverse LLMs—acts as an effective, general-purpose aggregation mechanism that can systematically improve accuracy over both individual model outputs and naive aggregation of independent responses. The work suggests that diversity of model families is a key active ingredient in realizing the benefits of deliberation, paralleling and extending human wisdom-of-crowds findings. This has practical implications for building AI systems that rely on ensembles of heterogeneous models and structured discussion protocols to enhance reliability in real-world decision-making tasks.

title: Beyond the Text: Verifying That Agent-Written Papers Are Backed by Their Artifacts
summary: Large language model agents are increasingly capable of conducting research autonomously, producing research documents alongside the code and experiments that ostensibly support them. Yet whether the reported findings are consistently supported by corresponding implementations and execution evidence remains largely unexplored: existing review practices primarily assess textual quality and cannot reliably identify inconsistencies such as hard-coded metrics, unimplemented methods, or unsupported experimental results. We present ReAgent, an automated auditing framework for assessing the consistency between agent-generated research documents and their associated repositories. ReAgent constructs structured representations of scientific claims from research documents and uses them to guide repository analysis and evidence collection. Static auditing examines whether claimed methodologies, implementations, and experimental configurations are consistently reflected in the repository, while dynamic auditing executes relevant experiments and collects execution evidence to assess empirical findings. By combining static analysis with dynamic evidence, ReAgent identifies inconsistencies that may remain hidden under either perspective alone, such as experiments that reproduce reported numbers while deviating from the claimed methodology. The collected evidence and audit decisions are organized into a structured repository-level audit report, enabling transparent evidence traceability. We evaluate ReAgent on a manually curated benchmark of agent-generated research document--repository pairs and compare it against representative static and reproduction-based baselines. Experimental results demonstrate that ReAgent effectively identifies inconsistencies between reported research findings and their supporting repository evidence.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ReAgent, an automated system that audits whether agent-written research papers are actually supported by the code and experiments in their repositories, using both static analysis and dynamic experiment execution to detect inconsistencies and generate structured audit reports.
AI.motivation: As large language model agents increasingly generate full research projects—papers plus code and experiments—traditional peer review, which focuses on textual quality, cannot reliably detect mismatches between the written claims and the actual code or experimental evidence. Problems like hard-coded results, missing implementations, or unfaithful experiment setups can go unnoticed, undermining trust in agent-generated research. There is a need for an automated way to systematically check that reported findings are genuinely supported by the associated repositories.
AI.method: The authors propose ReAgent, an automated auditing framework that: (1) parses agent-generated research documents to extract structured scientific claims about methods, implementations, and experimental results; (2) uses these claims to guide static analysis of the associated code repository, checking for the presence and consistency of claimed methods, configurations, and artifacts; (3) performs dynamic auditing by running selected experiments or scripts to collect execution evidence related to the reported results; and (4) integrates static and dynamic evidence into a structured, repository-level audit report that records findings and evidence links. ReAgent is evaluated on a curated benchmark of document–repository pairs and compared against static-only and reproduction-based baselines.
AI.result: On the benchmark of agent-generated paper–repository pairs, ReAgent detects inconsistencies between written claims and repository contents more effectively than static analysis alone or pure reproduction-based baselines. It can uncover subtle issues such as experiments that numerically reproduce reported metrics but use different methodologies or configurations than those described in the paper. The system generates detailed audit reports that enable traceability of evidence for each decision.
AI.conclusion: ReAgent provides an effective automated approach to auditing the consistency of agent-generated research by combining structured claim extraction with both static and dynamic repository analysis. This dual-perspective method uncovers inconsistencies that single-perspective approaches miss and produces transparent, evidence-backed audit reports. The work suggests that such tools can play a crucial role in maintaining the integrity and reliability of increasingly autonomous, agent-generated scientific research.

title: Agreement Overstates Evidence: Error Dependence in LLM Judge Consensus
summary: Consensus among LLM judges is often taken as strong evidence that a decision is correct. This assumes that judges make their errors independently. In practice, LLM judges are often trained and evaluated in similar ways, so they can make the same mistakes. We study how this dependency affects the reliability of consensus. We find substantial error correlation across both open-weight and frontier LLM judges. In our main bank of ten judges, the average pairwise correlation between judge errors is 0.21. As a result, the ten judges only provide roughly as much statistical information as 3.5 independent judges. The dependency is even stronger among the high-accuracy frontier judges we evaluate, including judges from different providers. In up to 28% of our comparisons, ignoring shared errors leads to the conclusion that one system is significantly better, while accounting for them does not. We also find that the pattern of errors matters. Errors shared by most judges and errors concentrated among a smaller group affect consensus differently and favor different voting methods. Measuring the overall amount of correlation alone is therefore insufficient. Our results suggest a simple approach: use a small set of trusted examples to estimate judge accuracy and identify shared mistakes. These shared errors should then be considered when analyzing the results, and the voting method should be chosen using trusted examples before it is applied to new data.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that agreement among LLM judges can be misleading because their errors are correlated, so 10 judges may only provide the information of about 3.5 independent judges, and it proposes using trusted examples to estimate accuracy, detect shared errors, and choose appropriate voting rules.
AI.motivation: LLM outputs are increasingly evaluated by other LLMs acting as judges, and practitioners often trust consensus among multiple judges as strong evidence of correctness. This implicitly assumes that each judge’s errors are independent. However, many LLM judges are trained and evaluated similarly, making it likely that they share systematic weaknesses. The paper is motivated by the need to understand how correlated errors affect the reliability of consensus-based evaluation and model comparison, and to design more principled strategies for aggregating LLM-judge opinions.
AI.method: The authors empirically measure error correlations among multiple LLM judges, including both open-weight and proprietary frontier models. Using a bank of ten judges, they compute average pairwise error correlations and translate this into an ‘effective’ number of independent judges. They compare different providers’ judges and examine how often ignoring versus accounting for shared errors leads to different conclusions about which system is better. They also analyze how different patterns of error sharing (e.g., errors common to most judges vs. concentrated in a subset) interact with alternative voting/aggregation rules. Finally, they propose and evaluate a simple procedure that uses a small, trusted labeled set to estimate judge accuracies, identify shared mistakes, and select voting methods before applying them to new data.
AI.result: They find substantial error correlation across LLM judges: in their ten-judge bank, average pairwise error correlation is 0.21, meaning that these ten judges collectively provide information equivalent to roughly 3.5 independent judges. Dependency is even stronger among higher-accuracy frontier judges, including those from different providers. In up to 28% of evaluated comparisons, treating judges as independent yields a statistically significant difference between systems that disappears once shared errors are accounted for. They also show that the structure of error sharing matters: broadly shared errors and errors concentrated in a subset of judges influence consensus differently and interact in distinct ways with various voting methods. Measuring only a single scalar ‘correlation’ is therefore inadequate for choosing aggregation rules.
AI.conclusion: Consensus among LLM judges is not a reliably strong signal of correctness when their errors are correlated, as is common due to similar training and evaluation regimes. Substantial error correlations reduce the effective number of independent judges and can produce misleading conclusions about system quality. A practical mitigation is to use a small, trusted evaluation set to (1) estimate individual judge accuracies, (2) detect shared errors, and (3) select and calibrate a voting/aggregation scheme before applying it at scale. Properly accounting for both the amount and the structure of error correlation is necessary for trustworthy LLM-based evaluation and model comparison.

title: Privacy Personalization Trade offs in LLMs: The Impact of Stylometric Signal Reduction on User-Specific Text Generation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated the ability to generate user-specific text with high stylistic fidelity. However, the personal data that enables such personalization frequently embeds demographic, cultural, and stylistic markers that raises concerns about stylometric re- identification. This paper investigates whether reducing identifiable stylistic signals affects personalization in text generation by LLMs. We introduce a controlled framework to isolate stylometric signals in LLM personalization using the LaMP-7 Twitter benchmark. Experiments on 250 sampled users compare two settings: paraphrasing conditioned on the original profile and paraphrasing conditioned on an anonymized converted profile in which demographic identifiers, cultural references, personal details, and informal linguistic cues have been systematically neutralized. Outputs are assessed by two independent LLM judges and a complementary human evaluation. Our pairwise evaluation shows that outputs conditioned on original profiles are nearly indistinguishable from human-authored ground truth, indicating that modern LLMs can closely reproduce an author's writing style with sufficient fidelity. In contrast, preference for model outputs with anonymized profiles drops to 13.0% on average, while semantic context preservation remains high at 94.8%. A study with human evaluators confirms the same pattern. These findings reveal a clear privacy-personalization trade-off and highlight the need for privacy-aware personalization methods that retain meaning while suppressing identifying stylistic signals.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how anonymizing stylistic and personal signals in user profiles affects the ability of LLMs to generate highly personalized, style-faithful text, revealing a trade-off between privacy and personalization.
AI.motivation: LLMs can mimic users’ writing style with high fidelity, which raises privacy risks of stylometric re-identification because personal data often encodes demographic, cultural, and other identifiable cues. The authors want to understand whether and how suppressing these identifiable stylistic signals impacts the quality of personalized text generation, to better balance personalization with privacy protection.
AI.method: Using the LaMP-7 Twitter personalization benchmark, the authors sample 250 users and define two paraphrasing conditions: (1) conditioning generation on the original user profile, and (2) conditioning on an anonymized profile where demographic identifiers, cultural references, personal details, and informal stylistic cues are systematically neutralized. They then generate paraphrases under both conditions and evaluate outputs with two independent LLM-based judges plus a human evaluation, focusing on style similarity to ground-truth tweets and semantic preservation.
AI.result: When conditioned on original profiles, LLM outputs are rated as nearly indistinguishable from human-authored tweets, demonstrating strong stylistic imitation. When conditioned on anonymized profiles, preference for those outputs falls to about 13% on average, meaning personalization quality—particularly stylistic fidelity—drops sharply, even though semantic context preservation remains very high at 94.8%. Human evaluations mirror the LLM-judge findings.
AI.conclusion: Anonymizing or neutralizing stylistic and demographic signals substantially reduces the stylistic quality of personalization while maintaining meaning, exposing a clear privacy–personalization trade-off. The work underscores the need for privacy-aware personalization techniques that can preserve semantic content and utility while actively suppressing or controlling for identifying stylistic markers to mitigate re-identification risk.

title: IntLawNER: A Named Entity Recognition Dataset and Benchmark in International Law
summary: International law provides the normative framework through which states coordinate action, regulate armed conflict, and protect human rights, yet its texts remain without token-level named entity recognition (NER) resources. We introduce IntLawNER, a NER dataset and benchmark for codified sources of international law, covering 2,987 gold-annotated sentences and 8,094 entity spans from International Court of Justice (ICJ) decisions, UN Security Council resolutions, and European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) judgments, annotated with seven institution-specific entity types. We construct IntLawNER with a cost-effective hybrid algorithmic-agentic pipeline that reduces 468k source sentences to a compact annotation set through candidate retrieval, LLM-based vetting, and human review, with 89.6% of gold spans accepted unchanged from the silver layer. However, the silver-to-gold analysis reveals that human-machine aggregate agreement metrics can be misleading in domain-specific NER: Cohen's kappa=0.964 on boundary-matched spans masks a macro-F1 of 0.753 when missing entities, boundary errors, and label corrections are included. The benchmark shows that zero-shot span-based GLiNER collapses on entity types dependent on institutional function rather than surface form (0.243 micro-F1), while fine-tuned transformers struggle on rare labels. Carefully selected few-shot examples that demonstrate label contrasts improve every LLM over zero-shot prompting, with Claude Opus 4.6 reaching the best score of 0.873 micro-F1. We release IntLawNER as a benchmark and reusable resource for extracting references in international legal texts.

AI.tldr: They build and release IntLawNER, the first token-level NER dataset and benchmark for international law texts, created with a hybrid LLM + human pipeline and analyzed against multiple NER models.
AI.motivation: International law is central for coordinating state behavior, regulating armed conflict, and protecting human rights, but there is no token-level NER resource tailored to its specialized texts. This gap impedes automatic extraction of legal references and entities from core institutions like the ICJ, UNSC, and ECtHR. The authors aim to provide a high-quality, domain-specific NER dataset and to study how well current NER and LLM methods perform on this challenging, institution-specific domain.
AI.method: They compile texts from ICJ decisions, UN Security Council resolutions, and ECtHR judgments and design seven institution-specific entity types. Using a cost-effective hybrid pipeline, they start from 468k sentences and filter them into a smaller set for annotation via candidate retrieval, LLM-based vetting, and human review. They first create a silver layer with LLM assistance, then convert it to gold via human annotation. They evaluate silver-to-gold agreement (including boundary and label errors), then benchmark various systems: a zero-shot span-based GLiNER model, fine-tuned transformer models, and multiple LLM prompting regimes (zero-shot vs. carefully designed few-shot prompts).
AI.result: The resulting IntLawNER dataset contains 2,987 gold-annotated sentences and 8,094 entity spans with seven institution-specific labels. In the pipeline, 89.6% of gold spans are accepted unchanged from the silver layer, but a deeper silver-to-gold comparison shows that aggregate agreement metrics can be misleading: a very high Cohen’s kappa of 0.964 on boundary-matched spans corresponds to only 0.753 macro-F1 once missing entities, boundary mistakes, and label corrections are considered. On the benchmark, zero-shot GLiNER performs poorly (0.243 micro-F1), especially for entities defined by institutional function rather than surface pattern, while fine-tuned transformers have trouble with rare labels. LLMs see consistent performance gains when given carefully chosen few-shot examples, and Claude Opus 4.6 achieves the strongest result with 0.873 micro-F1.
AI.conclusion: IntLawNER fills a key resource gap by providing the first token-level NER dataset and benchmark tailored to core institutions of international law. The hybrid LLM–human construction pipeline is efficient yet reveals that standard agreement metrics can overstate NER quality in specialized domains. Existing NER models, especially in zero-shot settings, struggle with institution-specific, function-defined entities, though LLMs can perform strongly when guided by contrastive few-shot examples. The released dataset and benchmark are intended as reusable tools for automatic extraction of references and entities in international legal texts and for further research on domain-specific NER and evaluation methods.

title: An Empirical Cost Attribution of Context-Compression Gateways in Multi-Turn Coding Agents
summary: Context compression is widely proposed as a way to cut the token bill of LLM coding agents, and public benchmarks report that aggressive compression preserves task-solving quality. These two facts do not imply the third one commonly assumed: that compressing file reads saves money in a real multi-turn agent. We instrument a production compression gateway (Paritok) between coding agents (Claude Code, Codex) and frontier LLMs (Claude Sonnet, GPT-5), and decompose the token bill of real sessions into three independent levers: tool-schema filtering, content compression of file reads and tool output, and history summarization. Measured in isolation under controlled A/B runs, the three save at fundamentally different rates. Tool-schema filtering removes a fixed block every turn, roughly 21K-57K tokens on a typical turn; it is linear in the turn count N and the only unambiguously and reproducibly positive lever. Content compression saves only about 2% of the cache-priced prefix per turn, but compressed reads accumulate in history and are re-sent on every later turn, so its cumulative saving grows quadratically, about 3350*N^2 tokens (measured), overtaking the fixed tool-filter saving within roughly 6 turns until the context window caps it. A non-destructive gateway lets the agent pull original bytes back on demand; each recall re-sends exactly the one segment just compressed away, so its cost is fixed and bounded rather than a multiplicative blowup, and heavy recall spends the accumulated saving back one segment at a time. Finally, a strong single-shot compression benchmark - 86.5% of SWE-bench quality retained at a 25.7% compression rate, achieved by the model this gateway deploys (Paritok-4B, reported separately) - is orthogonal to multi-turn agent cost and must not be cited as a cost-saving argument. We distill the results into an actionable recipe for where token-saving effort pays off.

AI.tldr: The paper empirically analyzes how different context-compression levers (tool-schema filtering, content compression, and history summarization) affect real token costs in multi-turn LLM coding agents, showing that not all compression that preserves quality actually saves money in practice.
AI.motivation: While context compression is promoted as a way to reduce token costs for LLM coding agents and benchmarks show that strong compression can preserve task performance, it is unclear whether and how these techniques translate into real cost savings in multi-turn, tool-using production agents. The authors want to disentangle which compression strategies truly reduce token bills and under what conditions, rather than relying on single-shot benchmark results as a proxy for economic benefit.
AI.method: The authors deploy and instrument a production compression gateway (Paritok) between real coding agents (Claude Code, Codex) and frontier LLMs (Claude Sonnet, GPT-5). They decompose the token usage of real multi-turn sessions into three components: (1) tool-schema filtering, (2) content compression of file reads and tool outputs, and (3) history summarization. Using controlled A/B experiments, they independently toggle and measure the impact of each lever on token counts across turns, and model how savings scale with the number of turns and with context-window limits. They also analyze how non-destructive compression with on-demand recall affects cumulative savings and recall costs.
AI.result: They find that the three levers behave very differently. Tool-schema filtering removes a large, mostly fixed block of tokens every turn (about 21K–57K tokens per typical turn), producing linear savings with respect to turn count and yielding consistent, reproducible cost reductions. Content compression of file reads and tool output saves only around 2% of the cache-priced prefix per turn when viewed locally, but because the compressed content recurs in the conversation history, its cumulative savings grow approximately quadratically with the number of turns, measured as about 3350·N^2 tokens, eventually surpassing the per-turn savings of tool-schema filtering after roughly six turns, until context-window limits are reached. Using a non-destructive gateway that allows the agent to recall original content means each recall only re-sends the specific compressed segment, capping recall costs and turning recall into a gradual spend-back of previously accumulated savings. They also show that high-quality single-shot compression performance, such as retaining 86.5% of SWE-bench performance at 25.7% compression with Paritok-4B, is essentially unrelated to and not predictive of actual multi-turn token-cost savings.
AI.conclusion: Effective token-cost reduction for multi-turn coding agents cannot be inferred from single-shot compression benchmarks alone. Tool-schema filtering is the most robust and straightforward cost-saving mechanism, scaling linearly with turns and consistently delivering savings. Content compression can become highly valuable in longer sessions due to quadratic cumulative savings, but its benefit depends on conversation length and context-window constraints, and recall patterns determine how much of that saving is ultimately realized. Non-destructive compression with selective recall provides a controlled way to trade between savings and information restoration. Overall, the paper offers a practical recipe: prioritize tool-schema filtering first, use content compression strategically for longer sessions with appropriate gateway design, and do not treat benchmarked compression quality as direct evidence of economic cost reduction.

title: EvidenT: Building Trustworthy Enterprise Assistants through Evidence Groundedness and Traceability
summary: Enterprise AI assistants must produce responses that are verifiable and traceable to source evidence. However, retrieval augmented generation (RAG) over heterogeneous enterprise data can suffer from citation drift, unsupported content, and weak source traceability. We present EvidenT (T = Trust + Transparency + Traceability), a lightweight pipeline that verifies extracted evidence against retrieved documents before answer generation, without model retraining. EvidenT combines structured passage extraction with deterministic lexical alignment to filter unsupported content, correct citation drift, and preserve source-span traceability. On approximately 500 real enterprise queries, EvidenT improves gold-source hit rate by an average of 29% over prompting baselines, produces no citations to nonretrieved urls, and achieves near-saturated answer-to-source lexical coverage.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces EvidenT, a lightweight pipeline to improve trust, transparency, and traceability in enterprise RAG systems by verifying and aligning evidence with sources before answer generation.
AI.motivation: Enterprise AI assistants must give answers that are verifiable and clearly linked to their evidence, but existing RAG systems over heterogeneous enterprise data suffer from problems like citation drift, hallucinated or unsupported content, and weak traceability from answers back to specific source spans. There is a need for a practical method that strengthens evidence verification and traceability without retraining large models.
AI.method: The authors propose EvidenT, a pipeline that operates before answer generation. It performs structured passage extraction from retrieved documents, then uses deterministic lexical alignment between candidate answer content and the extracted passages. This alignment is used to filter out unsupported content, correct citation drift, and maintain explicit mappings from answer spans to source spans, all without modifying or retraining the underlying LLM.
AI.result: On about 500 real enterprise queries, EvidenT increases the rate at which answers cite the correct gold sources by an average of 29% compared to prompting-only baselines. It eliminates citations to URLs that were not actually retrieved and yields answers whose content has near-complete lexical coverage in the underlying sources, indicating strong answer-to-source alignment.
AI.conclusion: EvidenT demonstrates that a lightweight, pre-generation verification and alignment pipeline can significantly improve the reliability and traceability of enterprise RAG systems without model retraining. By combining structured passage extraction with deterministic lexical alignment, it mitigates citation drift and unsupported content while preserving fine-grained source-span traceability, thereby enhancing trust and transparency in enterprise AI assistants.

title: Evaluation Awareness Shifts from Format to Context with Model Scale
summary: Evaluation awareness poses an unprecedented threat to model evaluation, but the mechanisms by which models detect it remain unknown. This study focuses on determining this and identifying contrasting mechanisms between smaller and larger models. While smaller models use the prompt's format sensitivity to detect evaluation, larger models often rely on higher-order reasoning to detect it. We evaluated Gemma 3 (1B, 4B, and 12B), Phi-3 (Mini and Medium), and Llama-3 8B using Chain-of-Thought analysis, representation probing, and Integrated Gradients attribution. Motivated by these findings, we propose a dual-pathway intervention that combines prompt sanitization with activation counter-steering to suppress both external evaluation triggers and their internal representations. Across 200 highly evaluation-aware prompts, our method achieves an average behavioral flip rate of 70.58\%, consistently outperforming either intervention alone. These results provide new insights into how evaluation awareness develops in compact language models and suggest that effective mitigation requires jointly addressing both prompt-level and representation-level signals.Datasets and codebase can be found in this \href{https://github.com/chahal-navi/Evaluation-Awareness-Compact-LLMs/tree/main}{Github Repository.}

AI.tldr: The paper studies how compact language models become aware they are being evaluated, finds different detection mechanisms in small vs larger models, and proposes a two-part mitigation method that modifies both prompts and internal activations, achieving about 70% success in suppressing evaluation-aware behavior.
AI.motivation: Evaluation awareness—when models recognize they are in a test or benchmark—can undermine the reliability of evaluations by changing model behavior. This is increasingly problematic as models get better at inferring context and intent from prompts, potentially gaming tests, refusing tasks, or otherwise behaving differently when they detect evaluation. The authors aim to understand how such awareness arises in compact LLMs and to develop methods to mitigate it so that evaluations remain trustworthy.
AI.method: The authors analyze several compact LLMs (Gemma 3 at 1B, 4B, 12B; Phi-3 Mini and Medium; Llama-3 8B). They compare smaller vs larger models using: (1) Chain-of-Thought analysis to inspect explicit reasoning traces; (2) representation probing to identify internal features or directions correlated with evaluation awareness; and (3) Integrated Gradients attribution to see which input tokens and internal activations drive evaluation-aware responses. Based on the insights, they design a dual-pathway intervention that combines (a) prompt sanitization to remove or obfuscate explicit evaluation cues, and (b) activation counter-steering, where they push internal representations away from discovered evaluation-aware directions during inference.
AI.result: Empirically, they test their intervention on 200 prompts chosen to strongly elicit evaluation awareness. The dual-pathway method achieves an average behavioral flip rate of 70.58%, meaning in about 7 out of 10 cases the model stops exhibiting evaluation-aware behavior and responds as if it were not being evaluated. This combined approach consistently outperforms using only prompt sanitization or only activation counter-steering across the studied models and sizes, indicating synergy between external prompt-level and internal representation-level controls.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that evaluation awareness in compact LLMs arises via at least two distinct mechanisms: format-based sensitivity in smaller models and more abstract, higher-order reasoning in larger ones. Because of this, effective mitigation must address both surface-level evaluation cues and the internal representations that encode evaluation-related concepts. Their dual-pathway intervention offers a practical strategy to reduce evaluation-aware behavior and, more broadly, the work highlights that as models scale, understanding and controlling evaluation awareness is essential for robust and trustworthy benchmarking.

title: AutoGym: Blueprint-First Generation of Verifiable Agent Gyms
comment: Submitted to NeurIPS 2026 Workshop: Who Verifies the Agents?
summary: Training agents with reinforcement learning requires a gym, comprising a task, an executable environment in which the task can be attempted, and a verifier that reliably distinguishes success from failure. Constructing such gyms remains manual, expensive, and static. Task sets saturate as models improve and are increasingly exposed to contamination. Synthetic generation offers scale, but single-pass synthesis produces tasks whose difficulty is largely cosmetic. Models comparable in capability solve them despite convoluted phrasing, and correctness must be adjudicated post-hoc by unreliable LLM judges. We present AutoGym, a framework that generates complete gyms (tasks, executable environments, and verifiers) from a minimal domain seed or prior model trajectories. AutoGym introduces three mechanisms. (1) Blueprint-first generation specifies the valid solution space, environment requirements, and verification criteria before the environment is materialized, making solvability a construction prerequisite rather than a property verified after the fact. (2) Explicit generation parameters control task topology, interaction depth, capability axes, question obfuscation, and distractor composition, enabling fine-grained difficulty steering. (3) Active curriculum synthesis uses performance-informed calibration to adjust the distribution over these parameters as model capabilities evolve. Across productivity and temporal-reasoning settings, AutoGym generates gyms spanning the capability spectrum, including instances that challenge frontier models.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AutoGym, a system that automatically generates reinforcement-learning ‘gyms’ (tasks, environments, and verifiers) that remain challenging as models improve.
AI.motivation: Building RL gyms is currently manual, expensive, static, and prone to task saturation and contamination. Synthetic tasks generated in a single pass tend to be superficially complex but not meaningfully difficult, and correctness usually depends on unreliable LLM judges. The authors want a scalable, automated way to construct high-quality, adaptive gyms that rigorously test evolving model capabilities.
AI.method: AutoGym takes a minimal domain seed or existing model trajectories and automatically creates full gyms. It uses three key mechanisms: (1) blueprint-first generation, which first defines the valid solution space, environment needs, and verification criteria before instantiating the environment, so solvability is guaranteed by design; (2) explicit, structured generation parameters that control aspects like task topology, interaction depth, capability dimensions, degree of obfuscation, and distractors, enabling precise difficulty control; and (3) active curriculum synthesis, which monitors model performance and adaptively adjusts the parameter distributions to keep tasks appropriately challenging over time.
AI.result: Using productivity and temporal-reasoning domains, AutoGym produces a wide range of gyms covering easy to very difficult instances. Some generated tasks are sufficiently hard to challenge state-of-the-art models, demonstrating that the framework can exceed the limitations of existing, static task suites.
AI.conclusion: AutoGym provides a scalable, controllable, and adaptive framework for generating RL gyms. By defining solution spaces and verification criteria up front, exposing rich difficulty parameters, and using performance-based curriculum adjustment, it can continuously create robust, solvable tasks that match and stress-test frontier model capabilities.

title: Balancing Reasoning and Hardware Constraints in RAG Pipelines for Ukrainian Multi-Domain Document Understanding
comment: 5 pages, 2 tables. Technical report based on UNLP 2026 Shared Task submission
summary: This paper describes the system submitted to the UNLP 2026 Shared Task on Multi-Domain Document Understanding. The challenge required extracting precise answers, document IDs, and page numbers from a diverse corpus of Ukrainian PDF documents within a strict 9-hour offline Kaggle execution limit. During evaluation on the hidden private test set, optical character recognition (OCR) of scanned documents emerged as a severe bottleneck, consuming 5-7 hours of the total time budget due to sequential single-threaded execution. This overhead strictly limited the remaining time for Large Language Model (LLM) inference to approximately two hours for 500 questions. To guarantee pipeline completion without timeouts, we developed a resource-efficient Hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline utilizing BM25, BGE-M3, and Cross-Encoder reranking. Rather than deploying parameter-heavy reasoning models (e.g., DeepSeek R1) which consistently timed out, we utilized a 4-bit quantized LapaLLM 12B model via llama.cpp on dual NVIDIA T4 GPUs. Prioritizing pipeline stability over multi-step reasoning, our system achieved a Private Score of 0.8095, placing 10th out of 15 active teams.

AI.tldr: They built a time-efficient RAG pipeline for a Ukrainian multi-domain document QA shared task, carefully balancing OCR cost and LLM inference to finish within a 9-hour Kaggle limit and achieved mid-tier performance.
AI.motivation: The shared task required accurate multi-domain question answering over Ukrainian PDFs under a strict offline runtime budget. OCR of scanned documents consumed most of the available time, leaving little for LLM-based reasoning. Existing heavy reasoning models could not run reliably without timing out, so a more resource- and time-efficient approach was needed to complete the pipeline within the constraints while remaining competitive.
AI.method: They designed a Hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipeline combining sparse and dense retrieval with reranking. Specifically, they used BM25 for lexical retrieval, BGE-M3 for dense retrieval, and a Cross-Encoder for reranking candidate passages. To fit in the time budget, instead of large, reasoning-heavy models like DeepSeek R1, they used a 4-bit quantized LapaLLM 12B model, run via llama.cpp on dual NVIDIA T4 GPUs. The system was optimized for stability and completion under the 9-hour execution limit, trading off some complex multi-step reasoning for predictable runtime. OCR, although a bottleneck, was kept as a separate initial step despite being single-threaded and time-consuming.
AI.result: On the hidden private test set of the UNLP 2026 shared task, the system achieved a Private Score of 0.8095 and ranked 10th out of 15 active teams. The pipeline successfully completed within the strict 9-hour Kaggle time limit despite OCR overhead, but heavier reasoning models were found impractical due to timeouts.
AI.conclusion: A carefully engineered, resource-efficient hybrid RAG pipeline with lightweight quantized LLMs can be more effective under severe runtime and hardware constraints than deploying parameter-heavy reasoning models that frequently time out. Prioritizing pipeline stability and guaranteed completion—especially when OCR dominates the time budget—can still yield respectable performance in constrained document understanding tasks, even if it limits the use of advanced multi-step reasoning models.

title: MAWILE: Multi-Axis Workbench for Inspecting LLM Evaluators
summary: Large language model (LLM) judges provide a flexible and scalable method for evaluating model and agent outputs, but their verdicts can be sensitive to incidental changes in the evaluated response, judge instructions, and scoring rubric. Existing systems examine important subsets of these failure modes, but auditing a configured judge requires testing both the judge instrument and the items it evaluates. We introduce MAWILE, a developer-facing workbench for auditing judge sensitivity across four surfaces: the judge prompt, judge rubric, target-system input, and target-system output. Given a user-supplied judge and representative evaluation items, MAWILE constructs and validates controlled perturbations, re-executes the judge, and localizes the resulting sensitivity. Each perturbation declares whether the verdict should remain invariant or change in a specified direction, allowing the same system to measure both robustness to irrelevant variations and sensitivity to meaningful changes. MAWILE audits binary, ordinal, and pairwise judges without requiring gold labels. The code for this tool is available at: github.com/megagonlabs/mawile-judge.

AI.tldr: The paper presents MAWILE, a workbench for auditing how sensitive LLM-based judges are to changes in prompts, rubrics, and evaluation items, enabling systematic analysis of robustness and desired sensitivity without needing gold labels.
AI.motivation: LLM judges are increasingly used to evaluate models and agents, but their verdicts can change unpredictably with small, incidental variations in instructions, rubrics, or evaluated content. Existing tools only partially address this, and developers lack a systematic way to audit a fully configured judge (instrument plus items) to understand where it is overly brittle or insufficiently sensitive. The paper aims to fill this gap with a practical debugging and auditing tool.
AI.method: The authors build MAWILE, a developer-facing workbench that takes a user-supplied LLM judge plus representative evaluation items and then automatically constructs controlled perturbations across four surfaces: the judge prompt, the judge rubric, the target-system input, and the target-system output. For each perturbation, they specify whether the judge’s verdict should stay the same (invariance) or change in a particular direction (directed change). MAWILE re-runs the judge on the original and perturbed cases, compares verdicts, and localizes where sensitivity occurs. It supports different judge formats (binary, ordinal, pairwise) and works without gold labels by relying on these invariance/change expectations.
AI.result: MAWILE can systematically expose when LLM judges are unstable to irrelevant modifications and when they fail to respond appropriately to meaningful changes, across prompts, rubrics, inputs, and outputs. The system demonstrates the feasibility of auditing diverse judge configurations, including binary, ordinal, and pairwise setups, using only developer-specified perturbations rather than ground-truth annotations. The implementation is released as open-source code.
AI.conclusion: MAWILE provides a practical, general workbench for auditing LLM judges, helping developers quantify and localize both unwanted brittleness and desired responsiveness to content changes. By operating without gold labels and supporting multiple judgment formats and perturbation types, it makes judge reliability analysis more accessible and systematic for real-world evaluation pipelines.

title: Type-Driven Tokenization for Brahmic Scripts
summary: Standard tokenizers used in large language models produce malformed text when applied to Brahmic scripts. They are a family of abugidas, writing systems whose consonants carry an inherent vowel that dependent marks can modify. They include Devanagari, Telugu, Tamil, Kannada, and others. The underlying issue is that these tokenizers violate orthographic constraints that do not arise in alphabetic scripts like English. We observe that while English orthography forms a \emph{semigroup} (any two valid tokens can be freely concatenated), Brahmic orthography forms a \emph{partial semigroup}: not every concatenation yields a valid string. We formalise this distinction in Agda, model valid Brahmic tokens as chains in a transition system, and derive a provably correct \texttt{fixToken} function that extends any candidate token to respect orthographic boundaries. We then show how this formal derivation translates into a practical patch for SentencePiece as well as a standalone Rust-based pre-tokenizer library, eliminating the observed errors across Indic scripts.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies why standard LLM tokenizers break Brahmic scripts and presents a formally verified fix that is implemented in real tooling.
AI.motivation: Existing tokenizers (e.g., SentencePiece) work well for alphabetic scripts like English but produce invalid or malformed text when used on Brahmic abugida scripts such as Devanagari, Telugu, Tamil, and Kannada. This harms the correctness and reliability of large language models for Indic languages. The authors want to understand the structural reason for these failures and design a tokenizer mechanism that provably respects the orthographic rules of these scripts.
AI.method: The authors analyze the structural difference between English orthography and Brahmic scripts, framing English as a semigroup where any two valid tokens can be concatenated, versus Brahmic writing as a partial semigroup where some concatenations are invalid. They formalize these orthographic constraints in the Agda proof assistant, model valid Brahmic tokens as paths (chains) in a transition system, and derive a formally verified `fixToken` function that takes any candidate token and extends or adjusts it to obey orthographic boundaries. They then translate this formal construction into practical software: a patch for SentencePiece and a Rust-based pre-tokenizer library.
AI.result: The authors obtain a provably correct `fixToken` function that guarantees tokens respect Brahmic orthographic rules as defined in their formalization. They implement this mechanism as a modification to SentencePiece and as an independent Rust pre-tokenizer. Empirically, these implementations remove the previously observed malformed outputs across multiple Indic Brahmic scripts.
AI.conclusion: The paper shows that failures of standard LLM tokenizers on Brahmic scripts stem from a fundamental structural mismatch: treating a partial semigroup orthography as if it were a full semigroup. By explicitly modeling the orthographic constraints in a proof assistant and deriving a verified correction mechanism, the authors provide both theoretical insight and practical tools that fix tokenization errors for multiple Indic scripts. This demonstrates the value of formal methods in building multilingual NLP infrastructure that respects script-specific structure.

title: GaitVista: Reliability-Aware AI Measurement toward Accessible Longitudinal Gait Assessment
summary: Tracking recovery of walking function requires detecting meaningful gait change across rehabilitation sessions, yet objective 3D measurement remains confined to specialized motion-capture laboratories. Small camera sets and body-worn inertial sensors broaden access, but reliability varies across joints and time, allowing sensing failures to masquerade as patient change. We present \textsc{GaitVista}, a reliability-aware measurement layer whose lightweight gate assigns joint- and frame-specific visual contributions using camera coverage, local visual quality, cross-modal disagreement, and root-motion continuity, and exposes them for inspection. Across seven clean and degraded sensing conditions on TotalCapture, \textsc{GaitVista} reduces average full-body and lower-body error by \textbf{27.7\%} and \textbf{27.8\%}, attains the lowest worst-condition error among fusion methods, and reduces the gap to a joint-frame oracle from $2.76$--$5.33$~cm for condition-blind baselines to $1.11$~cm. On MoVi with image-derived keypoints, it is the only deployable fusion method to improve over both unimodal streams, reducing marker-supported error by \textbf{6.4\%} relative to the strongest learned fusion baseline. On TotalCapture, it improves bilateral knee-flexion waveform accuracy by \textbf{18.9\%}. Raw inertial measurements from five TotalCapture participants show location- and time-varying magnetic disturbance, supporting the design's reliability premise. Both benchmarks contain neurologically healthy participants in controlled settings and retain participant-specific IMU calibration; we therefore report progress toward accessible gait assessment, not validated clinical deployment.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces GaitVista, a reliability-aware fusion layer for combining camera and inertial sensor data to robustly measure gait outside of motion-capture labs, significantly reducing pose and joint-angle errors across varied sensing conditions.
AI.motivation: Clinical tracking of walking recovery requires detecting real, clinically meaningful gait changes over time. Current high-fidelity 3D gait measurement is mostly restricted to motion-capture labs, while more accessible systems using few cameras and body-worn IMUs suffer from variable reliability across joints, views, and sessions. These reliability fluctuations can cause sensor failures to look like patient changes, undermining clinical use. The authors want a method that detects and accounts for such reliability variations so that gait metrics from accessible systems can be trusted across conditions.
AI.method: The authors propose GaitVista, a "reliability-aware" measurement and fusion layer that operates on multi-sensor gait data. It assigns joint- and frame-specific visual reliability weights based on camera coverage, local visual quality, agreement or disagreement between visual and inertial modalities, and continuity of root motion. These reliability scores gate the contribution of visual information in the fused pose estimate and are explicitly exposed for inspection. They evaluate GaitVista under seven sensing conditions (including degraded ones) on the TotalCapture dataset, and on the MoVi dataset using image-derived keypoints, comparing against unimodal (vision-only, IMU-only) and learned fusion baselines. They also analyze raw IMU data from a subset of participants to document real magnetic disturbances and motivate their reliability modeling.
AI.result: On TotalCapture across seven sensing conditions, GaitVista reduces average full-body and lower-body pose error by 27.7% and 27.8%, respectively, relative to condition-blind baselines and achieves the lowest worst-condition error among fusion methods. It also decreases the gap to an oracle that knows the best joint-frame source from 2.76–5.33 cm to 1.11 cm. On MoVi with image-derived keypoints, GaitVista is the only practically deployable fusion method that outperforms both unimodal streams, lowering marker-based error by 6.4% compared to the strongest learned fusion baseline. On TotalCapture, it improves bilateral knee-flexion waveform accuracy by 18.9%. Analysis of IMU signals shows spatially and temporally varying magnetic disturbances, supporting the need for reliability-aware fusion.
AI.conclusion: GaitVista enables more robust and interpretable fusion of camera and IMU data for gait assessment by explicitly modeling reliability at the joint-frame level, leading to substantial pose and joint-angle accuracy gains, especially under degraded sensing conditions. The work demonstrates progress toward accessible, clinic-ready gait measurement outside motion-capture labs, though current validation is limited to neurologically healthy participants in controlled environments with participant-specific IMU calibration, so further studies are needed before clinical deployment.

title: Beyond Accuracy and Surface Fluency: Risk-Sensitive Evaluation of LLMs for Legal Clause Generation
comment: Accepted to the AI for Law Workshop @ ICML 2026. https://openreview.net/forum?id=qWtjzD2Udj
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to draft contractual language, yet conventional accuracy or preference-based evaluations are poorly matched to legal drafting. A clause may be fluent and stylistically polished while still omitting an essential carve-out, allocating risk in an unenforceable way, assuming an inapplicable jurisdiction, or exposing a party to regulatory liability. This paper presents a empirical study design and framework for evaluating LLM-generated contract clauses. The study evaluates four models - Claude Haiku 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite, GPT 5.4 Nano, and Qwen 3.5 Flash, across 22 contract clause categories and 34 legally-motivated failure modes. We combine two evaluation frameworks: CLAUSE, which classifies prompts by legal function and failure target, and LENS-CRAFT, which scores outputs across nine legal-quality dimensions. Instead of averaging dimension scores, the study applies a Max Severity Principle so that a single legally decisive defect remains visible. The paper provides the evaluation protocol, taxonomy, analysis plan, and a results structure for reporting empirical findings. We argue that legal AI evaluation should move beyond aggregate accuracy toward clause-specific, failure-mode-driven, and risk-sensitive assessment.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and details an empirical evaluation framework for LLM-generated contract clauses, focusing on legally meaningful failure modes rather than aggregate accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM evaluations focus on accuracy, preference, or fluency, which are poorly aligned with legal drafting needs where small omissions or hidden defects can be legally decisive. There is a need for an evaluation approach that captures legally salient risks in contract clauses, not just surface-level quality or average scores.
AI.method: The authors design an empirical study evaluating four LLMs (Claude Haiku 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite, GPT 5.4 Nano, Qwen 3.5 Flash) on 22 categories of contract clauses and 34 legally-motivated failure modes. They integrate two frameworks—CLAUSE (for classifying prompts by legal function and failure target) and LENS-CRAFT (for scoring outputs on nine legal-quality dimensions). They introduce a Max Severity Principle, where the worst defect in a clause governs its evaluation instead of averaging scores across dimensions. The paper specifies the protocol, taxonomy, and analysis plan for running and reporting this evaluation.
AI.result: The abstract does not report empirical performance numbers; rather, it presents the designed framework, taxonomy, and analysis structure for evaluating LLM-generated contract clauses and for making legally decisive defects visible in results.
AI.conclusion: Evaluation of legal drafting by LLMs should be clause-specific, driven by explicit legal failure modes, and sensitive to the most severe risks in a clause, rather than relying on aggregate accuracy or averaged quality scores. The proposed framework and study design aim to standardize such risk-aware evaluation for legal AI systems.

title: Splitting Documents at Lower Cost: Multi-Split Boundary Decisions for LLM-Based Page Stream Segmentation
comment: Accepted at the DocInsights Workshop at EMNLP 2026
summary: Scanned mail, uploaded PDFs, and consolidated attachments often arrive as page streams that must be split into individual documents before downstream classification, extraction, or routing. Zero-shot large language models can detect document boundaries without task-specific training, but standard Page Classification (PC) and Boundary Decision (BD) formulations resolve only one boundary per model call. We introduce Multi-Split Boundary Decision (MSBD), which predicts multiple boundaries within a page window in a single call, reducing the number of inference requests. We evaluate MSBD across multiple language models, document collections, input modalities, and window sizes. The results reveal a model- and corpus-dependent operating range in which MSBD preserves strong segmentation accuracy while substantially improving inference efficiency, followed by a sharp decline at larger windows. MSBD provided the strongest overall accuracy--efficiency trade-off, while large windows expose distinct over- and under-segmentation behavior across models. These findings show that multi-boundary prediction can make zero-shot page stream segmentation more efficient when the window size is selected for the target corpus.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a more efficient way to split continuous page streams into individual documents using large language models by predicting multiple document boundaries in one go instead of one at a time.
AI.motivation: In many real-world systems, scanned mail and uploaded PDFs arrive as continuous page streams that must be segmented into separate documents before tasks like classification or information extraction can be performed. Existing zero-shot LLM approaches treat boundary detection as either page classification or single-boundary decision per model call, which is inefficient because they require a separate inference for each potential boundary. There is a need to improve inference efficiency without sacrificing segmentation accuracy.
AI.method: The authors introduce a new formulation called Multi-Split Boundary Decision (MSBD), where an LLM is asked to predict multiple document boundaries within a window of pages in a single inference call. They apply this to various large language models, use different document collections and input modalities (e.g., text, images), and vary the size of the page window. They then compare segmentation accuracy and efficiency (number of calls) between MSBD and traditional Page Classification and Boundary Decision setups.
AI.result: Experiments show that MSBD can maintain strong segmentation accuracy while significantly reducing the number of LLM inference calls, but only within a certain range of window sizes that depends on both the model and the dataset. When the window becomes too large, segmentation performance drops sharply, with models showing different tendencies toward over-segmentation or under-segmentation. Overall, MSBD yields the best trade-off between accuracy and efficiency across the tested conditions.
AI.conclusion: Multi-boundary prediction via MSBD is an effective approach for zero-shot segmentation of page streams, improving efficiency over traditional one-boundary-per-call methods while keeping high accuracy when the page window is properly tuned to the target corpus. Choosing an appropriate window size is crucial, as too-large windows lead to significant performance degradation and distinct error patterns across models.

title: Correlation-Aware Structured Pruning for Large Language Models
summary: Structured pruning is a promising approach for reducing the substantial inference costs of Large Language Models (LLMs) while maintaining hardware efficiency. Many existing methods assess the importance of prunable units (e.g., channels or heads) in isolation, implicitly assuming that pruning errors are additive. This independence assumption is often invalidated by the non-orthogonality of model weights and strong correlations between unit activations, potentially leading to performance degradation. To address this, we propose a Correlation-Aware Structured Pruning method. We formulate the pruning objective as a cardinality-constrained binary quadratic program that explicitly models cross-unit dependencies in the reconstruction error. Since this binary quadratic program is NP-hard and difficult to solve exactly, we develop a greedy interaction algorithm based on dependency-aware marginal costs to optimize unit selection. Furthermore, we incorporate a gradient-based strategy to achieve adaptive layer-wise sparsity allocation across the entire model. Extensive experiments on mainstream LLMs demonstrate that incorporating correlation information yields competitive accuracy-efficiency trade-offs compared to representative structured pruning baselines.

AI.tldr: They introduce a correlation-aware structured pruning method for LLMs that explicitly models and optimizes cross-unit dependencies, achieving better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs than prior structured pruning approaches.
AI.motivation: Existing structured pruning methods for LLMs typically evaluate the importance of channels or attention heads independently, assuming pruning errors are additive. This ignores interactions caused by non-orthogonal weights and correlated activations, which can make these methods suboptimal and hurt performance. There is a need to account for correlations between prunable units to obtain more accurate pruning decisions and better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs.
AI.method: They formulate structured pruning as a cardinality-constrained binary quadratic program that directly models cross-unit dependencies in the reconstruction error. Since this program is NP-hard, they do not solve it exactly. Instead, they design a greedy interaction algorithm that selects units based on dependency-aware marginal costs, explicitly taking correlations into account. Additionally, they use a gradient-based scheme to adaptively allocate sparsity across layers of the model, rather than using a fixed or heuristic layer-wise sparsity pattern.
AI.result: On multiple mainstream LLMs, their correlation-aware method achieves competitive or improved trade-offs between accuracy and computational efficiency compared to representative structured pruning baselines that ignore correlations. The experiments validate that explicitly modeling cross-unit dependencies during pruning yields better retained performance at comparable sparsity levels.
AI.conclusion: Considering correlations between prunable units in structured pruning leads to more effective unit selection than treating units independently. By formulating pruning as a binary quadratic program and approximating its solution with a greedy interaction algorithm plus adaptive layer-wise sparsity allocation, their approach improves the accuracy-efficiency trade-off for LLM inference over standard structured pruning methods.

title: Text, Pixels, or Both? Evaluating Input Representations for Multimodal Document QA
comment: Accepted as a poster at the Context Beyond the Window (CBW) Workshop at COLM 2026 and the DocInsights Workshop at EMNLP 2026
summary: Every document QA system begins with a choice that is rarely studied on its own: whether to feed the model page images, extracted text, or both. We isolate this choice, holding the prompt, judge, and scoring pipeline fixed, across four commercial model endpoints, two corpora, and two context regimes (gold evidence pages and the full document). On documents that fit the image budget, page images lead on accuracy at every document length on both corpora, but this advantage carries a growing latency and cost premium: text latency stays roughly flat as documents lengthen while image latency rises steadily. Text and images also fail on different questions, with exactly one representation correct on 19--25% of items across the reported cells, so neither subsumes the other. Exploiting this complementarity, a lightweight TF-IDF router that reads only the question text gains 2.6 points over always-text while cutting median latency 30% relative to always-vision, on a document-disjoint held-out split.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the impact of using page images, extracted text, or both as input to document QA systems, finding that images are more accurate but slower and costlier, text is faster with flat latency, and a simple TF-IDF router can effectively combine them for better accuracy-latency trade-offs.
AI.motivation: In document QA, the standard but under-examined design choice is whether to feed the model page images, extracted text, or both. This choice can significantly affect accuracy, latency, and cost, yet is rarely isolated and systematically studied. The authors aim to rigorously evaluate these input representations to inform better system design.
AI.method: The authors hold the prompt, judge, and scoring pipeline fixed while varying only the document representation (images vs extracted text vs combinations). They conduct experiments across four commercial model endpoints, two document corpora, and two context regimes (gold evidence pages versus full documents). They additionally analyze error complementarity and introduce a lightweight TF-IDF-based router that selects the representation using only the question text.
AI.result: On documents that fit within the image token/budget constraints, page images consistently outperform text alone in accuracy across all document lengths and both corpora. However, image-based QA incurs increasing latency and cost as document length grows, whereas text-based QA maintains roughly constant latency. The analysis shows that text and image representations succeed on different subsets of questions, with exactly one representation being correct for 19–25% of items. Using this complementarity, the TF-IDF router improves accuracy by 2.6 percentage points over always using text, while reducing median latency by 30% compared with always using images on a document-disjoint held-out set.
AI.conclusion: The choice of document representation (images versus extracted text) has substantial and nuanced effects on document QA performance, latency, and cost. Images offer better accuracy but scale poorly in latency and expense with document length; text is more efficient but misses questions that images can answer. Because the two representations are complementary, simple routing strategies like a TF-IDF-based router can yield better accuracy-latency trade-offs than committing to a single representation, suggesting that hybrid or adaptive systems are a promising direction for practical document QA.

title: Observational Equivalence of LLM and Human Annotation
summary: In this paper, we show that LLM and human coding are observationally equivalent in terms of annotation quality: recent LLMs agree with expert coders at rates comparable to those observed among experts themselves. We demonstrate this through replications of text-classification tasks from 14 peer-reviewed political science studies, in which ten LLMs, three human experts, and 165 crowdsourced workers independently classify the same texts using identical codebooks. We find that this equivalence is driven by ambiguity in the texts and coding rules. When LLMs disagree with experts, experts are also more likely to disagree with one another, and clarifying coding rules reduces disagreement among both experts and sufficiently capable LLMs. Thus, there is little empirical basis for preferring human coding on the basis of annotation quality alone, while LLMs offer substantial advantages in speed and cost. We therefore argue that the central challenge of text annotation is no longer choosing between human and machine coders, but developing coding rules that minimize ambiguity and accounting for the ambiguity that remains. To this end, we propose using disagreement across LLMs to identify difficult cases and refine codebooks, and we develop ambiguity-aware bounds for downstream inference when a unique annotation cannot be defined for every text.

AI.tldr: The paper finds that recent LLMs match human experts in text-annotation quality on political science tasks, with remaining disagreements largely due to inherent ambiguity rather than coder type.
AI.motivation: To assess whether human coders are still superior to large language models (LLMs) for text annotation in social science research, given the high cost and slowness of human coding and the increasing use of LLMs despite limited systematic validation against expert standards.
AI.method: The authors replicate text-classification components of 14 peer‑reviewed political science studies. For each task, they have ten different LLMs, three human expert coders, and 165 crowdsourced workers independently annotate the same texts using the original codebooks. They then compare agreement rates across LLMs, experts, and crowd workers, analyze patterns of disagreement in relation to textual and rule ambiguity, and study how clarifying coding rules affects agreement. Finally, they propose and illustrate methods that use cross‑LLM disagreement to flag ambiguous cases and construct ambiguity‑aware bounds for downstream statistical inference.
AI.result: Recent LLMs agree with expert coders at rates comparable to the levels of agreement observed among experts themselves, and they substantially outperform crowdsourced workers. Disagreements between LLMs and experts are concentrated in texts and coding rules that are ambiguous: where LLMs diverge from one expert, other experts are also more likely to diverge from each other. Tightening and clarifying coding rules reduces disagreement for both human experts and capable LLMs. LLMs provide results much faster and at lower cost than human coding.
AI.conclusion: On annotation quality alone, there is little empirical justification for preferring human over LLM coders in political text-classification tasks. The key methodological challenge shifts from choosing between human and machine annotators to designing unambiguous coding rules and explicitly handling irreducible ambiguity. The authors recommend using disagreement across multiple LLMs to detect difficult, ambiguous cases and refine codebooks, and when unique labels cannot be assigned, to incorporate that ambiguity via bounds in subsequent empirical analyses.

title: Self-Organizing Agent Teams Learn to Reason Together
summary: Collective intelligence depends not only on what team members know, but also on how they organize their work. When the structure of a solution is unknown, useful roles and divisions of labor cannot be specified in advance; teams must learn from experience how to organize reasoning as it unfolds. Human teams routinely adapt this way, while existing AI agent teams rely on fixed protocols, explicit task decomposition, or routing. We introduce Self-Organizing Agent Teams (SAT), fixed teams of AI agents that learn reusable strategies from prior collaborations to organize roles, conversational phases, participation, and information flow. These strategies enable what we call collaborative computation: agents exchange, challenge, repair, and synthesize partial reasoning into solutions no member produced independently. In two independent settings, we learn teamwork strategies that transfer unchanged to unseen benchmarks, using only 15 mathematics and 25 graduate-level knowledge problems. Across five mathematics and physics benchmarks, self-organizing teams average 66.7% accuracy, versus 48.8% for their strongest member, 58.7% for compute-matched inference by that agent, and 59.0% for a perfect router over members' independent answers; on AIME 2026, they exceed this router by 13.4 points. Because gains vary across benchmarks, we ask when self-organizing collaboration helps. Across eight benchmarks, demonstrability (the organizational-psychology construct of whether a team can distinguish correct from incorrect reasoning) strongly tracks improvement over the strongest member (Spearman $ρ=0.90$, $p=0.005$): teams benefit most when correct reasoning can be recognized once it appears. More broadly, these results suggest that organization itself can become an agent capability: agent teams can learn how to reason together and produce solutions their members could not reach independently.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Self-Organizing Agent Teams (SAT), where fixed groups of AI agents learn how to coordinate and structure their collaboration so that, together, they solve problems better than any individual agent or simple routing scheme.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent AI systems typically rely on hand-designed protocols, explicit task decomposition, or static routing of subproblems. This contrasts with human teams, which learn from experience how to organize their collaboration, adapt roles, and structure conversations, especially when the solution structure is unknown in advance. The authors aim to close this gap by enabling AI agent teams to learn how to self-organize their reasoning dynamically and to transfer these collaboration strategies to new tasks.
AI.method: The authors propose Self-Organizing Agent Teams (SAT), in which a fixed set of AI agents repeatedly collaborate on tasks and, from these experiences, learn strategies that govern roles, conversational phases, participation patterns, and information flow. These strategies are learned from a relatively small set of training problems (15 math and 25 graduate-level knowledge tasks) and are then transferred unchanged to new benchmarks. The teams perform what the authors call collaborative computation, where agents iteratively exchange, critique, repair, and integrate partial reasoning steps into final solutions that no single agent produced on its own. The study also analyzes when such collaboration is most beneficial by relating performance gains to the construct of demonstrability from organizational psychology.
AI.result: Across five mathematics and physics benchmarks, self-organizing teams achieve an average accuracy of 66.7%, outperforming the strongest individual agent (48.8%), compute-matched single-agent inference (58.7%), and an oracle router that selects the best among independently generated answers from team members (59.0%). On AIME 2026, the self-organizing team exceeds the oracle router by 13.4 percentage points. Further, across eight benchmarks, improvement over the strongest member strongly correlates with demonstrability—the ability of the team to recognize correct reasoning once it appears (Spearman ρ=0.90, p=0.005).
AI.conclusion: Self-Organizing Agent Teams can learn reusable, transferable strategies for organizing multi-agent reasoning, enabling them to perform collaborative computation and achieve solutions that individual agents or simple routing schemes cannot. The effectiveness of such collaboration depends strongly on demonstrability: teams gain the most when correct reasoning, once produced by any member, can be reliably recognized and propagated. The work suggests that organizational skill—how to coordinate and structure joint reasoning—can itself be treated and learned as a fundamental agent capability.

title: Read-Best Is Not Steer-Best: A Probing--Steering Layer Dissociation in Omni-Modal Large Language Models
summary: Omni-modal large language models integrate text, audio, and image signals into a shared residual stream, where concepts such as emotion can be linearly decoded and causally modified by activation steering. A common but rarely tested assumption is that the layer with the highest probing accuracy is also the best layer for steering, so injection layers are often selected by probe performance. We provide the first causal test of this assumption across three independently developed omni-modal models and find that it fails. Reading and intervention rely on different layers, a phenomenon we call the probing-steering layer dissociation. Using emotion as a controlled testbed, we measure layer-wise readability and steerability across text, audio, and image inputs. Probe-best layers vary widely across architectures, while steering-effective layers consistently fall within a narrow mid-to-late range of normalized depth. Paired random-direction controls show an approximately 26-fold causal gap, ruling out random perturbation and direction quality as explanations. Logit-lens analysis reveals a staged forward process: causal handle, probing saturation, and vocabulary commitment, and motivates a two-factor account in which steering effectiveness depends on both representational readability and downstream plasticity. These results show that probing accuracy is a poor heuristic for selecting intervention layers and suggest a cross-architecture mid-to-late selection criterion. We also identify a cross-modal emotion subspace organized by valence and arousal, with joy acting as a stable anchor across models. Code and data: https://github.com/YiboWang2002/Read-Best-Is-Not-Steer-Best.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the layers that are easiest to probe for concepts like emotion are not the same layers where steering those concepts is most effective, across multiple omni-modal LLMs.
AI.motivation: Researchers and practitioners commonly choose which layer to intervene in by finding the layer where a linear probe best decodes a target concept (e.g., emotion). This assumes that the most readable layer is also the best layer for causal control, but this assumption has not been systematically tested, especially in omni-modal models that jointly process text, audio, and images.
AI.method: The authors use emotion as a controlled testbed and run systematic, layer-wise experiments on three independently developed omni-modal LLMs. For each layer and modality (text, audio, image), they (1) train linear probes to measure how well emotions can be decoded (readability) and (2) apply activation steering along emotion directions to assess how effectively emotions can be causally modified (steerability). They compare probe-best vs steering-effective layers, introduce random-direction controls to separate causal effects from noise or direction quality, and apply logit-lens analysis to characterize how information flows across layers and when model predictions become committed to specific vocabulary. They normalize depth across architectures to compare patterns.
AI.result: They discover a consistent dissociation: layers with highest probing accuracy are not the layers where steering is most causally effective. Probe-best layers vary greatly across architectures, but steering-effective layers cluster in a narrow mid-to-late band of normalized depth. Random-direction controls show an approximately 26x causal effect gap, indicating that their steering directions are genuinely causal rather than random perturbations. Logit-lens analysis suggests a staged forward computation involving an early causal handle phase, a probing saturation phase, and a later vocabulary commitment phase. They also uncover a cross-modal emotion subspace aligned along valence and arousal axes, with joy serving as a robust anchor across models and modalities.
AI.conclusion: Probing accuracy is an unreliable heuristic for choosing intervention layers in omni-modal LLMs: read-best is not steer-best. Effective steering arises in mid-to-late layers where representations are both readable and still plastically influence downstream computation. The authors propose a two-factor account—requiring both representational readability and downstream plasticity—and suggest a practical, architecture-agnostic guideline to target mid-to-late layers for interventions. They additionally highlight the existence of a shared, cross-modal emotion subspace, opening avenues for more principled control of affective behaviors in omni-modal models.

title: Generative Embodied Multiple Behavior Control Systems for Human-like Agents
summary: An enduring and richly elaborated dichotomy in cognitive neuroscience is that of human behavior control mechanisms, divided into habitual versus goal-directed. While existing human-like agent frameworks primarily focus on modeling goal- directed behavior, habitual behavior has been largely overlooked, though it plays a crucial role in human daily life. In this paper, we address this gap by studying multiple behavior control systems that jointly model goal-directed and habitual behaviors.
