We propose a human behavior control mechanism-inspired framework which the Habitual Controller retrieves cue-triggered behaviors from personal- ized habit memory, while the Goal-directed Controller employs a context-aware world model to predict action consequences and estimate their values. The Arbiter dynamically balances the influence of both systems according to individual differ- ences and momentary internal states. To reconstruct diverse human-level behavior instructions in 3D environments, we further develop a keyframe-guided 3D mo- tion generation module. Through extensive evaluation methods, human studies, and ablations studies, experimental results demonstrate that human-likeness per- formance is significantly improved by our approach. The efficacy of our approach indicates the benefits of leveraging habitual behavior and multiple behavior con- trol system coordination for believable embodied human-like agents.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a multi-controller framework combining habitual and goal-directed mechanisms to generate more human-like 3D behavior for embodied agents, significantly improving human-likeness in experiments.
AI.motivation: Most human-like agent frameworks focus on goal-directed behavior and neglect habitual behavior, despite its crucial role in everyday human actions. The authors aim to fill this gap by integrating both habitual and goal-directed control mechanisms to better model and reproduce realistic human behavior.
AI.method: They design a behavior control framework inspired by cognitive neuroscience with three main components: (1) a Habitual Controller that retrieves cue-triggered actions from a personalized habit memory; (2) a Goal-directed Controller that uses a context-aware world model to predict outcomes and estimate action values; and (3) an Arbiter that dynamically balances the contribution of the two controllers based on individual differences and internal states. On top of this, they introduce a keyframe-guided 3D motion generation module to reconstruct diverse human-level behavior instructions in 3D environments. They evaluate the system using extensive quantitative metrics, human user studies, and ablation analyses.
AI.result: The proposed framework substantially improves human-likeness performance of embodied human-like agents compared with baselines. Ablation and human studies confirm that explicitly modeling habitual behavior and its coordination with goal-directed control leads to more believable and realistic behaviors in 3D environments.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating a dual-system behavior control architecture—combining habitual and goal-directed controllers with a dynamic arbiter—enhances the realism and believability of embodied agents. Modeling and coordinating habitual behavior is beneficial and perhaps necessary for achieving human-level behavior generation in 3D virtual environments.

title: DiFA: Dual Evidence Fusion and Aggregation for Token-Level Text Anomaly Detection
comment: Accepted by ICDM 2026. 10 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables
summary: Text anomaly detection, the task of identifying text instances that deviate from normal language patterns, is crucial for language-driven applications. However, most existing methods can only perform document-level anomaly detection, making it hard to locate harmful phrases or support targeted prevention. Recently, there has been an emerging trend toward token-level text anomaly detection, which aims to address the above limitation by identifying anomalous words or fragments within a document. Nevertheless, one representative method mainly relies on representation-space distance measurement, neglecting the complementary roles of different anomaly cues in capturing diverse abnormal patterns. To bridge the gaps, we propose a Dual-evidence framework with adaptive Fusion and Aggregation (DiFA) for token-level anomaly detection. DiFA derives anomaly scores from form-structural and semantic views to capture visible structural abnormality and contextual inconsistency, respectively, thereby providing complementary evidence for identifying diverse anomalies. To combine these two scores with varying numerical scales, DiFA incorporates a calibration and fusion mechanism to adaptively balance the two views. Moreover, to obtain a discriminative document-level score, a multivariate aggregation method is designed to summarize token-level anomaly scores from multiple perspectives, preventing rare anomalous tokens from being diluted. Extensive experiments across various text anomaly detection benchmarks demonstrate that DiFA consistently achieves top performance while maintaining strong efficiency, robustness, and interpretability. The code and scripts are available at: https://github.com/qyy11-com/DiFA.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes DiFA, a dual-evidence token-level text anomaly detection framework that fuses structural and semantic cues with adaptive calibration and multivariate aggregation to achieve state-of-the-art performance and interpretability.
AI.motivation: Existing text anomaly detection methods mostly work at the document level, which cannot pinpoint harmful or abnormal phrases and thus limits targeted prevention and interpretability. Emerging token-level methods improve granularity but often rely mainly on distance in representation space and ignore the complementary nature of different anomaly cues (e.g., surface/formal structure vs. semantics), which reduces their ability to capture diverse abnormal patterns. There is a need for a token-level approach that integrates multiple anomaly signals and produces both accurate token-level and robust document-level scores.
AI.method: The authors introduce DiFA, a Dual-evidence framework with adaptive Fusion and Aggregation for token-level text anomaly detection. DiFA computes anomaly scores from two complementary views: (1) form-structural, capturing visible structural or surface abnormalities, and (2) semantic, capturing contextual inconsistency. These per-token scores often have different numerical scales, so DiFA includes a calibration and fusion module to adaptively balance and integrate the two views into a unified token-level anomaly score. For document-level detection, DiFA applies a multivariate aggregation strategy that summarizes token-level scores from multiple perspectives rather than simple averaging, so that rare but highly anomalous tokens are not washed out in long texts.
AI.result: Across multiple standard text anomaly detection benchmarks, DiFA delivers consistently top or state-of-the-art performance. The method is also reported to be efficient in computation, robust across different settings, and to provide interpretable outputs by highlighting anomalous tokens. The authors release code and scripts to support reproducibility.
AI.conclusion: DiFA effectively addresses the limitations of prior token- and document-level anomaly detection methods by jointly exploiting structural and semantic anomaly cues, adaptively fusing them at token level, and aggregating them into discriminative document-level scores. This dual-evidence, calibrated fusion and advanced aggregation design enables accurate, robust, and interpretable token-level anomaly detection suitable for a wide range of language-driven applications.

title: Toward Auditable and Calibrated AI for Dementia-Related Crash Severity Prediction: A Selective Deferral Framework to Support Human Review
comment: This is the author's preprint version of a paper accepted for presentation at HICSS 60 (Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences), 2027, Hawaii, USA. The final published version will appear in the official conference proceedings. Conference site: https://hicss.hawaii.edu/
summary: Public crash databases increasingly support automated safety analysis, but crash severity prediction remains difficult to translate into public-sector decision workflows when models are evaluated primarily as ordinary classifiers. This study reframes dementia-related crash severity modeling as a decision-aware triage problem in which a system must classify crashes into no-injury/property-damage-only (O), minor or moderate injury (BC), and fatal or severe injury (KA), while also controlling outcome leakage, reporting severe under-triage, calibrating confidence, and preserving every raw prediction for audit. Using 4,781 Texas crash records with structured fields and police narratives, we evaluate structured, narrative, fusion, calibrated fusion, BERT-family, and local large-language-model baselines under a stratified 70/15/15 split. In the reported split, leakage-controlled Gemma obtains the highest observed macro-F1 (0.545; 95% bootstrap CI [0.507, 0.583]). The best calibrated fusion model obtains macro-F1 of 0.522 and expected calibration error of 0.033. Selective deferral improves performance among cases retained for automatic classification. At 70% coverage, macro-F1 rises to 0.573 and severity cost falls to 0.577, while deferred cases are treated as candidates for a proposed human-review process and are not further evaluated in the present experiment. The study contributes a reproducible, leakage-controlled, and uncertainty-aware evaluation framework for crash AI systems, emphasizing auditability and selective deferral rather than accuracy alone.

AI.tldr: They develop and evaluate a decision-aware, audit-focused AI framework to predict dementia-related crash severity using both structured crash data and police narratives, emphasizing calibrated uncertainty and selective deferral to human review rather than raw accuracy.
AI.motivation: Traditional crash severity prediction models are treated as standard classifiers, which makes it hard to use them in public-sector decision workflows. In particular, agencies need models that support triage-like decisions, manage the risk of misclassifying severe crashes, avoid label leakage, provide calibrated confidence estimates, and leave an auditable record of predictions. There is also growing interest in exploiting both structured crash data and unstructured police narratives, but it is unclear how to best combine them for high-stakes decisions like dementia-related crash severity classification.
AI.method: The authors frame dementia-related crash severity prediction as a triage problem with three outcome categories: no-injury/property-damage-only (O), minor or moderate injury (BC), and fatal or severe injury (KA). They build and compare several model families on 4,781 Texas crash records with structured variables and police narratives: (1) structured-only models, (2) narrative-only models, (3) fusion models that combine both, (4) calibrated fusion models, (5) BERT-family models, and (6) local large-language-model (LLM) baselines, including Gemma. The setup enforces leakage control (preventing outcome information from leaking into inputs), uses a stratified 70/15/15 train/validation/test split, assesses macro-F1 and calibration (e.g., expected calibration error), and evaluates selective deferral strategies where uncertain cases are deferred for human review.
AI.result: Under the specified stratified data split, a leakage-controlled Gemma LLM achieves the best observed macro-F1 of 0.545 (95% bootstrap confidence interval [0.507, 0.583]). The best calibrated fusion model yields a macro-F1 of 0.522 with an expected calibration error of 0.033, indicating good probability calibration. Introducing selective deferral—where the model only automatically classifies cases above a confidence threshold and defers the rest—improves performance among the non-deferred cases: at 70% coverage, macro-F1 increases to 0.573 and a severity cost metric drops to 0.577. Deferred cases are reserved for a proposed human-review pipeline and are not scored in the experiment.
AI.conclusion: Recasting crash severity prediction as a decision-aware triage and audit problem yields more suitable evaluation for high-stakes public-sector use than standard classification metrics alone. The paper shows that carefully leakage-controlled LLMs and calibrated fusion models can provide strong performance and well-calibrated uncertainties on dementia-related crash severity, and that selective deferral meaningfully improves effective performance for automatically handled cases. Overall, the work delivers a reproducible, uncertainty-aware evaluation framework that prioritizes auditability, calibration, and safe deferral to human review rather than focusing solely on aggregate accuracy.

title: Does the Truthfulness Signal Survive Code-Mixing? Probing Hidden States for Hallucination Detection in Hinglish
summary: Hidden-state hallucination probing - training a linear classifier on an LLM's internal activations to detect whether a generated answer is faithful to the input - is an active area of 2026 research, with recent work reporting 0.90-1.00 AUROC across several benchmarks and languages. However, none of this work has tested probes on code-mixed input, despite the fact that a huge population of chatbot users write in Hindi-English code-mixed text ("Hinglish"). We address this gap directly: does a hallucination probe trained on clean-language hidden states transfer to Hinglish, or does the signal degrade under code-mixing? We construct a 5,674-item Hindi/English/Hinglish QA benchmark, generate and label 17,022 model responses across three open-weight 7-8B LLMs (Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B, Llama-3.1-8B), extract per-layer hidden states at two token positions, and train linear and MLP probes for in-distribution detection and cross-lingual transfer. We find that the hallucination signal survives code-mixing well: transfer AUROC ranges from 0.88 to 0.99, with gaps of mostly under 0.05 AUROC relative to in-distribution performance, and that Hindi-trained probes transfer to Hinglish more reliably than English-trained probes. As an independent, practically motivated finding, all three models hallucinate substantially more on Hindi and Hinglish than on English for matched facts. We release our code and synthetic Hinglish QA dataset to support further work on code-mixed hallucination detection.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether hallucination detectors trained on an LLM’s internal activations in clean languages still work on Hindi-English code-mixed (“Hinglish”) inputs, finding that the signal largely transfers with high AUROC and that models hallucinate more in Hindi/Hinglish than in English.
AI.motivation: Existing hallucination probes for large language models claim high performance but are only evaluated on clean, monolingual input. A large real-world user base writes in Hindi-English code-mixed text (Hinglish), and it is unknown whether such probes remain reliable under code-mixing. There is also limited understanding of how hallucination rates differ across English, Hindi, and Hinglish for the same facts.
AI.method: The authors build a 5,674-item QA benchmark spanning Hindi, English, and Hinglish. Using three open-weight 7–8B models (Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B, Llama-3.1-8B), they generate 17,022 responses and label them for hallucination. They then extract hidden states from each model at all layers and at two specific token positions, and train both linear and MLP probes to classify hallucinated vs faithful answers. Probes are evaluated in-distribution and for cross-lingual transfer, especially from clean languages (English, Hindi) to Hinglish.
AI.result: Hallucination probes achieve very high AUROC (0.90–1.00) on in-distribution languages. When transferred to Hinglish, AUROC remains high (0.88–0.99), with performance drops typically under 0.05 compared to in-distribution. Probes trained on Hindi transfer better to Hinglish than those trained on English. Independently, the underlying LLMs hallucinate significantly more often on Hindi and Hinglish than on English for matched factual questions.
AI.conclusion: Hidden-state hallucination probes are robust to Hindi-English code-mixing: the internal signal used for hallucination detection largely survives code-mixing, and simple probes transfer well to Hinglish. Hindi-based probes are particularly effective for Hinglish transfer. Nonetheless, underlying models are more prone to hallucinate in Hindi and Hinglish than in English, highlighting a multilingual reliability gap. The released code and synthetic Hinglish QA dataset aim to support further research on hallucination detection in code-mixed and low-resource language settings.

title: A Survey on the Linear Representation Hypothesis
summary: The term "linear representation hypothesis" (LRH) has appeared across diverse subfields of artificial intelligence, neuroscience, and cognitive science. But previous works have not consistently treated the LRH as a falsifiable scientific hypothesis; we analyze these inconsistencies and examine their implications for how prior theoretical and methodological results should be interpreted. Based on this analysis, we argue that claims regarding linear representations become well-defined only through careful examination of the model, representation location, feature definition, and evaluation dataset. We therefore propose a more rigorous formalization of the LRH that makes these dependencies explicit and allows the hypothesis to be evaluated as a falsifiable scientific claim. Finally, we identify some non-trivial open problems that warrant further attention from the research community.

AI.tldr: The paper clarifies and rigorously formalizes the Linear Representation Hypothesis (LRH), turning it into a precise, falsifiable claim about when and how linear structure in model representations should be expected and evaluated.
AI.motivation: The term "linear representation hypothesis" is widely used in AI, neuroscience, and cognitive science, but in inconsistent, often vague ways that do not clearly specify what counts as evidence for or against it. This lack of precision undermines the interpretation of existing theoretical and empirical results about linear structure in neural representations.
AI.method: The authors conceptually analyze how the LRH has been used across prior work, identifying inconsistencies and implicit assumptions. They decompose claims about linear representations into specific components: the model under study, where in the model the representation lives, how features are defined, and what evaluation dataset is used. Based on this analysis, they propose a formalization of the LRH that explicitly incorporates these dependencies and frames it as a falsifiable hypothesis. They then outline key open problems that follow from this refined formulation.
AI.result: The main result is a sharpened, formal version of the LRH that resolves prior ambiguities and clarifies under what conditions claims about linear representations are meaningful and testable. The work shows that many earlier interpretations of linearity-based findings depend crucially on choices of model, representation layer, feature definition, and data, and that without specifying these, LRH claims are underspecified. The paper also maps out several concrete, unresolved questions raised by the formalization.
AI.conclusion: Claims about linear representations cannot be treated as model- or domain-agnostic; they only become scientifically meaningful when key contextual factors are made explicit. By formalizing the LRH as a falsifiable hypothesis tied to specific models, representation locations, feature definitions, and datasets, the paper provides a more rigorous foundation for future empirical and theoretical work, and highlights non-trivial open problems that should guide subsequent research.

title: Using Composition Operators to Linearize LLM Semantic Transformations
summary: Machine learning learns functions: prompt to response, image to caption. What these functions are mathematically remains hard to say. We present a method to approximate these kinds of transformations using techniques from dynamical systems that fall under the umbrella of Koopmanism. We introduce the use of composition operators, which generalize the Koopman operator and, crucially, can map between distinct spaces, motivating the perspective that LLM transformations are rectangular infinite-dimensional operators. This formalism reveals useful structure: under natural assumptions on the prompt and response distributions, the LLM operator is an isometry, and misalignment between learned representations manifests as spectral pollution of its finite sections. We then outline a method of constructing finite-dimensional approximations of an LLM operator, and demonstrate how the singular value spectrum can be used to compare tasks and models.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Koopman-operator-inspired mathematical framework to model LLMs as infinite-dimensional linear operators between prompt and response spaces, and studies how to approximate and analyze them via finite-dimensional spectra.
AI.motivation: Although machine learning models are used as black-box function approximators (e.g., mapping prompts to responses or images to captions), we lack a clear, rigorous mathematical description of these transformations, especially for LLMs. The authors aim to provide a principled operator-theoretic view that can explain structural properties of LLMs, such as alignment and representation quality, and enable systematic comparison between models and tasks.
AI.method: The authors adopt tools from dynamical systems and Koopman operator theory, generalizing to composition operators that can map between different function spaces (prompt space to response space). They model an LLM as a rectangular infinite-dimensional linear operator acting on suitable function spaces over prompt and response distributions. Under assumptions on these distributions, they analyze when this operator becomes an isometry. They then study how finite-dimensional approximations (“finite sections”) of this operator can be constructed, and how misalignment in learned representations appears as spectral pollution in these finite sections. Finally, they propose using the singular value spectrum of these finite-dimensional approximations as a diagnostic to compare tasks and models.
AI.result: Conceptually, the paper shows that LLMs can be fruitfully modeled as composition operators between different function spaces, and that this operator can be isometric under natural probabilistic assumptions. Technically, they derive that representation misalignment corresponds to spectral pollution in truncated operator approximations. Empirically or methodologically, they demonstrate a procedure to build finite-dimensional approximations to the LLM operator and compute their singular value spectra, which then serve as features to compare different LLMs or tasks.
AI.conclusion: Viewing LLMs as rectangular infinite-dimensional operators within a composition-operator/Koopman framework yields structural insights into their behavior, especially about alignment and representation quality. Finite-dimensional approximations of these operators and their singular value spectra provide practical tools to analyze and compare models and tasks. This operator-theoretic viewpoint offers a new, mathematically grounded way to study and design machine learning systems beyond black-box experimentation.

title: Building Trustworthy Mental Health Benchmarks on Bluesky: A Validation-Aware Weak-Supervision Framework
comment: This is the author's preprint version of a paper accepted for presentation at HICSS 60 (Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences), 2027, Hawaii, USA. The final published version will appear in the official conference proceedings. Conference site: https://hicss.hawaii.edu/
summary: Decentralized social media platforms create new opportunities and challenges for computational mental health research because data access, moderation, labeling, and deployment responsibilities are distributed across multiple technical and governance layers. This paper presents a validation-aware weak-supervision system for constructing and evaluating suicidal ideation (SI) and broader mental health (MH) disclosure benchmarks on Bluesky, a decentralized social media platform built on the AT Protocol. The system integrates public firehose collection, task-specific lexicon filtering, Llama-3-8B-assisted binary annotation, human-adjudicated validation subsets, and transformer-based model benchmarking. Using this pipeline, we construct two task-specific corpora containing 8,346 SI-labeled posts and 9,988 MH-labeled posts. The evaluation shows that model performance depends strongly on both task definition and validation protocol. BERT+LSTM achieves the highest SI stratified cross-validation F1-score, RoBERTa achieves the strongest SI holdout F1-score, and DistilRoBERTa achieves the best MH cross-validation F1-score. Human validation reveals different weak-label failure modes across tasks, with SI labels dominated by false negatives and MH labels dominated by false positives. These findings show that decentralized social media can support reproducible mental health benchmarking, but only when system design, label provenance, validation strategy, and deployment constraints are evaluated together.

AI.tldr: The paper builds weakly supervised benchmarks for suicidal ideation and broader mental health disclosures on the decentralized platform Bluesky and shows how model performance and label quality depend on task definitions and validation strategies.
AI.motivation: Decentralized social media like Bluesky are becoming important spaces for mental health discourse, but their distributed architecture complicates how researchers access data, define labels, validate annotations, and deploy models. There is a need for reproducible, well-validated benchmarks for detecting suicidal ideation and other mental health disclosures in this new context.
AI.method: The authors design a validation-aware weak-supervision pipeline on Bluesky’s AT Protocol. The pipeline includes: (1) collecting data from the public firehose; (2) filtering posts using task-specific lexicons; (3) generating weak binary labels with an Llama-3-8B model; (4) creating human-adjudicated validation subsets; and (5) benchmarking several transformer-based models (e.g., BERT+LSTM, RoBERTa, DistilRoBERTa) for suicidal ideation (SI) and broader mental health (MH) detection tasks.
AI.result: They create two corpora: 8,346 posts labeled for suicidal ideation and 9,988 posts labeled for broader mental health disclosure. Benchmarking shows that model performance is highly sensitive to task definition and validation protocol. BERT+LSTM performs best on SI under stratified cross-validation, RoBERTa performs best on SI in holdout evaluation, and DistilRoBERTa performs best on MH in cross-validation. Human validation reveals that weak labels for SI are mostly affected by false negatives, whereas weak labels for MH have many false positives.
AI.conclusion: Decentralized social media can be used to build reproducible benchmarks for detecting suicidal ideation and mental health disclosures, but doing so reliably requires jointly considering system design, label provenance, validation strategy, and deployment constraints. Different tasks exhibit different weak-label error profiles, which impacts how benchmarks should be constructed and interpreted.

title: Multilingual Safety Signals Are Multi-Layered: Filtering Safety-Degrading Data for Safer LLMs
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 Main Conference. 16 pages, 11 figures
summary: Preserving safety alignment during large language models fine-tuning is critical, however, recent studies have demonstrated that even benign fine-tuning data may contain safety-degrading samples that silently undermine safety alignment. Existing approaches typically identify such samples using representations from a single safety-sensitive layer. While this assumption has shown effectiveness in monolingual settings, its validity for multilingual models remains unclear due to potential cross-lingual differences in representation patterns. Through a cross-lingual analysis, we show that sensitive layers are only partially shared across languages, with safety-relevant signals often distributed across multiple layers. Motivated by these observations, we propose MMSAFE, a multi-layer framework for multilingual safety-degrading data identification that captures both shared and language-specific safety signals. Extensive experiments across multiple models, languages, and safety benchmarks demonstrate that MMSAFE reduces the average harmful-response ratio by 60% compared with random filtering and achieves stronger average performance than the strongest single-layer baseline, demonstrating the effectiveness of multi-layer modeling for robust multilingual safety alignment.

AI.tldr: MMSAFE is a multi-layer method to identify and filter safety-degrading samples during multilingual LLM fine-tuning, improving safety alignment across languages.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning can unintentionally weaken a model’s safety alignment because even seemingly benign data may include safety-degrading examples. Existing defenses usually rely on representations from a single “safety-sensitive” layer, which has worked mainly in monolingual (often English) settings. For multilingual models, it is unclear whether the same layers encode safety information for all languages, given possible cross-lingual differences in how representations are structured. There is a need to understand where safety signals live across layers and languages, and to design methods that can robustly detect harmful training samples in a multilingual context.
AI.method: The authors first conduct a cross-lingual analysis of multilingual LLMs to locate and compare safety-sensitive layers across different languages. They examine how safety-relevant signals are distributed across the network and find that such signals are not confined to a single shared layer. Based on this, they propose MMSAFE, a framework that: (1) extracts representations from multiple layers, (2) models both shared (cross-lingual) and language-specific safety features, and (3) uses these to identify safety-degrading samples in fine-tuning data. MMSAFE is then evaluated across various multilingual models, languages, and safety benchmarks by filtering training data and measuring the resulting models’ harmful-response rates and task performance.
AI.result: Empirically, sensitive layers are only partially shared across languages, and safety signals are often spread over multiple layers rather than concentrated in a single one. Using MMSAFE for pre-filtering fine-tuning data reduces the average harmful-response ratio by about 60% compared with random filtering. It also consistently outperforms the best single-layer baseline in terms of safety metrics while maintaining strong overall performance across different models, languages, and benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Safety-relevant signals in multilingual LLMs are distributed across layers and are not fully captured by a single safety-sensitive layer shared across languages. Consequently, single-layer methods are insufficient for robust multilingual safety alignment. MMSAFE’s multi-layer modeling of both shared and language-specific safety features more effectively identifies safety-degrading training samples, leading to significantly improved safety outcomes in multilingual fine-tuning. This demonstrates that multi-layer, cross-lingual approaches are a promising direction for maintaining safety alignment in multilingual LLMs.

title: Hapi: A Multivariable Land-Surface Transformer for Medium-Range Hydrological Forecasting at Continental Scale
summary: Accurate flood forecasts several days in advance are essential for flood control, water-resource management, and emergency response. Producing them at high resolution over a continental domain calls for local hydrological detail together with spatial context extending from river basins to synoptic weather systems. We developed Hapi, a U-Net Swin Transformer that uses fine three-dimensional patches and hierarchical shifted-window attention to forecast discharge, surface runoff, snow water equivalent, and soil wetness across the contiguous United States. The model produces 24--72-hour forecasts at $0.05^{\circ}$ resolution, with learned Laplacian task weights adjusting each variable's contribution to training. On 2024 test data using reconstructed weather and land-surface inputs from ERA5-Land, Hapi outperformed an operational physics-based model and a state-of-the-art AI model in flood detection. Independent validation against 3,881 U.S. Geological Survey gauges and a Hurricane Helene case study supported its advantage over the physics-based model in reproducing daily discharge. Controlled experiments showed that learned task weighting strengthens rare-flood detection, which is particularly sensitive to changes in precipitation inputs. Hapi produced a four-variable, 72-hour forecast across the contiguous United States with an average inference time of 0.11 seconds on a single A100 GPU.

AI.tldr: Introduces Hapi, a U-Net Swin Transformer model that delivers fast, high-resolution, multi-variable flood-related forecasts over the contiguous U.S., outperforming both physics-based and prior AI baselines, especially for rare-flood detection.
AI.motivation: Reliable, high-resolution flood forecasts several days ahead are crucial for flood control, water-resource management, and emergency response, but existing physics-based and AI models struggle to combine detailed local hydrology with large-scale spatial weather context across a continental domain.
AI.method: Design a U-Net Swin Transformer architecture (Hapi) that ingests 3D spatiotemporal patches and uses hierarchical shifted-window self-attention to produce 24–72-hour forecasts of discharge, surface runoff, snow water equivalent, and soil wetness at 0.05° resolution over the contiguous U.S., incorporating a multi-task loss with learned Laplacian task weights to adaptively balance the contribution of each predicted variable during training; evaluate against an operational physics-based model and a strong AI baseline using ERA5-Land reanalysis as forcing, USGS gauge observations, and a focused hurricane case study, and run controlled ablation experiments on task weighting and precipitation changes.
AI.result: On 2024 test data, Hapi achieved better flood detection performance than both an operational physics-based model and a state-of-the-art AI baseline, showed superior skill in reproducing daily discharge at 3,881 USGS gauges and in a Hurricane Helene case study, demonstrated that learned task-weighting particularly improves detection of rare flooding events and reveals high sensitivity to precipitation input perturbations, and delivered 72-hour, four-variable forecasts for the entire contiguous U.S. in an average of 0.11 seconds on a single A100 GPU.
AI.conclusion: A continent-scale, high-resolution, multi-variable neural forecasting system based on a U-Net Swin Transformer and learned multi-task weighting can outperform existing physics-based and AI approaches for flood detection and discharge prediction while running orders of magnitude faster, highlighting the promise of attention-based architectures with adaptive task balancing for operational hydrologic forecasting and emergency management.

title: Beyond the Stitching Assumption: A Unified Framework for Multimodal Synthetic Data Evaluation via Semantic Quantization
comment: 10 Pages, 2 figures, 4 tables, accepted to PST 2026
summary: Multimodal synthetic datasets combine structured attributes with free text, but are often evaluated separately. Such metrics can remain high after tabular--text pairings are disrupted. We present a projection-based evaluator for tabular--text synthetic data. A fixed sentence encoder maps text to embeddings, \(k\)-means converts them to cluster states, and tabular variables are represented as categorical or quantile-binned states. Real and synthetic contingency tables are compared using Jensen--Shannon divergence (JSD), normalized mutual information (NMI), conditional JSD (cJSD), and joint-state entropy. We also report text-to-attribute (T2A) utility and a holdout-calibrated proximity flag rate (PFR) as a representation-level diagnostic. A text-permutation control preserves both marginal distributions while disrupting their pairing. Experiments on Amazon Reviews, Kiva Loans, and the Employment Scam Aegean Dataset show that modality-specific scores remain high under this control. The projection diagnostics detect disruption when real projected dependence exceeds a permutation baseline, but are less informative for weak or sparse projections. Some conditioned LLM baselines also exhibit stronger measured dependence than the corresponding real-data projections. These results support explicit cross-modal evaluation with permutation baselines and coverage reporting.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a projection-based method to evaluate multimodal tabular–text synthetic data by measuring how well cross-modal relationships are preserved, using permutation baselines to reveal when standard, modality-specific metrics are misleadingly high.
AI.motivation: Existing synthetic multimodal datasets that combine structured tables and free text are typically evaluated with separate metrics for the tabular and text components. These metrics can stay high even if the pairing between rows and text is scrambled, meaning they fail to capture whether the synthetic data preserves the true cross-modal relationships. There is a need for evaluation methods that explicitly measure and stress-test dependence between structured attributes and free text in synthetic data.
AI.method: The authors introduce a projection-based evaluation pipeline. First, a fixed sentence encoder maps each text instance into a continuous embedding space. Then, k-means clustering is applied to those embeddings to convert them into discrete cluster states. Tabular variables are similarly represented as discrete states via categorical encoding or quantile binning for continuous variables. With both modalities in a common discrete state space, the method builds real and synthetic contingency tables over joint text–tabular states. It then compares real vs synthetic using metrics such as Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD), normalized mutual information (NMI), conditional JSD (cJSD), and joint-state entropy. Additional diagnostics include text-to-attribute (T2A) utility, measuring how well text predicts attributes, and a proximity flag rate (PFR) based on holdout calibration, which flags overly similar synthetic samples at the representation level. A text-permutation control baseline is constructed by shuffling text across rows to preserve marginals but break cross-modal links, providing a reference for dependence that should be absent.
AI.result: On three datasets—Amazon Reviews, Kiva Loans, and the Employment Scam Aegean Dataset—the authors show that standard modality-specific evaluation scores stay high even after text is randomly permuted with respect to the tabular data, indicating these metrics do not detect broken cross-modal relationships. In contrast, the proposed projection-based diagnostics identify this disruption when the original real data exhibits substantial projected dependence, via elevated divergence and dependence measures compared to the permutation baseline. However, when projections are weak or the joint distribution is sparse, the diagnostics become less informative. Interestingly, some conditioned LLM-based synthetic baselines manifest stronger measured cross-modal dependence than the real data itself in these projected metrics.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that synthetic multimodal tabular–text data must be evaluated with explicit cross-modal dependence measures rather than relying solely on independent tabular or text metrics. Projection-based contingency analyses, informed by permutation baselines and accompanied by coverage reporting, can reveal when cross-modal structure is preserved, broken, or even exaggerated by generative models. This framework highlights the importance of stress-testing synthetic data for realistic cross-modal relationships and suggests that some LLM-based generators may overfit or over-strengthen apparent dependencies in the projected space.

title: Trustworthy Agentic AI: Failure Modes, Mitigation Strategies, and a Lifecycle Framework for Autonomous LLM Systems
summary: Agentic AI systems built on large language models can plan over multiple steps, use external tools, retain information in memory, and coordinate with other agents. These capabilities make them more useful than static language models, but they also introduce new security and operational risks. Untrusted content from websites, emails, documents, and databases can enter the same context as system instructions; persistent memory can carry compromised information across sessions; and access to external tools can turn an incorrect model response into a consequential real-world action. This article reviews the trustworthiness of agentic AI across five interconnected dimensions: safety and robustness, alignment and human oversight, transparency and auditability, privacy and data governance, and regulatory compliance. It organizes key failure modes, including indirect prompt injection, backdoor triggers, goal misgeneralization, memory contamination, and cross-session data leakage, into a unified taxonomy. It also examines major mitigation approaches, such as instruction hierarchies, context isolation, spotlighting, process-based supervision, constrained tool use, and privacy-preserving memory, while distinguishing techniques supported by empirical evidence from those that remain largely conceptual. Building on this analysis, we introduce the Trustworthy Agent Development Lifecycle (TADL), a six-phase framework covering specification, design, training, evaluation, deployment, and monitoring. For each phase, TADL identifies relevant trust activities, expected evidence, and risk-based decision gates. Although TADL has not yet been empirically validated, it provides a structured foundation for developing and evaluating more secure and accountable agentic systems. The article concludes by identifying gaps in current benchmarks and outlining priorities for future research.

AI.tldr: The paper surveys security and trust issues in agentic AI systems and proposes a lifecycle framework (TADL) to guide their safe and accountable development.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI systems, which can plan, use tools, and persist memory, are more powerful than static LLMs but introduce novel security, safety, and governance risks that are not yet systematically understood or managed.
AI.method: The authors conduct a structured review of failure modes and mitigation strategies for agentic AI, organize them into a five-dimensional trustworthiness taxonomy, and synthesize these insights into the six-phase Trustworthy Agent Development Lifecycle (TADL).
AI.result: The paper delivers (1) a unified taxonomy of trust dimensions and failure modes for agentic AI; (2) a categorized survey of mitigation techniques, clearly separating empirically supported methods from largely conceptual ones; and (3) the TADL framework that maps concrete trust activities, evidence requirements, and risk gates onto the stages of agent development and operation.
AI.conclusion: Despite limited empirical validation, the proposed taxonomy and TADL framework offer a structured basis for designing, evaluating, and governing trustworthy agentic AI systems, and the paper highlights benchmark gaps and research priorities needed to mature this area.

title: Do Language Models Know Their Own Constraints?
summary: We ask whether behavioral constraints acquired through post training remain explicitly reportable. Using constrained recipe generation as a testbed, five banned ingredients enforced via LoRA fine tuning of Llama 3.1 8B Instruct we compare supervised fine tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) against an untrained baseline on a four tier Constraint Awareness Benchmark. Averaged over three seeds, both methods raise behavioral compliance from 4% to about 90% while reducing explicit constraint reporting below the untrained model (0.48/5 to 0.16/5 for SFT, 0.07/5 for GRPO) and eroding retained third person knowledge (93% to 36% for SFT, 14% for GRPO; p less than 0.01 between methods). Contrary to our initial hypothesis, the reward based signal is the more destructive of the two: a reward that penalizes banned ingredient tokens regardless of framing learns a context independent suppression rather than a self directed constraint. A context conditioned reward designed to teach the self to other distinction fails, collapsing toward inclusion in both framings. Probing prompt time hidden states recovers per ingredient avoidance at 83.8% (layer 24 MLP), but only 6.4 points above a per ingredient base rate predictor (77.4%), and the model's own verbal self report is more accurate still (87.8%). A positive control adding explicit self description examples does not restore reporting. The failure is therefore specific to enumerating constraints on request, not a general loss of access to them.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether post-training behavioral safety constraints in language models remain consciously accessible and verbally reportable by the model, finding that strong behavioral compliance can coexist with degraded explicit self-report of constraints.
AI.motivation: To understand if safety and alignment training methods (supervised fine-tuning and RL-style GRPO) not only change behavior but also preserve the model’s ability to explicitly state and explain its own constraints, which matters for interpretability, transparency, and trust.
AI.method: Use constrained recipe generation with five banned ingredients on Llama 3.1 8B Instruct fine-tuned via LoRA. Compare supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to an untrained baseline across a four-level Constraint Awareness Benchmark. Measure behavioral compliance, explicit self-reported constraints, third-person factual knowledge, and perform probing on hidden states. Also test a positive control that adds explicit self-description examples.
AI.result: Both SFT and GRPO greatly increase behavioral compliance from 4% to ~90%, but they decrease the model’s ability to explicitly list its constraints and erode related third-person knowledge. GRPO is more destructive than SFT, driving third-person knowledge down to 14%. Reward schemes aimed at context-conditional suppression or self/other distinction fail and collapse to generic suppression. Probes can weakly decode constraint knowledge from hidden states (83.8% avoidance vs. 77.4% base rate), while the model’s own indirect self-report remains more accurate (87.8%). Explicit self-description training does not restore the ability to enumerate constraints on request.
AI.conclusion: Post-training behavioral constraints can be deeply internalized in model behavior while becoming difficult for the model to explicitly report, especially under RL-style reward shaping. This indicates a disconnect between behavioral safety and introspective transparency: models may comply with constraints yet be unable to consciously enumerate them, which complicates alignment auditing and suggests that certain reward designs promote context-independent suppression rather than explicit, self-directed constraint representations.

title: ProcessLight: Process Supervision for Large Language Model Based Traffic Signal Control
comment: This paper has been accepted by The 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2026)
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently been introduced into traffic signal control (TSC) as decision agents due to their strengths in human-readable reasoning generation. Yet, existing LLM TSC methods optimize only from final outcomes and fail to distinguish valid from flawed reasoning steps, causing useful or misleading steps to be jointly updated and thus impairing the model's learning of effective reasoning. To bridge this gap, we propose an LLM-based framework ProcessLight to decompose signal decisions into verifiable semantic steps. Building on ProcessLight, we further develop Step-wise Traffic Process Policy Optimization (STeP-PO), a novel reinforcement learning framework that optimizes structured reasoning processes through step-level credit assignment. Specifically, STeP-PO uses step quality scores to evaluate local reasoning quality and step importance to measure each step's influence on the final action, and then assigns step-level advantages over a semantic step tree structure. The resulting step-level advantages are propagated to reasoning tokens, enabling fine-grained policy optimization beyond outcome-only rewards. Extensive experiments over multiple real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of our methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/wenzhaoabc/processlight.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ProcessLight and STeP-PO, an LLM-based traffic signal control framework that optimizes not only final decisions but also intermediate reasoning steps via step-wise credit assignment, yielding superior performance on real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based traffic signal control methods treat the model as a black-box decision agent and optimize policies based solely on final outcomes (e.g., reward after a control action). This ignores whether the intermediate reasoning steps leading to actions are logically sound or flawed. As a result, both good and bad reasoning steps are updated together, which can hinder the learning of robust and interpretable decision policies. There is a need for a framework that can decompose LLM decisions into verifiable semantic steps and assign credit at a finer granularity than only outcome-level rewards.
AI.method: The authors propose ProcessLight, an LLM-based framework that decomposes traffic signal control decisions into a sequence (or tree) of semantic reasoning steps that can be individually verified. Building on this, they introduce STeP-PO (Step-wise Traffic Process Policy Optimization), a reinforcement learning framework that performs step-level credit assignment. STeP-PO computes two key quantities for each reasoning step: (1) a step quality score that captures the local correctness or usefulness of that step; and (2) a step importance measure that captures the influence of that step on the final action. Using these, the method assigns step-level advantages over a semantic step tree and propagates these advantages back to the underlying reasoning tokens. This enables fine-grained policy optimization, where gradients are shaped by the quality and influence of each reasoning step rather than only by the terminal reward signal.
AI.result: In extensive experiments conducted on multiple real-world traffic signal control datasets, the proposed ProcessLight framework with STeP-PO outperforms existing baselines. The empirical results demonstrate that step-wise optimization of reasoning processes leads to better traffic control performance than outcome-only optimization. While the abstract does not provide numerical details, it emphasizes consistent superiority across various datasets, indicating that the method generalizes well and provides tangible improvements in traffic signal control effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that decomposing LLM-based traffic signal control decisions into verifiable semantic steps and applying step-wise credit assignment yields more effective and fine-grained policy optimization than traditional outcome-only approaches. ProcessLight and STeP-PO show that optimizing the reasoning process itself—via step quality and importance scores propagated down to reasoning tokens—can significantly enhance both the performance and interpretability of LLM agents in complex sequential decision-making tasks like traffic signal control.

title: Is Imagination Derived from Hallucination? A Cross-Taxonomy Evaluation of Imagination and Hallucination in Large Language Models
summary: Imagination performs as a high-level function of large language models (LLMs) which determines the potential of how an LLM creates unseen or creative content. While existing works have built a rich family of creativity benchmarks for this ability, they only measure how far an output departs from common answers and never check whether the departure is licensed by the prompt. Moreover, hallucination, the closest neighbor of imagination, is always measured in a separate pipeline on different generations, so the influential claim that imagination and hallucination stem from the same generative mechanism has never been directly testable. In this paper, we propose Whiteboard, the first LLM imagination evaluation benchmark. Its design follows the authoritative cognitive instruments developed to measure human imagination: seven mechanism-grounded imagination subtypes are adapted from classic paradigms, then crossed with ten support-boundary hallucination subtypes and scored jointly on the same generation. Different from previous creativity or hallucination benchmarks, Whiteboard gates every imagination score with an explicit support check and computes both axes deterministically through an auditable atom matrix, with no LLM judge on the primary path. The full Whiteboard item bank contains 1,660 prompts; on its shared 80-item anchor set, we evaluate 79 state-of-the-art LLMs and validate the instrument against 13,280 human judgments. Additionally, we further explore whether imagination derives from the same generative tendency as hallucination and what key factors shape it. Our analysis indicates a counterintuitive correlation between hallucination and imagination: Most of the subtype couplings are negative, every one of the anchor items reproduces the negative coupling on its own.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Whiteboard, the first benchmark that jointly measures imagination and hallucination in LLMs, using cognitively grounded subtypes and explicit support checks to disentangle creative yet valid output from unsupported hallucinations, and finds that imagination and hallucination are often negatively, not positively, correlated.
AI.motivation: Existing creativity benchmarks only quantify how unconventional a model’s answer is, without verifying whether such deviation is appropriate given the prompt, while hallucination benchmarks are evaluated on separate generations, making it impossible to directly test the widely held belief that imagination and hallucination arise from the same generative mechanism. There is a need for a unified, human-theory-grounded benchmark that can precisely and jointly evaluate imagination and hallucination on the same outputs.
AI.method: The authors design Whiteboard, an LLM imagination evaluation benchmark inspired by established human cognitive tests. They define seven mechanism-grounded imagination subtypes and ten support-boundary hallucination subtypes, adapt them into LLM prompts, and jointly score both imagination and hallucination for each model output via an explicit support check and a deterministic atom matrix instead of LLM judges. The benchmark comprises 1,660 prompts, with an 80-item anchor set used to evaluate 79 state-of-the-art LLMs, and is validated against 13,280 human judgments.
AI.result: Whiteboard provides a structured, auditable measurement of both imagination and hallucination on the same responses across many LLMs. Analysis of the scores reveals that, contrary to the prevailing assumption, the coupling between most imagination and hallucination subtypes is negative rather than positive, and this negative relationship is consistently reproduced across all anchor items.
AI.conclusion: Imagination in LLMs can be measured reliably and separately from hallucination using a cognitively grounded, support-checked benchmark. The empirical findings challenge the common belief that imagination and hallucination share the same underlying generative tendency, showing instead that higher imagination does not generally entail more hallucination and, in most subtype pairings, is associated with less. This has implications for how we design, tune, and evaluate LLMs for creative yet faithful behavior.

title: CTSpinoPelvic1K: spine, pelvis, ribs and femora in one coordinate frame, annotated for lumbosacral transitional anatomy
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures, 6 tables. Dataset (802 annotated CT records, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22139642; code at https://github.com/OpenSpineConsortium/CTSpinoPelvic1K. Submitted to Medical Physics as a Medical Physics Dataset Article
summary:
Purpose: A vertebra at the lumbosacral junction is named by counting caudally from C2 on whole-spine imaging, but a lumbar case is planned on lumbar-only imaging (T12 to S1), without C2. Abdominopelvic CT holds that span plus the lowest ribs and pelvis. Where a lumbosacral transitional vertebra (LSTV) alters the count, the local anatomy is ambiguous: four rib-free vertebrae may be an L1 with a lumbar rib or an L5 assimilated to the sacrum, and six may be a sixth lumbar vertebra, a T12 with aplastic ribs, or a lumbarized S1. CTSpinoPelvic1K asks whether local morphology resolves it without the count. CTSpine1K's vertebrae and CTPelvic1K's pelvis covered these patients but were never joined; this release joins them on one series and adds the bones neither had. It provides 802 CT records with per-level ribs and femora, levels anchored on the lowest rib-bearing vertebra and S1, and classes for L6, T13, a separate S1 and lumbar ribs, so anomalies are recorded as such.
  Acquisition and Validation Methods: Records pair CTSpine1K and CTPelvic1K labels on each patient's bone-richest series under a VerSe-native scheme. Validation covered geometric invariants (802/802 pass), rib-vertebra incidence across 5,749 ribs (0.035% offset), and spinopelvic measures matching published values.
  Data Format and Usage Notes: NIfTI image/label pairs with patient-grouped LSTV-stratified five-fold splits and a loader; archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22139642.
  Potential Applications: Classifying a vertebra from local features; updating cadaveric morphometry; spinopelvic assessment; opportunistic screening; and, absent a public preoperative lumbar cohort, surgical planning research (377 records prone). Limitations: thoracic ground truth is field-of-view limited; postural angles supine; no held-out test set; ribs are triaged-review pseudolabels; Castellvi grades two-reader consensus on 33 records.

AI.tldr: CTSpinoPelvic1K is a CT dataset linking spine and pelvis labels to resolve vertebral numbering ambiguities at the lumbosacral junction, especially in the presence of lumbosacral transitional vertebrae (LSTV).
AI.motivation: Clinicians and algorithms usually number lumbosacral vertebrae by counting from C2 on whole-spine imaging, but many clinical scans are limited to the lumbar region or abdomen/pelvis and do not include C2. In such local scans, especially when lumbosacral transitional vertebrae (LSTV) are present, identifying and naming the vertebra at the lumbosacral junction becomes ambiguous (e.g., distinguishing L1 with a lumbar rib from L5 sacralization or detecting an extra lumbar vertebra). Existing public datasets separately label spine or pelvis but do not link them or cover the full spinopelvic anatomy needed to resolve these ambiguities.
AI.method: The authors merge labels from two prior datasets (CTSpine1K for vertebrae and CTPelvic1K for pelvis) for the same patients into a unified, bone-rich CT series per subject. They re-annotate or extend labels so that each record includes vertebral levels anchored to the lowest rib-bearing vertebra and S1, along with detailed rib presence per vertebral level and femoral bones. They introduce explicit classes for anatomical variants such as L6, T13, separate S1, and lumbar ribs, thereby encoding lumbosacral anomalies directly. Validation includes checking geometric invariants across all 802 cases, assessing rib-to-vertebra incidence for thousands of ribs, and comparing derived spinopelvic measurements with values from the literature.
AI.result: The resulting CTSpinoPelvic1K dataset comprises 802 CT records with consistent, joined spine–pelvis labels on the richest available series per patient. All 802 pass geometric consistency checks; rib-to-vertebra mapping shows a very low mismatch rate (0.035% across 5,749 ribs), and spinopelvic parameters derived from the dataset align with published morphometric data. The data are provided as NIfTI image/label pairs with patient-grouped, LSTV-stratified five-fold splits and a dedicated loader, and are publicly archived at the provided Zenodo DOI.
AI.conclusion: CTSpinoPelvic1K offers a validated, publicly available spinopelvic CT dataset that explicitly encodes lumbosacral transitional anatomy and links vertebral, rib, pelvic, and femoral labels. This enables research on vertebral classification from local morphology without whole-spine counting, improves the basis for morphometric and spinopelvic analysis, and supports applications like opportunistic screening and preoperative planning studies. The authors note limitations including restricted thoracic field-of-view, supine-only posture, absence of a held-out test set, reliance on partially pseudolabeled ribs, and limited expert grading for Castellvi classification.

title: Beyond Raw Context Transfer: Representation-based Federated Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves the factuality of large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) by grounding generation in external knowledge. However, most existing RAG frameworks assume a centralized retrieval corpus, which is often impractical in sensitive domains such as healthcare, where data are inherently distributed and raw content cannot be directly shared across institutions. Recent efforts on decentralized RAG primarily follow prompt-based paradigms that exchange raw, human-readable retrieved content, leading to substantial inference-time computational overhead and direct exposure of retrieved information. To address these limitations, we propose Representation-based Federated RAG (FedRepRAG), a decentralized RAG framework that keeps raw documents at their owning clients and exchanges only compact latent representations during cross-client retrieval. To integrate retrieved knowledge, we introduce a collaboratively trained projector that converts retrieval embeddings into generator-compatible representation tokens for a frozen LLM/VLM backbone. Experiments across decentralized visual question answering (VQA) and question answering (QA) benchmarks show that FedRepRAG consistently outperforms direct inference and local retrieval baselines while substantially reducing retrieval-context length and inference-time computational overhead compared with raw-context transfer. Further analyses confirm the importance of query-relevant retrieved representations and characterize the residual representation-level leakage associated with representation exchange. Overall, FedRepRAG provides an effective and efficient framework for federated RAG without transferring raw retrieved content.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes FedRepRAG, a federated retrieval‑augmented generation framework that exchanges only latent representations instead of raw documents, improving performance and efficiency while preserving data locality.
AI.motivation: Centralized RAG requires aggregating all documents in one place, which is infeasible in sensitive, distributed domains like healthcare. Existing decentralized RAG methods either share raw retrieved text/images—violating privacy and causing long, costly prompts—or perform only local retrieval, missing cross‑institution knowledge. There is a need for a RAG framework that supports cross‑client retrieval without exposing raw content or incurring large inference overhead.
AI.method: FedRepRAG keeps raw documents on local clients and performs cross‑client retrieval through compact latent embeddings. Retrieved embeddings are not used directly; instead, the authors introduce a collaboratively trained projector that maps retrieval embeddings into special representation tokens compatible with a frozen LLM/VLM backbone. This enables the backbone model to consume cross‑client knowledge without seeing raw documents. The framework is evaluated on decentralized VQA and QA settings, comparing against direct inference (no retrieval), local-only retrieval, and raw-context transfer baselines.
AI.result: Across decentralized VQA and QA benchmarks, FedRepRAG achieves higher accuracy than direct inference and local retrieval baselines. Compared with methods that send raw retrieved content in the prompt, it significantly reduces context length and inference-time computation. Additional analyses show that (1) having query-relevant retrieved representations is crucial for performance and (2) while raw data are not shared, there remains some measurable information leakage at the representation level, which the authors characterize empirically.
AI.conclusion: FedRepRAG is an effective federated RAG approach that enables cross-client knowledge sharing through latent representations instead of raw documents, improving factuality and efficiency under data locality constraints. It demonstrates that representation-level exchange plus a learned projector can unlock multi-institution retrieval benefits while limiting—but not completely eliminating—information leakage, offering a practical path for RAG in sensitive, distributed domains.

title: DVA-Neurons: Design and Verification of Adaptive LIF Neurons: From Single-Neuron Dynamics to Multi-Neuron Spiking Networks
summary: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer a promising path toward ultra-low-power artificial intelligence inference by emulating the event-driven computation of biological neurons. However, two challenges limit their practical deployment. First, fixed-parameter Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neurons lack the adaptation mechanisms observed in biology, where neurons modulate their excitability based on firing history. Second, scaling from single neurons to multi-neuron networks introduces challenges in synaptic weight distribution and inter-neuron spike routing that are absent in isolated designs. This paper addresses both issues through the extension, verification, and physical implementation of adaptive LIF neurons at three architectural scales. This work contributes: a 2nd-order neuron with two-stage synaptic filtering for richer temporal dynamics; a fully-connected 6-neuron spiking network with configurable weights (100 to 5) demonstrating weight-based inter-neuron communication; and a direct verification methodology enabling per-cycle observation of all internal states. All designs were synthesized targeting Selected Area Electron Diffraction (SAED) 14 nm Complementary Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor (CMOS) technology at 1 GHz and verified with Cocotb-based Python testbenches under pulsed current stimuli (amplitude 80, ISI=3). The results show that adaptation effectively modulates firing: 31% suppression in the 2nd-order neuron (25 vs.\ 36 spikes) and 31% reduction in postsynaptic firing in the network (18 vs.\ 26 spikes). Physically, the 2nd-order neuron costs 1.77x more area and 1.52x more power than the 1st-order baseline, while the 6-neuron network demonstrates near-linear scaling (5.7x area, 5.3x power). Seven verification bugs spanning testbench connectivity, fixed-point overflow, and Verilog expression-width semantics are documented.

AI.tldr: They design and implement adaptive spiking neurons and a small spiking neural network in 14 nm CMOS, showing adaptation reduces spike rates ~31% with moderate area/power overhead and near-linear network scaling.
AI.motivation: Spiking Neural Networks are energy-efficient but current hardware usually uses simple fixed-parameter LIF neurons without biological-like adaptation, and most prior designs focus on isolated neurons rather than scalable multi-neuron networks with realistic synaptic connectivity and routing. There is also a need for rigorous, cycle-accurate verification methods for such mixed-signal-like digital neuron implementations.
AI.method: They extend standard LIF neurons to adaptive, higher-order variants including a 2nd-order neuron with two-stage synaptic filtering, design a fully connected 6-neuron SNN with configurable synaptic weights, and create a direct verification flow that exposes all internal neuron and network states per cycle. All designs are synthesized in SAED 14 nm CMOS at 1 GHz and functionally verified using Cocotb-driven Python testbenches applying pulsed current stimuli, while area and power are extracted from synthesis results. They also systematically log and classify verification bugs encountered.
AI.result: Adaptive dynamics significantly reduce firing rates under the same stimulus: the 2nd-order neuron fires 25 vs 36 spikes (~31% suppression), and the postsynaptic neuron in the 6-neuron network fires 18 vs 26 spikes (~31% reduction). The 2nd-order neuron requires 1.77x area and 1.52x power compared to a 1st-order baseline, while the 6-neuron network scales to ~5.7x area and 5.3x power, indicating near-linear scaling. Seven distinct verification issues were identified related to testbench wiring, fixed-point overflows, and Verilog expression widths.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive LIF neurons can be practically implemented in advanced CMOS with modest resource overhead while providing substantial control over firing activity, and small SNNs with configurable synaptic weights can scale almost linearly in area and power. The proposed per-cycle visibility verification methodology is effective for catching subtle design and testbench bugs, making it a useful approach for developing larger, more reliable neuromorphic systems.

title: MechaTerp-TRACE: A Novel Approach for Component Ablation Analysis in Language Models
summary: Interpretability research on large language models has produced accounts of factual recall in feed-forward layers and of token relationships in self-attention, but little work offers a unified way to compare the causal contribution of different architecture components to a model's output. We introduce MechaTerp (the Mechanistic Interpretability suite) -TRACE (subset for Teacher-forced Registry of Ablated Component Effects), an architecture and study that measures how much each registered component of a language model supports the production of a named entity. TRACE ablates one component at a time and measures the resulting change in the output distribution at a fixed answer token, so component types from whole transformer blocks down to individual neurons and output logits can be compared on a common scale. We apply it to thirteen instruction-tuned dense decoder models spanning five families and one to thirty billion parameters, ablating 49,656 components across 48 medical and 42 general-knowledge prompts. We find that the components carrying the most effect are the same few, positionally fixed components in every model, regardless of which entity a prompt asks about, and that once these are removed, the remaining support is close to evenly spread in eleven of the thirteen models. Apparent localisation of entity knowledge is therefore largely attributable to generic generation machinery, which has direct consequences for methods that assume entity knowledge sits in a findable place, including targeted knowledge editing.

AI.tldr: They propose TRACE, a systematic way to measure how much different components of transformer LLMs causally contribute to generating specific entities, and show that a small, fixed set of components dominates this effect across models and prompts.
AI.motivation: Existing mechanistic interpretability studies look at specific aspects (like factual recall in MLPs or relationships in attention) but lack a unified, causal, and comparable measure of how different architectural components (layers, heads, neurons, logits) contribute to model outputs. This makes it hard to rigorously evaluate claims about where knowledge is stored or how localized it is, and limits methods like knowledge editing that assume entity knowledge is in discrete locations.
AI.method: They introduce TRACE within the MechaTerp framework: for a given prompt and a specific answer token (teacher-forced), they systematically ablate one component at a time (ranging from whole blocks to individual neurons and output logits) in decoder-only LLMs. For each ablation, they measure how the output probability distribution at the target token changes, which quantifies that component’s causal support for producing a named entity. They apply this across 13 instruction-tuned dense decoder models (1–30B parameters, 5 model families) using 48 medical and 42 general-knowledge prompts, and analyze the contributions of 49,656 components.
AI.result: Across all models and prompts, a small, positionally fixed subset of components carries the largest causal effect on entity production. These high-impact components are largely the same regardless of which entity is queried. After ablating this small subset, the remaining contribution to entity prediction is spread relatively evenly across the rest of the network in 11 of 13 models, with no strong residual localization of entity knowledge to particular other components.
AI.conclusion: Apparent localization of entity knowledge to specific components is largely due to generic, shared generation mechanisms rather than entity-specific storage in isolated neurons or layers. Consequently, entity knowledge is more diffusely represented than some prior work assumes. This challenges approaches like targeted knowledge editing that rely on the idea that entity knowledge is stored in identifiable, manipulable locations, and suggests that editing or inspecting LLM knowledge must account for the dominant role of generic generation machinery and more distributed representations.

title: From Research Frontier to Laboratory Bench: Design of a Four-Tier Experimental Teaching System for Multimodal Medical Image Intelligent Diagnosis
summary: Undergraduate programmes in intelligent medical engineering are expanding, yet laboratory curricula lag behind the multimodal, long-tailed, and distributionally shifting realities of clinical AI. This design paper presents an advanced experimental teaching system that translates an ongoing multimodal deep learning research project on endometrial carcinoma into a structured undergraduate lab sequence. We identify three educational gaps (modality, authenticity, and deployment) and derive four pedagogical principles from constructive alignment, experiential learning, the research teaching nexus, and the CDIO framework. The curriculum comprises four progressive tiers plus an engineering layer, with 32 laboratory units over 64 contact hours, delivered via a custom virtual clinical workstation using de-identified multi-institutional data. Each tier maps to a specific technical bottleneck, prerequisite coursework, and criterion-referenced deliverables. Data governance, safety, and assessment protocols are specified. Learning outcome data will be collected across two implementation cycles.

AI.tldr: The paper designs an advanced lab curriculum that mirrors a real multimodal clinical AI research project on endometrial carcinoma for intelligent medical engineering undergraduates.
AI.motivation: Existing undergraduate intelligent medical engineering labs do not reflect the real-world complexity of clinical AI, which is multimodal, long-tailed, and subject to distribution shifts. There is a gap between fast-growing programmes and outdated or oversimplified laboratory curricula, especially around realistic data, authentic workflows, and deployment issues.
AI.method: The authors convert an ongoing multimodal deep learning research project on endometrial carcinoma into a structured undergraduate laboratory sequence. They first identify three educational gaps—modality (lack of multimodal data/tasks), authenticity (limited resemblance to real clinical AI work), and deployment (insufficient coverage of end-to-end deployment challenges). They then derive four pedagogical principles from constructive alignment, experiential learning theory, the research–teaching nexus, and the CDIO (Conceive–Design–Implement–Operate) engineering education framework. Based on these, they design a curriculum with four progressive tiers plus an engineering layer, totaling 32 lab units over 64 contact hours, implemented on a custom virtual clinical workstation using de-identified multi-institutional clinical data. Each tier is aligned with specific technical bottlenecks, prerequisite courses, and criterion-referenced assessments, with explicit data governance, safety, and evaluation protocols.
AI.result: The paper specifies a complete advanced lab curriculum and infrastructure: a tiered set of 32 labs, a virtual clinical workstation, and detailed mapping of each tier to technical challenges, prerequisites, and assessment criteria. It also defines protocols for data governance, safety, and assessment, and a plan to collect learning outcome data over two implementation cycles. Empirical learning outcome data are not yet reported; the main result is the instructional design itself.
AI.conclusion: A research-aligned, multimodal, authenticity-focused, and deployment-aware lab curriculum for intelligent medical engineering is feasible and can be systematically derived from established educational frameworks and an active clinical AI research project. This design aims to better prepare undergraduates for real-world clinical AI challenges, with future work to evaluate its educational impact across multiple implementation cycles.

title: A Multi-Agent Pipeline for Source-Grounded Synthetic Note Generation from Longitudinal Structured EHR
comment: Accepted at the FMSD Workshop, ICML 2026
summary: Structured EHR is abundant but sparse, coded, and difficult to use directly for note-centric clinical modeling. We present MedNotes, a multi-agent synthetic data generation pipeline that converts longitudinal structured EHR into source-grounded clinical note representations under explicit quality control. MedNotes treats structured-data-to-text synthesis as a closed-loop agentic process: a generator proposes a note, evaluator agents diagnose factual, coverage, structural, and hallucination-related failures, and a router accepts, revises, or rejects the draft. On 1,485 EHRSHOT encounters, MedNotes achieves a 91.4% pass rate, with mean factual accuracy of 0.980, completeness of 99.1%, structural fidelity of 0.761, and 0.028 critical hallucinations per encounter. Iterative refinement improves acceptance from 69.4% to 91.4%. The resulting synthetic corpus improves downstream CPT prediction and paragraph-level section prediction when combined with limited real data.

AI.tldr: MedNotes is a multi‑agent system that transforms sparse structured EHR data into high‑quality synthetic clinical notes through iterative generation and critique, yielding a corpus that boosts downstream clinical modeling tasks.
AI.motivation: Structured EHR data are plentiful but hard to use directly for tasks that are naturally note‑centric, such as modeling clinical narratives, because they are sparse, coded, and lack the rich free‑text context.
