Real clinical notes, in contrast, are difficult to share due to privacy and are limited in quantity. The paper is motivated by the need for a scalable, privacy‑preserving way to obtain realistic, source‑grounded clinical notes derived from structured EHR that can support and improve downstream clinical NLP and prediction tasks.
AI.method: The authors design MedNotes, a closed‑loop multi‑agent pipeline that synthesizes clinical notes from longitudinal structured EHR. A generator model first produces a draft note conditioned on the structured data. Multiple evaluator agents then independently assess the draft along several dimensions: factual consistency with the EHR, completeness/coverage of relevant information, structural fidelity to clinical note conventions, and presence of hallucinations. Based on the evaluators’ feedback, a router agent decides whether to accept the note, ask the generator to revise it, or reject it entirely. This iterative refinement continues until the note meets preset quality thresholds or a stopping condition is reached. The system is empirically evaluated on the EHRSHOT dataset of 1,485 encounters.
AI.result: On 1,485 EHRSHOT encounters, MedNotes attains a 91.4% final pass rate for generated notes. Among the accepted notes, it achieves mean factual accuracy of 0.980, completeness of 99.1%, structural fidelity of 0.761, and an average of only 0.028 critical hallucinations per encounter. Iterative refinement is crucial, raising the acceptance rate from 69.4% after initial drafts to 91.4% after revisions. Using the resulting synthetic note corpus alongside limited real notes improves performance on downstream tasks including CPT code prediction and paragraph‑level section prediction, indicating that the synthetic data are useful for enhancing clinical models.
AI.conclusion: MedNotes demonstrates that a closed‑loop, multi‑agent, structured‑data‑to‑text pipeline can reliably produce high‑quality, source‑grounded synthetic clinical notes from structured EHR data. The system substantially reduces hallucinations, ensures high factual accuracy and coverage, and yields synthetic corpora that materially improve downstream clinical prediction and section classification when paired with scarce real data. This suggests that carefully controlled synthetic note generation is a practical path to unlocking the value of structured EHR for note‑centric clinical modeling while mitigating data scarcity and privacy constraints.

title: ISA-Bench: A Benchmark for Computational Reasoning Across Instruction Set Architectures
summary: Large language model code generation benchmarks primarily evaluate well-resourced languages like Python and Java, where models benefit from abundant training data. They provide limited evidence about reasoning in unfamiliar computational models: deriving arithmetic from a single subtract instruction, coordinating parallel programs across communicating nodes, or wiring logic gates into circuits. We present ISA-Bench, a benchmark of programming games with constrained instruction sets. For each game we provide a full execution stack (parser, VM, and verifier), enabling automated evaluation with structured feedback for iterative refinement. Reasoning models achieve higher average solve rates than code-specialized and general-purpose models, but unfamiliar syntax remains a major source of failure. Models solve more tasks with iterative feedback, though the gains vary substantially across architectures. We introduce a reasoning--execution gap (REG) analysis that reveals a recurring disconnect between identifying a plausible computational strategy and expressing it as a correct program in the target ISA. Code is open-sourced.

AI.tldr: Introduces ISA-Bench, a benchmark of programming games using minimal instruction sets to test LLM reasoning in unfamiliar computational models, and analyzes the gap between reasoning and correct code execution.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM code benchmarks mostly cover popular, well-resourced languages (e.g., Python, Java), so they don’t tell us much about how models reason in unfamiliar or low-resource computational settings. The authors want to stress-test models on tasks that require understanding computation from first principles—like building arithmetic from a single instruction, orchestrating parallel programs, or constructing circuits from logic gates—while also enabling automated, feedback-rich evaluation.
AI.method: They design ISA-Bench, a collection of programming games built around constrained instruction set architectures (ISAs). For each game, they implement the full execution pipeline: a parser, a virtual machine to run the code, and a verifier to check correctness. They then evaluate different LLM families—reasoning-oriented models, code-specialized models, and general-purpose models—on these tasks, with and without iterative feedback, and analyze performance using a proposed “reasoning–execution gap” (REG) framework that distinguishes between finding a valid computational strategy and implementing it correctly in the given ISA.
AI.result: Reasoning-focused models achieve higher average solve rates than code-specialized and general-purpose models on ISA-Bench tasks. Iterative feedback generally improves performance, but the degree of improvement varies widely across model architectures. A dominant failure mode is dealing with unfamiliar syntax: even when models appear to understand the computational problem, they struggle to express correct programs in the target ISA. REG analysis shows that models often identify plausible strategies but fail to translate them into fully correct executable code within the constrained instruction sets.
AI.conclusion: ISA-Bench exposes limitations of current LLMs in transferring reasoning to unfamiliar, low-level computational formalisms. While reasoning-oriented models perform best and benefit from iterative feedback, there remains a substantial reasoning–execution gap: models can often conceptualize solutions but cannot reliably implement them in the target ISA, especially under unusual syntax and constraints. The benchmark and accompanying infrastructure provide a tool for future work on improving the alignment between high-level reasoning and low-level program synthesis in new computational domains.

title: Monocultural Biases: Correlated biases in large language models lead to unequal systemic exclusion rates in hiring
summary: Employers are increasingly using large language models (LLMs) to automate their hiring process. This paper investigates the risk of monocultural biases, in which the widespread deployment of large language models homogenizes biases across the labor market, leading to greater systemic exclusion for certain demographic groups. For ten LLMs, we measure hiring biases across their base and post-trained versions to identify which stage, pre-training or post-training, lead to monocultural biases. We find that, compared to their base models, post-trained models are 3.6% less likely to callback older applicants. This negative shift occurs in eight of the ten models that we evaluate. Post-trained models have much more correlated decisions than base models which is likely driven by human capital traits like skills or college major. However, greater consensus among models increases global systemic exclusion rates from 5.6% to 17.3% and exacerbates demographic inequalities, with intersectional systemic exclusion rates ranging from 12.2% to 21.7% for post-trained models. We find that this inequality is primarily driven by age-based discrimination that is exacerbated in post-training. These results indicate that while post-training techniques may improve models' abilities to select the best applicants, they may raise systemic inequality risks for those at the margin by uniformly introducing new biases.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how using large language models (LLMs) in hiring can create “monocultural” bias, where many employers’ tools share similar discriminatory patterns, particularly against older applicants, and shows that post-training of models increases systemic and intersectional exclusion even while improving apparent applicant selection quality.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are adopted at scale in hiring pipelines, their errors and biases no longer remain isolated to single firms; instead, if many organizations use similarly tuned models, they can create market-wide, monocultural patterns of exclusion. The authors want to quantify whether and how base versus post-trained LLMs contribute to such aligned biases, with a focus on systemic and demographic inequality risks (especially age-related discrimination) in automated hiring decisions.
AI.method: The authors evaluate ten different LLMs, comparing each model’s base version with its post-trained (e.g., instruction-tuned or RLHF-tuned) version. They simulate or measure “callback” decisions for applicants with varied demographic attributes and human capital traits (such as skills and college major). They then compute (1) changes in callback likelihood for groups (e.g., older vs. younger applicants), (2) the correlation of decisions across models to capture monocultural convergence, and (3) systemic exclusion rates—how often applicants are excluded by all models—overall, by demographic group, and at intersectional levels.
AI.result: Post-trained models become 3.6% less likely to callback older applicants compared to their base counterparts, with this negative shift occurring in eight out of ten models. Post-trained models’ decisions are more highly correlated with each other, especially around human capital traits, indicating stronger monocultural behavior. This heightened agreement raises global systemic exclusion—being rejected by all models—from 5.6% to 17.3%. Intersectional systemic exclusion rates for post-trained models lie between 12.2% and 21.7%. The main driver of these exacerbated inequalities is age-based discrimination, which worsens during post-training.
AI.conclusion: Post-training, while making LLMs appear better at identifying top candidates, also makes their decisions more similar and systematically biased, especially against older applicants. This convergence generates higher systemic and intersectional exclusion risks across the labor market. Therefore, standard post-training practices can unintentionally amplify inequality at scale, suggesting that fairness-aware or diversity-sensitive approaches to post-training are needed to mitigate monocultural bias when LLMs are deployed for hiring.

title: When Should a VLM Look? Paying Only for Visual Calls That Were Needed and Used
comment: 30 pages, 7 figures, 14 tables. Preprint under review
summary: Vision-language agents that crop and zoom are trained with rewards that credit a successful tool call, yet a successful call does not show that the model needed to look or used the pixels it received. On our cold-start checkpoint only 10% to 12% of visual calls were both needed and used, and released agents make spurious calls 36% to 87% of the time on individual benchmarks. Outcome rewards, judge rewards, and branch probes each observe one side of this failure, and about two thirds of what an outcome reward pays goes to calls that were neither needed nor used. CounterCredit asks both questions of every image-returning call at its realized pre-call state, using the policy's own gold-answer score. A decision value compares the realized visual branch with answering immediately; an evidence value compares the returned crop with random same-size patches substituted into the same call. A call verified on both earns cashback and every other executed call pays rent; the price is bounded so that every correct trajectory outranks every wrong one, and a dual-channel GRPO advantage keeps the price in its own units. From the same cold start, prompt pool, and budget, CounterCredit reaches 89.5% on V*, 80.2% on HR-Bench-4K, and 76.4% on HR-Bench-8K, 6.3 to 9.4 points above outcome-only GRPO at 1.78 against 1.84 calls per question, and lowers the spurious-call rate to 31% to 36%, the lowest among the agents evaluated. The same recipe lifts a Qwen3-VL-8B base from 75.4 to 80.8 on average.

AI.tldr: Proposes CounterCredit, a reward scheme that explicitly checks whether each vision tool call was necessary and whether its visual input was actually used, leading to more efficient and accurate vision-language agents with fewer spurious image crops/zooms.
AI.motivation: Existing vision-language agents that can crop and zoom images are rewarded for successful tool calls, but this does not ensure the calls were needed or that the returned pixels influenced the answer. Empirically, most visual calls are unnecessary or unused, and standard outcome-based rewards overpay for such spurious calls, wasting compute and harming performance.
AI.method: Introduce CounterCredit, a credit-assignment mechanism that evaluates each image-returning call at the moment it is made. It computes (1) a decision value by comparing the model’s gold-answer score if it used the visual branch versus if it answered immediately without looking; and (2) an evidence value by comparing performance when using the actual crop versus random same-size patches in the same call. Only calls that are both necessary (decision value positive) and truly using the visual evidence (evidence value positive) receive positive credit (“cashback”), while all executed calls pay a bounded “rent” cost, enforced via a dual-channel GRPO advantage formulation to keep the price in consistent units and preserve correct-trajectory dominance over incorrect ones.
AI.result: From the same cold start, prompt pool, and training budget, CounterCredit significantly improves benchmark performance versus outcome-only GRPO: it achieves 89.5% on V*, 80.2% on HR-Bench-4K, and 76.4% on HR-Bench-8K, gaining 6.3–9.4 points at essentially the same average tool usage (1.78 vs 1.84 calls per question) and reducing spurious visual calls to 31–36%, the lowest among evaluated agents. Applying the method to a Qwen3-VL-8B base model also raises its average score from 75.4 to 80.8.
AI.conclusion: Carefully attributing credit to vision-tool calls based on both their necessity and effective use of visual evidence leads to substantially better vision-language agents. CounterCredit aligns rewards with genuinely useful visual reasoning, cuts down on unnecessary cropping/zooming, and improves accuracy across multiple benchmarks and model backbones without increasing tool-call budget.

title: Quantifying Hidden Salt for Precision Healthcare: Sodium Assessment via Joint-Factor Retrieval and Chain-of-Thought Inference
comment: Accepted in EMNLP 2026 Main Conference; 16 pages, 7 figures
summary: Precision healthcare, particularly for conditions like hypertension and cardiovascular disease, necessitates monitoring of dietary sodium intake. However, tracking this is hindered by the prevalence of hidden salt in cooking, such as sodium in soy sauce and ketchup. While recipes offer a valuable data source for dietary analysis, sodium-rich seasonings are frequently omitted or described ambiguously in instructions. To solve this issue, we propose SALT, a Sodium Assessing & Level Tracking framework adopting an RAG framework to assess sodium content in recipes. Our framework first introduces a Joint-Factor Embedding Retrieval module to locate similar recipes with specified sodium content for addressing the lack of contextual references. These retrieved samples provide contexts for subsequent inference. Then we design a structured 4-hop Chain-of-Thought inference module to refine the vague estimation from language models through a multi-step sodium estimation. To facilitate our study, we further construct a recipe dataset SALT54k with $54,151$ entries labeled with sodium quantities across $11$ common seasonings. Results on SALT54k demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in sodium estimation. Additional real-world validations confirm the effectiveness of our method, demonstrating its potential as a practical solution for AI-assisted precision healthcare.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SALT, a framework that automatically estimates hidden sodium content in recipes using retrieval-augmented generation and multi-step reasoning, achieving state-of-the-art performance and supporting precision healthcare.
AI.motivation: Accurate monitoring of dietary sodium is essential for precision healthcare, especially for hypertension and cardiovascular disease, but sodium intake is hard to track because much of it comes from hidden salt in cooking (e.g., soy sauce, ketchup). Existing recipe texts often omit or ambiguously describe sodium-rich seasonings, limiting their usefulness for nutritional analysis. The authors aim to build an AI system that can robustly infer sodium content from incomplete or vague recipe information to support practical health applications.
AI.method: The authors propose SALT, a Sodium Assessing & Level Tracking framework based on a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) paradigm. First, they design a Joint-Factor Embedding Retrieval module that retrieves recipes with known sodium content that are similar across multiple factors, supplying contextual references for the target recipe. Then they introduce a structured 4-hop Chain-of-Thought inference module, which guides a language model through a multi-step reasoning process to refine initial rough estimates into precise sodium quantity predictions across seasonings. To train and evaluate the system, they build SALT54k, a dataset of 54,151 recipes labeled with sodium amounts for 11 common seasonings.
AI.result: On the SALT54k dataset, the SALT framework attains state-of-the-art accuracy in estimating sodium content compared with baseline methods. The authors also conduct real-world validations beyond the curated dataset, showing that SALT maintains strong performance when applied to practical cooking and dietary scenarios. These experiments suggest improved reliability and robustness in handling ambiguous or missing information about sodium-rich seasonings in recipes.
AI.conclusion: SALT effectively addresses the challenge of hidden sodium in recipes by combining retrieval of similar, labeled recipes with structured multi-step reasoning to infer sodium amounts. The constructed SALT54k dataset enables systematic development and evaluation of sodium estimation models. Empirical results and real-world validations show that SALT can serve as a practical AI-assisted tool for precision healthcare, particularly for individuals needing careful sodium monitoring, and the approach could be extended to other nutritional components or dietary analysis tasks.

title: Beyond Linear Context: Graph-Guided Evidence Navigation for Long-Novel Reasoning with a Local 9B Language Model
comment: 10 pages, 11 figures, 2 tables. Code, graph data and an interactive demo: https://github.com/fuxiaoji/novel-graph-lab
summary: Long-context models read a novel the way a person reads a printout: one token after another, in narrative order, with the whole history competing for a fixed budget of attention. A detective does not work that way. They sort what happened when, and they keep a map of who relates to whom, so a clue from chapter one can meet a question asked at the end of the book. We test whether a frozen knowledge graph can give a small local model that same freedom. Thirty detective novels and 234 multiple-choice questions are answered by one fixed qwen3.5:9b reader under nine conditions: five graph routes, a recent-window baseline, whole-book compression, ordinary vector retrieval, and a question-only control. The strongest graph route reaches 53.85% (126/234) against 46.15% for the recent window, 51.28% for compression, 51.71% for vector retrieval and 40.17% for question-only. On the subset that no model can answer without the book, the graph route reaches 42.86%. None of the fifteen graph-baseline contrasts survives Holm correction, so we present the result as exploratory evidence about a design. Two structural findings survive scrutiny better than the headline number: annotated evidence concentrates in the topological core of these graphs (2.35x enrichment, pooled), and the two graph-building pipelines differ so much in annotation coverage (16% versus 73% of clue paragraphs) that pooled accuracy alone would hide which bottleneck is being measured.

AI.tldr: The paper explores whether augmenting a small frozen LLM with an external, frozen knowledge graph improves question answering on full detective novels compared to standard long-context baselines. Results are modest and exploratory but suggest structural advantages and important implementation bottlenecks in graph construction and coverage.
AI.motivation: Long-context LLMs process text sequentially with a fixed attention window, which is poorly matched to tasks like mystery novels where scattered clues must be connected across the whole book. Humans instead build structured mental models of events and relationships. The authors want to know whether giving an LLM something analogous—a frozen knowledge graph of the book—allows a small, fixed model to answer questions about long narratives more effectively and more interpretably than standard approaches (recent window, compression, or vector search) without scaling up the model size or context length.
AI.method: They evaluate a single frozen qwen3.5:9B model on 234 multiple-choice questions about 30 detective novels under nine reading conditions. Five are different graph-based “routes” that query a pre-built knowledge graph of the novel; the others are baselines: a recent-context window, whole-book compression, ordinary dense vector retrieval, and a question-only control. They compare accuracies and apply Holm correction for multiple comparisons. They also analyze graph structure: where human-annotated evidence lies in the graph (e.g., in the topological core) and how differences in graph-building pipelines affect coverage of key clue paragraphs.
AI.result: The best knowledge-graph route attains 53.85% (126/234) accuracy, outperforming the recent-window baseline (46.15%) and slightly surpassing whole-book compression (51.28%) and vector retrieval (51.71%), and greatly improving over question-only (40.17%). On questions that cannot be answered without the novel, the top graph route achieves 42.86%. However, after Holm correction for multiple testing, none of the graph versus baseline differences are statistically significant, so claimed improvements are only exploratory. Structurally, human-annotated evidence paragraphs are 2.35× enriched in the graph’s topological core, indicating that important clues concentrate in central graph regions. They also find that two graph-construction pipelines differ dramatically in annotation coverage (16% vs. 73% of clue paragraphs), implying that naïve pooling of results obscures which step—graph quality or query routing—is the main performance bottleneck.
AI.conclusion: Augmenting a small LLM with an external knowledge graph for long-novel question answering yields promising but not statistically conclusive gains over standard long-context strategies. The more robust findings concern graph structure and pipeline design: crucial evidence tends to live in the graph’s core, and graph-building coverage has a large impact, so future work should focus on higher-quality, more complete graph construction and on exploiting graph topology. The work is best viewed as exploratory support for a particular graph-augmented reading architecture rather than as definitive performance gains.

title: SCoR: A Hierarchical Framework for Forecasting Relations Between Scientific Concepts
comment: 15 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables; includes supplementary material. Jingze Wang and Fred Sun contributed equally; Shangqi Guo is the corresponding author
summary: Anticipating emerging research directions is a critical goal of AI-assisted science. Existing methods mainly predict which concepts will co-occur in future papers, but co-occurrence captures shared attention rather than the scientific meaning of a connection, such as whether one method uses, combines, replaces, or contradicts another. We formulate research-direction discovery as hierarchical scientific-relation forecasting over a shared candidate-pair space, comprising three temporally aligned tasks: first co-occurrence, first scientific-relation formation, and relation type at formation. We construct SCoR-Graph from 187,848 cs.CV papers published between 2017 and 2026, yielding 270,687 consolidated concepts, 7.45 million co-occurrence edges, and 615,036 typed, directed relation edges. From cutoff-specific graph snapshots, we derive SCoR-Bench, a leakage-audited benchmark for these three capabilities, with expert-verified gold labels for the entire relation-type test set. We further introduce HiSCoR, a task-adapted model family that models relation emergence as a temporally evolving, hierarchically constrained process by encoding pre-cutoff event histories and conditioning relation formation on future co-occurrence. On the held-out 2025-2026 window, HiSCoR achieves an AUROC of 0.9515, a 2.4% relative improvement over the strongest temporal-graph baseline, and improves population-AUPRC by 14.0%; its relation-type variant achieves a Macro-AUROC of 0.7795. Ablations show that semantic, co-occurrence, and typed-relation views provide complementary predictive evidence. SCoR advances research-direction forecasting from predicting which concepts will co-occur to anticipating whether and how evidence-backed scientific relations will emerge.

AI.tldr: They build a graph and benchmark of computer-vision concepts and relations over time, and a model (HiSCoR) that forecasts not just future co-occurrence of concepts but when and what kind of scientific relations between them will emerge.
AI.motivation: Current AI methods for forecasting scientific trends mostly predict future co-occurrence of concepts in papers, which only reflects shared attention, not the nature of the scientific relationship (e.g., using, combining, replacing, contradicting). The authors want to move from shallow co-attention prediction to deeper, relation-level forecasting that better reflects genuine research directions.
AI.method: 1) Define a hierarchical forecasting problem over concept pairs: (a) predict if/when two concepts will first co-occur, (b) if/when a genuine scientific relation between them will first form, and (c) the type of that relation at formation. 2) Build SCoR-Graph from ~188k cs.CV arXiv papers (2017–2026), extracting and consolidating concepts, co-occurrence edges, and typed, directed scientific-relation edges. 3) Create SCoR-Bench by taking time-specific snapshots, auditing for temporal leakage, and obtaining expert-verified gold labels for the relation-type test set. 4) Propose HiSCoR, a model family that treats relation emergence as a temporally evolving, hierarchically constrained process, encoding pre-cutoff event histories and conditioning relation formation on forecasted co-occurrence. 5) Conduct experiments and ablations comparing against strong temporal-graph baselines and isolating the contributions of semantic, co-occurrence, and typed-relation signals.
AI.result: On a held-out 2025–2026 prediction window, HiSCoR attains AUROC of 0.9515 for relation-formation prediction, a 2.4% relative gain over the best temporal-graph baseline, and improves population-level AUPRC by 14%. For relation-type classification at first formation, it reaches Macro-AUROC of 0.7795. Ablation studies demonstrate that combining semantic information, co-occurrence patterns, and typed-relation structure yields the best performance, indicating these views capture complementary evidence for forecasting scientific relations.
AI.conclusion: The work reframes research-direction forecasting from simply predicting which concepts will co-appear to predicting whether and how concrete, evidence-backed scientific relations between them will arise. By releasing SCoR-Graph and the leakage-audited SCoR-Bench, and by introducing the HiSCoR model that explicitly models hierarchical, temporal relation emergence, the paper provides both data and methods that substantially advance the fidelity and usefulness of AI-assisted forecasting of emerging research directions.

title: AgentRouter: Heterogeneous Model Routing for Cost-Optimal Multi-Step Agentic Workflows
comment: Accepted at the AgenticUQ Workshop, ICML 2026. Camera-ready version
summary: Enterprise agentic systems that route every trajectory step to a frontier model waste 60-80% of their inference budget on subtasks that smaller models handle equally well. Existing routing solutions optimize single-turn query assignment but ignore a property unique to agentic workflows: subtask complexity varies widely within a single trajectory. A planning step may require frontier-class reasoning while a subsequent formatting step needs only a 7B model. We formalize step-level model routing as a sequential assignment problem over agent trajectories and propose AgentRouter, a lightweight classifier (12M parameters, <5ms overhead per step on an A100 GPU) that maps each trajectory step to one of four model tiers using five features extractable at routing time. Trained on 50,000 annotated agent trajectory steps spanning planning, coding, research, and data analysis tasks, AgentRouter achieves 72% cost reduction relative to frontier-only baselines, retaining 97.3% of frontier-only quality (less than 3% degradation in end-to-end task completion); per-step routing accuracy reaches 91% on minimal-complexity steps and 85% on efficient-tier steps, with 76-82% on the harder mid-range and frontier tiers. On the same benchmarks, RouteLLM and FrugalGPT (applied per-step) achieve only 31% and 44% cost reduction respectively, because their single-turn training signal misses trajectory-level quality dependencies.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AgentRouter, a lightweight classifier for step-level model routing in multi-step agent workflows, achieving large cost savings with minimal quality loss compared to always using a frontier model.
AI.motivation: Enterprise agentic systems currently overuse expensive frontier models for all steps in a trajectory, even though many subtasks are simple enough for smaller models. Existing routing methods are designed for single-turn queries and fail to capture the varying complexity across steps within a trajectory, leading to wasted inference budget and suboptimal cost-performance trade-offs.
AI.method: The authors formalize step-level routing as a sequential assignment problem over agent trajectories. They design AgentRouter, a 12M-parameter classifier that, using five features available at routing time, assigns each trajectory step to one of four model tiers. The system is trained on 50,000 annotated trajectory steps covering planning, coding, research, and data analysis, and evaluated on its routing accuracy, end-to-end cost, and task quality relative to baselines. They also compare to applying existing routing approaches like RouteLLM and FrugalGPT at the per-step level.
AI.result: AgentRouter reduces inference cost by 72% relative to a baseline that always uses the frontier model, while preserving 97.3% of the frontier-only task quality, corresponding to less than 3% degradation in task completion. Per-step routing accuracy reaches 91% on minimal-complexity steps and 85% on efficient-tier steps, with somewhat lower but still strong accuracy (76–82%) on more difficult mid-range and frontier tiers. Competing methods, RouteLLM and FrugalGPT, when naively applied per-step, achieve only 31% and 44% cost reduction, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Step-level, trajectory-aware routing is crucial for efficient agentic systems, as subtask complexity varies widely within a single workflow. A small, fast classifier such as AgentRouter can substantially cut costs while retaining near-frontier quality, outperforming single-turn routing methods that ignore trajectory-level dependencies. This suggests that future systems should treat routing as a sequential decision problem over trajectories rather than independent single queries.

title: Fairness Beyond Anonymization? Demographic Leakage in German LLM-Generated Resumes
comment: Accepted at ECML PKDD 2026 Workshop on Bias and Fairness in AI [BIAS 2026@ ECML/PKDD]
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into AI-assisted hiring pipelines, including automated resume generation and screening. Under the EU AI Act, the hiring domain is classified as high-risk, making fairness and transparency critical requirements. Existing work has primarily focused on explicit hiring decisions, while less attention has been paid to whether generated resumes themselves encode recoverable demographic information. In this work, we conduct a two-stage audit of demographic leakage in German-language LLM-generated resumes. First, we use ChatGPT (GPT-4o-mini), Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite, and multiple scales of the open-weight Qwen 3 model family (4B, 8B, and 14B) to generate resumes from real anonymized job-matching profiles, systematically varying gender- and ethnicity-associated names while holding qualifications constant. Second, we simulate a downstream resume screening scenario, where the generated resumes are first anonymized and gender-neutralized, before demographic leakage classifiers are trained on the resulting texts. We find that, despite these interventions, classifiers reliably distinguish between resumes generated with male and female names. This leakage is not driven by overtly gendered wording, but by subtle differences in the usage of semantically equivalent, formally gender-neutral terms in German. In contrast, ethnicity-related leakage remains comparatively weak across models. Our findings demonstrate that apparently neutral resume generation can still preserve highly predictive demographic signals, raising concerns about anonymization-based fairness interventions in multilingual AI hiring pipelines.

AI.tldr: The paper audits whether LLM-generated German résumés leak demographic information (gender, ethnicity) even after anonymization and gender-neutralization, and finds substantial residual gender leakage but limited ethnicity leakage.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly used in high-risk hiring contexts regulated by the EU AI Act, it is crucial to ensure fairness and transparency. While prior work has mainly examined explicit hiring decisions, there is a gap in understanding whether the supposedly neutral résumés generated by LLMs still encode demographic information that can be recovered downstream, undermining anonymization-based fairness strategies.
AI.method: The authors run a two-stage audit. Stage 1: They prompt several LLMs (GPT-4o-mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite, and Qwen 3 models of 4B/8B/14B) to generate German résumés from real anonymized job-matching profiles, systematically varying only gender- and ethnicity-associated names while keeping qualifications constant. Stage 2: They simulate a screening pipeline by anonymizing and gender-neutralizing these generated résumés, then train demographic leakage classifiers on the resulting texts to test how well gender or ethnicity can still be inferred.
AI.result: Classifiers can reliably distinguish between résumés generated with male vs. female names, even after anonymization and gender-neutralization. The leakage is not due to obviously gendered words but arises from subtle patterns in how semantically equivalent, formally gender-neutral German terms are used. In contrast, models show relatively weak leakage related to ethnicity across the tested LLMs.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based résumé generation, even when followed by anonymization and gender-neutralization, can preserve strong predictive signals for gender, casting doubt on the effectiveness of naïve anonymization-based fairness interventions in multilingual AI hiring systems. Fair AI hiring requires deeper controls on how LLMs encode and express demographic information, beyond surface-level removal of explicit identifiers.

title: A Compact Stance-Indexed Anterior-Posterior COP Representation for Parkinson's Disease Classification from Plantar VGRF
comment: 24 pages, 7 figures; supplementary material is included in the same PDF
summary: Parkinson's disease alters gait and bilateral coordination, but machine-learning performance also depends on how continuous gait signals are represented. This study investigates whether preserving anterior-posterior center-of-pressure (AP-COP) information at fixed locations across normalized stance provides a compact and informative representation of plantar-force gait signals. Bilateral vertical ground reaction force recordings from 165 participants in the Gait in Parkinson's Disease Database were evaluated using repeated fully nested participant-level cross-validation. We propose AP-COP10, comprising AP-COP position and bilateral asymmetry across five stance windows. AP-COP10 achieved an AUC of 0.894 and outperformed three harmonized literature-derived COP representations under the same evaluation pipeline. The complementary 25 non-AP-COP descriptors alone achieved an AUC of 0.856, while the complete 35-feature representation achieved 0.908. Removing AP-COP10 from the complete representation produced a statistically supported loss in discrimination, whereas adding the complementary descriptors to AP-COP10 yielded only a small, unsupported improvement. Feature competition indicated that the most informative stance-indexed descriptors were concentrated in early and early-mid stance, while source-study holdout and sensor-perturbation analyses supported the robustness of the representation. These findings indicate that stance-indexed AP-COP retains discriminative information that is not readily recovered by broader engineered gait descriptors, supporting compact and interpretable representations for machine-learning analysis of pathological gait.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a compact, stance-indexed representation of anterior-posterior center-of-pressure (AP-COP) from plantar-force gait signals that improves machine-learning based discrimination of Parkinson's disease gait over existing COP feature sets.
AI.motivation: Gait in Parkinson's disease is altered and bilaterally uncoordinated, but machine-learning performance for detecting these changes depends strongly on how continuous gait signals are encoded as features. Existing center-of-pressure (COP) representations may be suboptimal, and there is a need for a compact, interpretable feature set that preserves key discriminative information while remaining robust and suitable for cross-study applications.
AI.method: Using bilateral vertical ground reaction forces from 165 participants in the Gait in Parkinson's Disease Database, the authors computed stance-normalized features describing anterior-posterior center-of-pressure (AP-COP) position and asymmetry across five stance windows, yielding a 10-feature set called AP-COP10. They evaluated it with repeated fully nested participant-level cross-validation, compared it against three harmonized literature-based COP feature representations, combined it with 25 additional non-AP-COP gait descriptors, and conducted feature competition, source-study holdout, and sensor-perturbation analyses to assess informativeness and robustness.
AI.result: AP-COP10 alone achieved an AUC of 0.894 and outperformed three existing COP representations under the same evaluation framework. The 25 non-AP-COP descriptors alone achieved an AUC of 0.856. The full 35-feature set (AP-COP10 plus 25 additional descriptors) reached an AUC of 0.908. Removing AP-COP10 from the full set caused a statistically significant drop in discrimination, whereas adding the 25 complementary descriptors to AP-COP10 offered only a small, statistically unsupported gain. The most informative stance-indexed features were concentrated in early and early-mid stance, and the representation remained robust under source-study holdout and sensor-perturbation tests.
AI.conclusion: A stance-indexed AP-COP representation provides a compact, interpretable, and robust encoding of plantar-force gait signals that captures discriminative information about Parkinsonian gait not recovered by broader engineered gait descriptors. This supports using such low-dimensional, physiologically meaningful features for machine-learning analysis of pathological gait and suggests that early stance phases contain particularly valuable information for classification.

title: The Situated Identity Test: Distinguishing Persistent Cognitive Identity from Persona Imitation
comment: 28 pages, 1 figure, 9 tables; open-source benchmark and reference implementation available at https://github.com/openkedge/sitbench
summary: Large language models can convincingly adopt personas, recall past dialogues, and weave rich autobiographies. Yet this conversational eloquence conceals a fundamental attribution problem: looking the part does not mean having lived the life. Two individuals can share identical public profiles--the same age, hometown, occupation, and personality traits--while possessing entirely distinct private histories, relationships, and acquired skills. When conditioned solely on that shared profile, an agent lacks the information required to determine which lineage is correct. We introduce the Situated Identity Test (SIT), an architecture-independent framework that evaluates whether an agent's behavior is functionally attributable to a specific developmental lineage. Grounded identity requires both appropriate knowledge of recorded experiences and appropriate ignorance of ungrounded ones, bounded by what the identity has actually acquired rather than what its underlying foundation model knows. We prove that any policy conditioned solely on a compressed profile is bounded by an average situated validity of at most 1/m across m colliding life histories on lineage-discriminative queries (at most 50% for paired lineages). We instantiate this framework in SITBench, an evaluation suite designed for 25 profile-collision pairs (50 distinct lineages) across 10,000 planned probes and nine architectural configurations. Supported by an open-source reference implementation, deterministic test fixtures, and empirical pilot evaluations on frontier foundation models (GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 5), we formalize the failure modes of persona prompting under profile collision and provide an assurance harness for evaluating episodic continuity, structured state, and epistemic boundaries.

AI.tldr: They propose a test (SIT) and benchmark (SITBench) to check whether an AI agent’s claimed persona is actually grounded in a specific life history, not just plausible-sounding role-play.
AI.motivation: LLMs can role-play convincing personas and autobiographies, but this surface coherence hides a fundamental issue: the model may not actually be tied to a specific, coherent developmental history. When multiple distinct life histories share the same high-level profile (age, job, traits, etc.), an agent prompted only with that profile cannot know which detailed history is correct. This undermines claims about grounded identity, episodic continuity, and correct limits on what the agent should or should not know.
AI.method: They formally define the Situated Identity Test (SIT), an architecture-agnostic framework to test whether an agent’s behavior can be attributed to a particular developmental lineage. They require both correct knowledge of experiences that the identity actually had and correct ignorance of experiences it did not have, relative to the underlying foundation model’s knowledge. They provide theoretical bounds showing that any policy relying only on a compressed profile will perform poorly (on average 1/m correctness across m colliding life histories) on questions that distinguish those histories. They then build SITBench, a concrete benchmark with 25 pairs of colliding profiles (50 total lineages), ~10k probes, and nine different architectural setups, plus an open-source implementation and deterministic fixtures for evaluation.
AI.result: They derive a formal upper bound on situated validity for policies conditioned only on compressed profiles under profile collisions, highlighting inherent limitations of persona prompting. They implement SITBench and run pilot empirical evaluations on strong foundation models (GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 5), demonstrating and characterizing failure modes in how these models handle persona, memory, and knowledge boundaries when identities collide.
AI.conclusion: Persona prompting over compressed profiles cannot reliably produce agents whose behavior is grounded in a specific life history when multiple life histories share that profile; performance is fundamentally bounded and often poor on discriminative queries. The SIT framework and SITBench provide a principled way to test and analyze whether agents maintain coherent episodic continuity and proper epistemic boundaries, offering an assurance harness for future identity- and memory-sensitive agent designs.

title: R-GEAN: Regimen-Guided Edit Action Network for Within-Admission Medication Change Prediction
summary: The medications prescribed to a patient often change during a hospital admission as clinicians start, stop, or continue therapies. We study whether models can predict which medication classes are added or removed between 24 hours after admission and discharge. Metrics that compare the complete discharge regimen can reward models for copying medications that remain unchanged, even when they identify no actual changes. We therefore introduce a leakage-controlled benchmark that predicts net ATC3 additions and removals using only prior completed admissions and information available within the first 24 hours of the current admission. Addition candidates are classes not active at 24 hours, whereas removal candidates are classes active at that time. We also introduce R-GEAN, an asymmetric candidate-scoring network with independent addition and removal predictors. Across 240,480 admissions from 82,286 patients, R-GEAN achieves the highest predefined summary of addition, removal, changed-regimen, and action-pattern performance, termed the edit composite (0.464), compared with 0.435 for the strongest primary comparator. Reimplemented RETAIN, GAMENet, and MICRON baselines obtain 0.428, 0.420, and 0.288, respectively. R-GEAN's advantage is concentrated in correctly identifying medication classes no longer active at discharge, while rare additions and admissions with multiple medication changes remain difficult. Rankings based on micro-F1 over the reconstructed discharge regimen and the edit composite correlate weakly across the evaluated models (Spearman r = 0.20). The continuation baseline achieves the highest complete-regimen score despite predicting no additions or removals. These results show that complete-regimen and edit-level evaluation measure different aspects of medication prediction. The benchmark evaluates observed prescribing changes, not treatment appropriateness

AI.tldr: They propose a new, leakage-controlled benchmark and a specialized model (R-GEAN) to predict which medication classes will be added or removed between 24 hours after hospital admission and discharge, showing that edit-level evaluation reveals different model behavior than full-regimen prediction.
AI.motivation: Existing medication prediction work often evaluates models on the complete discharge regimen, which can over-credit models that simply reproduce medications that stay the same and may even reward models that predict no changes at all. The authors want to focus specifically on clinically meaningful changes—medication classes added or removed during a hospitalization—while avoiding information leakage from future data and disentangling evaluation of edits from overall regimen similarity.
AI.method: They define a leakage-controlled benchmark that uses only data from prior completed admissions plus information available in the first 24 hours of the current admission to predict net additions and removals of medication classes at the ATC3 level. Addition candidates are drug classes not active at 24 hours, while removal candidates are those active at that time. They introduce R-GEAN, an asymmetric candidate-scoring network that has separate predictors for additions and removals, and compare it against reimplemented baselines such as RETAIN, GAMENet, MICRON, and a continuation baseline. Performance is summarized via an "edit composite" metric that combines addition, removal, changed-regimen, and action-pattern performance; they also compare with micro-F1 over reconstructed discharge regimens.
AI.result: On 240,480 admissions from 82,286 patients, R-GEAN attains the best edit composite score (0.464), outperforming the strongest competitor (0.435) and other baselines (RETAIN 0.428, GAMENet 0.420, MICRON 0.288). Its main gains come from correctly identifying medication classes that are no longer active at discharge, but it still struggles with rare additions and cases with many medication changes. Rankings of models differ substantially depending on whether one uses micro-F1 over the reconstructed discharge regimen or the edit composite (Spearman r = 0.20), and the trivial continuation baseline gets the highest complete-regimen score while predicting no edits.
AI.conclusion: R-GEAN is more effective than established baselines at predicting which medication classes will be stopped or changed during a hospital stay, especially for removals. However, predicting rare additions and complex multi-change admissions remains challenging. The work demonstrates that edit-level metrics and complete-regimen metrics capture different capabilities: a model can look strong on full-regimen reconstruction while failing to predict actual prescribing changes. Their benchmark is designed to assess observed prescribing changes, not whether the underlying treatments are clinically appropriate.

title: The Role of AI in Online Reviews
summary: The rapid adoption of large language models (LLMs) creates new opportunities for strategic content generation on online platforms, including potentially harmful forms of manipulation that may undermine platform effectiveness and reshape platform dynamics. However, measuring such activity is difficult because AI-generated content is rarely directly observable. We introduce an empirical approach that leverages discrete LLM supply shocks - abrupt changes in model prices and capabilities, and contrasts verified with non-verified reviews to identify changes in platform activity associated with generative AI supply improvements. We apply this approach to more than 13 million reviews from Trustpilot, one of the leading online platforms for business reviews. A robust finding is that following LLM supply shocks, unverified reviews shift toward greater negativity: more 1-stars, fewer 5-stars, and lower ratings, with effects driven primarily by new model releases and concentrated among firms with the lowest and highest review volumes, suggesting that strategic AI use may reshape platform competition dynamics. We further find that LLM supply shocks trigger short, concentrated bursts of review activity. Together, these findings suggest that generative AI is already reshaping how reputation and competition operate on online platforms.

AI.tldr: The paper empirically studies how large language model (LLM) improvements affect online review platforms, finding that AI availability coincides with more negative, strategically generated unverified reviews and bursts of activity.
AI.motivation: As LLMs become widespread, actors can strategically generate large volumes of persuasive or manipulative content on review platforms, but it is hard to measure this because AI-generated reviews are not directly observable. The authors aim to understand whether and how advances in generative AI are already reshaping reputation systems and competition dynamics on major review platforms.
AI.method: The authors exploit discrete "supply shocks" in LLMs—sudden changes in model prices and capabilities—to identify behavioral changes on a large review platform. They compare trends in verified vs. unverified reviews on Trustpilot using over 13 million reviews, focusing on periods around new LLM releases and price changes, and examine shifts in rating distributions and temporal patterns of review activity.
AI.result: After LLM supply shocks, unverified reviews become systematically more negative: more 1-star ratings, fewer 5-star ratings, and lower average scores. These effects are driven mainly by new model releases and are strongest for firms at the extremes of review volume (very low or very high). Additionally, the shocks are associated with short, concentrated bursts of review submissions.
AI.conclusion: Generative AI is already affecting how online reputations and competitive dynamics evolve on review platforms. The patterns observed—more negative unverified reviews and bursty activity around LLM supply shocks—are consistent with strategic, AI-assisted manipulation, suggesting that platforms and policymakers need to account for AI-driven behavior in the design and governance of reputation systems.

title: OptiSkill: A Hierarchical and Evolving SkillBank for LLM-Based Optimization Modeling
summary: Automated operations research (OR) modeling requires LLMs to translate natural-language decision problems into correct mathematical programs. Existing methods can improve individual formulations, but they often solve problems in isolation, retaining little reusable experience and repeating similar formulation errors. Prior memory-based approaches store examples, thoughts, or insights as references, while OR modeling requires reusable formulation skills that transfer across problem narratives and guide concrete modeling decisions. We propose OptiSkill, a skill-augmented framework that builds a hierarchical and evolving SkillBank for LLM-based OR modeling. SkillBank stores solver-verified experience as reusable skills, with Global Strategies for problem-level formulation skeletons and Step Experiences for local error-prevention rules. It is further refined through stable batch-level test-time evolution, where candidate skills are incorporated only after validation. Experiments on eight OR modeling benchmarks show that OptiSkill improves formulation accuracy across LLM backbones, outperforms strong agentic baselines, and gains further by expanding SkillBank coverage and reliability. Code and data are available at https://github.com/rachhhhing/OptiSkill

AI.tldr: OptiSkill is a framework that augments LLMs with a hierarchical, evolving bank of reusable optimization-modeling skills, significantly improving automated OR problem formulation accuracy over prior approaches.
AI.motivation: LLMs can translate natural-language decision problems into mathematical programs, but they tend to repeat similar formulation mistakes and fail to reuse past experience. Existing memory-based methods mostly store examples or reflections tied to specific problems, which don’t generalize well across diverse OR narratives. There is a need for a mechanism that captures reusable, solver-verified modeling skills that can transfer to new tasks and systematically reduce repeated formulation errors.
AI.method: The authors propose OptiSkill, which introduces a hierarchical SkillBank for LLM-based OR modeling. SkillBank has two main components: (1) Global Strategies, which represent high-level, problem-level formulation skeletons (e.g., how to structure decisions, objectives, and constraints for a given OR task type); and (2) Step Experiences, which encode fine-grained, local rules that prevent recurring formulation errors (e.g., common constraint mis-specifications). These skills are extracted and updated from solved problems with solver verification, ensuring correctness. The framework employs a batch-level test-time evolution process: candidate skills learned from new solved instances are only integrated into SkillBank after being validated on a batch to ensure stability and reliability. During inference, LLMs consult the SkillBank to guide both the overall model structure and local formulation decisions.
AI.result: On eight OR modeling benchmarks, OptiSkill yields higher formulation accuracy than baseline LLM systems, including strong agentic approaches that use tools or multi-step reasoning. The improvements hold across different LLM backbones, and performance further increases as the SkillBank is expanded and refined, demonstrating positive returns from accumulating solver-verified skills.
AI.conclusion: By organizing solver-verified modeling knowledge into an evolving hierarchical SkillBank, OptiSkill enables LLMs to reuse abstract formulation strategies and concrete error-prevention rules across OR tasks. This leads to more accurate and robust automated OR modeling compared to prior methods that treat each problem in isolation or rely on less structured memory. The results suggest that skill-centric, verifiable knowledge accumulation is an effective direction for improving LLM-based modeling systems in operations research and potentially other structured reasoning domains.

title: PII-TRACE: A Benchmark for Context-Aware PII Detection in Multi-Turn LLM Conversations
summary: LLM assistants and agentic systems log long multi-turn conversations. AI providers often scan these conversations for Personally Identifiable Information (PII) and mask the PII before storing or processing conversation data. Yet most PII detectors and benchmarks target self-contained records rather than cross-turn evaluation. To evaluate PII detection across turns in multi-turn conversations, we introduce PII-TRACE (Tracing Recurring PII Across Conversational Exchanges), to our knowledge the first PII benchmark to assess whether detectors identify PII in conversational contexts and cover every mention of a recurring identifier across turns. PII-TRACE contains 13,148 synthetic multi-turn dialogues in 13 languages with character-level spans and identifier clusters. Across eleven baselines, including frontier LLMs, no detector achieves full entity-level coverage without substantial false positives on PII-free conversations, and single-pass reading loses a third of the gold characters on long dialogues. To close this gap, we introduce PII-Tracer, a compact 0.6B-parameter detector trained with conversation-level supervision. PII-Tracer attains the highest entity-level coverage of any system we evaluate and also performs strongly on standard single-record benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PII-TRACE, a multilingual benchmark for detecting and tracking recurring PII across multi-turn conversations, and PII-Tracer, a compact model that achieves state-of-the-art entity-level PII coverage with fewer false positives than existing systems.
AI.motivation: Existing PII detectors and benchmarks are designed mainly for isolated, self-contained records (like single documents or forms) rather than long, multi-turn conversational logs produced by LLM assistants and agentic systems. In such conversations, PII can be spread across turns, recur, and appear in context-dependent ways. Providers need reliable, conversation-aware PII detection to safely log, store, and process conversational data without leaking sensitive information. There was no benchmark specifically designed to test whether detectors can (a) recognize PII in conversational contexts and (b) consistently capture all mentions of the same identifier across turns, especially in multiple languages.
AI.method: The authors construct PII-TRACE, a benchmark of 13,148 synthetic multi-turn dialogues in 13 languages. Each dialogue includes character-level PII spans and clusters that link recurring mentions of the same identifier across turns. They evaluate eleven baseline detectors, including strong frontier LLMs, under cross-turn and entity-level metrics, as well as measuring performance on PII-free conversations to assess false positives. They also study the effect of single-pass reading on long dialogues, showing how much gold PII is missed. To improve performance, they propose PII-Tracer, a 0.6B-parameter model trained with supervision at the conversation level so it can track entities and PII mentions across turns.
AI.result: On PII-TRACE, none of the eleven baseline systems achieves full entity-level coverage without incurring many false positives on conversations with no PII, and approaches that only read the conversation once miss about one-third of gold PII characters in long dialogues. PII-Tracer, despite being compact, achieves the highest entity-level coverage among all evaluated systems while maintaining strong precision on PII-free data. Furthermore, it also performs competitively on standard, single-record PII benchmarks, indicating that its improvements in conversational settings do not come at the expense of performance on traditional tasks.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that conversational, cross-turn PII detection is substantially harder than detecting PII in isolated records and that existing methods and LLMs are inadequate for reliable entity-level coverage in long, multilingual dialogues. PII-TRACE fills an important benchmarking gap by focusing on recurring PII across turns and languages. The proposed PII-Tracer model, trained with conversation-level supervision, sets a new state-of-the-art on this benchmark while remaining strong on standard PII tasks, suggesting that specialized, conversation-aware detectors are needed to safely process LLM conversation logs at scale.

title: PINNForge: Execution-Grounded Evolutionary Design of Physics-Informed Neural Networks for PDE Solving via Large Language Models
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) require coordinated choices over network representation, sampling, loss construction, and optimization, while effective configurations often vary substantially across partial differential equations (PDEs). Existing automated PINN design methods can search candidate configurations, but information revealed during actual training is still used mainly for evaluation rather than to improve subsequent design, leading to repeated trial-and-error and inefficient use of training budget. We propose PINNsForge, an LLM-driven evolutionary framework for execution-feedback-based automated PINN design. PINNsForge generates diverse candidate configurations from PDE-related prior knowledge, evaluates them through actual training, and feeds high-performing designs together with accumulated execution evidence back to the LLM. Guided by observed optimization behavior, the LLM then refines, recombines, and explores coupled PINN design components, forming a continual cycle of generation, execution, feedback, and evolution. Unlike one-shot search or evaluation-only feedback, PINNsForge progressively converts training experience into improved design decisions for the target PDE. Across 25 PDE benchmarks, PINNsForge achieves the lowest mean MSE on 24 tasks compared with RoPINN, PINNsFormer, and PINNsAgent. Ablation studies further confirm the importance of the PDE knowledge base, execution feedback, and evolutionary search: removing these components increases the mean MSE to 3.74$\times$, 12.10$\times$, and 10.10$\times$ that of the full PINNsForge, respectively.

AI.tldr: PINNsForge is an LLM-driven evolutionary framework that automatically designs physics-informed neural networks by iteratively using training execution feedback to refine network and training configurations for specific PDEs, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy on most of 25 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Designing effective PINNs for different PDEs requires many coupled decisions about architecture, sampling, loss, and optimization. These choices are problem-dependent and current automated methods mainly treat training runs as passive evaluations, leading to repeated trial-and-error and inefficient use of computational budget. There is a need for a framework that can actively use information from the training process itself to continually improve PINN designs for a given PDE.
AI.method: The authors introduce PINNsForge, an LLM-driven evolutionary design loop. First, an LLM generates diverse PINN configuration candidates based on prior PDE knowledge. These candidates are then instantiated and evaluated via actual training runs. Performance metrics and detailed execution evidence (e.g., optimization behavior) are fed back into the LLM. Guided by this feedback, the LLM refines and recombines high-performing designs, jointly exploring architecture, sampling, loss construction, and optimization. This cycle of generation, execution, and feedback is repeated, forming an evolutionary search process that progressively tailors PINN designs to the target PDE.
AI.result: On a suite of 25 PDE benchmarks, PINNsForge achieves the lowest mean MSE on 24 tasks when compared with prior automated PINN design methods including RoPINN, PINNsFormer, and PINNsAgent, demonstrating superior accuracy and robustness. Ablation studies show that removing the PDE knowledge base, the execution feedback mechanism, or the evolutionary search substantially degrades performance, increasing mean MSE by factors of 3.74x, 12.10x, and 10.10x respectively relative to the full system.
AI.conclusion: Execution-feedback-based, LLM-driven evolutionary search is an effective approach for automated PINN design. By continually converting training experience into improved design decisions and leveraging PDE-specific prior knowledge, PINNsForge outperforms existing methods on a broad range of PDE problems. The components of PDE knowledge, explicit use of execution feedback, and evolutionary refinement are all critical contributors to its performance.

title: Evaluating Personal Information Output from Conversational Interactions in Generative AI Systems
comment: Accepted at the 19th IIAI International Congress on Advanced Applied Informatics (IIAI-AAI 2026)
summary: This exploratory pilot study evaluates the scope and perceived accuracy of personal information output from ongoing conversational interactions in generative AI systems using GPT-5.2 Instant and GPT-5.2 Thinking, categorized into three output types: Fact, Inference, and Confidence. Based on the evaluation results obtained from 15 Japanese participants, differences in model design have limited impact on personal information output tendencies. Compared with the Inference type, the Fact type shows a more conservative output pattern. Regarding attribute categories, the findings indicate that Core Personal attributes associated with identification are treated relatively conservatively, whereas Behavioral and Linguistic attributes show higher accuracy across both Fact and Inference outputs. Furthermore, Holistic Profile, Psychological and Cognitive, and Residual attributes are more readily inferred, even when not supported by explicit factual outputs. Notably, the lack of null outputs for these attributes in the Inference type suggests that such inferred profiles may be constructed from indirectly available contextual information. The findings may contribute to future discussions regarding privacy awareness and personal information inference in generative AI systems.

AI.tldr: The paper explores what kinds of personal information generative AI systems infer or state during ongoing conversations, and how accurate and conservative these outputs are across different attribute categories and model designs.
AI.motivation: With the increasing use of conversational generative AI, there is a concern that such systems may infer or expose personal information about users, even beyond what is explicitly provided. However, there is limited empirical evidence on what kinds of personal attributes are output, how accurate they are, and how model design affects these patterns. This study aims to provide initial empirical insight into the scope and nature of personal information outputs, informing privacy and safety discussions.
AI.method: The authors conducted an exploratory pilot study with 15 Japanese participants interacting with two generative AI variants (GPT-5.2 Instant and GPT-5.2 Thinking). They categorized the AI’s personal-information-related outputs into three types—Fact (stated as factual), Inference (derived or guessed information), and Confidence (self-reported certainty)—and analyzed them across different attribute categories (Core Personal, Behavioral and Linguistic, Holistic Profile, Psychological and Cognitive, Residual). They then compared output tendencies and perceived accuracy between model types and output types.
AI.result: Model design differences between GPT-5.2 Instant and GPT-5.2 Thinking had limited impact on overall personal information output tendencies. Fact-type outputs were more conservative than Inference-type outputs. Core Personal attributes related to identification were handled conservatively, while Behavioral and Linguistic attributes showed relatively high accuracy for both Fact and Inference types. Holistic Profile, Psychological and Cognitive, and Residual attributes were more frequently inferred even when not grounded in explicit factual outputs. In the Inference type, these attributes rarely had null outputs, implying continuous profile construction from context.
AI.conclusion: Generative AI systems can infer a wide range of personal attributes from conversational context, often going beyond explicitly provided information, especially for profile-like, psychological, and residual attributes. While core identifying attributes are treated more conservatively and behavior/linguistic traits are inferred with relatively high accuracy, many higher-level personal characteristics are readily inferred without explicit factual basis. These results highlight the need for stronger privacy-awareness, transparency, and controls around personal information inference in conversational AI design and policy.

title: Spatial-Interactor: Learning Spatial Reasoning through Interaction with the Observable Physical World
summary: Spatial reasoning is essential for vision-language models (VLMs) to understand and act in the physical world. Reasoning in dynamic environments requires VLMs to perceive local state transitions caused by object motion and viewpoint changes and integrate them over long trajectories to maintain an updated spatial state, yet existing VLMs remain limited in both capabilities. Current spatial training primarily focuses on static questions about object attributes and spatial relations, providing limited direct supervision for state transitions; in contrast, interaction trajectories naturally connect a preceding observation, an action, and a subsequent observation, offering direct supervision for local state transitions, while complete trajectories reveal dependencies among consecutive transitions. We therefore introduce Spatial-Interactor, a framework that trains VLMs to model physical-world state transitions through interaction, organizing this learning process into a three-level curriculum covering L1 passive world-state transitions, L2 active self-state transitions, and L3 long-horizon interaction trajectories. Accordingly, we construct the Learning from Spatial Interaction dataset (LSI-108K) from simulated and real interaction trajectories, with tasks aligned with the objective of each level. Our two-stage training strategy applies Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) to L1 and L2 for local transition modeling, and On-Policy Distillation (OPD) then uses privileged self-distillation: a teacher branch given segment-level transition descriptions supervises the student's on-policy CoT, helping the student learn to integrate consecutive transitions over L3 long trajectories. Experiments across multiple VLMs and spatial benchmarks show consistent gains in local transition modeling and long-horizon integration.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Spatial-Interactor, a training framework and dataset (LSI-108K) that teach vision-language models to understand and update spatial states in dynamic environments via a three-level interaction-based curriculum and a two-stage training strategy, significantly improving both local transition modeling and long-horizon spatial reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing vision-language models struggle with spatial reasoning in dynamic environments, particularly in tracking how the world changes due to object motion and viewpoint shifts and in integrating these changes over long trajectories. Current training data mostly offer static supervision (object attributes and relations in single snapshots), providing little direct guidance on state transitions. However, interaction trajectories naturally encode how actions change the world and how consecutive changes depend on each other. The paper is motivated by the need to leverage such interaction data to explicitly train VLMs to model physical-world state transitions and maintain an updated spatial state over time.
AI.method: The authors propose Spatial-Interactor, a three-level curriculum that structures spatial interaction learning as: (L1) passive world-state transitions (observing how the environment changes without the agent acting), (L2) active self-state transitions (how the agent’s own actions and viewpoint changes affect observations), and (L3) long-horizon interaction trajectories (integrating many local transitions over time). They build a dataset, LSI-108K, from simulated and real interaction trajectories, with tasks tailored to each level. Training occurs in two stages: (1) Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on L1 and L2 tasks to learn local transition modeling; (2) On-Policy Distillation (OPD), where a teacher model that has access to segment-level transition descriptions supervises a student model’s on-policy chain-of-thought over L3 trajectories, effectively distilling privileged transition knowledge into the student to master long-horizon integration.
AI.result: Across multiple underlying VLM architectures and various spatial reasoning benchmarks, Spatial-Interactor yields consistent performance improvements. Models trained with this framework show better accuracy in predicting local state transitions and enhanced ability to integrate sequences of transitions for long-horizon spatial reasoning tasks compared to baselines trained only on conventional static spatial data.
AI.conclusion: Interaction trajectories can serve as effective supervision for teaching VLMs to model physical-world state transitions and maintain updated spatial representations in dynamic environments. The Spatial-Interactor framework, with its three-level curriculum, specialized LSI-108K dataset, and two-stage SFT+OPD training, significantly enhances both local and long-horizon spatial reasoning. This suggests that structuring training around explicit state transitions and leveraging privileged teacher information is a promising direction for making VLMs more competent in real-world interactive scenarios.

title: Dissecting Training-Free Uncertainty Estimation in Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across a wide range of multimodal tasks, yet understanding and quantifying their predictive uncertainty remains underexplored despite being central for safety critical applications. In this work, we present a systematic study of training-free uncertainty quantification strategies for MLLMs, categorizing existing approaches into three conceptual families: token-level methods, which operate directly in the text output space; verbalized methods, which elicit uncertainty estimates or abstention signals via natural language prompts; and semantic methods, which measure uncertainty in a semantic meaning space. We benchmark these strategies across multiple datasets, model families, generations, and scales, and find that no single family dominates: token-level entropy (at sampling temperature 1.0) wins on short answers, verbalized abstention on sentence-length responses, and semantic methods on long-form generation.

AI.tldr: The paper systematically studies and benchmarks training-free ways to estimate uncertainty in multimodal large language models (MLLMs), showing that different strategies work best for different answer lengths.
AI.motivation: While MLLMs perform well on many multimodal tasks, their predictive uncertainty is poorly understood and rarely quantified, which is problematic for safety-critical settings that require calibrated confidence and principled abstention.
AI.method: The authors define and categorize training-free uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods for MLLMs into three families—token-level methods based on output token distributions, verbalized methods that ask the model to express its own uncertainty or abstain via prompts, and semantic methods that assess variability in the underlying meaning space. They then benchmark these approaches across diverse datasets, MLLM architectures, model generations, and scales, comparing their effectiveness under different answer types and lengths.
AI.result: The benchmarking shows no universally best UQ strategy: token-level entropy at temperature 1.0 is superior for short answers; verbalized abstention methods work best for sentence-length outputs; and semantic-based UQ is most effective for long-form generations.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty quantification in MLLMs is inherently context-dependent, and practitioners should match the UQ strategy to the response format and task type rather than relying on a single method. The study provides an empirical guide for selecting training-free UQ approaches in multimodal settings, highlighting that different uncertainty families specialize in different generation regimes.

title: Enforcing Narrative Reliability and Epistemic Pacing in LLM-Driven Detective Games via Structured Knowledge Trees
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) enable open-ended dialogue in interactive games, but their non-deterministic outputs make it difficult to preserve authorial control, factual consistency, and the intended sequence of information disclosure. These challenges are particularly significant in detective games, where premature revelation or fabricated details can undermine the logic of player progression. We present a Structured Knowledge Tree architecture coupled with a tri-agent LLM pipeline for controlling dialogue in an open-ended interrogation game. The system separates knowledge retrieval, dialogue generation, and response verification to ensure that the virtual suspect reveals only information permitted by the current narrative state. We evaluate the approach through The Interrogation of Adrian Gale, a playable detective-game testbed, and a formal user study examining hallucination reduction, adherence to authored disclosure sequences, and perceived logical progression. Our results demonstrate that the structured architecture reduces critical hallucinations by 64.78% and entirely prevents premature narrative disclosure. While the strict mechanical constraints introduced usability trade-offs regarding forced conversational reveals, the system successfully enforces rigorous epistemic pacing and provides players with a clear, subjective sense of progression toward solving the case.
