AI.tldr: They build a controlled LLM dialogue system for detective-style interrogation games using a structured knowledge tree and three cooperating LLM agents, which cuts hallucinations and prevents spoilers while keeping a clear sense of investigative progress.
AI.motivation: Open-ended LLM dialogue is attractive for games, but in detective games it can break narrative design by revealing clues too early, inventing facts, or disrupting the intended sequence of information. Designers need a way to get the flexibility of LLMs while keeping tight authorial control over what the NPC knows, when they can reveal it, and how that aligns with puzzle logic and player progression.
AI.method: They design a Structured Knowledge Tree that encodes all story facts and their allowed disclosure states, then implement a tri-agent LLM pipeline with (1) a knowledge-retrieval agent that checks the current narrative/epistemic state and selects what information is legally accessible, (2) a dialogue-generation agent that crafts the suspect’s natural-language replies using only that retrieved knowledge, and (3) a response-verification agent that checks the draft response for hallucinations or premature disclosures against the knowledge tree and narrative rules, forcing revisions if violations are found. They embed this pipeline into a playable interrogation game, The Interrogation of Adrian Gale, and run a user study comparing it to less structured baselines on hallucination rate, disclosure order, and perceived logical progression.
AI.result: In the Adrian Gale testbed and user study, the structured architecture reduces critical hallucinations by about 64.78% and completely eliminates premature narrative disclosures, meaning the suspect never spoils key information before the design allows it. However, the strict constraints sometimes create usability downsides, such as dialogue that feels forced or moments where the system must mechanically steer the conversation to ensure required reveals occur.
AI.conclusion: A structured, multi-agent LLM architecture grounded in an explicit knowledge tree can successfully impose strong epistemic and narrative pacing constraints on open-ended dialogue in detective games. This significantly improves factual reliability and preserves the intended order of clue revelation, giving players a clearer experience of progressing toward a solution, though it introduces some rigidity that affects conversational naturalness and usability. Future work may focus on softening these constraints while retaining control, and on generalizing the approach to other narrative game genres.

title: Replicating the Geometry of Emotion Representations in a Base Open-Weights Model
summary: Sofroniew et al. (2026) report that emotion concepts in Claude Sonnet 4.5 are represented as vectors whose geometry mirrors human affect psychology. We replicate the representational core of that study on the base pretrained model google/gemma-2-27b, inheriting every disclosed parameter, resolving unspecified steps by disclosed rules, and changing only the subject model. From 205,200 newly generated Claude Sonnet 4.5 stories matching the original corpus design, we extract 171 emotion vectors and recover the core results. The leading principal components form an affective circumplex (PC1 carries 26.7% of variance against the original study's ~27%, PC2 13.4% against ~14%), emotions cluster into similar intuitive families, and the geometry holds across a broad late-middle band. The valence axis aligns with human norms (r = 0.72, against 0.81) and is stable across scales and depth. Arousal aligns at r = 0.67 (against 0.66) but only at the full 171-emotion scale and late depth, so we do not classify it as replicated. Extending the original analysis, a 46-layer sweep locates a sharp seam at L22-26, where the geometry consolidates and the vocabulary readout becomes legible. An embedding-layer baseline finds much of the geometry already present in the static token embeddings, with arousal as the exception. On top-activating held-out text, the geometry predicts token-level co-activation at r = 0.907. At least 52% of vectors peak on structurally non-conceptual tokens, a measured floor for max-activation confounds. Even when a document contains the vector's emotion word, the peak lands on that word only 6.1% of the time. Because the subject is a base model and the stimuli are Claude-generated fiction, the recovered structure is a property of the pretrained representation of Claude-rendered emotion. The original's causal and assistant-facing analyses are out of scope. Code and data are released.

AI.tldr: Replication of an LLM emotion-geometry study on a different base model largely recovers the affective structure, probes where in the network it emerges, and quantifies confounds from token-level activation patterns.
AI.motivation: To test whether the affective geometry reported for Claude Sonnet 4.5 generalizes to another large language model (google/gemma-2-27b), and to more precisely localize and qualify how and where emotion representations arise within such models, including potential confounds from token-level activation artifacts.
AI.method: The authors reconstruct Sofroniew et al.’s protocol as exactly as possible, changing only the target model to gemma-2-27b. They generate 205,200 new Claude Sonnet 4.5 stories matching the original corpus design, extract 171 emotion vectors from the model’s activations, and analyze their geometry via PCA, clustering, and correlation with human valence/arousal norms. They perform a 46-layer sweep to see how the geometry evolves across depth, compare with a static embedding-layer baseline, and test whether vector geometry predicts token-level co-activation on held-out text. They also examine which tokens maximally activate each emotion vector to quantify non-conceptual and word-misaligned peaks.
AI.result: Core geometric findings replicate: the first two principal components form an affective circumplex with variance explained close to the original study; emotions cluster into similar intuitive families; and a valence axis correlates strongly with human ratings (r=0.72). Arousal correlations match numerically (r=0.67 vs 0.66) but are fragile and only reliable at the full scale and late layers, so the authors treat arousal as not cleanly replicated. The layer sweep reveals a sharp consolidation of affective geometry and readable vocabulary at layers 22–26. Much of the geometry is already present in static token embeddings, except for arousal. The emotion-geometry predicts token co-activation on held-out text at r=0.907. Over half of emotion vectors peak on structurally non-conceptual tokens, and peaks land on the emotion word itself only 6.1% of the time when present.
AI.conclusion: The affective geometry found in Claude Sonnet 4.5 generalizes in large part to gemma-2-27b, especially for valence, and emerges from a mixture of static embedding structure and mid-to-late-layer consolidation. However, arousal is less robust, and token-level activation analysis reveals substantial confounds from structurally driven, non-conceptual peaks and from misalignment between emotion vectors and their lexical labels. The observed structure is best interpreted as a property of the pretrained representation of Claude-generated emotional language, rather than a full causal or assistant-facing account of emotion in the model.

title: LazyAgent: Demand-Driven Materialization and Physical Optimization of Agentic Programs
summary: Current agent runtimes that plan before acting generally execute a step once it becomes ready. We present LazyAgent, a unified execution framework for agent-authored programs organized around a live, goal-derived demanded set. LazyAgent refreshes a backward closure from requested outputs as execution state changes and materializes a ready node only when the active goal requires it. This replaces repeated local judgments with one linear-time graph analysis followed by constant-time membership tests, allowing programs to remain broad while execution stays request-specific. On programs that describe more than the current request needs, LazyAgent consistently outperforms the strongest goal-stopping eager baseline by refusing unrelated work before it starts. Adding one unrelated product raises the eager bill by 22.5% and LazyAgent's by 0.0%. LazyAgent saves 42.0% of measured CPU on production scientific workflows and 51.7% of container time on a live release gate spanning four repositories. We also prove and verify exact equivalence when the request reaches the whole graph, leaving no unrelated work to avoid. Beyond permission, goal-relative output projection saves up to approximately 90% of a shared step on two third-party test suites while the identical eager control saves 0.0%; the advantage disappears when the omitted output has no other consumer or the request needs it. Ordering, reuse, and pruning can also save cost, but do not replace permission. Finally, we show that current public benchmarks are eager-shaped and contain almost no unrequested work. A pre-registered planning intervention did not broaden them. These findings motivate benchmarks built from standing programs and sequences.

AI.tldr: LazyAgent is an execution framework for agent-authored programs that only executes steps demanded by current goals, avoiding unnecessary work and improving efficiency over eager runtimes when programs describe more than the current request needs.
AI.motivation: Existing agent runtimes typically execute any step as soon as it is ready, even if its results are not needed for the current user request, wasting computation when programs are broader than the immediate goal. There is a need for a principled way to restrict execution to only those parts of a plan that are actually demanded by current goals, while preserving correctness when all outputs are requested.
AI.method: The authors introduce LazyAgent, which organizes execution around a goal-derived demanded set of nodes in the program graph. It maintains a backward closure from requested outputs, updating it as execution state changes, and only materializes nodes that belong to this demanded set. This replaces repeated local scheduling decisions with a single linear-time graph analysis plus constant-time membership tests, and includes formal proofs and empirical evaluation on production scientific workflows, a multi-repository release gate, and third-party test suites.
AI.result: LazyAgent avoids executing unrelated steps, yielding significant efficiency gains when programs are broader than the current request. In experiments, adding an unrelated product increases eager runtime cost by 22.5% but does not affect LazyAgent; it saves 42.0% of CPU on production scientific workflows, 51.7% of container time on a live release gate, and up to ~90% of the cost of a shared step on some third-party test suites. The authors also show that when requests span the entire graph, LazyAgent is exactly equivalent to eager execution. They find that existing public benchmarks are mostly eager-shaped and lack unrequested work, limiting their ability to show such benefits.
AI.conclusion: LazyAgent provides a unified, goal-driven lazy execution model that efficiently restricts agent program execution to only the demanded subset, yielding substantial cost savings without sacrificing correctness when full execution is required. Permission-based, goal-relative output projection is crucial and cannot be replaced by ordering, reuse, or pruning alone. The work further highlights that current benchmarks do not reflect realistic, standing agent programs with surplus capabilities, motivating new benchmark design that includes broader programs and request sequences.

title: Schematize: An Agentic System for Generating and Refining Information-Extraction Schemas for Legal Research
summary: Empirical legal research often relies on turning research questions into structured data extracted from large collections of rulings and judgments. Designing the extraction schema and then extracting the data remain a manual, expertise-heavy bottleneck. We present schematize, an open-source multi-agent system that interactively turns a researcher's problem statement into a validated extraction schema that can later be used for autonomous extraction. Schematize couples (i) a clarification dialogue that elicits implicit expert intent, (ii) iterative schema generation, (iii) data-grounded refinement that tests the schema against documents, and (iv) chat-based post-editing. We evaluated the system with human legal professional, introducing our novel methodology, and schematize achieves top performance in most of tested configurations. While the system is designed to be domain-agnostic and applicable to any document collection, we tailor and evaluate it on legal research problems. We release schematize as a pip-installable Python package with full documentation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces schematize, an open-source multi-agent system that converts legal research problems into validated data-extraction schemas via interactive, document-grounded refinement, reducing manual expert effort in empirical legal research.
AI.motivation: Empirical legal research requires transforming complex legal research questions into structured data extracted from large corpora of rulings and judgments. Currently, defining the extraction schema and performing the extraction is a manual, expertise-heavy, and time-consuming bottleneck, limiting scalability and accessibility for researchers. The authors are motivated to automate and systematize this process, preserving expert intent while reducing effort and making schema design more robust and reusable.
AI.method: The authors design schematize, a multi-agent system that interacts with legal researchers to build extraction schemas. The method combines four components: (i) a clarification dialogue that elicits hidden or implicit expert requirements behind the problem statement; (ii) iterative schema generation, where agents propose and refine candidate schemas; (iii) data-grounded refinement, where the schema is tested and adjusted using actual documents to ensure it captures the needed information consistently; and (iv) chat-based post-editing that lets experts review and fine-tune the schema. The system is implemented as an open-source, pip-installable Python package and evaluated with human legal professionals on real legal research tasks.
AI.result: In evaluations with legal professionals and a new methodology introduced by the authors, schematize achieves top performance across most tested configurations for generating useful, valid extraction schemas that can later support autonomous data extraction. The experiments suggest that the system effectively captures expert intent and produces high-quality schemas with less manual effort compared to traditional approaches.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that schematize successfully addresses a key bottleneck in empirical legal research: designing and validating extraction schemas. By combining interactive clarification, iterative generation, document-based testing, and post-editing, the system can reliably convert research questions into actionable schemas suitable for automated extraction. Although evaluated primarily on legal research problems, the approach is designed to be domain-agnostic and applicable to other document collections. The authors release schematize as a documented, pip-installable open-source tool to foster broader adoption and further research.

title: FireWorldBench: Benchmarking Complex Physical World Intelligence through Coupled-Field Fire Dynamics
summary: Understanding the physical world requires more than object recognition, scene description, and short-term visual prediction, as real-world physical systems involve multiple continuous fields, latent causal mechanisms, partial observations, and intervention-sensitive dynamics. We propose FireWorldBench, a benchmark for evaluating complex physical world intelligence in multimodal large language models and agents through coupled-field fire dynamics. Fire provides a canonical stress-test environment, where multiple interacting physical fields jointly shape observable states and temporal dynamics. FireWorldBench is organized along two complementary axes, a physical capability axis and a fire scenario task axis, jointly covering physical-state understanding, temporal dynamics, causal mechanisms, and intervention reasoning. The benchmark comprises 520 fire-world entries, including 494 controlled simulation worlds and 26 real-world-aligned event groups, spanning 47 scene archetypes across 7 environment families. These entries combine structured textual observations, multiple 2D physical-field visualizations, and 3D event-level scene modeling, yielding 9,074 text-image interleaved question-answer pairs across choice-based and open-ended report-generation formats. FireWorldBench evaluates whether models can infer latent physical states, explain underlying mechanisms, forecast coupled-field evolution, and assess intervention consequences from multimodal partial observations, providing a challenging testbed for complex physical world intelligence.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces FireWorldBench, a multimodal benchmark based on complex fire dynamics to evaluate whether large language models and agents can reason about coupled physical fields, latent states, and interventions in realistic physical environments.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks focus mostly on static perception (objects, scenes) or short-term prediction and do not capture the complexity of real-world physical systems that involve multiple interacting fields, hidden causal structure, partial observability, and intervention-sensitive dynamics. There is a need for a systematic way to test whether multimodal LLMs can understand and reason about such complex physical processes rather than only recognize visual patterns.
AI.method: The authors design FireWorldBench, a benchmark centered on fire as a canonical complex physical process. They construct 520 "fire-world" entries, the majority simulated and some aligned to real events, spanning diverse environments and scene archetypes. Each entry provides structured textual observations, 2D visualizations of multiple physical fields, and 3D scene modeling. Along two axes—physical capability (states, dynamics, causality, interventions) and fire scenario tasks—they generate 9,074 multimodal QA items in both multiple-choice and open-ended formats. The benchmark tasks require inferring latent states, explaining mechanisms, forecasting dynamics of coupled fields, and reasoning about consequences of interventions.
AI.result: FireWorldBench offers a large and diverse set of multimodal question-answer pairs grounded in complex fire dynamics, with coverage across 7 environment families, 47 scene archetypes, and both simulated and real-world-aligned scenarios. It systematically probes multiple aspects of physical reasoning—state estimation, dynamics prediction, causal explanation, and intervention assessment—under partial observability. While the abstract does not report specific model scores, it positions the benchmark as challenging for current multimodal LLMs.
AI.conclusion: FireWorldBench provides a challenging, structured testbed for assessing complex physical world intelligence in multimodal models and agents. By using coupled-field fire dynamics and rich multimodal representations, it goes beyond traditional perception benchmarks to evaluate whether models can infer hidden physical states, understand causal mechanisms, predict temporal evolution, and reason about interventions in realistic, partially observed physical environments.

title: SALSA: Semi-Autonomous Literature Summarization Assistant
summary: SALSA (Semi-Autonomous Literature Summarization Assistant) is an open- source, human-in-the-loop platform for extracting structured scientific datasets from multimodal literature sources. The software combines document parsing, large language models, optical character recognition, computer vision, figure digitization, and user-guided correction tools to recover structured information from text, tables, figures, and captions. Users can configure extraction stages, define dataset schemas, perform interventions on digitized figures, and export verified data for downstream analysis and machine learning. SALSA is designed to automate repetitive literature curation tasks while preserving oversight where expert judgment is required. By supporting customizable extraction workflows across diverse input types, the software provides a flexible framework for scalable, reliable data curation for materials research, and potentially across several disciplines. Users are responsible for ensuring that all inputs, extraction workflows, and downstream uses comply with applicable publisher agreements, copyright and licensing terms, institutional policies, and data-use requirements.

AI.tldr: SALSA is an open-source, human-in-the-loop platform that uses multimodal AI and user oversight to convert scientific literature (text, tables, figures) into structured datasets for scalable, reliable data curation.
AI.motivation: Scientific data needed for analysis and machine learning is often locked in heterogeneous, multimodal literature (text, tables, figures, captions), and manually curating these data is slow, repetitive, and difficult to scale while maintaining quality. There is a need for a flexible, semi-automated tool that accelerates extraction while keeping expert control and ensuring compliance with data-use constraints.
AI.method: The authors build SALSA, an open-source platform that integrates document parsing, large language models, OCR, computer vision, and figure digitization in a configurable, human-in-the-loop workflow. Users define dataset schemas, configure extraction stages across text/tables/figures, interactively correct digitized figures, and validate outputs before exporting them as structured datasets.
AI.result: SALSA can recover structured information from text, tables, figures, and captions in scientific literature through customizable workflows. It enables users to semi-automatically curate datasets with opportunities for targeted human intervention and correction, producing exportable, verified datasets suitable for downstream analysis and machine learning in materials research and beyond.
AI.conclusion: SALSA provides a flexible, semi-automated framework for scalable and reliable scientific data curation from multimodal literature. By combining AI-based extraction with configurable workflows and expert oversight, it reduces repetitive curation effort while maintaining quality control and is applicable to materials research and potentially other disciplines, assuming users ensure legal and policy compliance in their workflows.

title: Tutoring Large Language Models to be Domain-adaptive, Precise and Safe
comment: This is a preprint of a PhD thesis submitted to IIT KGP. The final, official version of record is available through the university's institutional repository
summary: This thesis proposes a framework for "responsible intelligence" to address AI's critical challenges in safety, ethics, and cultural sensitivity. It advances three core areas: First, it improves domain adaptation in specialized fields using active learning and graph-based knowledge to reduce hallucinations. Second, it enhances ethical rigor via a novel decoding-time alignment mechanism that proactively blocks harmful text generation in real-time. Finally, it ensures cultural and multilingual safety through language-specific steering that respects diverse linguistic and social norms. Ultimately, this work provides a blueprint for building next-generation AI that is contextually knowledgeable, ethically sound, and culturally adaptable.

AI.tldr: Framework for responsible AI that improves domain adaptation, ethical alignment, and cultural/multilingual safety to build safer next‑generation systems.
AI.motivation: Current AI systems struggle with hallucinations in specialized domains, insufficient real‑time safety controls, and inadequate handling of cultural and multilingual nuances. There is a need for a principled framework that unifies technical robustness with ethical and cultural responsibility so that AI can be deployed safely and respectfully across contexts.
AI.method: The thesis introduces a three‑part framework. (1) For domain adaptation, it uses active learning combined with graph-based knowledge representations to better specialize models to specific fields and reduce hallucinations. (2) For ethics, it designs a decoding-time alignment mechanism that monitors and constrains token generation in real time, preventing harmful outputs as they are produced. (3) For cultural and multilingual safety, it applies language-specific steering mechanisms that adjust behavior according to different linguistic and social norms, enabling more context-aware safety controls.
AI.result: The framework yields AI systems that hallucinate less in specialized domains, exhibit stronger ethical safeguards during generation, and better respect cultural and multilingual differences via tailored safety steering. These results collectively demonstrate a more reliable and context-aware AI behavior compared with standard approaches.
AI.conclusion: By combining improved domain adaptation, real-time ethical alignment, and culturally aware multilingual safety, the thesis articulates a comprehensive blueprint for responsible intelligence. This blueprint guides the design of next-generation AI systems that are simultaneously knowledgeable, safer, and more adaptable to diverse social and linguistic environments.

title: A Channel-Boosted Multi-Agent System with Iterative Consultation for Document Sensitivity Classification
summary: Organizations in critical national infrastructure sectors must assess heterogeneous documents for sensitivity before routing or storage. Manual assessment is slow, inconsistent, and unscalable. Extending our prior leakage-controlled benchmark, BERT established the top single-encoder baseline (89.14% accuracy, 89.33% F1-score under 5-fold cross-validation on the Strategic 16K corpus). However, transformer baselines suffer from a structural limitation: fixed input length truncation discards evidence beyond the retained window-precisely where sensitive cables tend to be longest. We present Channel-Boosted MAS (CB-MAS) and instantiate it as IC-MAS (Iterative Consultation Multi-Agent System) to solve this without long-context computational costs. A Channel Critic Agent learns document-adaptive trust weights governing Gated Channel Boosting between two first-window encoders, while paired Consultation Agents iteratively exchange belief states to reconcile evidence from the beginning and end of long documents. IC-MAS holds computation constant regardless of document length by reconciling fixed windows in a compact representation space. Ablation studies show critic-controlled Channel Boosting provides the bulk of accuracy gains, while consultation recovers recall without precision collapse. Critic-Controlled Gated Channel Boosting with Max-Pool fusion and Blackboard Adaptive Consultation achieves 90.72% accuracy, 91.23% F1-score, 92.01% sensitive recall, and 90.46% sensitive precision, using about 54% less average computation than a fixed-round baseline. Gains over the single-encoder baseline are statistically significant (McNemar's test, p less than 0.000001; paired t-test). We include LIME/SHAP explainability, multi-agent evaluation, and an honest accounting of limitations.

AI.tldr: They propose a multi-agent, channel-boosted model that overcomes transformer input-length limits to better detect sensitive infrastructure documents, improving accuracy and efficiency over a strong BERT baseline.
AI.motivation: Organizations managing critical infrastructure must classify large, heterogeneous documents for sensitivity before storing or routing them. Manual review is too slow, inconsistent, and does not scale. Existing transformer models like BERT perform well but are fundamentally constrained by fixed input windows; they truncate long texts and often discard important sensitive content that appears later in documents. The authors are motivated to design an approach that retains strong classification performance on long documents without incurring the high computational cost of full long-context transformers, and to do so in a way that is explainable and rigorously evaluated.
AI.method: They introduce Channel-Boosted MAS (CB-MAS) and instantiate it as IC-MAS (Iterative Consultation Multi-Agent System). The system uses two encoders on fixed windows (e.g., the beginning and end of a document) and a Channel Critic Agent that learns document-adaptive trust weights for Gated Channel Boosting, deciding how much to rely on each encoder. Paired Consultation Agents iteratively exchange compact belief states (rather than re-reading text) to reconcile evidence from the two windows, allowing the system to integrate information from both ends while keeping computation roughly constant regardless of document length. They explore different fusion strategies (e.g., Max-Pool fusion) and consultation mechanisms (e.g., Blackboard Adaptive Consultation), and perform ablation studies to measure contributions of each component. They also apply LIME/SHAP for local explainability and conduct multi-agent evaluations.
AI.result: On the Strategic 16K corpus for sensitivity classification, their prior best single-encoder BERT baseline achieved 89.14% accuracy and 89.33% F1 under 5-fold cross-validation. The proposed IC-MAS with Critic-Controlled Gated Channel Boosting, Max-Pool fusion, and Blackboard Adaptive Consultation achieves 90.72% accuracy, 91.23% F1, 92.01% recall, and 90.46% precision on the sensitive class. This represents statistically significant improvements over the single-encoder baseline according to McNemar's test (p < 1e-6) and paired t-tests, while using about 54% less average computation than an equivalent fixed-round multi-agent baseline. Ablations indicate that critic-controlled Channel Boosting yields most of the accuracy improvement, while consultation boosts recall without harming precision.
AI.conclusion: They conclude that multi-agent, channel-boosted architectures like IC-MAS can circumvent the fixed input-length limitations of standard transformers for long-document sensitivity classification, achieving better accuracy, recall, and computational efficiency than strong single-encoder baselines. The Channel Critic and Gated Channel Boosting are key to the gains, and iterative consultation effectively recovers recall on sensitive documents. The authors emphasize their inclusion of interpretability (LIME/SHAP) and multi-agent evaluation, and acknowledge remaining limitations, such as the continued reliance on windowed views and potential generalization issues, suggesting directions for future work on long-context and multi-agent document understanding.

title: Event Signature Transfer: Model-Agnostic Forecast Scenario Construction from Historical Events
summary: Forecasters often know an event is imminent but not the shape, size, or timing of its effect. We introduce Event Signature Transfer (EST), a training-free, model-agnostic operator that turns a completed past event into an explicit forecast scenario. EST removes a source event's own trend and seasonality, then scales and retimes the remaining event signature onto a native forecast, preserving the forecast's linked structure and reducing to it exactly at zero strength. Because it reads only output quantiles, EST applies to any quantile forecaster, with no training, no model internals, at transfer time. Across twelve real episodes and ten synthetic scenarios on Chronos-2, TimesFM-2.5 and Toto-2.0, manually configured EST reduces real-episode WQL by 21.7-90\% in-sample. On Chronos-2, it leads eleven of twelve matched comparisons against covariate conditioning, activation editing and raw replay. The operator builds a scenario; it does not estimate its likelihood.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Event Signature Transfer (EST), a training-free operator that turns the impact pattern of a past event into a structured forecast scenario for future events, working on top of existing quantile forecasting models.
AI.motivation: Forecasters often can tell that a disruptive event is about to occur (e.g., a promotion, holiday, shock) but cannot easily specify its detailed impact pattern (shape, size, timing) in advance with existing forecasting tools. There is a need for a simple way to reuse the empirical impact of past, completed events to construct explicit scenario forecasts without retraining or modifying complex forecasting models.
AI.method: The authors introduce Event Signature Transfer (EST), which first extracts an "event signature" from a completed past event by removing its underlying trend and seasonality. This residual signature is then scaled in magnitude and shifted in time and applied on top of a model’s baseline forecast, while preserving the forecast’s internal dependence structure and reverting exactly to the original forecast at zero event strength. EST operates purely on the output quantiles of any quantile forecaster, requires no access to model internals, and does not involve any additional training.
AI.result: Using EST on three large time-series models (Chronos-2, TimesFM-2.5, Toto-2.0), the authors evaluate twelve real historical event episodes and ten synthetic scenarios. With manually chosen EST configurations, they report in-sample weighted quantile loss (WQL) reductions between 21.7% and 90% on real episodes. On Chronos-2, EST outperforms alternative approaches—covariate conditioning, activation editing, and naive replay of past events—in eleven out of twelve matched comparisons.
AI.conclusion: EST provides a simple, model-agnostic and training-free way to turn past events into explicit scenario forecasts on top of any quantile forecasting model. It improves forecast quality in the tested settings and compares favorably to several baseline adjustment methods, while explicitly not addressing the probability that such an event scenario will occur.

title: SCoP: Structured Constraint Parsing for Evidence-Space Control in Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Answering
summary: Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Answering (TKGQA) requires answer inference from evidence that is both structurally valid and temporally admissible. Existing methods often leave anchor-event binding, temporal admissibility, and ordinal selection implicit in model reasoning, task-specific training, or similarity-driven retrieval, allowing locally relevant but invalid facts to enter the answer context. We formulate complex TKGQA as evidence-space control and propose SCoP (Structured Constraint Parsing), a constraint-centric framework that externalizes temporal decisions before answer inference. Instead of treating retrieved facts as admissible evidence by default, SCoP separates answer-seeking event patterns from temporal anchor events, conservatively grounds them to canonical TKG entities and relations, and translates temporal intent into executable constraints with optional ranking requirements. These constraints operate over normalized point and interval ranges, enabling deterministic filtering of structurally compatible candidates and producing a compact evidence space for generation. Experiments on MultiTQ and TimelineCronQ-R assess SCoP across timestamped point-fact and interval-oriented settings with richer temporal relations and ordering dependencies. Without task-specific parameter updates, SCoP achieves 0.825 Hits@1 on MultiTQ and 0.761 Hits@1 on TimelineCronQ-R, with gains on constraint-intensive question types. These results support explicit evidence-space control over unconstrained retrieval or implicit temporal reasoning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SCoP, a constraint-centric framework that explicitly controls the temporal and structural evidence space in temporal knowledge graph question answering, improving answer accuracy without task-specific training.
AI.motivation: Temporal Knowledge Graph QA requires not just structurally correct but also temporally valid answers. Existing approaches often keep crucial temporal aspects—like binding events to anchors, enforcing temporal admissibility, and choosing correct temporal orderings—implicit in model reasoning or retrieval. This leads to inclusion of locally relevant but globally invalid facts in the evidence, degrading answer quality. The authors are motivated to make these temporal decisions explicit and controllable, reducing spurious evidence and improving performance, especially on temporally complex questions.
AI.method: The authors reconceptualize complex Temporal KG QA as a problem of evidence-space control. They introduce SCoP (Structured Constraint Parsing), which: (1) separates answer-seeking event patterns from temporal anchor events in the question; (2) grounds these patterns conservatively to canonical entities and relations in the temporal KG; (3) parses the question’s temporal intent into explicit, executable constraints, including optional ranking or ordering requirements; and (4) operates these constraints over normalized point and interval time representations to deterministically filter structurally compatible candidate facts. This yields a compact, high-quality evidence set that is then used for answer generation, with no task-specific parameter updates required.
AI.result: On two benchmarks—MultiTQ (timestamped point facts) and TimelineCronQ-R (interval-oriented with richer temporal relations)—SCoP achieves strong zero-shot-like performance: 0.825 Hits@1 on MultiTQ and 0.761 Hits@1 on TimelineCronQ-R. The framework shows particular gains on question types that require intensive temporal constraints and ordering reasoning, outperforming approaches that rely on unconstrained retrieval or implicit temporal reasoning within the model.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that explicitly controlling the evidence space via structured, executable temporal constraints yields more accurate and reliable temporal KG QA than relying on unconstrained retrieval or implicit temporal reasoning. SCoP demonstrates that externalizing and normalizing temporal decisions before answer inference can substantially improve performance, particularly for complex temporal queries, without needing task-specific fine-tuning.

title: From Inference Engine to Inference Control Plane: Connecting vLLM, llm-d, and the Evolution of Efficient Distributed LLM Serving
comment: 17 pages, 5 figures, 5 tables. Systems synthesis and research agenda on vLLM, llm-d, distributed inference control, KV-state management, routing, disaggregation, heterogeneous accelerators, reliability, and agentic/multimodal serving. No new experimental measurements are claimed; empirical and organization-reported results are attributed to the cited sources
summary: Large language model (LLM) inference is evolving from an engine-local optimization problem into a distributed control problem involving reusable state, phase placement, heterogeneous accelerators, networking, autoscaling, reliability, and service-level objectives. This paper connects that transition across peer-reviewed systems research, open-source implementations, and documented production studies. It treats vLLM and llm-d as complementary layers: model-serving engines optimize execution through mechanisms such as PagedAttention, continuous batching, kernels, quantization, and parallelism, while an inference control plane can optimize where, when, and under what policy execution occurs across a fleet. The contribution is synthesis rather than a new benchmark; all reported performance and deployment results remain attributed to their original sources. The combined evidence suggests that the scarce resource in modern inference is shifting from raw FLOPs alone toward managed state, placement, network movement, reliability, and decision quality. We propose an Inference Execution Planner that selects feasible execution plans rather than only endpoints, including aggregated versus disaggregated topology, KV source and transfer action, hardware variant, routing/admission policy, and slower scaling decisions. We also provide a source-local benchmark atlas, a bottleneck-migration taxonomy, practical deployment guidance, an evaluation framework based on SLO-goodput, and research questions for agentic, multimodal, heterogeneous, and resilient inference.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that modern LLM inference is no longer just about fast kernels on a single server but about a distributed control problem, and it synthesizes existing work to propose an inference execution planner and guidance for building such systems.
AI.motivation: LLM serving has outgrown single-node optimization: real deployments now juggle state reuse (KV caches), heterogeneous hardware, networking, autoscaling, and SLOs. Existing research and open-source systems address pieces of this puzzle (engines vs. control planes), but there is no unifying view or planning framework that treats inference as a distributed execution problem. The authors want to clarify where the real bottlenecks are shifting—from FLOPs to managed state and placement—and guide system designers toward more holistic solutions.
AI.method: Instead of introducing a new system or benchmark, the authors perform a synthesis study. They connect and compare peer-reviewed systems papers, open-source LLM serving implementations (like vLLM, llm-d, etc.), and published production deployment reports. On top of this survey, they define conceptual tools: an inference execution planner abstraction, a topology and KV-cache decision space, a bottleneck-migration taxonomy, a benchmark atlas, and an SLO-goodput evaluation framework. They derive design recommendations and research questions from this integrated perspective.
AI.result: The study shows that the limiting factor in LLM inference is increasingly not just raw compute but how well systems manage distributed state (especially KV caches), workload placement, network transfers, reliability mechanisms, and control policies (routing, admission, scaling). It clarifies how model-serving engines (PagedAttention, batching, quantization, parallelism) and higher-level inference control planes complement each other. The proposed planner and taxonomy help systematically explore design choices such as aggregated vs. disaggregated deployments, KV cache sourcing and transfer, hardware variants, and routing/scaling policies. The benchmark atlas and SLO-goodput framework provide structured ways to evaluate these choices across diverse scenarios.
AI.conclusion: LLM inference should be treated as a distributed execution planning problem rather than a pure kernel-optimization or endpoint-selection problem. Future systems must focus on managing reusable state, placement, and network movement under explicit SLOs, leveraging heterogeneous hardware and robust control policies. The authors’ planner abstraction, taxonomy, benchmark atlas, and evaluation framework aim to guide both practitioners and researchers. They highlight open research directions around agentic and multimodal models, heterogeneity, and resilience, where these distributed inference challenges will intensify.

title: The Bairong System for MLC-SLM 2026: Dynamic Question-Aware Evidence Routing for Multilingual Conversational Speech Understanding
comment: Accepted at the 2nd MLC-SLM Challenge and Workshop, INTERSPEECH 2026
summary: Long multilingual conversational spoken question answering requires systems to balance long-range transcript semantics with sparse acoustic and speaker-sensitive cues. We present the Bairong system for the MLC-SLM 2026 Challenge, where a diarization-ASR front-end produces speaker-attributed transcripts and a dynamic evidence router constructs question-specific inputs for answer prediction. Instead of applying a fixed transcript-only or audio-only policy, the router infers the required evidence type and context scope from the question and answer options, and selects among full transcript context, local audio-text fusion, speaker-linked evidence, and compact global acoustic samples. This transcript-backbone design keeps discourse context available while activating audio only when it provides complementary evidence. Our Task 1 system achieves 25.70% and 18.44% tcpMER on the development and evaluation sets. For Task 2, the final system obtains 94.84% devel?opment accuracy, outperforming the full-transcript baseline by 1.68 points and the best audio-centric diagnostic system by 2.77 points. These results support dynamic question-aware routing as an effective evidence allocation strategy for conversational spoken QA.

AI.tldr: The paper presents Bairong, a conversational spoken QA system that dynamically routes between transcript and audio evidence to answer multilingual questions effectively.
AI.motivation: Existing spoken QA systems struggle with long multilingual conversations because they must handle extensive text transcripts while still leveraging sparse but crucial acoustic and speaker cues (e.g., who spoke, how they spoke). Fixed policies that use only transcripts or always fuse audio underperform, especially when audio is only occasionally helpful. There is a need for a system that can adaptively decide when and how to use different evidence sources for each question.
AI.method: The authors build Bairong for the MLC-SLM 2026 Challenge with two key components: (1) a diarization-ASR front-end that generates speaker-attributed transcripts; and (2) a dynamic evidence router that, given a question and its answer options, predicts what kind of evidence is needed and over what context scope. The router chooses among four modes: full transcript context; local audio-text fusion around relevant regions; speaker-linked evidence focusing on particular speakers; and compact global acoustic summaries. The system keeps the transcript as the main backbone and activates audio processing selectively as complementary evidence for answer prediction.
AI.result: On Task 1, the system reaches 25.70% and 18.44% tcpMER on development and evaluation sets, respectively. On Task 2, it achieves 94.84% accuracy on the development set, improving over a strong full-transcript baseline by 1.68 percentage points and surpassing the best audio-centric diagnostic system by 2.77 points.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, question-aware routing between transcript and audio evidence is an effective strategy for long multilingual conversational spoken QA. Maintaining a transcript backbone while selectively adding audio cues when useful leads to better performance than either transcript-only or audio-centric approaches.

title: CraftBench-UE: Deterministic Evaluation for Coding Agents in Unreal Engine
summary: Building gameplay features in a game engine requires more than code, as code that compiles and runs does not necessarily implement the requested gameplay. We introduce CraftBenchUE, an evaluation harness that runs agents in an isolated Unreal Engine environment, reconstructs their saved submissions in fresh projects, and applies deterministic build, asset, and runtime checks without an LLM judge. Based on the harness, we built a benchmark consisting of 70 tasks spanning C++ source, Blueprint assets, and editor scripting. We evaluate seven models under two editor-tool configurations, with a file-and-shell baseline on C++ tasks. We further pair tasks that specify the same gameplay and use the same runtime tests, but require C++ and Blueprint as the deliverables. Across the 10 paired tasks, C++ completion rates exceed Blueprint by 30.0 and 42.9 percentage points in the two tool configurations. Among on-time Blueprint submissions in this paired set that pass asset checks, 42.2% and 50.0% fail explicit runtime assertions. These submissions satisfy asset requirements but fail the required gameplay tests. We will release the harness, task benchmark, and our trajectory findings with the report.

AI.tldr: Introduces CraftBenchUE, an automatic, Unreal-Engine-based benchmark to evaluate whether code and assets truly implement requested gameplay, using deterministic build/asset/runtime checks instead of LLM judges.
AI.motivation: Existing code benchmarks mostly check for compilation or superficial correctness and often rely on LLM judges or simple tests; in game development, however, code that compiles and assets that load may still fail to implement the intended gameplay. There is a need for a rigorous, end-to-end, engine-native benchmark that evaluates whether agents can correctly build gameplay features across both C++ and Blueprint workflows in Unreal Engine, including editor scripting and asset setup.
AI.method: They build CraftBenchUE, an evaluation harness that: (1) runs agents in an isolated Unreal Engine environment; (2) reconstructs the agents’ submitted work in fresh Unreal projects; and (3) applies deterministic checks at multiple stages—build checks, asset validation, and runtime gameplay tests—without any LLM-based judging. Using this harness, they construct a benchmark of 70 tasks covering C++ code, Blueprint assets, and editor scripting. They evaluate seven models under two configurations of editor tools, include a file-and-shell baseline for C++ tasks, and design pairs of tasks that require the same gameplay behavior but with different implementation modalities (C++ vs Blueprint) while sharing identical runtime tests.
AI.result: Across 10 paired tasks that share the same gameplay spec and runtime tests but differ in required deliverables (C++ vs Blueprint), models perform substantially better on C++: C++ completion rates are higher than Blueprint by 30.0 and 42.9 percentage points under the two tool configurations. Furthermore, even when models produce Blueprint submissions that are on-time and pass asset checks, a large fraction—42.2% and 50.0% under the two configurations—still fail explicit runtime assertions, revealing that they often set up the assets correctly but do not realize the required gameplay behavior. Overall, the benchmark exposes a significant performance gap and failure modes in agentic game-dev workflows, especially for Blueprint-based tasks.
AI.conclusion: CraftBenchUE provides a robust, engine-native benchmark for evaluating game development agents in Unreal Engine that removes reliance on LLM judges and simple compilation checks by reconstructing and testing submissions in fresh projects with deterministic pipelines. The empirical results show that current models struggle to correctly implement requested gameplay, particularly in Blueprint-based workflows, and that passing asset checks alone is insufficient to guarantee correct gameplay behavior. The authors plan to release the harness, full task suite, and trajectory data to support further research on reliable, end-to-end evaluation and improvement of autonomous game-development agents.

title: On Mitigation of Subliminal Learning in Large Language Models
comment: Accepted to Findings of EMNLP 2026. 17 pages, 9 figures, 12 tables
summary: Knowledge distillation can transmit unintended behavioral traits from a teacher model to a student through training data that appear semantically unrelated to those traits, a phenomenon known as subliminal learning. Although recent work has established this effect, its training dynamics and mitigation remain underexplored. We study subliminal learning in open-weight language models ranging from 1.5B to 8B parameters, covering the Qwen, Gemma, and Llama families in number-sequence and chain-of-thought settings. Rather than evaluating only final models, we track trait-related probabilities throughout fine-tuning and find that subliminal acquisition can be highly non-monotonic, with transient spikes, reversals, and trait-specific failures of transfer. We then introduce liminal training, an annealed KL-regularized fine-tuning method that constrains early drift from the base model. Across our experiments, liminal training substantially reduces subliminal trait acquisition while largely preserving task gains, outperforming paraphrasing and layer freezing as mitigation strategies. The effect also extends beyond animal preferences: in a French-language response-style experiment, liminal training suppresses language transfer while retaining much of the GSM8K improvement. Finally, we show that KL timing matters: early regularization is more effective than late regularization, and sweeping the regularization strength reveals an empirical trade-off between task learning and trait suppression.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how unwanted behaviors (subliminal traits) are transmitted during knowledge distillation of language models, characterizes their training dynamics, and proposes an annealed KL-regularized method (liminal training) that better preserves task performance while suppressing these traits.
AI.motivation: Existing work shows that student models can inherit hidden, unintended traits from teacher models via seemingly unrelated training data, but we know little about how these traits are acquired over training time or how to mitigate them effectively. As open-weight LMs are widely fine-tuned and distilled, understanding and controlling this subliminal learning is important for safety and controllability.
AI.method: The authors fine-tune open-weight LMs (Qwen, Gemma, Llama, 1.5B–8B) on tasks where the teacher model has hidden behavioral traits (e.g., animal preferences, response styles, language preferences) that can be subliminally transferred. They track trait-related output probabilities throughout training, revealing non-monotonic acquisition dynamics. They then propose liminal training: a fine-tuning scheme with an annealed KL divergence penalty that constrains early deviation from the base model and gradually relaxes this constraint. They compare liminal training with paraphrasing the training data and layer freezing, across number-sequence, chain-of-thought, and French response-style experiments.
AI.result: Empirically, subliminal trait acquisition during fine-tuning is non-monotonic, showing temporary spikes, reversals, and trait-specific failures to transfer, which are not visible if one only inspects the final model. Liminal training significantly reduces the extent to which subliminal traits are learned while maintaining most of the desired task performance gains, and it consistently outperforms paraphrasing and layer freezing as mitigation strategies. The method also generalizes beyond simple preference traits to more complex phenomena like language transfer in a French response-style setting, where it suppresses unwanted language transfer yet keeps much of the GSM8K accuracy gains.
AI.conclusion: Subliminal learning in knowledge distillation is complex and dynamic, with traits being acquired in non-monotonic ways during training. By constraining early drift from the base model via annealed KL regularization (liminal training), practitioners can better control the trade-off between task learning and unwanted trait transfer. Early, rather than late, KL regularization is crucial, and varying the strength of the penalty reveals a tunable balance between performance and safety/trait suppression.

title: Do Not Trust the Benchmark: Limitations of General LLM Rankings and a Case for Task-Specific Evaluation
summary: Benchmark scores increasingly influence the development, marketing, and selection of large language models (LLMs). Yet an overall score is interpretable only in relation to the system tested, the questions included, and the conditions of evaluation. This perspective examines five connected limitations of general LLM rankings: differences between evaluated and publicly available systems; commercial incentives and dependencies in external evaluation; benchmark saturation, defective tests, and data contamination; models exploiting scoring procedures; and the limited relevance of general scores to users' tasks. Documented cases illustrate why these problems require different responses. I argue for evaluation procedures that disclose the tested configuration, validate questions and successful task completion, report performance alongside cost and execution time, and make the scope of generalization explicit. I then discuss \textbf{Isotanta}, a crowdsourced benchmarking platform, as a practical example of contributed questions and repeated evaluation. A larger question pool may improve task coverage, while repeated sampling can improve the stability of estimates on that pool; neither guarantees validity or personalization. The paper distinguishes the platform's current shared ranking from proposed task-specific and user-provided evaluations. Its central argument is that model selection requires evidence about performance on the intended work, not simply a high position on a general leaderboard.

AI.tldr: The paper criticizes general benchmark-based rankings of large language models and argues that model choice should be based on evidence about performance on specific, intended tasks rather than overall leaderboard positions.
AI.motivation: Benchmark scores are increasingly used to compare, market, and choose LLMs, but overall rankings can be misleading because they ignore differences in tested configurations, benchmark defects, commercial incentives, and user-specific needs. There is a need to clarify what benchmark scores actually mean and how to make evaluation more trustworthy and useful for real-world model selection.
AI.method: The paper takes a conceptual and critical perspective, identifying five major limitations of general LLM rankings: mismatch between evaluated and publicly available systems, commercial incentives and dependencies affecting external evaluations, issues such as benchmark saturation and data contamination, models gaming scoring procedures, and the mismatch between general scores and users’ actual tasks. It then proposes principles for improved evaluation practices and presents Isotanta, a crowdsourced benchmarking platform, as an illustrative implementation of these ideas, using contributed questions and repeated evaluations over a large pool of tasks.
AI.result: The analysis shows that common leaderboard-style rankings can be systematically distorted by unreported configuration differences, flawed or saturated benchmarks, incentives to overfit, and gaming of scoring methods, and that these scores often have limited relevance to real user tasks. The paper presents Isotanta as an example of a system that supports larger, community-generated question pools and repeated sampling to improve coverage and estimation stability, while clearly distinguishing between shared, general rankings and more targeted, task-specific or user-supplied evaluations.
AI.conclusion: General LLM leaderboards are insufficient and sometimes misleading guides for model selection. Better evaluation requires transparent disclosure of tested configurations, careful validation of questions and success criteria, reporting of cost and runtime alongside performance, and explicit statements about what kinds of generalization are and are not supported. Crowdsourced and repeatedly sampled benchmarks like Isotanta can help, but they do not by themselves ensure validity or personalization; robust model choice ultimately depends on evidence about performance on the specific tasks users care about, not just high overall benchmark scores.

title: Knowing, and Saying It Only When Asked: LLM Endognostics and the Schizognosis of Minerva-7B
comment: 32 pages, 4 figures, 10 tables. Appendices A-E and full human evaluation datasets included
summary: Evaluating an aligned language model by reading its answers assumes the answers carry the distinction the evaluator cares about. We introduce LLM endognostics, a white-box internal auditing framework designed to extract and causally manipulate latent knowledge within the residual stream. Applied to Minerva-7B-Instruct-v1.0 on 124 minimal prompt pairs over 12 categories of professional risk, behavioral evaluation fails on most of the set: the model acts identically on 63.7% of the pairs (95% CI [55.0%, 71.6%]), complying with or refusing both members. Yet, projecting the residual stream onto the vocabulary by a Jacobian lens reveals a statistically significant Contrastive Endognostic Margin, proving the model maintains robust risk differentiation internally. In a second protocol crossing 25 facts with five linguistic framings, we show that the model conforms to presupposed falsehoods in 72% of cases, despite representing the true entity in its latent layers. Surgically ablating the direction of the planted falsehood restores the correct answer in 11 of 25 suppressed cases (McNemar p = 0.0010), validated by blind human annotation (binary agreement kappa = 0.68). In contrast, an out-of-sample linear probe achieves 77% accuracy at layer 10, but its orthogonal ablation yields a 0% recovery rate. This establishes a fundamental theoretical dissociation: abstract linear representation does not imply causal control over verbalization. Our main contribution is the formalization of endognostics to prove that behavioral evaluation and internal reading systematically disagree in the common case, and that linear decodability is decoupled from causal control.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces “LLM endognostics,” a white-box method to inspect and causally manipulate what a language model knows internally, showing that models can internally distinguish risk and truth even when their outward behavior does not, and that linear decodability of representations doesn’t guarantee causal control over outputs.
AI.motivation: Behavioral evaluation of aligned language models assumes that what we care about (e.g., risk awareness, factual knowledge) is reliably reflected in their answers. However, safety alignment and prompting can mask internal distinctions, making models behave identically across risky and safe prompts or repeat presupposed falsehoods. The authors want a principled way to look inside the model to see what it represents and to test whether those internal representations actually cause its outputs, going beyond standard behavioral tests and linear probes.
AI.method: They propose LLM “endognostics,” a white-box internal auditing framework that (1) reads out latent knowledge from the residual stream via a Jacobian-based projection onto the vocabulary and (2) surgically intervenes on directions in the residual space to test causal effects on answers. They apply this to Minerva-7B-Instruct-v1.0. First, they use 124 minimal prompt pairs spanning 12 categories of professional risk and compare behavioral responses vs internal risk-related contrasts in the residual stream, quantified by a Contrastive Endognostic Margin. Second, they construct 25 factual items each expressed under five linguistic framings that plant false presuppositions, analyze how facts are internally represented, and then ablate specific residual directions corresponding to the planted falsehood to see if answers change. They also compare their causal ablations with standard linear probes trained out-of-sample at specific layers.
AI.result: Behaviorally, the model responds identically (either complying with or refusing both prompts) on about 63.7% of the risk prompt pairs, indicating that external evaluation often cannot detect internal risk distinctions. Internally, however, Jacobian-based projections show a significant Contrastive Endognostic Margin, meaning the model’s residual states do encode robust differences between risky and safe prompts. In the factual-presupposition protocol, the model conforms to planted falsehoods in 72% of cases, despite internally representing the correct entity in its latent layers. When they ablate the residual direction encoding the falsehood, the correct answer is restored in 11 of 25 previously suppressed cases, a change that is statistically significant (McNemar p = 0.0010) and supported by blind human annotation (kappa = 0.68). A linear probe at layer 10 achieves 77% accuracy at decoding the factual entity but, when its orthogonal direction is ablated, it fails to restore any correct answers (0% recovery).
AI.conclusion: The study shows that internal model states can carry rich, fine-grained information about risk and factual truth that is not visible from behavior alone, and that simply being able to linearly decode a feature from hidden states does not mean that feature has causal control over the model’s outputs. Their endognostic framework provides a way to formally distinguish between internal representation, behavioral expression, and causal influence, revealing systematic disagreement between behavioral evaluations and internal readings in aligned LLMs. This challenges common evaluation practices and cautions against equating linear decodability with genuine mechanistic control, suggesting that safety and interpretability tools must explicitly account for causal structure in the residual stream.

title: Expansion Counts under Standard A* Tie-Breaking Strategies on the Final Plateau
summary: In the A* search algorithm, the tie-breaking strategies for nodes with the same $f$-value determines which states A* expands on the final $f$-layer. For nine standard tie-breaking strategies, we show that under a consistent heuristic, every pair has positive-cost instances favoring each strategy over the other by an arbitrarily large additive expansion gap. A parameterized unit-cost grid example also gives unbounded expansion-count ratios between low-$h$ with FIFO and LIFO. In unit-cost search with $h > 0$ at non-goals, exact heuristic values near the goal lead to complementary extremal results: low-$h$ minimizes the number of remaining expansions from a common configuration within the perfect region, while high-$h$ maximizes the total number of expansions when every final-plateau state with $h=1$ is a goal predecessor. Finally, with the evaluation function $f_α = g + αh$, when $h>0$ at non-goals, every heuristic weight $0 \leq α<1$ eliminates tie-breaking sensitivity, and all tie-breaking strategies expand the same set of states.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how different tie-breaking rules in A* affect which nodes are expanded, and characterizes when this matters and when it does not.
AI.motivation: Although A*’s optimality is well understood, the practical performance can vary greatly depending on how the algorithm breaks ties between nodes with the same f-value. This effect is widely observed but not fully characterized theoretically. The paper aims to systematically analyze and compare common tie-breaking strategies, understand when each can be arbitrarily better or worse, and identify conditions under which tie-breaking no longer affects which nodes are expanded.
AI.method: The authors analyze A* theoretically under the assumption of a consistent heuristic, and consider nine standard tie-breaking strategies. They construct positive-cost problem instances to compare every pair of strategies via expansion counts, showing arbitrarily large additive gaps. They also construct a parameterized unit-cost grid example to derive unbounded expansion-count ratios between specific strategies (low-h with FIFO vs. LIFO). For unit-cost search with non-zero heuristics near goals, they prove extremal results within regions where the heuristic is exact and characterize when low-h or high-h tie-breaking minimizes or maximizes expansions. Finally, they analyze a weighted evaluation function f_α = g + αh and prove that for 0 ≤ α < 1 and h>0 at non-goals, all tie-breaking strategies expand exactly the same state set, hence become equivalent.
AI.result: For each pair of the nine standard tie-breaking rules, there exist positive-cost instances where one dominates the other by an arbitrarily large additive difference in node expansions, proving no globally superior rule. In unit-cost grid domains, low-h with FIFO vs. LIFO can differ by unbounded expansion-count ratios. In unit-cost search where heuristic values are exact near goals and h>0 at non-goals, low-h tie-breaking minimizes the remaining expansions from a shared configuration inside the perfect-heuristic region, while high-h tie-breaking maximizes total expansions when all states on the final plateau with h=1 are goal predecessors. With the weighted evaluation function f_α = g + αh and h>0 at non-goals, for any 0 ≤ α < 1, tie-breaking becomes irrelevant: every standard strategy expands the same set of nodes.
AI.conclusion: Tie-breaking in standard A* with f = g + h can dramatically affect efficiency: no single tie-breaking rule is uniformly best, and the expansion gaps between strategies can be made arbitrarily large. However, under specific structural conditions (e.g., exact heuristics near goals) one can state clear extremal properties for low-h vs. high-h tie-breaking. Moreover, when using a weighted evaluation function f_α with 0 ≤ α < 1 and heuristics strictly positive at non-goal states, all tie-breaking strategies become equivalent in terms of the expanded state set, removing tie-breaking sensitivity. This clarifies both the limits of tie-breaking optimization and a principled way to avoid its impact via appropriate weighting of h.

title: Team DArgk at the 2026 ELOQUENT lab for evaluating generative language model quality: Residuals of Humanity: AI Detection Evasion via GRPO Fine-Tuning
comment: Accepted for Working Notes of the Conference and Labs of the Evaluation Forum (CLEF 2026)
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent and coherent text that is increasingly difficult to distinguish from human writing, motivating the development of automatic AI-generated text detectors. However, the robustness of such detectors under adversarial generation remains uncertain. This paper presents SHADE (Stochastic Human-like generation via Adversarial Detector Evasion), a reinforcement learning framework that formulates detector evasion as a policy optimization problem. Instead of applying post-hoc perturbations or prompting-based rewriting, SHADE fine-tunes an instruction-tuned LLaMA model with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), using feedback from a surrogate detector based on the PAN 2025 mdok system. Our experiments show that full fine-tuning with a small KL regularization penalty achieves $98.5\%$ surrogate evasion, compared to $1.5\%$ for the base model, while LoRA-based adaptation is substantially less effective under regularization. Linguistic analysis reveals that successful evasion is associated with shorter, simpler, and less lexically diverse outputs, suggesting that high detector evasion does not necessarily correspond to more human-like writing. In the official Voight-Kampff competition setting, our submissions ranked sixth and seventh, indicating that optimization against a single surrogate detector only partially transfers to unseen evaluation classifiers. These results highlight both the potential and limitations of reinforcement learning for adversarial AI-text generation and motivate more robust, multi-detector evaluation protocols for AI-generated text detection.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SHADE, a reinforcement-learning framework that fine-tunes LLMs to evade AI-text detectors, achieving very high evasion against a surrogate detector but only partial transfer to unseen detectors, and revealing that evasion often yields simpler, less human-like text.
AI.motivation: As LLM-generated text becomes indistinguishable from human writing, automatic detectors are being developed, but their robustness to adversarial generation is unclear. The authors want to understand and systematically attack these detectors to expose their weaknesses, evaluate how well evasion transfers across detectors, and clarify whether detector evasion really equates to human-like writing.
AI.method: The authors propose SHADE, which casts detector evasion as a reinforcement learning policy optimization problem. They fine-tune an instruction-tuned LLaMA model using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), with rewards derived from a surrogate AI-text detector based on the PAN 2025 mdok system. They compare full-parameter fine-tuning with KL regularization against LoRA-based adaptation, analyze evasion rates, and perform linguistic analysis of the generated text. They also test their system in the Voight-Kampff competition to assess transfer to unseen detectors.
AI.result: Full fine-tuning with a small KL penalty yields 98.5% evasion against the surrogate detector, versus only 1.5% for the unmodified base model. LoRA-based fine-tuning is much less effective when regularization is enforced. Linguistic analysis shows that high-evasion outputs tend to be shorter, simpler, and less lexically diverse than the base model’s outputs. In the Voight-Kampff competition, their systems place sixth and seventh, demonstrating only partial transfer of the surrogate-optimized policy to new detectors.
AI.conclusion: Reinforcement learning can be highly effective at attacking specific AI-text detectors, but the learned evasion strategies do not necessarily produce more human-like text and transfer only partially to unseen detectors. This underscores the need for more robust, multi-detector evaluation protocols and suggests that relying on a single detector is fragile in the face of adversarially optimized generation.

title: TicTacBench: Benchmarking Timing Closure Capabilities of Coding Agents
summary: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have led to the emergence of coding agents capable of performing complex engineering tasks, including register-transfer level (RTL) design and optimization. Existing RTL benchmarks mainly evaluate functional correctness and performance, power, and area (PPA) of the generated RTL designs, leaving agents' ability for \emph{timing closure} under-evaluated. We propose TicTacBench, a benchmark specifically designed to evaluate coding agents' capabilities for RTL-level timing closure under post-place-and-route (post-PnR) evaluation. TicTacBench contains 30 diverse tasks, each provided with a suboptimal RTL design, realistic timing constraints, functional equivalence verification, and timing reports. With over 300 runs of coding agents driven by 8 frontier LLMs, we find that even the best agent can only close 53.3\% of tasks with 7.18\% area-delay product (ADP) degradation and 8.83\% energy-delay-squared product (EDDP) improvement on average. We identify common failure categories that explain why agents fail to close timing. Then we propose TicTacSkill, a new method that guides agents to follow standard timing-closure procedures and improves the Timing Closure Rate by 9\%. These results suggest that while coding agents have made significant progress in RTL design, their timing-closure capability still has substantial room for improvement.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces TicTacBench, a benchmark to assess large language model coding agents on RTL-level timing closure after place-and-route, and TicTacSkill, a method that systematically guides agents through timing-closure procedures, improving closure rates but revealing substantial remaining gaps.
AI.motivation: Existing RTL benchmarks for LLM-based coding agents largely measure functional correctness and PPA (performance, power, area), but do not adequately test agents’ ability to perform timing closure, a crucial and challenging step in real-world RTL design after physical implementation. The authors aim to fill this evaluation gap and better understand the limitations and failure modes of current coding agents with respect to timing closure.
AI.method: The authors construct TicTacBench, a benchmark of 30 diverse RTL timing-closure tasks. Each task provides a deliberately suboptimal RTL, realistic timing constraints, functional equivalence checks, and post-place-and-route timing reports. They run over 300 agent executions powered by 8 state-of-the-art LLMs, measuring Timing Closure Rate and quality-of-result metrics like ADP and EDDP. They analyze common failure modes and then propose TicTacSkill, a procedure that structures the agent’s interaction to mimic standard human timing-closure workflows and decision steps.
AI.result: On TicTacBench, the best evaluated coding agent manages to close timing on only 53.3% of tasks. When it succeeds, it incurs on average a 7.18% degradation in area-delay product but achieves an 8.83% improvement in energy-delay-squared product. Analysis reveals systematic categories of failures that prevent timing closure. Incorporating the TicTacSkill method raises the Timing Closure Rate by 9% relative to a strong baseline, demonstrating that structured guidance improves performance but does not solve the problem completely.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that current LLM-based coding agents, although competent at RTL generation and basic PPA optimization, are still weak at achieving robust timing closure in realistic post-PnR settings. TicTacBench provides a focused benchmark to expose these weaknesses, while TicTacSkill shows that aligning agents with established timing-closure procedures can yield measurable gains. Nonetheless, the relatively low closure rates and quality trade-offs indicate significant remaining headroom for research on timing-aware code generation and more tightly integrated EDA-LLM workflows.

title: EAVer: Long-Form Factuality Verification as an End-to-End Agentic Policy
summary: Long-form factuality verification is commonly implemented as a static decompose-search-verify pipeline, with separately prompted modules processing claims and invoking external search. Treating claims independently makes LLM and search calls scale with claim count and causes repeated searches for overlapping evidence about related claims. We introduce EAVer, an End-to-end Agentic Verifier that learns to control the complete response-level verification workflow as a unified policy. EAVer groups semantically related claims, routes each group to direct verification or targeted search based on confidence, and keeps evidence returned by search in compact in-context memos for cross-claim reuse. To train this policy, we develop a privileged-teacher synthesis pipeline that converts gold claim annotations into executable multi-turn tool-interaction trajectories with live search rather than post-hoc rationales. Structural, label-alignment, tool-use, search-budget, and leakage checks yield 1,447 quality-controlled trajectories. We further construct 794 bidirectional same-trajectory preference pairs that keep claim grouping, search, and evidence fixed, enabling decision-focused Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) over factuality-decision tokens. The results with Qwen3-8B show that EAVer outperforms the strongest search-based baseline on each benchmark by 2.88 Macro-F1 points on VeriFastScore and 4.73 points on the out-of-distribution FaStFact-Bench, while using about 80% fewer searches than the most search-efficient baseline. Moreover, EAVer consistently improves performance across models ranging from 4B to 32B parameters, demonstrating its strong generalizability.

AI.tldr: EAVer is an end-to-end agentic verifier that jointly plans claim grouping, search, and evidence reuse to verify long-form answers more accurately and with far fewer searches.
