AI.motivation: Existing long-form factuality verification systems use a static decompose-search-verify pipeline where each claim is treated independently. This leads to high cost because the number of LLM and search calls scales with the number of claims, and it wastes effort by repeatedly searching for overlapping evidence across related claims. There is a need for a unified, response-level policy that can coordinate verification decisions, reuse evidence across claims, and reduce search overhead while improving factuality performance, especially in out-of-distribution settings and across model scales.
AI.method: The authors propose EAVer, an end-to-end agentic verifier that learns a single policy to control the full verification workflow for an entire response. EAVer: (1) groups semantically related claims; (2) decides for each group whether to directly verify with the model or invoke targeted external search based on confidence; and (3) stores retrieved evidence in compact in-context memos for reuse across multiple claims. To train this policy, they build a privileged-teacher synthesis pipeline that turns gold claim-level annotations into executable multi-turn tool-use trajectories involving live search, rather than static rationales. They curate 1,447 high-quality trajectories using structural, label-alignment, tool-use, search-budget, and leakage checks. Additionally, they derive 794 bidirectional preference pairs over the same trajectories that hold grouping, search, and evidence fixed; these are used for decision-focused Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) specifically on factuality-decision tokens.
AI.result: Using Qwen3-8B, EAVer outperforms the strongest search-based baseline by 2.88 Macro-F1 on VeriFastScore and 4.73 Macro-F1 on the out-of-distribution FaStFact-Bench. It also achieves about 80% fewer search calls than the most search-efficient baseline, indicating substantial savings in tool usage. Beyond a single model size, EAVer yields consistent performance gains across models ranging from 4B to 32B parameters, suggesting robustness and strong generalizability of the learned policy.
AI.conclusion: EAVer demonstrates that treating long-form factuality verification as an end-to-end agentic control problem, rather than a static per-claim pipeline, improves both accuracy and efficiency. By learning to group claims, selectively route to search, and reuse evidence across claims, the system can outperform strong search-based baselines while greatly reducing search calls. The training framework, which converts gold annotations into live tool-interaction trajectories and uses decision-focused DPO, provides a viable recipe for building scalable, generalizable verification agents across model sizes and benchmarks.

title: Leaky-integrator reconstruction: taming error accumulation in recursive differenced time-series forecasting
summary: We introduce leaky-integrator reconstruction, a training-free method that cures the error accumulation of recursive differenced forecasting. Our first contribution is diagnostic: predicting one-step changes and integrating them by cumulative summation, the standard remedy for non-stationarity, is a discrete integrator with a pole on the unit circle, and we show this makes recursive rollout of a nonlinear model diverge, its 336-step error reaching several times that of a well-behaved forecaster (normalised MAE 1.6-3.8 versus about 0.8) across every neural architecture tested. Our second, central contribution is the fix: move the pole inside the unit circle with a leaky integrator H(z) = 1/(1 - gamma z^-1), gamma < 1, which provably bounds the accumulated error variance. Applied at reconstruction time with a single fixed gamma=0.9 (no retraining, a two-line change to any deployed one-step or foundation-model forecaster), it shrinks error at every horizon, the mean gain over seven diverging architectures and twenty datasets growing from ~3% at H=24 to 23% at H=96, 37% at H=192 and 51% (43-74% across those architectures) at H=336 (78% with an oracle pole). Crucially, it is provably inert where no pathology exists (stable or joint predictors already at the irreducible rate), making it a safe, general default.

AI.tldr: Proposes a simple, training-free leaky-integrator reconstruction that fixes error blow‑up in recursive differenced time‑series forecasting, giving large long‑horizon accuracy gains across models and datasets while being provably harmless when not needed.
AI.motivation: Recursive forecasting on differenced (change-based) predictions is widely used to handle non-stationary time series. However, integrating predicted changes with a standard cumulative sum is equivalent to using a discrete-time integrator with a pole on the unit circle. For nonlinear forecasters, this leads to unbounded error accumulation and divergence over long horizons, as empirically seen in large normalized MAE for 336-step forecasts across many neural architectures. The authors aim to understand this pathology formally and design a simple, universally applicable method that can be applied post‑hoc—without retraining—to stabilize and improve long-horizon forecasts.
AI.method: 1) Theoretically analyze the standard differencing-plus-cumulative-sum reconstruction, modeling it as a discrete integrator with a pole on the unit circle. They show that when this is combined with nonlinear one-step change predictors and recursively rolled out, the forecast errors can grow without bound. 2) Propose replacing the pure integrator with a leaky integrator characterized by a transfer function H(z) = 1 / (1 - gamma z^-1) with gamma < 1, which moves the pole inside the unit circle, thereby bounding the accumulated error variance. 3) Apply this leaky integrator only at reconstruction time, using a fixed gamma (e.g., 0.9), without changing or retraining the underlying forecaster, which can be any one-step or foundation model predictor. 4) Provide theoretical guarantees that this modification is inert—that is, does not harm performance—when the original forecasting system is already stable or operating near the irreducible error rate. 5) Empirically evaluate across seven diverging neural architectures and twenty datasets, comparing error metrics such as normalized MAE over various horizons.
AI.result: Diagnostic results show that the standard cumulative-sum reconstruction causes recursive nonlinear forecasters to diverge, with 336-step normalized MAE in the range 1.6–3.8, far worse than a well-behaved forecaster at about 0.8. Introducing the leaky integrator reconstruction, with a single fixed gamma = 0.9 and no retraining, consistently reduces error at all horizons for all diverging architectures and datasets tested. The average accuracy gains grow with forecasting horizon: approximately 3% at horizon 24, 23% at horizon 96, 37% at horizon 192, and 51% at horizon 336, with architecture-specific gains between 43–74% at horizon 336. With an oracle choice of the pole, improvements can reach around 78%. Theoretical analysis confirms that the leaky integrator bounds error variance and is effectively neutral where the original predictor is already stable and close to optimal.
AI.conclusion: Standard differencing-plus-cumulative-sum reconstruction in recursive forecasting embeds an unstable integrator that can cause severe long-horizon error blow‑up for nonlinear models. A simple, training-free leaky integrator reconstruction, implemented as H(z) = 1 / (1 - gamma z^-1) with gamma < 1 and applied only at inference, stabilizes this process by moving the pole inside the unit circle and provably bounding error variance. Empirically, with a single fixed gamma value, it delivers substantial and growing gains over longer horizons across a variety of neural architectures and datasets, while being provably harmless when the underlying system is already stable. Thus, leaky-integrator reconstruction is proposed as a safe, general default for recursive differenced time‑series forecasting.

title: From Trait Vectors to Circuits: Tracing Refusal and Sycophancy Through Language Models
summary: A direction in activation space that changes safety-relevant behavior when steered is not necessarily one the model uses to produce that behavior on its own. We therefore ask whether steering acts through the computation of the unmodified model or through a different set of components, studying two traits whose directions have been extracted and validated in prior work: refusal and sycophancy in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. For each, we use the trait vector to split the computation into a reconstruction circuit before the vector and a transmission circuit after it. We then test whether restoring the coordinate returns behavior removed by ablation. For refusal, both circuits are compact and faithful, restoring the coordinate alone recovers almost all of the refusal signal lost to ablation, and a circuit built around the vector matches the faithfulness of a direct input-to-output circuit at roughly half the edges. For sycophancy, transmission is compact, but reconstruction is broader and only partially faithful. Circuits that transmit a steering intervention are therefore not automatically the circuits that produce the behavior, and we report the counterfactual, target, and behavioral test for every circuit accordingly.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether activation steering directions that change model behavior are actually used by the original model to produce that behavior, by dissecting circuits around known “trait vectors” (refusal and sycophancy) in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct.
AI.motivation: Prior work has shown that you can find activation-space directions (trait vectors) that, when steered, significantly alter safety-relevant behaviors like refusal or sycophancy. However, it is unclear whether these directions lie on the model’s native computation path or are merely convenient control handles that work via alternative circuits. This distinction matters for mechanistic interpretability, safety guarantees, and reliable use of steering methods.
AI.method: The authors take existing, validated trait vectors for refusal and sycophancy in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. For each vector, they conceptually cut the forward pass into two parts: (1) a reconstruction circuit that computes the trait coordinate up to the layer where the vector lives, and (2) a transmission circuit that propagates that coordinate to outputs. They ablate the trait signal and then try to restore only the coordinate to test how well each circuit accounts for behavior. They build and evaluate sparse circuits, comparing their faithfulness and size to direct input-to-output circuits, and they perform counterfactual, target, and behavioral tests for each circuit.
AI.result: For refusal, both the reconstruction and transmission circuits are small and highly faithful. Simply restoring the trait coordinate recovers almost all refusal behavior lost through ablation, and a circuit centered on the vector achieves faithfulness comparable to a full input–output circuit with about half as many edges. For sycophancy, the transmission circuit is compact but the reconstruction circuit is much more diffuse and only partially faithful. This implies that the steering direction for sycophancy does not neatly capture the natural computation that produces sycophantic behavior.
AI.conclusion: Steering directions that effectively alter safety-relevant behavior are not guaranteed to coincide with the circuits the unmodified model actually uses to generate that behavior. Refusal appears to have a clean, compact circuit aligned with its steering vector, but sycophancy does not. As a result, circuits that transmit a steering intervention cannot be assumed to be the same as those that produce the trait naturally; each proposed circuit must be evaluated with counterfactual, target, and behavioral tests to understand what it truly represents.

title: AgentBetta: Verification-Driven Adaptive Configuration of an AI Nano-Agent through Selective Expansion and Verified Contraction
summary: Large language model agents are typically deployed with predefined configurations, although the required model capability, context, tools, permissions, memory, and computational resources can vary substantially across tasks. This study develops and evaluates AgentBetta, an adaptive AI Nano-Agent framework that represents these factors as an executable configuration and updates them through verification-driven diagnosis, selective expansion, and verification-based counterfactual contraction. The evaluation distinguishes controlled mechanism validation from external agent comparisons. On the AB-ConfigBench benchmark, AgentBetta achieved 91.38% verified success while reducing median context allocation from 64,000 to 8,000 context characters and median tool exposure from five tools to zero compared with the fully provisioned configuration. The configuration-deficiency diagnosis achieved a macro-F1 score of 0.819 with precision of 1.000 across the evaluated dimensions, and selective expansion avoided unnecessary changes to unrelated configuration dimensions. Post-success contraction preserved verification outcomes in 56.41% of evaluated one-dimension contraction probes, indicating that some successful configurations contained removable capability under the tested conditions. External evaluations indicate that adaptive configuration can improve the balance between verified task completion and capability exposure; however, the results vary across benchmarks and agent families. In particular, the cross-family replication did not reproduce the primary-backbone accuracy ordering, and specialized systems remained advantageous for certain task domains. These results support interpreting AgentBetta as a configuration-adaptation mechanism that regulates capability allocation and inference expenditure rather than as a universal replacement for specialized agent architectures.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AgentBetta, an adaptive AI agent framework that dynamically configures its own capabilities, tools, and resource use, achieving high verified success while significantly reducing context and tool usage.
AI.motivation: Most large language model agents are deployed with fixed, over-provisioned configurations, even though different tasks require different levels of capability, tools, memory, and computation. This wastes resources and exposes unnecessary capabilities, raising efficiency and safety concerns. The paper is motivated by the need for a principled mechanism that can automatically adapt an agent’s configuration to the specific demands of each task, balancing performance, resource use, and capability exposure.
AI.method: The authors propose AgentBetta, which treats an agent’s configuration (model capability, context length, tools, permissions, memory, and compute) as an executable object that can be diagnosed and modified. It uses verification-driven diagnosis to detect configuration deficiencies, selective expansion to add only the missing capabilities or resources, and verification-based counterfactual contraction to remove possibly unnecessary elements after success and test whether success is preserved. They evaluate AgentBetta using a dedicated benchmark (AB-ConfigBench) and separate external benchmarks, distinguishing controlled mechanism validation from cross-system agent comparisons.
AI.result: On AB-ConfigBench, AgentBetta reached 91.38% verified task success while substantially reducing resources compared with a fully provisioned setup: median context dropped from 64,000 to 8,000 characters and median tool exposure from five tools to zero. Its configuration-deficiency diagnosis achieved a macro-F1 of 0.819 with perfect precision (1.000), and selective expansion avoided disturbing unrelated configuration dimensions. Post-success contraction kept verification success in 56.41% of one-dimensional contraction tests, showing that many successful runs were over-provisioned and could be simplified. External evaluations showed that adaptive configuration can better trade off verified completion versus capability exposure, but performance varied by benchmark and agent family, and did not consistently mirror the usual backbone model accuracy rankings.
AI.conclusion: AgentBetta is best viewed as a general configuration-adaptation mechanism that manages how much capability and computation an agent uses, rather than as a replacement for specialized agent architectures. Adaptive configuration can maintain high verified success while significantly reducing resource use and unnecessary capabilities, but its benefits are benchmark- and system-dependent, and specialized systems still excel in some domains.

title: Do LLMs Choose Like Humans? Using Cognitive Theory to Evaluate LLM Decision-Making
summary: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit a range of human-like decision-making behaviors, but whether these reflect similar underlying mechanisms or surface-level mimicry remains unclear. We evaluate whether LLM context sensitivity aligns with a cognitive economic theory that explains human behavior through problem categorization and attention allocation. Across 12 open-source and commercial LLMs on a novel 140,000-trial product choice benchmark, context induces human-like shifts in choice and problem categorization, but does not reliably reweight attention between features like price and quality. Neither scale nor chain-of-thought reasoning reliably attenuates context sensitivity or generates human-like behavior. These results suggest that LLM decision mechanisms are distinct from human ones.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether large language models’ context-sensitive choices follow the same cognitive mechanisms as humans, and finds key mismatches in how models allocate attention to decision features, implying different underlying decision processes.
AI.motivation: Although LLMs can mimic many human-like decision behaviors, it is unclear whether they use similar cognitive mechanisms or just reproduce patterns from data. Cognitive economics offers theories about how humans categorize problems, attend to different features (like price vs. quality), and shift decisions with context. The authors are motivated to see if LLMs’ context sensitivity and decision patterns genuinely align with these human theories, which matters for using LLMs as models of human cognition or as proxies in behavioral research and economic policy simulations.
AI.method: The authors construct a large product-choice benchmark with 140,000 trials where options vary along features such as price and quality, and contextual information is manipulated. They test 12 open-source and commercial LLMs on this benchmark, measuring how context affects: (1) choices among products, (2) how problems are categorized, and (3) how attention is allocated across features (operationalized as the implicit weighting of attributes like price vs. quality). They also test the impact of model scale and prompting style, including chain-of-thought reasoning, on these behaviors and context effects. The LLM behaviors are then compared to predictions from a cognitive economic theory of human decision-making based on categorization and attention allocation.
AI.result: Across models, contextual cues lead to shifts in product choices and problem categorizations that qualitatively resemble human context effects: LLMs change what they choose and how they label or frame the decision when context changes. However, unlike humans in the cognitive theory, LLMs do not consistently reweight attention between features such as price and quality in response to context, indicating a lack of human-like attribute-level attentional shifts. Moreover, increasing model size or using chain-of-thought prompting does not systematically reduce context sensitivity or bring LLM behavior closer to the human-like pattern predicted by the theory.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that while LLMs display human-like context sensitivity at the level of observed choices and problem categorizations, their internal decision mechanisms differ meaningfully from those posited for humans in cognitive economics. Specifically, LLMs fail to exhibit the theoretically expected context-driven reallocation of attention across attributes. Neither scaling models nor eliciting explicit reasoning via chain-of-thought closes this gap. Therefore, LLMs should not be straightforwardly treated as mechanistic models of human decision-making, and caution is warranted when using them as stand-ins for human agents in behavioral and economic analyses.

title: Are Human-Aligned Models Models of Humans? A Turing-Test Gap in Preference Alignment
summary: Human-feedback alignment has made language models useful assistants and is commonly described as aligning them with humans. However, the responses people prefer from an AI need not be the responses they themselves would give. We distinguish alignment with human preferences from alignment with human behavior, and show that alignment with human preferences can make model behavior less human-like even when both preferences and responses come entirely from humans. We call this the Turing-test gap. We show that preference alignment preserves the human response distribution only under a restrictive condition, and find no consistent evidence that real human preferences satisfy it. Empirically, the loss of human-response likelihood increases with the strength of preference weighting, regardless of its direction, and the gap also appears under standard DPO. These results establish human-likeness as an explicit dimension of alignment rather than something assumed to follow from preference alignment.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that aligning language models to human preferences can make them less human-like in behavior, and formalizes this mismatch as the “Turing-test gap.”
AI.motivation: Although human-feedback alignment aims to make language models match what people want, it is usually assumed this also makes them behave more like humans. The authors question this assumption: Are the answers that people prefer from AI the same as the answers humans themselves would naturally give? If not, current alignment approaches may unintentionally push models away from human-like behavior. Clarifying this is important for safety, interpretability, and for applications where human-likeness or Turing-test behavior matters.
AI.method: The authors conceptually distinguish two targets: alignment with human preferences (what responses people say they like) and alignment with human behavior (what responses people actually produce). They analytically derive conditions under which optimizing for human preferences leaves the original human response distribution unchanged, and show these conditions are restrictive. They then run empirical experiments using human-generated responses and preference labels, applying preference-weighting and standard DPO-style optimization, and measure how the likelihood of human responses changes as preference strength increases.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis shows that matching human preferences preserves the human response distribution only if preferences satisfy a strong, special condition that is unlikely in practice. Empirically, as the strength of preference weighting increases, models become worse at assigning high likelihood to human responses, independent of whether the preferences favor or disfavor those responses. The same pattern—called the Turing-test gap—appears when using standard DPO training. Thus, preference alignment systematically pushes models away from human-like response distributions.
AI.conclusion: Human-feedback alignment should not be equated with making models more human-like. Preference alignment and behavioral human-likeness are distinct axes of alignment, and optimizing for the former can widen a measurable Turing-test gap with the latter. Future alignment methods need to explicitly consider human-likeness as its own objective if Turing-test behavior or close behavioral mimicry of humans is desired.

title: Swiss-Knife: A Framework for Reconfigurable Externalised Multi-Objective Alignment at Decode Time
comment: 19 pages, 3 figures, includes technical appendix and proofs
summary: Decode-time alignment methods steer a frozen language model by scoring candidate continuations with an external reward and selecting the maximiser. We argue that this shared design is a single degenerate point in a much larger space. We introduce Swiss-Knife, a framework for externalised multi-objective alignment in which the alignment specification is a first-class runtime object: hot-swappable scoring blades, a batch normaliser, a pairwise aggregation operator, and a selection rule. Six axioms characterise the admissible aggregation operators, and we prove a representation theorem: every operator satisfying them has the form $R_i = \sum_{j \neq i} g((μ_i - μ_j)/s(σ_i,σ_j))$, a two-parameter family containing probit and logistic comparison rules and pointwise argmax as named coordinates. Within it, pairwise aggregation is Lipschitz-stable under adversarial reward contamination while argmax is not, and Candidate-Batch Normalization (CBN) makes the weight simplex invariant to the rescalings under which reward models are only ever identified. Our reference instantiation pairs DPO-LoRA blades with an uncertainty-aware pairwise tournament. Sweeping the helpfulness/honesty/harmlessness simplex, it attains the best balanced frontier of six decode-time methods (harmonic $F_1$ 0.797 vs. 0.750 for the strongest baseline, $p < 10^{-14}$) with the lowest refusal rate and highest helpfulness of any arm, and reconfigures its objectives in 0.05 ms with no gradient computation. Ablating CBN costs 0.217 $F_1$, and the metadata confirms the predicted mechanism: the lowest-variance blade retains 9% of its nominal 33% influence, and the collapse follows the predicted ordering.

AI.tldr: The paper presents Swiss-Knife, a flexible framework for multi-objective, decode-time alignment of language models using external reward models, with theoretical guarantees and strong empirical results.
AI.motivation: Existing decode-time alignment methods all share a narrow, degenerate design: they apply a single external reward model and choose the highest-scoring continuation, offering limited flexibility, poor robustness to reward scaling/contamination, and weak support for multiple simultaneous objectives (e.g., helpfulness, honesty, harmlessness). The authors aim to generalize and systematize decode-time alignment into a principled, modular framework that can: (1) handle multiple objectives as first-class components, (2) be robust to noise and adversarial corruption in reward signals, (3) be invariant to arbitrary rescalings of reward models, and (4) be reconfigurable at runtime without retraining the base language model.
AI.method: The authors propose Swiss-Knife, a modular framework where the alignment specification is a runtime object composed of “blades” (external reward models), a candidate-batch normalizer, a pairwise aggregation operator, and a selection rule. They axiomatize the class of admissible pairwise aggregation operators and prove a representation theorem that any such operator must have the form R_i = Σ_{j≠i} g((μ_i - μ_j)/s(σ_i,σ_j)), parameterized by a comparison function g and a scale function s over reward means μ and uncertainties σ. This family includes probit, logistic, and pointwise argmax as special cases. They analyze Lipschitz stability under adversarial reward contamination, showing that pairwise aggregation can be stable while simple argmax is not, and introduce Candidate-Batch Normalization (CBN) to make the weight simplex invariant to rescalings of reward models. Their concrete instantiation combines DPO-LoRA reward “blades” with an uncertainty-aware pairwise tournament for multi-objective decoding.
AI.result: Empirically, the Swiss-Knife instantiation, using DPO-LoRA blades and uncertainty-aware pairwise tournaments, is evaluated on a multi-objective alignment setting balancing helpfulness, honesty, and harmlessness. When sweeping over different trade-offs (the simplex over these three objectives), it achieves the best balanced frontier among six decode-time alignment methods, improving the harmonic F1 from 0.750 (best baseline) to 0.797 with statistical significance (p < 1e-14). It also achieves the lowest refusal rate and highest helpfulness across methods. Swiss-Knife supports rapid reconfiguration of objective weights (0.05 ms, no gradients). An ablation removing Candidate-Batch Normalization causes a large performance drop (−0.217 F1), and diagnostic metadata shows that, without CBN, the lowest-variance blade’s actual influence collapses to 9% instead of the nominal 33%, in the order predicted by their theoretical analysis.
AI.conclusion: Swiss-Knife reframes decode-time alignment as a general, principled, and modular framework rather than a single fixed design. By treating alignment as an externalized, multi-objective, and runtime-configurable specification—equipped with theoretically grounded pairwise aggregation and normalization—the method provides improved robustness, better utilization of multiple reward models, and stronger empirical performance than existing decode-time approaches. Theoretical results (representation theorem, stability analysis) and empirical studies (F1 gains, ablation of CBN) jointly support that carefully designed aggregation and normalization are critical for stable, effective multi-objective alignment without retraining the base language model.

title: PhysAI-Bench: A Benchmark for LLM-Based Agentic Decision-Making in Autonomous UAV-Centric Physical AI
summary: Recent advances in Physical AI have accelerated the use of foundation models in autonomous systems such as unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), which must perceive, reason, plan, and act in dynamic environments. Existing benchmarks assess physical perception, intuitive physics, embodied navigation, and collaborative reasoning, but rarely evaluate the agentic decision-making required for reliable autonomy. We introduce \textit{PhysAI-Bench}, a benchmark for evaluating this capability. It contains 10,178 standardized decision instances automatically extracted from conversational traces of autonomous UAV missions. Each instance preserves mission context, temporal dependencies, physical constraints, Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool calls, Agent-to-Agent (A2A) interactions, sensor observations, and AI-native 6G network conditions, including latency, packet loss, throughput, edge load, and network slicing. We expose only information preceding each decision, preventing future-event leakage and approximating online decision-making. We evaluate 29 foundation models using a two-stage protocol. We select model-specific configurations from 12 combinations of zero-, three-, and five-shot prompting and four temperatures, tested in three runs on a 35-instance, human-verified development set. We then freeze each selected configuration and evaluate it in three runs on a fixed, episode-disjoint set of 500 instances. GPT-5.3 achieves the highest accuracy (52.00%), followed by GPT-5.2 (49.40%) and Grok~4.5 (49.07%). Few-shot prompting generally improves performance, while temperature has limited influence. The results demonstrate that reliable agentic decision-making in Physical AI remains an open challenge. The dataset is available at https://github.com/maferrag/physai-bench

AI.tldr: PhysAI-Bench is a large-scale benchmark to test how well foundation models make real-time decisions for autonomous UAV missions under realistic physical and network constraints.
AI.motivation: While many benchmarks test perception, navigation, and reasoning in embodied or physical settings, they rarely target the specific, high-stakes decision-making needed for reliable autonomy in real-world systems like UAVs, especially under realistic networking conditions. There is a gap between current benchmarks and the complex, temporally grounded decisions autonomous agents must make when operating with tools, other agents, and constrained communications.
AI.method: The authors construct PhysAI-Bench by automatically extracting 10,178 standardized decision points from conversational traces of autonomous UAV missions. Each decision instance preserves rich mission context, temporal structure, physical constraints, available MCP tools, agent-to-agent interactions, sensor inputs, and detailed AI-native 6G network conditions (latency, packet loss, throughput, edge load, network slicing). For each instance, only information available before the decision is exposed, approximating online operation. They then evaluate 29 foundation models using a two-stage protocol: (1) hyperparameter/model-configuration selection on a small, human-verified development set of 35 instances using 12 prompt/temperature combinations and three runs each; (2) freezing the best configuration per model and running three evaluation passes on a disjoint test set of 500 instances.
AI.result: Across 29 models, GPT-5.3 performs best with 52.00% decision accuracy, followed by GPT-5.2 at 49.40% and Grok 4.5 at 49.07%. Few-shot prompting (3- or 5-shot) generally improves accuracy compared to zero-shot prompting, while varying the temperature has only minor impact. Overall accuracies remain moderate, showing substantial room for improvement in agentic decision-making for autonomous UAVs under realistic constraints.
AI.conclusion: PhysAI-Bench offers a standardized, context-rich benchmark for evaluating agentic decision-making in Physical AI, going beyond perception and navigation to capture real-time, constraint-aware choices in autonomous UAV operations. Current state-of-the-art foundation models achieve only modest accuracy, indicating that robust, reliable autonomous decision-making in such settings is still unsolved. The benchmark and released dataset provide a foundation for future research on models and methods better suited to online, tool-using, network-constrained autonomy.

title: Assessing Adversarial Robustness of Latent Reasoning Models
summary: Large language models increasingly rely on long chain-of-thought (CoT) trajectories for complex reasoning, but autoregressive generation brings substantial memory and inference costs. Latent reasoning models (LRMs) offer a more efficient alternative by compressing intermediate reasoning into a small number of continuous latent vectors. Despite their efficiency, however, the adversarial robustness of LRMs remains largely underexplored. In this work, we systematically evaluate the robustness of latent reasoning across textual and multimodal settings, covering eight models and six benchmarks. We find that, across our evaluated settings, LRMs are generally less robust than explicit CoT baselines under adversarial perturbations, with particularly severe degradation under white-box attacks. Further analysis reveals distinct failure modes across modalities: textual latent states exhibit brittle dynamics and high sensitivity to specific input patterns, while latent states in multimodal models can remain largely invariant to input perturbations and have limited influence on final predictions. These findings expose robustness limitations of current latent reasoning approaches and highlight the need to jointly consider efficiency and robustness when designing implicit reasoning systems. We have open-sourced our code to facilitate reproduction of our research https://github.com/PKU-ML/latent-reasoning-model-assessment.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates how robust latent reasoning models (LRMs)—which compress chain-of-thought into continuous latent vectors—are to adversarial attacks, and finds they are generally less robust than explicit chain-of-thought approaches.
AI.motivation: While LRMs improve efficiency by avoiding long explicit chain-of-thought text, it is unclear how this compression affects robustness, especially under adversarial perturbations in text and multimodal inputs. As LLM-based systems are increasingly deployed in safety-critical and cost-sensitive settings, understanding the trade-off between efficiency and robustness in implicit reasoning mechanisms is important.
AI.method: The authors systematically benchmark latent reasoning models against explicit chain-of-thought baselines. They evaluate eight models across six textual and multimodal benchmarks, applying adversarial perturbations (including strong white-box attacks) to inputs. They then analyze how perturbations affect latent states and final predictions, identifying modality-specific failure modes by inspecting latent dynamics and their influence on outputs.
AI.result: Empirically, latent reasoning models are consistently less robust than explicit CoT baselines to adversarial input changes. The performance gap is especially large under white-box attacks. In text-only settings, latent states change sharply in response to small adversarial perturbations and show high sensitivity to certain patterns. In multimodal settings, latent states often fail to reflect input perturbations and exert limited control over the final prediction, suggesting a form of latent under-utilization or decoupling from the decision process.
AI.conclusion: Current latent reasoning approaches suffer from notable robustness issues: compressed latent trajectories can be either overly brittle (text) or under-influential and insensitive (multimodal). These vulnerabilities mean that efficiency gains from LRMs come with a robustness cost. The authors argue that future work on implicit reasoning should treat robustness as a first-class design objective alongside efficiency, and they support further research by open-sourcing their evaluation code.

title: ScholarStack: Layered Research Asset Orchestration and Cross-Task Reuse for Scientific Agents
summary: Scientific agents support a range of literature-based research tasks, such as retrieval, question answering, evidence-grounded generation, and claim assessment. Most existing systems, however, are organized around individual tasks: the same papers are repeatedly retrieved, segmented, and interpreted, and the understanding built in one task is difficult to reuse in the next. We present ScholarStack, a layered research asset framework that compiles a paper collection into reusable, versioned, and provenance-preserving assets at three complementary levels: source-grounded paper-level statements, domain-level organization, and evidence-grounded cross-paper syntheses. A common access interface returns task-specific views at the evidence granularity each task requires, preserving study conditions, source traceability, and verification status. We instantiate the framework on four task families spanning ten task settings, comparing agents that use the compiled assets with task-specific baselines under matched base models. Quality gains concentrate on tasks that require cross-paper evidence, such as multi-paper question answering and literature review generation, and query-time token cost falls on every task where it is measured, with assets compiled once and reused across tasks. These results suggest that layered research assets can serve as shared infrastructure for scientific agents, shifting literature-based assistance from isolated document processing toward cumulative, evidence-grounded workflows.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ScholarStack, a framework that compiles scientific papers into reusable research assets to support multiple literature-based tasks more efficiently and accurately.
AI.motivation: Existing scientific agent systems handle tasks like retrieval, QA, and claim checking in isolation, repeatedly reprocessing the same papers and failing to reuse understanding across tasks. This redundancy wastes computation and limits performance, especially for workflows that require synthesizing evidence across multiple papers.
AI.method: The authors design ScholarStack, a layered research asset framework that converts a paper collection into structured, versioned assets at three levels: (1) paper-level, source-grounded statements, (2) domain-level organization of those statements, and (3) cross-paper, evidence-grounded syntheses. They expose a unified interface that returns task-specific views at the appropriate evidence granularity while preserving study conditions, provenance, and verification status. They then instantiate this framework across four task families and ten task settings, and compare agents using ScholarStack assets against task-specific baselines using the same base models.
AI.result: Across the evaluated tasks, agents that use ScholarStack’s compiled assets achieve higher quality on tasks requiring cross-paper reasoning—such as multi-paper QA and literature review generation—and reduce query-time token costs wherever measured, because assets are compiled once and reused instead of recomputed for each task.
AI.conclusion: Layered, reusable research assets can act as shared infrastructure for scientific agents, enabling more cumulative and evidence-grounded literature workflows. ScholarStack demonstrates that organizing scientific knowledge into reusable, provenance-preserving layers improves efficiency and performance over isolated, per-task document processing.

title: EvalMem: An Operation-Level Diagnostic Framework for Long-Term Memory Systems
summary: Long-horizon interactions with LLM-based assistants require memory systems that preserve and update user states, preferences, and interaction histories. Existing evaluations report end-to-end QA accuracy and cannot determine whether errors arise from encoding, retrieval, or generation. We introduce EvalMem, an operation-level diagnostic framework with three parallel Examiners. For each query, the Encoding Examiner checks whether the target fact is stored, the Retrieval Examiner assesses whether the native retriever returns usable evidence, and the Generation Examiner tests whether the model can answer from oracle evidence. Their outputs form fine-grained multi-label defect codes. To improve store-level diagnosis, we adapt agentic RAG with a recall-first strategy that searches using both the query and source evidence, increasing recall of present evidence on LoCoMo from 70.2% to 95.6%. Evaluations of seven memory systems on LoCoMo, LongMemEval-S, and dynamic DynaMem-Bench identify retrieval as the most frequently attributed failure layer; in default LoCoMo, retrieval defects reach 22.1%, compared with 7.7% for encoding and 6.5% for generation. Guided by this diagnosis, MemWiki, a search-friendly auxiliary structure built from each system's memory export, improves mean accuracy by 2.5 and 2.3 percentage points on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S, respectively.

AI.tldr: EvalMem is a diagnostic framework that pinpoints where memory systems for LLMs fail—at encoding, retrieval, or generation—and uses these insights plus a recall-first RAG strategy and an auxiliary MemWiki to boost long-horizon QA performance.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon LLM assistants need reliable memory of user-specific information, but current evaluations only give aggregate QA accuracy, making it impossible to tell whether errors come from storing facts, retrieving them, or using them in generation. This lack of layer-wise diagnosis hinders systematic improvement of memory systems.
AI.method: The paper proposes EvalMem, which decomposes memory evaluation into three operation-level Examiners: (1) an Encoding Examiner checks if target facts are actually stored; (2) a Retrieval Examiner measures whether the system’s retriever surfaces usable evidence; (3) a Generation Examiner tests whether the model can answer correctly given oracle evidence. Their outputs yield multi-label defect codes for each query. The authors further enhance store-level diagnosis via an agentic RAG setup with a recall-first strategy that searches using both the user query and source evidence to maximize evidence recall. They then benchmark seven memory systems across LoCoMo, LongMemEval-S, and DynaMem-Bench and introduce MemWiki, a search-optimized structure automatically built from each system’s memory export, to test diagnosis-guided improvements.
AI.result: Agentic recall-first RAG increases recall of present evidence on LoCoMo from 70.2% to 95.6%. Across three benchmarks and seven memory systems, retrieval emerges as the dominant failure source; on default LoCoMo, retrieval defects are 22.1%, versus 7.7% for encoding and 6.5% for generation. Deploying MemWiki guided by these findings boosts mean QA accuracy by 2.5 points on LoCoMo and 2.3 points on LongMemEval-S.
AI.conclusion: Fine-grained, operation-level evaluation of LLM memory systems reveals that retrieval, not encoding or generation, is typically the main bottleneck. EvalMem’s diagnostic framework, together with recall-focused RAG and auxiliary retrieval-friendly structures like MemWiki, can both localize and mitigate these failures, leading to measurable improvements in long-horizon interaction performance.

title: On Probabilistic Inference Through Parametric Tensor Decomposition in Base Tensor Networks
comment: Accepted at: The 17th International Conference on Scalable Uncertainty Management (SUM 2026)
summary: Probabilistic inference is generally only tractable in low-treewidth graphical models, limiting its effective applicability in high-treewidth settings. Many existing methods improve efficiency by exploiting specific parametric structure, such as symmetries. However, they typically require such structure to be explicitly present, limiting their applicability to a broader range of graphical models. To address this limitation, we propose a framework where tractable inference is controlled by latent parametric structure exploitation, rather than requiring it to be explicitly present a priori. Our approach first reparameterises a graphical model as a specific tensor network representation, which we call a base tensor network. This representation yields two key properties that allow inference tractability to be controlled by parametric structure: 1) First, the complexity of inference is mainly determined by the parametric structure of a single tensor, called the base tensor. We characterise several tractable classes of base tensors for which the entire base tensor network can be contracted efficiently. 2) Second, decomposing the base tensor yields again a collection of base tensor networks. This allows inference to be naturally reduced to decomposing the base tensor into tractable components with sufficient parametric structure. We call this procedure parametric tensor decomposition. By exploiting parametric structure within the base tensor, our framework enables a novel view on inference beyond settings where such structure is explicitly present.

AI.tldr: They propose a new tensor-network-based framework that makes probabilistic inference tractable in high-treewidth graphical models by exploiting latent parametric structure rather than requiring explicit structure in the original model.
AI.motivation: Exact or efficient probabilistic inference is usually only feasible in graphical models with low treewidth. Existing speedups depend on explicit parametric structure (e.g., symmetries) in the model, making them inapplicable to more general, unstructured high-treewidth models. There is a need for a way to control inference complexity via structure that may be latent or implicit, not manifest in the initial representation.
AI.method: They reparameterize any given graphical model into a special tensor network called a base tensor network, dominated by a single key tensor (the base tensor). They then analyze how the parametric structure of this base tensor governs overall inference complexity. They identify classes of base tensors that yield tractable full-network contraction, and introduce parametric tensor decomposition: decomposing the base tensor into components with sufficient parametric structure so that the resulting base tensor networks can all be contracted efficiently.
AI.result: They show that the complexity of performing inference on the base tensor network is primarily controlled by the parametric structure of the base tensor and that certain structured classes of base tensors yield globally tractable inference. Furthermore, they demonstrate that decomposing the base tensor into structured components effectively reduces general inference problems to a sequence of tractable subproblems over these structured components.
AI.conclusion: By shifting the focus to exploiting latent parametric structure of a single base tensor within a reparameterized tensor-network form of the model, they provide a new, more general lens on making inference tractable. This approach extends inference techniques beyond models with explicit structure, potentially broadening the class of high-treewidth graphical models for which efficient inference is possible.

title: Seeing Through Conflicts: Improving Instruction Hierarchy Alignment in Vision-Language Models
summary: Instruction hierarchy (IH) alignment teaches language models to prioritize higher-level instructions when inputs conflict. While studied primarily in text-only settings, vision-language models (VLMs) introduce new challenges for IH: instructions may be embedded in images, split across modalities, visually transformed, or encountered during agentic tasks. Positing multimodal IH alignment as a reasoning problem, we train VLMs using reinforcement learning with rule-based rewards, comparing text-only, image-only, and mixed-modality supervision. We find that text-only IH training partially transfers to multimodal attacks, failing when models must decode, reconstruct, or reason over instructions across modalities. Image-based training improves robustness beyond text-only supervision, while mixed-modality training performs best overall. Importantly, the benefits generalize beyond the synthetic typographic training setting to real-image and web-agent safety tasks, while largely preserving general multimodal capability, showing that lightweight, verifiable supervision can meaningfully improve VLM robustness under adversarial, cross-modal, and interactive instruction conflicts.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to align vision-language models (VLMs) to obey higher-level instructions when text and images provide conflicting commands, using reinforcement learning with rule-based rewards across different modality setups.
AI.motivation: Existing instruction hierarchy (IH) alignment work focuses on text-only language models, but VLMs face harder scenarios: instructions can appear in images, be split between text and vision, be visually obfuscated, or arise in interactive agent tasks. Current models can be manipulated by such multimodal, adversarial instructions, posing safety and robustness risks. The authors aim to understand and improve how VLMs prioritize high-level user instructions across modalities, even under cross-modal and adversarial conflicts.
AI.method: They formulate multimodal IH alignment as a reasoning problem and apply reinforcement learning with rule-based, verifiable rewards. They train VLMs under three supervision regimes: (1) text-only IH training, (2) image-only IH training using typographic or visual instructions, and (3) mixed-modality training where instructions and conflicts span both text and images. They then evaluate robustness under multimodal instruction attacks that require decoding, reconstructing, or reasoning over instructions across modalities, and test generalization to real-image and web-agent safety tasks while monitoring general multimodal capabilities.
AI.result: Text-only IH training gives some robustness to multimodal instruction attacks but breaks down when success requires complex cross-modal decoding, reconstruction, or reasoning. Image-based IH training improves robustness relative to text-only. Mixed-modality IH training yields the strongest robustness overall, handling more challenging cross-modal and adversarial conflicts. These gains persist when moving from synthetic typographic settings to more realistic real-image and web-agent tasks, and the trained models largely retain their general multimodal performance.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal instruction hierarchy alignment is crucial for safe, robust VLM behavior under cross-modal and adversarial instruction conflicts. Lightweight reinforcement learning with rule-based, verifiable rewards can substantially improve VLM robustness, especially when training includes mixed-modality instruction supervision. Benefits transfer from controlled synthetic setups to real-world-like tasks without significantly harming general multimodal capabilities, suggesting a practical path for safer, more reliable VLM deployment in interactive and agentic settings.

title: Total Cost of Agency: Exact Attribution of Memory Injection Cost in Multi-Agent LLM Workflows
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables. Code, data, and evaluation harness in github: https://github.com/vsingh45/tca-compiler
summary: Every node in a multi-agent large language model (LLM) workflow retrieves context from memory and injects it into its prompt, where those injected tokens are billed as input tokens at the same per-token price as the system prompt and the user query. Production observability tools report total token cost but do not separate the tokens a node generates from the tokens it is handed, so this component of the bill is invisible to the teams paying it. We introduce the Total Cost of Agency (TCA), a decomposition of multi-agent workflow cost into base prompt, inference, memory injection, miss penalty and context-accumulation components, and an exact attribution method: a two-pass, non-billable token count that measures injected tokens directly rather than estimating them from word-count proxies. On a 200-task enterprise benchmark executed against real model APIs, memory injection accounts for 13.6 percent of the variable cost a compile-time optimizer can act on, about 12 percent of the full billed cost, and its share rises from a structural zero at workflow depth one to 27.6 percent at depth six. Injected tokens grow linearly with depth over the measured range (R^2 = 0.9974, depths two through six); a quadratic fit yields a negative leading coefficient, so the data do not exhibit convex growth at these depths. We show the component is controllable at fixed model tier: reducing the retrieval window capacity from 32 to 2 entries lowers injected tokens by 28.7 percent with an accuracy change within seed-level variation. We report in full that our graph-rewriting transforms are approximately cost-neutral in isolation, that two of the five decomposition terms are zero by construction in this harness, and that total workflow cost is dominated by model tier assignment, which we hold fixed and treat as prior work. Prompt caching is not evaluated; all figures are for the uncached case.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces and measures a new cost metric, Total Cost of Agency (TCA), for multi-agent LLM workflows, isolating the often-hidden cost of memory injection and showing it is significant, measurable exactly, and controllable without hurting accuracy.
AI.motivation: In multi-agent LLM systems, each node retrieves and injects context from memory into prompts, but current observability tools only show aggregate token costs. This hides how much teams actually spend on injected context vs. generated text, making it hard to optimize workflows or understand where money goes. The authors aim to expose and decompose these costs so practitioners can optimize multi-agent designs more effectively.
AI.method: They define Total Cost of Agency (TCA), decomposing workflow cost into base prompt, inference, memory injection, miss penalty, and context-accumulation components. They propose an exact attribution method based on a two-pass, non-billable token counting procedure that directly measures injected tokens rather than inferring them from proxies. They then run a 200-task enterprise benchmark using real LLM APIs and apply graph-rewriting optimizations and retrieval-window variations to observe how these components behave and how controllable memory injection is.
AI.result: On the benchmark, memory injection accounts for about 13.6% of the variable cost available to compile-time optimization and about 12% of total billed cost. Its share of cost grows with workflow depth: from effectively zero at depth 1 to 27.6% at depth 6. Injected tokens increase linearly with depth between 2–6 (R^2=0.9974), with quadratic fits indicating no convex growth in that depth range. Reducing the retrieval window capacity from 32 to 2 entries cuts injected tokens by 28.7% with no accuracy loss beyond seed-level variation. Their graph-rewriting transforms are roughly cost-neutral on their own, two TCA terms are zero by harness construction, and overall workflow cost remains dominated by model tier choices (held fixed in this study).
AI.conclusion: The hidden cost of memory injection in multi-agent LLM workflows is measurable, material, and structurally grows with workflow depth, but it is also controllable without sacrificing performance. Total Cost of Agency and the associated exact attribution method provide a practical framework for understanding and optimizing these costs, while model tier selection continues to dominate overall spend. Prompt caching is left for future work, as all reported results exclude caching effects.

title: BizSage: A Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Framework for Business Research with Efficient Knowledge Retrieval
summary: While multi-agent systems based on large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in automating the progressive workflow of academic research, extending them to economics and business research, where specialized domain knowledge spans neighboring disciplines yet remains difficult to access in a structured way, presents two challenges. First, existing methods mostly retrieve at the paper level, yet the evidence needed for research tasks is often distributed across different sections, creating a granularity mismatch that hinders retrieval coverage and precision. Second, these fields demand strict empirical rigor, yet current systems provide limited mechanisms for learning from evaluation feedback. We present \textbf{BizSage}, a multi-agent framework combining corpus-level fine-grained retrieval with quality-driven self-evolution. We build a Lateral Knowledge Graph (LKG) by merging section-level knowledge graphs and apply Personalized PageRank (PPR) to surface semantically relevant and structurally important sections. Seven specialized agents collaborate under a Meta-Review self-evolution mechanism that distills failure modes from evaluation traces into reusable strategies. On a benchmark spanning four domains and three tasks, BizSage ranks first on the majority of metrics, achieves pairwise win-rates above 60\% against six baselines, and produces zero hallucinated citations. We hope BizSage paves the way for reliable research assistance in economics, business, and the broader social sciences.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces BizSage, a multi-agent LLM framework for economics and business research that uses fine-grained section-level retrieval via a Lateral Knowledge Graph and a self-evolving meta-review mechanism to improve reliability and empirical rigor, achieving state-of-the-art performance with no hallucinated citations.
AI.motivation: LLM-based multi-agent systems can automate academic workflows but struggle in economics and business because domain knowledge is dispersed across paper sections rather than whole papers, making retrieval too coarse, and because these fields demand strict empirical rigor that existing systems cannot meet due to weak use of evaluation feedback for self-improvement.
AI.method: The authors propose BizSage, which constructs a Lateral Knowledge Graph (LKG) by merging section-level knowledge graphs from a corpus and then applies Personalized PageRank to identify sections that are both semantically relevant and structurally important for a query. On top of this fine-grained retrieval layer, they design seven specialized LLM agents that collaborate to perform research tasks. A Meta-Review self-evolution mechanism analyzes evaluation traces, identifies failure modes, and turns them into reusable strategies that guide future agent behavior, effectively enabling the system to learn from its own mistakes over time.
AI.result: On a benchmark covering four domains and three tasks in economics and business-related research, BizSage outperforms six baseline systems on most metrics, achieves pairwise win-rates above 60% in head-to-head comparisons, and crucially shows zero hallucinated citations, indicating strong reliability and empirical grounding of retrieved evidence and generated content.
AI.conclusion: BizSage demonstrates that combining corpus-level, section-granularity retrieval via an LKG with a quality-driven, meta-review based self-evolution mechanism can substantially improve the reliability and performance of LLM-based research assistants in economics and business. The approach suggests a promising path toward robust, low-hallucination AI tools for the broader social sciences, where complex, dispersed evidence and high standards of empirical rigor are essential.

title: WorkWorlds: An Infrastructure for Evaluating AI Agents on Workplace Tasks
summary: Many knowledge-work benchmarks are constructed around individual tasks, with the context needed for each task selected together with or after the task has been specified. This design measures performance on workplace-like tasks in an environment assembled for the task. When task specification guides which context is selected, the evaluation can encode task information into the environment and pre-complete part of the information-localization work that workplace performance normally requires. We introduce WorkWorlds, an evaluation infrastructure that separates organizational state from task specification. A world first fixes a revision, date, and employee seat and materializes the organizational state that employee can access; tasks are introduced only afterward. We implement WorkWorlds in a primary synthetic pharmaceutical company with 8 measured tasks across 6 employee seats, and construct additional organizational worlds. Across 192 matched evaluations, moving from task-curated context to the full role-visible workplace reduced evidence access from 90.4% to 74.5% and criterion pass from 79.4% to 68.2%, while pass conditional on evidence access remained nearly unchanged; most of the measured difference occurred before the agent reached sufficient evidence.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces WorkWorlds, an evaluation framework that more realistically measures AI performance on knowledge work by separating organizational context from task specification, showing that current task-centric benchmarks overestimate performance by implicitly giving away part of the work.
AI.motivation: Existing knowledge-work benchmarks usually build the context around each task after the task is known, which unintentionally encodes task information into the environment. This setup makes AI systems look better than they would in real workplaces because it pre-solves the hard problem of finding and localizing relevant information in a large organizational state. The authors want a more realistic way to test AI agents that must operate inside complex organizational environments, where context is fixed and not curated per task.
AI.method: The authors design WorkWorlds, an evaluation infrastructure where an organizational “world” is defined by a fixed revision, date, and employee seat, and then all information that this employee can access is materialized. Only after this world is frozen are tasks instantiated, so the task cannot influence which context is available. They implement this in a synthetic pharmaceutical company setting, defining 6 employee roles (seats) and 8 tasks. They then compare agent performance under two settings: (1) task-curated context, where information relevant to the task is pre-selected, and (2) full workplace context, where the agent must search within everything the role can access. They run 192 matched evaluations to quantify differences.
AI.result: When moving from task-curated to full-role workplace context, the agent’s access to needed evidence dropped from 90.4% to 74.5%, and the overall task pass rate dropped from 79.4% to 68.2%. However, the conditional pass rate given that the agent had accessed sufficient evidence stayed nearly the same. This indicates that most of the performance drop is due to difficulty in locating and gathering the right information in a large environment, rather than in reasoning over evidence once obtained. The largest measured differences appear before the agent reaches sufficient evidence.
AI.conclusion: WorkWorlds shows that current task-centric benchmarks overestimate AI performance on realistic knowledge work because they bake part of the information-localization step into the evaluation design. By fixing organizational state independently of tasks and measuring performance in full workplace contexts, the framework reveals that information discovery and access are major bottlenecks. The authors conclude that future evaluations and systems for AI in knowledge work must explicitly account for and test this information-localization component, not only reasoning on pre-curated evidence.

title: Knowledge Graph-Augmented Ambient AI for Clinical Note Generation
summary: Ambient AI is increasingly adopted in healthcare to automatically generate clinical notes from patient-clinician conversations, with the potential to substantially reduce clinician documentation burden. However, generated notes may omit clinically relevant information discussed during the encounter, creating information gaps that can affect downstream care. Knowledge graphs (KGs) constructed from encounter transcripts can provide a structured representation of what was discussed and enable systematic identification of missing information from generated notes that are critical for patient care. In this study, we introduce Coverage-Directed Revision (CDR), a model-agnostic framework that constructs a KG from the encounter transcript, identifies medical concepts absent from an initially generated note, and directs large language models (LLMs) to restore the missing information without modifying the underlying note-generation system. We evaluate CDR on two datasets: 1) Pitt-Bench, a local dataset comprising rehabilitation sessions, and 2) ACI-Bench, a public dataset for benchmarking clinical note generation. We tested four underlying LLMs widely used in ambient AI systems. The results show that CDR consistently improves content recall across all evaluated conditions. Our study provides a practical approach for improving the completeness of ambient AI-generated clinical documentation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Coverage-Directed Revision (CDR), a framework that uses knowledge graphs built from clinical encounter transcripts to detect and restore medically relevant content missing from AI-generated clinical notes, thereby improving recall without changing the original note-generation model.
AI.motivation: Ambient AI systems that auto-generate clinical notes can reduce clinician documentation burden, but they often omit clinically important information that was discussed during patient-clinician encounters. Such omissions create information gaps that may negatively impact downstream care. There is a need for a systematic, model-agnostic way to detect and recover missing but clinically relevant content in generated notes, using the full encounter transcript as reference.
AI.method: The authors construct a knowledge graph (KG) from the encounter transcript to represent discussed medical concepts and their relations. They then compare the KG-derived concepts with the content of an initially generated clinical note to identify concepts present in the transcript but absent from the note. These missing concepts are used to guide a Coverage-Directed Revision (CDR) step, where large language models (LLMs) are prompted to revise or augment the original note to restore the missing information. This framework is model-agnostic, operating as a post-processing layer on top of any underlying note-generation LLM. CDR is evaluated on two datasets—Pitt-Bench (rehabilitation sessions) and ACI-Bench (a public benchmark for clinical note generation)—using four different LLMs commonly used in ambient AI.
AI.result: Across both datasets and all four tested LLMs, applying the CDR framework consistently increases content recall of the generated clinical notes compared to the original, unmodified LLM outputs. That is, more clinically relevant concepts mentioned in the encounter transcripts are successfully captured in the final notes after CDR is applied, demonstrating robustness of the approach across settings and models.
AI.conclusion: Coverage-Directed Revision (CDR) offers a practical, model-agnostic approach to enhance the completeness of ambient AI-generated clinical documentation. By exploiting knowledge graphs derived from encounter transcripts to detect and restore missing medical concepts, CDR improves content recall without requiring changes to the underlying note-generation systems. This makes it suitable for deployment as an add-on layer in existing ambient AI workflows to reduce clinically important omissions in generated notes.

title: Pretraining of Medical Visual Encoders Toward Multi-modal Large Language Models
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) commonly reuse visual encoders pretrained with CLIP, although the features of these ViTs are ultimately consumed by autoregressive LLMs. We refer to this mismatch as the semantic-interface gap and introduce MedMLIP, a framework that pretrains the visual encoder through report generation with a frozen LLM, while employing Local Relational Distillation (LRD) to preserve relationships among visual patches to avoid visual collapse. We pretrain MedMLIP on IU-Xray and Open-PMC-300K and evaluate the resulting encoders on VQA-RAD and SLAKE. Only the ViT is transferred, while the guiding LLM and projector are replaced, allowing us to assess cross-LLM transferability. Our cross-LLM transfer experiments demonstrate the value of pretraining visual encoders for their autoregressive LLM interface while trying to preserve more fine-grained visual information. Code and the pretrained model are available at https://github.com/SkyCol/MedMLIP

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MedMLIP, a framework to pretrain visual encoders for multimodal LLMs using medical report generation with a frozen LLM, aiming to better match the autoregressive interface while preserving fine-grained visual relations.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal LLMs usually reuse CLIP-pretrained visual encoders whose features are optimized for contrastive objectives, not for consumption by autoregressive LLMs. This semantic-interface gap can hurt downstream performance, especially in domains like medical imaging that require detailed visual understanding. The authors aim to design a pretraining scheme that produces visual features tailored to LLM-based report generation while retaining rich local visual structure.
AI.method: MedMLIP freezes an LLM and trains the visual encoder via medical report generation, so that vision features are directly optimized for an autoregressive language interface. To avoid visual collapse, they introduce Local Relational Distillation (LRD), a mechanism that preserves local relationships among visual patches during training. The system is pretrained on IU-Xray and Open-PMC-300K. After pretraining, only the ViT encoder is transferred, while the LLM and projector used during pretraining are replaced to test cross-LLM transferability.
AI.result: Visual encoders trained with MedMLIP are evaluated on medical visual question answering benchmarks VQA-RAD and SLAKE. When the pretrained ViT is plugged into different LLMs, the models show improved performance compared to baselines that rely on standard CLIP-based encoders, indicating better cross-LLM transfer and more useful visual features for autoregressive language generation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Pretraining visual encoders via report generation with a frozen LLM reduces the semantic-interface gap between visual features and autoregressive LLMs. The proposed Local Relational Distillation helps preserve fine-grained patch-level information, avoiding visual collapse. MedMLIP yields visual encoders that transfer well across LLMs and enhance medical VQA performance, suggesting a promising direction for domain-specific multimodal pretraining. The authors release code and models to facilitate further research.

title: H2LooP Telecom Model v1: From Telecom Comprehension to Autonomous Issue and PR Resolution
summary: We present H2LooP Telecom Model v1, a domain-specialized large language models fine-tuned for the telecommunications industry. We release two domain-adapted model variants serving complementary use cases: a comprehension-focused variant for telecom domain question answering and reasoning, and an agentic variant for autonomous telecom code generation, pull request resolution, and code commits on production repositories. H2LooP Telecom achieves strong results on the GSMA Open Telecom Lite (OT-Lite) benchmark and a proprietary telecom code generation benchmark, outperforming frontier closed-source models such as GPT-5 and Claude Opus on independent leaderboard evaluation, while preserving general-purpose capabilities. The Comprehension variant achieves 81.8% weighted average on OT-Lite Pass@3, and, independently, ranks 5th overall on the official community-run Open Telco AI Leaderboard* at only 31B parameters-ahead of frontier closed-source systems including Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3 Flash, Grok-4-fast, and Kimi K2.5. Our agentic variant obtains a relative improvement of +8.8% in AST Similarity and +20.0% in Location IoU over the base model on telecom code generation, while maintaining identical MMLU (74.0%) and BFCL v3 multi-turn function calling (79.0%) performance, indicating zero catastrophic forgetting. Domain specialization on curated telecom corpora, spanning 3GPP standards, O-RAN specifications, network telemetry, and real repository commits, yields substantial improvements over general-purpose models of equivalent scale, approaches frontier closed-source models on domain-specific evaluation, and is independently corroborated by our official leaderboard standing.

AI.tldr: Introduces H2LooP Telecom Model v1, telecom-specialized LLMs (comprehension and agentic variants) that outperform larger closed-source frontier models on telecom benchmarks while retaining general capabilities.
AI.motivation: General-purpose LLMs underperform on highly specialized telecom tasks (e.g., interpreting 3GPP/O-RAN specs, working with network telemetry, and modifying production telecom code). Industry needs models that deeply understand telecom standards and codebases, can be evaluated on domain benchmarks, and support both knowledge-intensive reasoning and autonomous coding/DevOps workflows without sacrificing general performance.
AI.method: Fine-tune a base 31B LLM on curated telecom corpora, including 3GPP standards, O-RAN specifications, network telemetry data, and real repository commits. Produce two variants: (1) a comprehension-focused model optimized for telecom question answering and reasoning; (2) an agentic model optimized for autonomous telecom code generation and repository operations such as pull request resolution and code commits. Evaluate on GSMA OT-Lite benchmark, a proprietary telecom code generation benchmark, general benchmarks like MMLU and BFCL v3, and on the community Open Telco AI Leaderboard.
AI.result: The comprehension variant achieves 81.8% weighted Pass@3 on OT-Lite and ranks 5th on the community Open Telco AI Leaderboard, outperforming several larger closed-source models (e.g., Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3 Flash, Grok-4-fast, Kimi K2.5) despite having only 31B parameters. The agentic variant yields +8.8% AST Similarity and +20.0% Location IoU over the base model on telecom code generation tasks, while keeping general benchmarks unchanged (MMLU 74.0%, BFCL v3 79.0%), indicating no catastrophic forgetting. Both models approach frontier closed-source performance on telecom-specific tasks.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specializing a mid-sized LLM on carefully curated telecom data produces models that substantially outperform general-purpose LLMs of similar scale and rival frontier closed-source systems on telecom benchmarks, without degrading general reasoning or tool-use abilities. Differentiating between a comprehension-focused and an agentic code-focused variant effectively covers key telecom use cases such as standards reasoning and autonomous code workflows, as supported by both internal benchmarks and independent leaderboard evaluations.

title: Explainable Recommendations at Scale: LLM Rationales for YouTube Music Artist Discovery
summary: Modern music streaming platforms face a persistent tradeoff: exploiting familiar content versus driving the exploration of novel items. While users frequently desire discovery, they hesitate to select unknown artists over proven favorites. Providing transparent, natural language rationales that explain why an unexplored item is recommended lowers this barrier. However, while Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at this nuanced explainability, their real-time deployment is severely bottlenecked by prohibitive inference costs and computational overhead. In this paper, we present an industry case study of a decoupled recommendation architecture that successfully scales exploration without compromising latency. Our system isolates LLM inference asynchronously offline, pre-computing personalized candidate pools of undiscovered artists alongside tailored rationales. Large-scale online A/B experiments validate our design. We demonstrate that combining LLM-backed recommendations with these explanatory rationales significantly reduces the trust barrier for new content, yielding statistically significant improvements in both user exploration and overall engagement on the discovery surfaces.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an industry-scale system that uses LLMs offline to generate explanations and candidate pools for music recommendations, enabling more exploration of new artists without hurting latency or costs.
AI.motivation: Music streaming platforms struggle with the tradeoff between recommending familiar content users are likely to click and encouraging discovery of new artists that users say they want but are hesitant to select. Transparent, natural-language explanations can lower this trust barrier for unknown items, but running LLMs online in real time is too expensive and slow at scale.
AI.method: They design a decoupled recommendation architecture where LLM inference is run asynchronously and offline. The system pre-computes, for each user, a pool of undiscovered-artist candidates plus personalized natural-language rationales explaining why each is recommended. At serving time, the platform only retrieves from this pre-computed pool, so online latency and compute remain low. They evaluate the system through large-scale online A/B experiments on discovery surfaces in a real music streaming product.
