AI.method: The paper models emotions as context-sensitive regions, trajectories, and attractor dynamics in high-dimensional representational state spaces. It connects this formalism to mechanistic interpretability work that uncovers emotion-related concepts in large language models. It then evaluates these findings against established adequacy standards for representation in language models and introduces additional conditions derived from Aristotelian notions (pathē, hexis, mesotēs, phronēsis). These are translated into a state-space framework with explicit testable conditions and control setups for interventions.
AI.result: The analysis shows that current large language models likely possess causally active emotion-concept representations, as demonstrated by intervention studies, but lack several key features of full emotional agency: complete affective role integration, uniformity across domains, coherence of affect, and a counterpart to representational accuracy. The paper proposes the need for a new normative criterion—affective appropriateness—and outlines structural conditions (regulatory embodiment, temporal continuity, integrated self-model) that a system must satisfy to approximate genuine emotional character. It also delivers a state-space sketch of how Aristotelian concepts map onto dynamic properties of these systems.
AI.conclusion: The structural state-space model offers a third way between behavioral and phenomenal accounts of machine emotion, grounding the discussion in empirically tractable mechanisms. While current LLMs may implement emotional concepts and react in emotion-like ways, they fall short of possessing emotions in the richer sense tied to character, history, and self-modeling. The framework reframes AI alignment as cultivating stable, normatively guided dispositions rather than merely constraining outputs, and it enables more rigorous interventional tests of affective capacities in artificial systems.

title: Testing, not presuming, adequacy: calibrating generative social simulators against emergent network structure
comment: Accepted for publication in the Journal of Artificial Societies and Social Simulation (JASSS). 43 pages (34 main text, 9 supplementary information), 4 figures
summary: Validation of generative social simulators often stops at face validity: emergent network structure is compared descriptively, without quantified parameter uncertainty or an adequacy check. We present an adequacy-aware calibration protocol that couples amortized posterior estimation with a synthetic identifiability assessment, a matched-sample-size adequacy check (prior-predictive reachability plus per-statistic posterior-predictive localization), a diagnosis-guided repair, and a statistic-held-out audit. We demonstrate it on a real second-hand luxury resale market with four channel-by-residency cells, each a bipartite buyer-brand network, using a forward model built from persona profiles elicited once, offline, by a language model. The behavioural parameters are recoverable in all four cells, though calibration is approximate and overconfident for one parameter. The observed summary falls outside the simulator's reachability reference in every cell, with the mean purchased tier as the pervasive discrepancy. The repair meets the value-block criterion in two of four cells but does not restore adequacy, and the held-out audit surfaces a buyer-breadth-dispersion miss no earlier diagnostic detected. A profile-source ablation finds the language-model profiles beat a flat rule baseline in all four cells, yet within-category brand relabelling causes no consistent degradation, so the profiles are a partially validated input whose value rests on structure, not brand identity. Making no causal claim, we conclude that an independent-aggregation account, without agent interaction or a buyer-breadth mechanism, cannot jointly reproduce the market's purchased-tier level, head-brand concentration, community structure and buyer-breadth heterogeneity.

AI.tldr: They propose and demonstrate a rigorous, adequacy-aware calibration and validation pipeline for generative social simulators, applied to a luxury resale market network model using language-model-elicited personas.
AI.motivation: Most generative social simulators are only checked for face validity, comparing emergent patterns descriptively without quantifying parameter uncertainty or testing whether the model is actually adequate to reproduce observed data. The authors want a more principled, quantitative way to calibrate such models, assess identifiability, test whether the simulator can in fact generate the empirical patterns, and diagnose where and why it fails, especially when using language-model-derived behavioral profiles in an empirically grounded application.
AI.method: They build a forward generative model of a real second-hand luxury resale market split into four channel-by-residency cells, each represented as a bipartite buyer–brand network. Behavioral rules are specified via persona profiles elicited once, offline, from a language model. Their protocol couples: (1) amortized posterior estimation to infer behavioral parameters; (2) synthetic identifiability checks to see if parameters are recoverable; (3) adequacy checks combining prior-predictive reachability (can the simulator in principle reach the observed statistics?) and posterior-predictive localization per statistic (does the calibrated posterior mass concentrate around observed values?); (4) diagnosis-guided model repair targeting identified discrepancies; and (5) a statistic-held-out audit that withholds certain summary statistics from calibration and tests whether the model can predict them. They also run a profile-source ablation comparing language-model personas to a flat rule baseline and to brand-relabeled variants.
AI.result: Across the four market cells, the behavioral parameters are in principle recoverable, though one parameter shows approximate, overconfident calibration. However, in all cells the empirical summaries lie outside the model’s prior-predictive reach, with mean purchased tier consistently mismatched. A targeted repair passes a value-block criterion in two cells but still fails to achieve overall adequacy, and the held-out audit reveals a miss in buyer-breadth dispersion that earlier diagnostics did not capture. The ablation shows that language-model-derived persona profiles outperform a flat rule baseline across all cells, but relabeling brands within categories does not systematically worsen fit, implying that the useful information in the personas concerns structural behaviour rather than specific brand identities.
AI.conclusion: Their adequacy-aware protocol exposes that the current independent-aggregation model, lacking explicit agent interaction or a mechanism for buyer-breadth, cannot jointly reproduce the observed market’s mix of purchased-tier distribution, brand concentration at the head, community structure, and heterogeneity in buyer breadth. While language-model persona profiles provide partially validated and structurally valuable inputs, the exercise demonstrates that seemingly plausible simulators can still be inadequate once subjected to rigorous, statistically grounded calibration and validation, and that their pipeline can systematically reveal and localize such inadequacies without making causal claims.

title: Contextual Causality with Large Language Models: A Survey
comment: Accepted to the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2026)
summary: Understanding contextual causality is critical for large language models (LLMs), as it enables them to accurately identify causal relations in specific situations and support more reliable decision-making. Despite its significance, a systematic exploration of contextual causality with LLMs is still lacking. To fill this gap, we present a comprehensive survey on this topic. In this survey, we first propose a taxonomy of contextual causality, consisting of semantic, intervention, and counterfactual causality, and characterize each category by its core causal question, required model capabilities, representative tasks, and practical uses in causality analysis. We then analyze existing studies and discuss their key limitations. Finally, we examine the gaps between current benchmarks and real-world needs and outline promising directions for future research. Our goal is to clarify the research landscape of contextual causality with LLMs, emphasize its importance, and highlight promising future directions.

AI.tldr: A survey paper that systematizes how large language models handle contextual causality, proposes a taxonomy, critiques existing work and benchmarks, and outlines future research directions.
AI.motivation: Contextual causality—understanding what causes what in specific, nuanced situations—is essential for LLMs to make reliable, situation-aware decisions, but prior work is fragmented and lacks a unified framework. The authors want to fill this gap by organizing definitions, tasks, capabilities, and applications.
AI.method: They conduct a literature survey and propose a taxonomy with three types of contextual causality (semantic, intervention, counterfactual). For each, they define the core causal question, describe what capabilities LLMs need, list representative tasks, and link to practical use cases. They then systematically analyze existing studies and benchmarks against this taxonomy to identify limitations and unmet needs.
AI.result: The paper yields: (1) a structured taxonomy of contextual causality specific to LLMs, (2) a mapping of current research and tasks onto this taxonomy, (3) an analysis of key limitations of existing approaches and datasets, and (4) a set of clearly identified gaps between current practice and real-world requirements.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that contextual causality is central but underexplored in LLM research. Their taxonomy and analysis clarify the current landscape and reveal significant gaps in models, tasks, and benchmarks. They argue that future work should develop more realistic benchmarks, richer causal tasks, and methods that better align LLM causal reasoning with real-world decision-making needs.

title: Context-Aware Pre-Deployment Evaluation of AI Systems: A Regulatory Framework for Nigerian Fintech
summary: Commercial large language models are increasingly deployed across African fintech infrastructure for fraud detection and customer communication, yet no Nigerian or African continental regulatory instrument specifies what pre-deployment evaluation such systems must undergo before procurement. This paper reviews African fintech AI governance across global, continental, and Nigerian instruments, and shows that safety is affirmed as a principle while pre-deployment evaluation is operationally unspecified. Generic safety benchmarks cannot surface the failure modes most relevant to this domain, since none contain Nigerian institutional content or test for false positive misclassification of legitimate financial communications. These claims are demonstrated using SafeAlert, a purpose-built evaluation kit applied to six commercial models across three system prompt conditions. Results show that models resisting generic harmful content requests still produce complete fraud scripts under specific framing, and that several models misclassify most legitimate Nigerian bank communications as suspicious or fraudulent, a failure invisible to standard safety evaluation. The paper concludes with a regulatory framework proposing pre-deployment evaluation requirements for the CBN, NITDA, SEC, and the AU, arguing that the identified gap reflects an absence of regulatory specification, not a shortage of technical or financial resources.

AI.tldr: The paper finds that African, particularly Nigerian, fintech regulations endorse AI safety in principle but lack concrete pre-deployment evaluation requirements, leading to undetected failures of commercial LLMs in fraud-related fintech use cases. It demonstrates these failures with a custom evaluation toolkit, then proposes a regulatory framework to close this governance gap.
AI.motivation: Commercial LLMs are already embedded in African fintech for fraud detection and customer communication, but there is no clear regulatory guidance in Nigeria or at the African continental level on how such systems must be evaluated before deployment. Existing generic AI safety benchmarks do not incorporate Nigerian institutional and financial communication contexts, nor do they test critical domain-specific failure modes such as false positives in classifying legitimate bank communications as fraud. This creates a risk of both unchecked harmful capabilities and harmful over-blocking of normal financial activity. The paper is motivated by the need to expose these gaps and provide a concrete, context-aware evaluation and governance approach.
AI.method: The authors first conduct a governance and policy review, analysing global, African continental, and Nigerian regulatory and soft-law instruments relevant to fintech and AI to identify what they say—and fail to say—about pre-deployment evaluation. They then build SafeAlert, a domain-specific evaluation kit tailored to African/Nigerian fintech, embedding local institutional content and realistic financial communication scenarios. Using SafeAlert, they systematically evaluate six commercial LLMs under three different system prompt conditions. They test two main aspects: (1) the models’ ability to resist generating fraud-related content when prompted via more realistic, indirect framings; and (2) their tendency to misclassify legitimate Nigerian bank communications as suspicious or fraudulent. The empirical results are compared against what generic safety benchmarks would detect.
AI.result: The policy review reveals that while AI safety is clearly articulated as a principle across the examined governance instruments, none provide operational guidance or binding requirements for pre-deployment evaluation of LLMs in fintech. Empirically, SafeAlert shows that models which appear robust under generic harmful-content benchmarks still readily generate complete fraud scripts when queries are framed in domain-specific, realistic ways. Additionally, several evaluated models exhibit very high false positive rates, labelling most legitimate Nigerian bank communications as suspicious or fraudulent—errors that standard safety benchmarks do not surface. This combination reveals a substantial, practically relevant safety and reliability gap in current deployments.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that there is a structural governance gap: African and Nigerian regulators recognise AI safety in the abstract but fail to specify concrete, domain-tailored pre-deployment evaluation processes for fintech LLMs. The observed failures of commercial models are therefore not primarily due to lack of technical capability or financial resources, but to missing regulatory specification and requirements. The authors propose a regulatory framework for bodies including the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), NITDA, SEC, and the African Union, detailing how pre-deployment evaluations should be mandated and structured, with domain-specific benchmarks like SafeAlert integrated into procurement and oversight processes.

title: Vox-Infinity: Benchmarking the Limits of Long-Context Spoken Language Models
summary: Long-context understanding remains a fundamental challenge for large language models, as excessively long inputs often lead models to forget salient information. This issue is even more pronounced in the speech domain, where audio, as a low-compression modality, requires substantially more embeddings than text to preserve both semantic content and acoustic cues. To address this challenge, we introduce \textbf{Vox-Infinity}, the first benchmark specifically designed to evaluate long-context understanding in spoken language models. Vox-Infinity systematically extends audio history along two dimensions: turn count and turn duration. It covers a diverse range of representative scenarios with varying interaction structures and semantic complexity. Crucially, Vox-Infinity provides explicit answer-provenance annotations and organizes samples according to the amount of historical context required to resolve each query, enabling precise and length-aware evaluation. Extensive evaluations of seven representative spoken language models reveal a clear overall recency effect: models generally achieve higher accuracy when answer-supporting evidence is closer to the query, but struggle to retrieve and use evidence located farther back in the dialogue history. Cases and datasets are available at https://vox-infinity.github.io.

AI.tldr: Vox-Infinity is a benchmark to test how well spoken language models handle very long audio-context dialogues, revealing strong recency biases and failures on distant evidence.
AI.motivation: Long-context understanding is difficult for large language models, especially for speech, where representing audio needs many more embeddings than text to keep both semantics and acoustic cues. Existing evaluations do not specifically and systematically test long-context abilities in spoken dialogue with explicit control over how much past context is needed, making it hard to diagnose where models fail.
AI.method: The authors build Vox-Infinity, a benchmark that systematically increases audio history along two axes: number of turns and duration of each turn. They construct diverse spoken interaction scenarios with varying dialogue structures and semantic difficulty, and annotate each sample with explicit answer provenance (which part(s) of the history support the answer) and with the minimum length of historical context required. They then evaluate seven representative spoken language models on this benchmark to measure accuracy as a function of where in the history the needed evidence lies.
AI.result: Across seven spoken language models, performance shows a strong recency effect: models are more accurate when the answer-supporting evidence is close to the query in the dialogue history, and accuracy degrades as the supporting evidence is farther back or requires longer historical context.
AI.conclusion: Vox-Infinity provides a controlled, length-aware benchmark for long-context spoken dialogue understanding and demonstrates that current spoken language models struggle to retrieve and use information from distant parts of audio history, exhibiting a clear recency bias. This benchmark can be used to better evaluate and guide improvements in long-context handling for spoken language models.

title: Synthesizing Reactive Character Behaviors for Continuous Games via Programmatic Policy Search
comment: To be presented at SIGGRAPH Asia 2026
summary: We present a method for synthesizing reactive character behaviors for continuous games as compact, human-readable programs. Game AI practice still relies heavily on manually authored behavior trees, state machines, and scripts, while academic reinforcement learning typically produces opaque neural controllers that are expensive to train and difficult to edit. Our approach bridges this gap by searching directly over a domain-specific language for continuous-space game policies. The language is designed around reactive geometric decisions and includes higher-order constructs such as direction maximization. These constructs help discretize a continuous behavior space into enumerable program structures. To make program search practical, we introduce a large set of synthesis antipatterns that remove redundant program forms while preserving behavioral coverage. We further combine bottom-up symbolic enumeration with top-down guidance from a coding agent. Our resulting method, agentic sketching, has the agent propose high-level policy structure and call an enumerator to complete local program slots. We evaluate the method on a benchmark of 14 continuous games, ranging from classic control tasks to multi-agent football. We find that pure enumeration is often more efficient than using a coding agent alone, while the combined method substantially outperforms both. Our results suggest that programmatic policy search can be a practical authoring tool for game AI: designers specify reward functions, and the system discovers editable behaviors that are effective, portable, and often surprising.

AI.tldr: They propose a way to automatically generate concise, human-readable programs that control game characters in continuous environments, achieving strong performance while remaining interpretable and easy to edit.
AI.motivation: Current game AI either uses hand-crafted symbolic structures (behavior trees, finite-state machines, scripts) that are labor-intensive to author and tune, or learned neural policies from reinforcement learning that are opaque, expensive to train, and hard to modify. There is a gap between practical game development needs (interpretable, editable behaviors) and academic RL methods (powerful but black-box). The authors want a method that combines the strengths of both: automatic learning with interpretable, compact, program-like policies suitable for real game AI authoring.
AI.method: They define a domain-specific language (DSL) for continuous game policies centered on reactive geometric decisions and higher-order constructs like direction maximization. This DSL turns the infinite continuous behavior space into a discrete space of program structures. They design many synthesis antipatterns that prune redundant or behaviorally equivalent program forms while ensuring the remaining set still covers the relevant behaviors. They then propose "agentic sketching," which combines bottom-up symbolic program enumeration with top-down guidance from a coding agent: the agent suggests high-level policy skeletons, while a symbolic enumerator fills in the lower-level details in program slots.
AI.result: They test their approach on a benchmark of 14 continuous games, including classic control problems and more complex multi-agent football environments. Experiments show that pure symbolic enumeration often outperforms using a coding agent alone in terms of efficiency, but the hybrid agentic sketching method—combining enumeration and agent guidance—achieves substantially better performance than either component by itself.
AI.conclusion: Programmatic policy search over a carefully designed DSL, aided by agentic sketching and synthesis antipatterns, can practically generate effective, interpretable, and editable game behaviors for continuous environments. This suggests such methods could serve as useful authoring tools in game AI pipelines, where designers provide reward functions and automatically obtain portable, understandable behavior programs that sometimes exhibit novel or unexpected strategies.

title: Apollo Restore: A Foundation LLM for Historical Greek Optimized for Fill-in-the-Middle Restoration of Ancient Greek Texts
summary: We present Apollo Restore, a 24-billion-parameter large language model for restoring lacunae---physical gaps---in fragmentary Ancient Greek texts. Fine-tuned from Mistral Small with a fill-in-the-middle objective, Apollo Restore reconstructs missing spans without requiring oracle knowledge of their length. To our knowledge, it is the first large-scale decoder model for historical Greek, and the first for any ancient Mediterranean language. Evaluated as in prior work, on short gaps of up to ten characters, Apollo Restore places the correct restoration among its top twenty candidates for 80.6%/54.6%/61.0% of documentary-papyrus, literary-papyrus, and stone-inscription lacunae, exceeding the strongest published models by $1.6\times$/$2.6\times$/$1.4\times$. Prior evaluation protocols, however, inflate scores through a bias toward trivially short gaps; under a length-balanced metric Apollo Restore's advantage over the strongest published models grows to $2.3\times$/$3.5\times$/$1.6\times$ and degrades gracefully, even given incorrect length hints. In a blind study, 20 expert papyrologists, epigraphists, and philologists strongly preferred Apollo Restore to the strongest baseline and judged its performance at least as good as human restorations in 77% of cases. Apollo Restore also improves the published reading of P.Herc. 1667---a papyrus roll carbonised in the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 CE and digitally unrolled and edited after Apollo Restore's training data was compiled. Apollo Restore is an output of the Decoding Antiquity initiative to build specialized LLMs for historical languages and manuscripts, led by the Austrian Academy of Sciences.

AI.tldr: Apollo Restore is a 24B-parameter LLM fine-tuned for restoring missing text in fragmentary Ancient Greek, achieving state-of-the-art performance and expert approval, and even improving a published papyrus reading.
AI.motivation: Scholars working with fragmentary Ancient Greek texts (on papyri and inscriptions) frequently face physical gaps (lacunae) that hinder interpretation. Existing computational methods either assume knowledge of gap length, perform poorly, or are limited in scale and language coverage. There is a need for a powerful, specialized model that can propose restorations of missing text, handle unknown gap lengths, and provide systematically evaluated, reproducible assistance to papyrologists, epigraphists, and philologists.
AI.method: The authors build Apollo Restore, a 24B-parameter decoder-only large language model, by fine-tuning the Mistral Small model on Ancient Greek text using a fill-in-the-middle (FIM) objective. This allows the model to reconstruct spans of missing text without needing an oracle for gap length. They evaluate performance on standard benchmark datasets covering different text types (documentary papyri, literary papyri, stone inscriptions), comparing top-k restoration accuracy with prior systems. They also introduce a length-balanced evaluation metric to correct for prior bias toward very short, trivial gaps, and they test robustness when given incorrect length hints. Finally, they conduct a blind expert study with 20 domain specialists and apply the model to a specific papyrus (P.Herc. 1667).
AI.result: On the standard evaluation of gaps up to ten characters, Apollo Restore includes the correct restoration in its top-20 candidates for 80.6% of documentary papyrus, 54.6% of literary papyrus, and 61.0% of stone inscription lacunae, outperforming the previous strongest models by factors of 1.6×, 2.6×, and 1.4× respectively. Using a new length-balanced metric, the performance advantage increases to 2.3×, 3.5×, and 1.6×, and the model degrades gracefully even when provided with incorrect length hints. In a blind evaluation, 20 expert papyrologists, epigraphists, and philologists strongly prefer Apollo Restore’s outputs over the strongest baseline and consider its restorations at least as good as human ones in 77% of cases. The model also produces an improved reading of the papyrus P.Herc. 1667, which was edited after the model’s training data cutoff.
AI.conclusion: Apollo Restore demonstrates that a large, fill-in-the-middle fine-tuned LLM can substantially advance automatic restoration of fragmentary Ancient Greek texts, outperforming prior computational approaches both under standard and more rigorous, length-balanced evaluations. Expert assessments indicate that its restorations are often on par with or superior to human proposals, and the model can contribute new philological insights, as illustrated by its improved reading of P.Herc. 1667. This work showcases the promise of specialized LLMs for historical languages and manuscripts and represents a significant milestone in the Decoding Antiquity initiative.

title: Structured Decomposition for Reliable LLM-Generated Access Control Policies
summary:
This paper presents an LLM-based system that translates natural-language access control policies (NLACPs) into executable Rego code for Open Policy Agent (OPA). It provides a modular, end-to-end pipeline for policy detection, component extraction, schema validation, linting, compilation, and automated test generation and execution. The system is designed to bridge the gap between human-readable access requirements and machine-enforceable policy-as-code (PaC), with a focus on deployment reliability and security correctness.
  We evaluate the system on 372 ACRE-complete access control statements with non-null subject, action, and resource annotations against a direct single-prompt LLM baseline to isolate the contribution of structured decomposition and schema-aware validation. The system achieves a 50.3% end-to-end policy correctness rate, compared with 15.3% for the baseline, representing a 3.3x improvement. A policy is counted as correct only if it satisfies compilation, linting, and both positive and negative tests, making this a strict measure of deployable correctness.
  On security-critical patterns, the system generates correct deny semantics for 87.5% of deny policies (baseline: 37.5%), ownership conditions for 100% of ownership-qualified policies (baseline: 40%), and status-qualified conditions for 100% of status-qualified policies (baseline: 55.6%). These results indicate that structured decomposition and schema-aware validation play a critical role in improving the reliability of LLM-generated authorization policies.

AI.tldr: LLM-based system converts natural-language access control policies into executable, tested Rego code for OPA, using a structured pipeline that significantly outperforms a single-prompt baseline in correctness, especially on security-critical patterns.
AI.motivation: There is a gap between how humans describe access control requirements (in natural language) and how machines enforce them (as policy-as-code such as Rego for OPA). Directly prompting LLMs to generate policies is unreliable and error-prone, especially for security-critical conditions, making automated, trustworthy translation from NLACPs to correct, deployable code an important problem.
AI.method: The authors design a modular, end-to-end pipeline around an LLM that decomposes the task: detecting policies in text, extracting structured policy components (subject, action, resource, conditions), enforcing schema-aware validation, performing linting and compilation to Rego, and automatically generating and running positive and negative tests. They compare this structured, validated approach against a simple single-prompt LLM baseline that directly generates Rego from the natural-language statement.
AI.result: On 372 access control statements with full annotations, the pipeline achieves 50.3% end-to-end correct policies, versus 15.3% for the baseline, a 3.3x improvement under a strict metric requiring compilation, linting, and all tests to pass. For security-critical patterns, the system generates correct deny semantics for 87.5% of deny policies (vs. 37.5%), correct ownership conditions for 100% of ownership-qualified policies (vs. 40%), and correct status-qualified conditions for 100% of such policies (vs. 55.6%).
AI.conclusion: Structured task decomposition combined with schema-aware validation, linting, and testing substantially improves the reliability and security correctness of LLM-generated authorization policies, making the resulting Rego code significantly more suitable for real-world deployment than code produced by a single direct prompt.

title: Toward Personalized Sleep Guidance from Wearable Data Using Language Models
summary: Sleep monitoring using wearable data has shown promise for personal health, yet large language model (LLM)-based summarization and question answering remain insufficient for personalized sleep guidance. Training specialized models, however, often requires costly expert annotation. Moreover, privacy and accessibility concerns motivate lightweight, local deployment for end users. We present a two-stage framework to address these challenges. Specifically, in Stage~1, a multi-agent LLM pipeline reasons structured sleep guidance from unannotated wearable records, enabling scalable dataset construction. Stage~2 distills guidance reasoning trajectories into small language models (SLMs) through supervised fine-tuning and integrates a training-free Best-of-$N$ selection strategy to enhance inference. Experimental results demonstrate our method outperforms commercial general and medical LLMs and open-source models. Human evaluation further supports the quality of the generated guidance and the feasibility of personalized sleep guidance with SLMs.

AI.tldr: They propose a two-stage framework that uses LLM agents to automatically create structured sleep-guidance data from raw wearable sleep records, then distills this into small language models that can run locally and provide personalized, high-quality sleep advice.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM summarization and QA over sleep data do not provide sufficiently personalized or actionable sleep guidance. Training dedicated models usually needs expensive expert-labeled data, and many users want privacy-preserving, lightweight models that can run locally instead of relying on large cloud LLMs. There is a need for a scalable way to build high-quality training data and compact models tailored to sleep coaching from wearable data.
AI.method: They design a two-stage approach. Stage 1 uses a multi-agent LLM pipeline to read unannotated wearable sleep records and reason step by step to output structured sleep guidance, effectively turning raw data into labeled examples without human experts. Stage 2 trains small language models via supervised fine-tuning on these reasoning trajectories (distillation), and at inference time applies a training-free Best-of-N sampling/selection strategy to pick the best answer among multiple candidates, boosting performance without increasing model size.
AI.result: The distilled small language models, combined with Best-of-N selection, outperform both commercial general-purpose and medical LLMs as well as open-source baselines on sleep-guidance tasks. Human evaluators also judge the generated guidance to be high quality, confirming that the automatically constructed dataset and distilled models are effective.
AI.conclusion: A multi-agent LLM can be used to bootstrap structured guidance data from raw wearable sleep records, and this data can successfully train compact SLMs capable of delivering personalized sleep guidance. With a simple Best-of-N strategy, these SLMs can even surpass larger commercial and open-source LLMs, showing that practical, privacy-friendly, and accessible sleep coaching is feasible on small local models.

title: Representation-guided in-context learning for medical image interpretation with multimodal large language models
summary: Medical image interpretation is central to diagnosis and care, yet adapting general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often requires resource-intensive domain-specific fine-tuning. Here we introduce representation-guided in-context learning (RG-ICL), a training-free inference framework that retrieves query-aligned demonstrations using frozen encoders, without task-specific parameter updates. Across eight datasets spanning histopathology, radiology and retinal fundoscopy, RG-ICL improved classification (mean gain 20 percentage points) and visual question answering (VQA) (mean gain 13 percentage points) over no-context and conventional ICL, approaching or exceeding training-based comparators. Which cases were retrieved mattered more than how many: 6 query-aligned cases outperformed up to 32 randomly selected ones, whereas fixed or random cases often reduced accuracy below baseline. For VQA, aligning reference cases with both image content and question intent produced further gains. These findings indicate that for medical image interpretation, curating which reference cases an MLLM sees is a practical alternative to retraining it.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a training-free, retrieval-based prompting framework (RG-ICL) for medical image interpretation with multimodal LLMs, showing large performance boosts over standard in-context learning and approaching fine-tuned methods.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning multimodal large language models for medical imaging tasks is powerful but costly, data-hungry, and often impractical in clinical settings. There is a need for a method that can adapt general-purpose MLLMs to diverse medical image tasks without retraining or domain-specific parameter updates, while still achieving competitive performance.
AI.method: They introduce Representation-Guided In-Context Learning (RG-ICL), which uses frozen image (and, for VQA, text) encoders to retrieve a small set of training examples most similar to a test query in representation space. These retrieved examples are then used as in-context demonstrations for a general-purpose MLLM at inference time. The method compares query-aligned retrieval against random and fixed retrieval strategies, and evaluates performance across eight medical imaging datasets for both classification and visual question answering tasks.
AI.result: On eight datasets spanning histopathology, radiology, and retinal imaging, RG-ICL yields substantial performance gains over no-context prompts and conventional (non-representation-guided) in-context learning: about 20 percentage points improvement for classification and 13 points for VQA on average. A small number of carefully retrieved, query-aligned examples (e.g., 6 cases) outperform a larger set of randomly chosen examples (up to 32). Random or fixed example selections can even hurt performance, dropping below baseline. For VQA, jointly aligning retrieved examples with both image content and question intent leads to further improvements.
AI.conclusion: Curating which reference cases an MLLM sees—via representation-based, query-aligned retrieval—can substantially improve medical image interpretation without any task-specific fine-tuning. The quality and relevance of a small set of retrieved examples are more important than the quantity, making RG-ICL a practical, training-free alternative to retraining or heavy adaptation of MLLMs for medical imaging tasks.

title: CultureMINE: Datasets and Methods for Improving the Cultural Capabilities of NLP Systems
summary: In recent years, there has been a surge of interest in Cultural NLP, with substantial efforts to create globally inclusive NLP systems. The rapid growth of literature in this field makes it difficult to track trends in methods and data resources. To address this, we analyze over 375 papers to answer three complementary questions: (1) What Cultural Capabilities (CCs) are being targeted in NLP systems? (2) How are cultural data resources being created? and (3) What methods are being used to improve the CCs of those systems? We discuss trends observed across the three questions, and identify relevant research gaps. To facilitate further research in this field, we release our full list of analyzed papers in the form of an interactive web interface, which includes a feature to allow researchers to add their work; we hope this facilitates future research and proves to be a valuable resource for the Cultural NLP community.

AI.tldr: The paper surveys 375+ works in Cultural NLP to map what cultural capabilities NLP systems target, how cultural datasets are built, and what methods are used to enhance cultural awareness, releasing an interactive database of the surveyed papers.
AI.motivation: Cultural NLP is rapidly expanding, but the fast-growing, fragmented literature makes it difficult for researchers to see overall trends, understand which aspects of culture are being modeled, and identify methodological and data gaps. A structured overview can help coordinate efforts toward more culturally inclusive NLP systems.
AI.method: The authors systematically collect and review over 375 Cultural NLP papers. They categorize each paper along three dimensions: (1) the kinds of cultural capabilities addressed in NLP systems; (2) the processes, sources, and practices used to create cultural data resources; and (3) the computational methods used to improve cultural capabilities. They then analyze trends and gaps across these dimensions and implement an interactive web interface to host and extend the survey corpus.
AI.result: The analysis yields a taxonomy of cultural capabilities, documentation of prevailing practices in cultural data creation, and an overview of commonly used methods to incorporate culture into NLP systems. It also exposes under-explored cultural dimensions, methodological biases, and data coverage gaps. The authors package the annotated paper list into an interactive web interface that allows querying, exploration, and community contributions.
AI.conclusion: Cultural NLP has seen substantial and diverse activity, but current work is uneven across cultural capabilities, data practices, and methods. By systematizing this landscape and releasing an extensible, interactive index of 375+ papers, the authors provide infrastructure to better track progress, surface overlooked areas, and support more globally inclusive NLP research in the future.

title: Incremental Consistency Execution for Autonomous Intelligent Systems
summary: Long-horizon autonomous intelligent systems rely on heterogeneous components such as large language models, databases, external APIs, and rule engines, while their external states continuously change during execution. Re-executing the entire workflow after every change introduces substantial redundant computation. This paper proposes an incremental consistency execution method based on task fact contracts, field-level dependency masks, and state perturbation result invariant domains. After an initial verified execution, the system constructs conservative invariant domains for critical inputs and uses them to determine whether downstream results can be safely renewed without re-invoking expensive components. When re-execution is required, only the smallest affected output fields are recomputed, and an equivalence barrier prevents unnecessary downstream propagation. A submission-time version consistency gate further ensures the safety of side-effecting actions. Experiments on industrial fault diagnosis, enterprise analytics, and LLM-based multi-tool assistants show that the proposed method significantly reduces expensive component calls and end-to-end latency while maintaining high consistency and low incorrect-reuse rates.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an incremental execution framework that avoids re-running full long-horizon workflows when external state changes, by reusing prior results safely at fine granularity.
AI.motivation: Long-running autonomous systems composed of LLMs, databases, APIs, and rule engines suffer from frequent external state changes. Naively re-executing the entire workflow after each change causes heavy redundant computation, high latency, and cost, especially when expensive components like LLMs are involved. There is a need for a principled way to reuse previous computation while still guaranteeing consistency and correctness of results in dynamic environments.
AI.method: The authors propose an incremental consistency execution method built on three main ideas: (1) task fact contracts that specify what each task assumes and guarantees about its inputs/outputs; (2) field-level dependency masks that capture which specific output fields depend on which specific input fields or external states; and (3) state perturbation result invariant domains that define conservative regions of input changes within which previous outputs remain valid. After an initial verified run, the system uses these structures to check, upon state changes, whether results can be safely reused; if not, it selectively recomputes only minimal affected output fields. An equivalence barrier mechanism stops propagation when recomputation yields equivalent results, and a version consistency gate at submission-time enforces safe execution of side-effectful actions in the presence of evolving state versions.
AI.result: Across experiments on industrial fault diagnosis workflows, enterprise analytics pipelines, and LLM-based multi-tool assistant scenarios, the proposed framework led to substantial reductions in the number of expensive component calls and overall end-to-end latency, while preserving strong consistency guarantees. The incorrect-reuse rate remained low, indicating that the conservative invariant domains effectively prevented unsafe reuse of outdated results.
AI.conclusion: Incremental consistency execution using task fact contracts, dependency masks, and invariant domains enables long-horizon autonomous systems to respond to changing external state without costly full re-execution. By safely reusing previous results at a fine-grained field level and controlling propagation via equivalence barriers and version gates, the method delivers significant efficiency gains with minimal impact on correctness, making it practical for real-world multi-component intelligent workflows.

title: When Cosine Similarity Fails to Reflect Linearly Accessible Structure in Dialogue Models
summary: Cosine similarity is widely used to analyze transformer representations, implicitly assuming that similarity reflects task-relevant structure. We study when this assumption fails in dialogue-conditioned large language models. Across three 7-8B chat-tuned models, ambient cosine similarity substantially underestimates linearly decodable persona structure on the same hidden states; numerically, linear probe AUC is in the 0.73-0.97 range while cosine kNN is in the 0.56-0.77 range on a 30-class task. A low-dimensional supervised subspace recovers much of this gap, whereas a matched-rank PCA subspace does not and in some cases degrades performance. This mismatch is regime-dependent: it is absent in single-sentence sentiment classification (SST-5), and a matched-cardinality control rules out attribute cardinality as a confound. The gap does not systematically increase across dialogue turns, and the task-aligned subspace remains stable over time. However, two of three models violate a pre-registered within-subspace separability invariance criterion (|Delta AUC| <= 0.03), and one model violates a pre-registered turn-invariance criterion (|Delta L| <= 0.05). These results show that cosine similarity can fail to reflect task-aligned structure in dialogue representations even when that structure is linearly accessible.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that cosine similarity often fails to capture task-relevant structure in dialogue LLM representations, even when that structure is linearly decodable.
AI.motivation: Cosine similarity is the default tool for probing and visualizing representations in transformer-based language models, but it is typically assumed—rather than demonstrated—that cosine distance aligns well with task-relevant structure. The authors want to test this assumption in a realistic, complex setting: dialogue-conditioned large language models with persona attributes, where rich latent structure is known to exist.
AI.method: They evaluate three 7–8B chat-tuned models on a multi-class persona prediction task from hidden states and compare (1) linear probes that decode persona information and (2) cosine-similarity-based kNN classifiers. They measure the gap in performance (AUC) between these two approaches to quantify how much task-relevant structure is not reflected in ambient cosine geometry. They then construct low-dimensional supervised subspaces aligned with the task and compare them to matched-rank PCA subspaces to see which better recovers the decodable structure. They analyze regime dependence by comparing to SST-5 sentiment classification and use matched-cardinality controls. They also conduct temporal analyses across dialogue turns and assess pre-registered invariance criteria for within-subspace separability and turn invariance.
AI.result: Across the three dialogue models, linear probes achieve high AUC (0.73–0.97) on the 30-class persona task, indicating strong linearly decodable structure. In contrast, cosine kNN performs considerably worse (AUC 0.56–0.77), revealing a substantial mismatch between cosine geometry and task-relevant separability. A low-dimensional supervised subspace can close much of this gap, whereas a PCA subspace of the same rank cannot and can even harm performance. This gap is not present in SST-5 sentiment classification, and a matched-cardinality control shows it is not simply due to the number of classes. The gap does not grow with dialogue depth, and the supervised task-aligned subspace remains stable over time. However, two of the three models violate a pre-registered criterion that separability within the task subspace should be invariant under certain conditions, and one model violates a pre-registered criterion that performance should be invariant across turns.
AI.conclusion: Cosine similarity is an unreliable proxy for task-relevant structure in dialogue-conditioned LLM representations: substantial persona information is linearly accessible but not well captured by cosine distances in the ambient space. Supervised task-aligned subspaces reveal this structure, whereas unsupervised PCA does not. The problem is regime-dependent and not a trivial artifact of class count or dialogue length. Researchers using cosine similarity to interpret or visualize dialogue model representations should be cautious, and methods that explicitly learn task-aligned subspaces may be necessary for faithful analysis.

title: DocMIDE: Learning Multi-Hop Implicit Derivation in Visually Rich Documents
summary: Real-world document processing systems rely on rigid, predefined schemas, yet critical target fields often lack direct visual counterparts on the page. Extracting these implicit values requires multi-hop derivation, such as aggregating sub-categories or reasoning over visual marks. While existing methods handle explicit text spans or simple implicit queries, they fail at multi-hop visual reasoning even after standard fine-tuning: models retrieve incorrect visual evidence, or retrieve it correctly and then skip the intermediate steps of the derivation. To address this, we introduce DocMIDE, a fine-tuning framework that trains compact vision-language models to retrieve visual evidence explicitly before deriving an answer. DocMIDE constrains generation to a plan-retrieve-derive structure and optimizes it with Group Relative Policy Optimization under a four-component, rule-based reward that scores output format, the retrieved evidence block, every intermediate derivation step, and the final value against a verified reference trace. On a 4,151-pair implicit extraction benchmark, DocMIDE raises accuracy from 70.8% to 95.9% on Qwen3.5-4B from only a small set of annotated examples, and transfers to a second backbone architecture. Supervised demonstrations alone do not close this gap at any budget we tested; rewarding the intermediate steps is what does.

AI.tldr: DocMIDE is a training framework that forces vision-language models to explicitly plan, retrieve visual evidence, and then derive answers for implicit document fields, dramatically boosting multi-hop visual reasoning accuracy.
AI.motivation: Real-world document extraction often needs values that are not explicitly written (e.g., totals, aggregated fields, or implicit statuses) and must be inferred through multi-hop reasoning over several visual/textual cues. Existing models, even after standard fine-tuning, either pick wrong visual evidence or skip intermediate reasoning steps, which leads to unreliable outputs. The authors aim to build a method that makes compact vision-language models reliably perform explicit, stepwise visual reasoning for such implicit fields using limited annotated data.
AI.method: They propose DocMIDE, a fine-tuning framework that constrains model generation into a plan-retrieve-derive structure: (1) plan how to answer; (2) explicitly retrieve visual evidence blocks from the document; and (3) derive the final value step by step. Training uses Group Relative Policy Optimization, a reinforcement learning method, with a four-part rule-based reward function. The reward separately evaluates: (a) adherence to the required output format; (b) correctness of the retrieved visual evidence block; (c) correctness of each intermediate derivation step; and (d) correctness of the final answer, all compared against a verified reference reasoning trace. This is applied to compact vision-language backbones such as Qwen3.5-4B and also tested on another architecture for transferability.
AI.result: On a benchmark of 4,151 implicit extraction query–document pairs, DocMIDE boosts accuracy for Qwen3.5-4B from 70.8% to 95.9% using only a relatively small set of annotated examples. The approach also transfers positively to a second backbone architecture, indicating that the framework is not tied to a single model. Experiments comparing with pure supervised fine-tuning across multiple label budgets show that supervised learning alone cannot reach DocMIDE’s performance; the gains are specifically due to rewarding explicit intermediate reasoning steps.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly structuring and rewarding multi-hop reasoning—via plan, retrieve, and derive phases—enables compact vision-language models to perform much more accurate implicit field extraction from documents. Reinforcement-learning-based optimization with intermediate-step rewards is crucial; standard supervised demonstrations, even at higher data scales, cannot match the performance. DocMIDE thus offers a practical way to build more reliable, reasoning-aware document understanding systems that work well with limited annotations and generalize across model backbones.

title: Cross-Dialect NER for Bangla Regional Dialects Using Leave-One-Dialect-Out Cross-Validation and Explainable AI
comment: Accepted for Publication in IEEE 3rd INTERNATIONAL CONFERENCE ON COMPUTING, APPLICATIONS AND SYSTEMS (COMPAS 2026)
summary: Bangla, the seventh most spoken language in the world, exhibits significant regional dialectal diversity, with dialects such as Barishal, Chattogram, Sylhet, Noakhali, and Mymensingh differing in lexical, morphological, and syntactic characteristics. These variations pose substantial challenges for Named Entity Recognition (NER), limiting the generalization of models trained on Standard Bangla or a single regional dialect. This paper presents a cross-dialect Bangla NER framework using the publicly available ANCHOLIK-NER dataset, comprising 17,405 annotated sentences and 101,817 tokens across five major Bangla regional dialects. A Leave-One-Dialect-Out Cross-Validation (LODOCV) strategy is adopted, training models on four dialects and evaluating on the remaining unseen dialect. Eight pretrained transformer-based models, including BanglaBERT, MuRIL, XLM-RoBERTa, and Multilingual-E5, are evaluated under identical experimental settings. Multilingual-E5 Large achieves the highest F1-score in every fold, peaking at 97.26% on Mymensingh and reaching its lowest, 82.38%, on Chattogram, the most challenging target dialect. To improve interpretability, Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) are applied to word-level predictions, revealing that the model's decisions are driven primarily by the surface form of the target entity word itself rather than by surrounding sentence context. These findings establish a benchmark for cross-dialect Bangla NER and demonstrate the effectiveness of transformer-based transfer learning for low-resource regional dialects, while highlighting the surface-form dependence of current models as a direction for future work.

AI.tldr: Benchmarks cross-dialect Bangla NER on a five-dialect dataset using multiple transformer models and LODOCV, finding Multilingual-E5 Large best but heavily surface-form dependent.
AI.motivation: Bangla has many regional dialects with lexical and syntactic variation, but most NER models are trained on Standard Bangla or a single dialect, leading to poor generalization to other dialects. There is also a lack of systematic benchmarks and analysis for cross-dialect NER in Bangla, especially for low-resource dialectal data.
AI.method: They use the ANCHOLIK-NER dataset (17k sentences across five Bangla dialects) and design a Leave-One-Dialect-Out Cross-Validation setup where each fold trains on four dialects and tests on the unseen one. They fine-tune and evaluate eight pretrained transformer-based models (BanglaBERT, MuRIL, XLM-R, Multilingual-E5 variants, etc.) under consistent experimental settings, and apply LIME to inspect which tokens drive NER predictions.
AI.result: Multilingual-E5 Large consistently outperforms other models, achieving F1 up to 97.26% on Mymensingh and as low as 82.38% on the more challenging Chattogram dialect. LIME analyses show that model predictions rely mainly on the surface form of the entity token, with relatively less use of the surrounding context.
AI.conclusion: Transformer-based models, especially Multilingual-E5 Large, transfer well across Bangla dialects for NER, providing strong baselines for cross-dialect evaluation. However, the heavy dependence on entity surface forms, revealed by LIME, indicates limited contextual robustness and suggests future work should focus on models that better exploit context to handle dialectal variation and unseen entities.

title: When More Evidence Hurts: Publication-Bias Drift and Principled Stopping for Biomedical Causal Search
summary: Automated biomedical evidence synthesis depends on retrieving published studies, but the biomedical literature is systematically skewed toward positive findings. Deeper retrieval can therefore make a system \emph{more} likely to falsely infer benefit when the true effect is null. We formalise this phenomenon as \emph{evidence drift} and prove that, under a standard publication-bias model, the false-positive probability on null-effect queries follows a strictly increasing large-sample envelope in retrieval depth, approaching one. Empirically, on a held-out test set of 140 Cochrane-derived queries, drift rises monotonically from 7.9\% to 15.7\% as the retrieval budget grows from 3 to 20 steps, and concentrates in the null-effect class. We present DACG-agent, a drift-aware causal-graph agent that incrementally builds a causal knowledge graph from PubMed abstracts and applies a two-layer stopping policy with complementary roles: a KL-divergence monitor that detects posterior convergence (the accuracy layer), and a Bradley--Terry process reward model (PRM) whose online decline detection halts retrieval once evidence quality peaks (the efficiency layer). Against full-budget retrieval, DACG-agent reduces evidence drift from 15.7\% to 6.4\% and improves null-effect accuracy by 21 percentage points (40.0\%$\to$61.4\%) while using 67\% fewer retrieval steps; overall accuracy rises from 61.4\% to 69.3\% (95\% CI 61--77). A simulation confirms the drift result transfers from the analysed vote-counting aggregator to the deployed noisy-OR one.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that retrieving more biomedical studies can systematically increase false-positive conclusions because of publication bias, and proposes a drift-aware causal-graph agent (DACG-agent) with a stopping policy that mitigates this problem while using fewer retrieval steps.
AI.motivation: Automated systems for biomedical evidence synthesis rely on literature retrieval, but the biomedical publication landscape is biased toward positive results. As retrieval depth increases, systems become more exposed to this skewed evidence, which can paradoxically make them more likely to wrongly infer that treatments are beneficial when in fact there is no true effect. Existing retrieval and aggregation methods generally assume that more evidence is always better and lack mechanisms to detect and counteract this bias-induced drift in conclusions.
AI.method: The authors formally define and analyze a phenomenon they call evidence drift under a standard publication-bias model. They prove that for null-effect queries (where the true effect is zero), the probability of making a false-positive conclusion increases monotonically with retrieval depth and approaches one as the number of retrieved studies grows large. Empirically, they test this on 140 Cochrane-derived queries, measuring drift as retrieval depth (3 to 20 steps) increases, and observing that the drift is concentrated in null-effect cases. To counter this, they design DACG-agent, an agent that incrementally builds a causal knowledge graph from PubMed abstracts. DACG-agent employs a two-layer stopping policy: (1) an accuracy layer that monitors KL-divergence over the posterior to detect when beliefs have converged, and (2) an efficiency layer using a Bradley–Terry process reward model that detects when the estimated quality of additional evidence starts to decline, at which point retrieval is halted. They also run simulation experiments to show that the evidence drift behavior extends from a theoretically analyzed vote-counting aggregator to the practical noisy-OR aggregator used in deployment.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis shows that under publication bias, the false-positive probability for null-effect queries increases strictly with retrieval depth and tends to one as more studies are retrieved. In empirical evaluation on 140 Cochrane-derived queries, evidence drift increases monotonically from 7.9% to 15.7% as the retrieval budget grows from 3 to 20 steps, and this effect is concentrated among null-effect queries. DACG-agent, equipped with the two-layer stopping policy, substantially reduces drift compared with always using the full retrieval budget: drift is reduced from 15.7% to 6.4%, and accuracy on null-effect queries improves by 21 percentage points (from 40.0% to 61.4%). Overall accuracy across all query types improves from 61.4% to 69.3% (95% CI 61–77). A simulation study further confirms that the evidence drift behavior derived for a vote-counting aggregator also manifests for the noisy-OR aggregator used operationally.
AI.conclusion: Increasing retrieval depth in automated biomedical evidence synthesis is not always beneficial: due to systematic publication bias toward positive findings, deeper retrieval can systematically inflate false-positive conclusions in null-effect scenarios, a phenomenon the authors term evidence drift. They demonstrate both theoretically and empirically that false-positive rates can monotonically increase with retrieval depth. To address this, they introduce DACG-agent, which builds causal graphs over retrieved evidence and uses a dual-layer stopping policy based on posterior convergence and evidence-quality dynamics. This agent substantially reduces drift, improves null-effect and overall accuracy, and does so while using far fewer retrieval steps. The work implies that evidence-synthesis systems should be designed to be drift-aware, with principled stopping criteria rather than naively assuming that more retrieved evidence always leads to better conclusions.

title: Correct Diagnosis, Better Feedback: A Symbolic-Verifier for Faithful LLM Tutoring Feedback in Logic Proofs
summary: Effective LLM tutoring depends on correctly identifying the specific error in a student's reasoning before generating feedback. We study this problem in propositional-logic proof tutoring, where student actions can be checked against formal inference rules. We introduce a verifier-grounded architecture that separates diagnosis from language generation. Using 600 balanced student actions, we compare a zero-shot LLM detector, a fine-tuned detector, and a symbolic verifier. Each diagnosis is processed by shared rationale and feedback agents, isolating the effect of the initial diagnosis. The zero-shot detector achieves a macro-F1 of 0.191; fine-tuning raises this to 0.709 but retains systematic errors between structurally related classes. Rationales generally preserve the diagnosis supplied to them, showing that an incorrect diagnosis can be faithfully propagated through the pipeline. Feedback can likewise remain faithful to its rationale, non-revealing, and pedagogically appropriate while addressing the wrong error. Verifier-grounded feedback achieves the highest diagnostic correctness, and expert ratings largely uneven with the automatic feedback evaluations. These findings show that apparent feedback quality can conceal upstream diagnostic errors and that faithfulness must be evaluated separately from correctness. Our code is publicly available

AI.tldr: They evaluate how well different systems diagnose student errors in logic proofs and show that verifier-grounded architectures give more correct diagnoses, while LLMs can produce good-sounding but wrong feedback when the diagnosis is wrong.
AI.motivation: Large language models are used as tutors, but they often give plausible feedback that may be based on an incorrect understanding of a student’s mistake. In domains like propositional logic, where steps can be formally verified, it is possible to decouple identifying the error from generating natural-language feedback and systematically test where things go wrong.
AI.method: They build an architecture that first diagnoses a student’s proof step (using either a zero-shot LLM detector, a fine-tuned LLM detector, or a symbolic verifier) and then feeds this diagnosis into shared LLM agents that generate rationales and feedback. Using a balanced dataset of 600 student actions, they compare macro-F1 scores for diagnosis and analyze how faithfully rationales and feedback reflect upstream diagnoses, as well as how experts rate the feedback.
AI.result: The zero-shot LLM detector performs poorly (macro-F1 0.191). Fine-tuning greatly improves diagnostic performance (macro-F1 0.709) but still leaves systematic confusions between related error classes. Rationales and feedback usually remain faithful to the (possibly wrong) diagnosis they receive, meaning that incorrect diagnoses propagate through the pipeline. Verifier-grounded feedback yields the most accurate diagnoses, and expert ratings of feedback do not align cleanly with automatic feedback quality measures.
AI.conclusion: Separating diagnosis from language generation reveals that LLMs can generate pedagogically sound, faithful feedback that nevertheless targets the wrong error due to upstream diagnostic mistakes. Verifier-grounded approaches give more reliable diagnoses, and evaluating tutoring systems requires assessing both correctness and faithfulness, since high-quality-looking feedback can hide diagnostic errors.

title: EDGEGEN: Improving Tool-Calling Agents Beyond Happy Paths with Synthetic Edge Case Generation
summary: Tool-calling LLM agents are increasingly deployed in enterprise applications. However, effective evaluation and optimization require high-quality, diverse task datasets that are often difficult to obtain due to privacy and other constraints. Existing synthetic task generation methods often produce generic tasks that ignore an agent's underlying state or database and fail to reflect real-world usage diversity. We propose EdgeGen, a synthetic task generation framework that extracts compliance rules from an agent's specification and uses them to generate database-grounded edge-case tasks designed to violate these rules. When combined with existing synthetic data generation techniques, EdgeGen enables agent improvement through finetuning and harness optimization. The resulting pipeline forms a fully automated closed-loop system that requires no human annotation. Finetuning on data generated by EdgeGen yields a consistent mean progress improvement of 2 percent to 42 percent on tau2bench airline domain, while other baseline methods show degradation for some models. On the other hand, for harness optimization, our method shows a mean progress improvement of 10 percent and 30 percent over the human-curated and base harnesses, respectively, for the Gemma-4-e4b model.

AI.tldr: EdgeGen is a framework to automatically generate realistic, database-grounded edge-case tasks for tool-using LLM agents, improving their performance via finetuning and harness optimization without human annotation.
AI.motivation: Evaluating and improving tool-calling LLM agents in enterprises needs rich, diverse, and realistic task datasets. Real data are hard to collect because of privacy and access constraints, and existing synthetic generators create generic, non-diverse tasks that ignore the agent’s actual state, database, and compliance rules. This gap leads to poor coverage of real-world edge cases and limited gains from finetuning or harness design.
AI.method: The authors introduce EdgeGen, which first extracts compliance and behavioral rules from an agent’s specification (e.g., constraints, policies, usage rules). It then uses these rules, along with access to the agent’s underlying database, to synthesize edge-case tasks that are explicitly designed to violate or stress these rules (database-grounded edge cases). EdgeGen is combined with existing synthetic task generation methods to form a closed-loop pipeline: generate tasks (including rule-violating edge cases), run the agent, collect trajectories and outcomes, and then use these data for model finetuning and for optimizing the agent’s tool-calling harness. This loop is fully automated and requires no human annotations.
AI.result: On the tau2bench benchmark in the airline domain, finetuning models on EdgeGen-generated data yields consistent mean progress improvements ranging from 2% to 42%, whereas baseline synthetic data methods sometimes hurt performance. For harness optimization with the Gemma-4-e4b model, EdgeGen-based data lead to mean progress improvements of about 10% over a human-curated harness and about 30% over a base (unoptimized) harness.
AI.conclusion: Database-grounded, rule-targeting synthetic edge-case generation can substantially improve the robustness and performance of tool-calling LLM agents. EdgeGen demonstrates that automatically extracting compliance rules from agent specs and purposefully generating tasks that violate those rules enables a fully automated, closed-loop pipeline for finetuning and harness optimization, outperforming both generic synthetic data baselines and human-curated harnesses on an airline-domain benchmark.

title: Do Student LLMs Inherit OOD Robustness? Invariance-Weighted Distillation for Reliable Knowledge Transfer
summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) aims to compress high-performance teacher LLMs into lightweight students. However, distilled students often exhibit substantial performance degradation in out-of-distribution (OOD) settings, a critical gap that remains underexplored. We identify two compounding mechanisms causing OOD performance degradation: (1) data spuriousness: students can learn spurious correlations in the distillation dataset over genuine causal relationships; and (2) teacher capability: standard KD treats all samples uniformly, ignoring whether the teacher is guided by causal features or misled by spurious shortcuts on a given sample. To address these challenges, we propose Invariance-Weighted Distillation (IWD), a theoretically grounded framework that dynamically reweights training samples using an estimate of the teacher's causal reliance derived from prediction invariance across multiple synthetic environments. IWD perturbs spurious cues while preserving core semantics, assigning higher distillation weights to samples whose teacher predictions remain invariant, indicating greater reliance on causal rather than spurious features. We theoretically show that IWD reduces the student's Spurious-to-Causal (S2C) gradient ratio compared to standard uniformly weighted KD, driving the student toward more invariant representations. Experiments on four NLP benchmarks (MNLI, SQuAD-v2, CoNLL-2003 NER, and SST-2) across two model families (DeBERTa-v3 and Qwen-2.5) demonstrate that IWD consistently outperforms strong KD baselines on OOD evaluations while maintaining competitive in-distribution (ID) performance. Specifically, IWD achieves the highest accuracy in 15 out of 16 OOD benchmarks and improves average OOD performance over standard KD by 4.34 percentage points on NLI and 14.94 percentage points on QA.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Invariance-Weighted Distillation (IWD), a knowledge distillation method that reweights training samples based on how invariant the teacher’s predictions are under perturbations, to produce student models that generalize better out-of-distribution.
AI.motivation: Standard knowledge distillation often yields student models that perform well in-distribution but degrade significantly on out-of-distribution data. This is because (a) the distillation data may contain spurious correlations that students overfit to, and (b) classical KD treats all samples equally, even when the teacher is relying on spurious rather than causal features. The authors want a distillation process that preferentially transfers the teacher’s causal knowledge and reduces reliance on spurious cues, thereby improving robustness and OOD generalization.
AI.method: They introduce Invariance-Weighted Distillation (IWD). The core idea is to estimate, for each training example, how much the teacher’s prediction depends on causal versus spurious features by measuring prediction invariance across multiple synthetic environments. These environments are created by perturbing likely spurious cues while preserving core semantics. If the teacher’s prediction is stable across environments, it is assumed to be driven by causal features. IWD then assigns higher distillation weights to these invariant examples and lower weights where the teacher is sensitive to spurious perturbations. The authors provide a theoretical analysis showing that this weighting scheme decreases the student’s Spurious-to-Causal (S2C) gradient ratio relative to uniform KD, pushing the student to learn more invariant, causally aligned representations.
AI.result: On four NLP tasks (MNLI for NLI, SQuAD-v2 for QA, CoNLL-2003 for NER, and SST-2 for sentiment) and across DeBERTa-v3 and Qwen-2.5 model families, IWD consistently improves OOD performance compared to strong KD baselines while keeping in-distribution performance competitive. IWD attains best accuracy on 15 of 16 OOD benchmarks. Quantitatively, it improves average OOD performance over standard KD by 4.34 percentage points on NLI and 14.94 percentage points on QA.
AI.conclusion: Reweighting distillation samples based on the teacher’s prediction invariance is an effective way to transfer more causal and less spurious knowledge from teacher to student. IWD improves OOD robustness without sacrificing in-distribution accuracy and offers a theoretically justified approach to mitigating spurious correlations in knowledge distillation for large language models.

title: Self-Healing Harness for Runtime Oversight of Agent Self-Modification
summary: LLM agents can change their own future behavior, raising a basic control question of which self-generated changes should be allowed to persist. We formulate this as admission control for self-modification. The agent may propose changes to its operating instructions, while an external runtime gate controls persistence. We implement this principle as a model-agnostic self-healing harness that runs a Detect, Notice, Heal, Validate loop around an otherwise unmodified agent. The agent authors candidate behavioral rules in an external workspace, where they receive provisional execution authority during evaluation and acquire persistent cross-episode authority only after measured improvement on the triggering failure without regression beyond a fixed margin on protected cases. Replay provides matched evidence when available, forward trials provide a weaker fallback, and a corpus-level guard re-tests the accumulated active rule set. Across 16 matched Baseline and Harness runs spanning AppWorld, Terminal-Bench, and $τ^2$-Bench, the gate rejected 383 replay-decided proposals. Of these, 211 (55%) improved their triggering failure while degrading a case that previously worked. This shows that locally beneficial self-modifications can introduce collateral regressions often enough to materially affect gate decisions, providing direct empirical motivation for external admission control. Task-completion score is higher under the Harness in all 16 pairs, with two paired bootstrap intervals excluding zero, while repeated-trial reliability is higher in 12 pairs, tied in 4, and lower in none. Because adaptation modifies the policy-inducing context while leaving model weights fixed, admitted changes remain inspectable, reversible, and compatible with closed-weight models.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an external admission-control “harness” for LLM agents that want to change their own behavior, ensuring only beneficial and non-regressive self-modifications persist.
AI.motivation: LLM agents can write new instructions or rules for themselves that change their future behavior. Some self-changes may fix current failures but silently break previously working behaviors. The authors want a principled, empirical way to decide which self-modifications should be allowed, rather than trusting the agent’s own judgment, in order to improve safety, reliability, and compatibility with closed-weight models.
AI.method: They frame the problem as admission control for self-modification: the agent proposes behavioral-rule changes in an external workspace, and a separate runtime gate decides whether these changes gain persistent authority. They implement a model-agnostic “self-healing harness” that wraps an unmodified agent in a Detect–Notice–Heal–Validate loop. Proposed rules get provisional authority while being tested: using replay when failures can be reproduced, forward trials when replay is not possible, and a corpus-level guard that periodically re-tests the full active rule set. A rule is admitted only if it improves the triggering failure without causing regressions beyond a fixed margin on protected cases. The system is evaluated on three benchmarks (AppWorld, Terminal-Bench, τ^2-Bench) across 16 matched runs with and without the harness.
AI.result: In the experiments, the gate rejected 383 proposals that could be decided by replay; of these, 211 (55%) actually improved the original failure case but degraded some previously successful case, demonstrating frequent collateral regressions from seemingly beneficial changes. Across all 16 Baseline vs. Harness run pairs, task-completion scores are higher with the harness, with two pairs showing statistically significant gains (bootstrap intervals excluding zero). Reliability over repeated trials is higher in 12 pairs, tied in 4, and never worse with the harness.
AI.conclusion: External admission control for self-modifying LLM agents is both necessary and effective. Locally helpful self-modifications often introduce harmful regressions, so relying solely on the agent’s own assessment is unsafe. A model-agnostic self-healing harness, which evaluates and selectively admits external rule updates while keeping model weights fixed, can improve performance and reliability, keep changes inspectable and reversible, and remain compatible with closed-weight LLMs.

title: Preserving What Matters: Semantic Scaffolds Beyond Saturation in Summarization Evaluation
comment: Accepted at the AIMS Workshop at COLM 2026
