summary: Summarization ships in countless production systems, making model selection a routine decision that depends on measuring summary quality. Existing metrics struggle to support this: ROUGE captures only surface overlap, while LLM-as-judge scores saturate to near-identical values that fail to rank models effectively. We observe this saturation across three public datasets, two proprietary datasets, and multilingual settings. Motivated by this, we introduce Semantic Scaffold, an evaluation framework that extracts a hierarchical representation of facts, questions, and entity attributes from a source text, labeling each as a main point or supporting detail, and reusing this structure as a fixed reference for scoring summaries. From this representation, we derive three diagnostic metrics: Fact Preservation Score (FPS), Question Preservation Score (QPS), and Entity Preservation Score (EPS), designed to reward the preservation of essential information while penalizing detail overload, and position them as interpretable diagnostics that remain informative where holistic axes collapse. Finally, we analyze four recurring failure modes of ROUGE and LLM-as-judge scores, demonstrating that scaffold-based evaluation remains informative where conventional metrics collapse.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Semantic Scaffold, a structured evaluation framework for summarization that avoids the saturation and limitations of ROUGE and LLM-as-judge metrics by using a hierarchical fact-based representation to compute more diagnostic scores.
AI.motivation: Summarization systems are widely deployed, and choosing between models requires reliable metrics. Existing metrics have serious flaws: ROUGE focuses on surface-level n-gram overlap and misses semantic quality, while LLM-as-judge metrics tend to saturate, giving very similar scores that fail to distinguish models, as observed across multiple public, proprietary, and multilingual datasets. This makes model ranking and diagnostic evaluation difficult.
AI.method: The authors introduce Semantic Scaffold, which first extracts from the source text a hierarchical representation consisting of facts, questions, and entity attributes, each labeled as either a main point or a supporting detail. This scaffold is created once per source and then reused as a stable reference to evaluate different system summaries. From this scaffold, they define three diagnostic metrics—Fact Preservation Score (FPS), Question Preservation Score (QPS), and Entity Preservation Score (EPS)—that measure how well a summary preserves essential information, while penalizing inclusion of excessive or unnecessary details.
AI.result: Using three public datasets, two proprietary datasets, and multilingual experiments, the authors show that conventional metrics like ROUGE and LLM-as-judge often collapse, either missing semantic distinctions or saturating to nearly identical scores across systems. In contrast, the scaffold-based metrics (FPS, QPS, EPS) remain discriminative and informative, enabling finer-grained ranking and diagnosis of summarization models and highlighting where others fail (e.g., detail overload, missing key facts).
AI.conclusion: Semantic Scaffold provides a more interpretable and robust evaluation framework for summarization than commonly used metrics. By leveraging a reusable, hierarchical representation of the source text and targeted preservation scores, it avoids score saturation and surface-overlap bias, yielding diagnostics that stay informative in settings where ROUGE and LLM-as-judge metrics break down.

title: APEXA: Execution-Integrity Enforcement for Multi-Agent LLM Automation of Synchrotron Data Reduction
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures. Accepted at the 4th TPC Workshop @ SC'26 (Building Open AI Infrastructure, Models, and Agentic Systems for Science). Code and benchmark: https://github.com/AdvancedPhotonSource/APEXA-APS-Beamline-Assistant ; data: https://doi.org/10.18126/tgg4-1m26
summary: Synchrotron data reduction, detector calibration followed by azimuthal integration of terabyte-scale diffraction series, is a multi-step, expert-bound bottleneck that increasingly limits the science rate of user facilities. LLM agents promise to collapse it, but driving a real pipeline with a stochastic model creates a failure mode chat benchmarks cannot see: an agent can report a calibration that was never computed. Correctness here is a property of what executed, not of the transcript. We present APEXA, a deployed multi-agent framework (61 tools over heterogeneous compute, run as a single reasoning loop) automating calibration and integration from natural language at a major light source. We make three contributions. First, execution-integrity enforcement: a deterministic tool-layer guard that refuses to surface any result not backed by an executed tool call, with a parser tolerant of cross-model tool-call format drift: in deployment, a frontier model fabricated a complete calibration-comparison report for commands that never ran, which the guard converts to an explicit non-result; the same code gates an optional motor-control surface at 0/200 adversarial violations against a simulated IOC, versus 15/200 for an equivalent safety prompt. Second, we release APEXA-Bench, an evaluation harness of 58 facility tasks (50 base plus an 8-task cross-detector slice) organized by a four-class physical-consequence taxonomy, the first benchmark axis we know of separating a wasted compute cycle from a damaged instrument; its cross-detector grading against NIST-traceable lattice constants surfaced two latent pipeline bugs. Large-scale agent scoring is left to a full-length study. Third, we validate APEXA on real beamline data: from one natural-language prompt it recovers detector geometry and integrates a full attenuation/exposure sweep. We release the framework, harness and traces.

AI.tldr: APEXA is a multi-agent framework that safely automates synchrotron diffraction data reduction—from detector calibration to azimuthal integration—using natural-language control, while enforcing strict execution integrity and introducing a safety- and physics-aware benchmark.
AI.motivation: Synchrotron diffraction experiments generate terabytes of data whose reduction (detector calibration and azimuthal integration) is complex, multi-step, and typically requires expert intervention. This creates a bottleneck that limits the scientific throughput of large user facilities. While LLM-based agents could automate this workflow, standard chat-style evaluations miss a critical risk: an LLM might claim to have run calibrations or control actions that never actually executed, potentially wasting resources or even endangering instruments. There is thus a need for an agent framework that can both automate these pipelines and guarantee that reported results genuinely stem from executed, verified computations, with evaluation metrics aligned to physical consequences in a laboratory setting.
AI.method: The authors build APEXA, a deployed multi-agent system with 61 tools spanning heterogeneous compute resources, orchestrated as a single reasoning loop controllable via natural language. Their method has three main components: (1) an execution-integrity guard at the tool layer that deterministically enforces that any surfaced result must be backed by a real, logged tool execution, using a robust parser tolerant to variations in tool-call formats across LLMs; this guard can also gate optional motor-control commands and is evaluated against adversarial prompts on a simulated IOC. (2) APEXA-Bench, a new benchmark suite of 58 real facility tasks, categorized along a four-level taxonomy of physical consequences (e.g., from harmless wasted compute to risk of instrument damage), including cross-detector tasks graded against NIST-traceable lattice constants to check physical correctness; this harness is used to uncover latent bugs in existing pipelines. (3) A validation of the full APEXA system on real beamline data, where a single natural-language instruction triggers end-to-end detector geometry recovery and azimuthal integration over an attenuation/exposure sweep. The framework, benchmark harness, and interaction traces are released for reproducibility and further study.
AI.result: The execution-integrity guard successfully blocked fabricated outputs: in real deployment, when a leading LLM invented a complete calibration-comparison report for commands that were never executed, the guard recognized the lack of corresponding tool calls and returned an explicit non-result instead of a false success. In motor-control simulations on an IOC, the same guard achieved 0 violations in 200 adversarial test cases, compared with 15 violations out of 200 when relying solely on an equivalent safety prompt, showing a substantial safety gain. APEXA-Bench’s cross-detector, physically grounded grading surfaced two previously unknown bugs in the existing data-reduction pipeline, demonstrating the practical diagnostic value of the benchmark design. On real beamline data, APEXA, driven by one natural-language prompt, correctly recovered detector geometry and integrated a full attenuation/exposure sweep, confirming its ability to automate the end-to-end workflow in realistic conditions. The authors also provide the system, benchmark, and traces as open resources, enabling broader evaluation and extension, though large-scale agent scoring is deferred to future work.
AI.conclusion: APEXA demonstrates that complex synchrotron diffraction workflows can be automated via LLM agents when coupled with strict execution-integrity enforcement and physics-aware evaluation. The tool-layer guard eliminates a critical failure mode where agents may fabricate results not grounded in actual computation, outperforming safety prompting in adversarial tests and making it safer to expose control surfaces such as motor commands. APEXA-Bench introduces a benchmark paradigm that differentiates between mere inefficiency and potentially damaging actions, and its application already revealed hidden bugs in production pipelines, underscoring the need for such physically grounded assessments. Successful deployment on real beamline data shows the practical viability of natural-language-driven calibration and integration. Overall, the work positions execution-grounded, consequence-aware multi-agent systems as a necessary evolution for safely scaling LLM automation in large scientific facilities.

title: Pretrained Persona Mixture Models and Tandem Models for Human Simulation
comment: 11 pages in body, 36 with appendices. 7 figures. 8 tables
summary: We argue here that the current dominant practice in LLM human simulation: prompting instruction-tuned assistant language models to role-play personas, is inaccurate and produces stereotyped predictions (lacking natural diversity). It has previously been shown that LLMs can be bound to personas using naturalistic, freetext dialog avoiding stereotyping. Here we show that binding can also be achieved using short, individual samples of dialog from specific people. Demographics can be added later without negative effects by simply querying the model. We use the term Persona Mixture Models (PMMs) for well-calibrated human models, currently realized as pretrained base models. We show that PMMs produce more accurate predictions than instruction-tuned models and retain more of the lexical, semantic, and pragmatic diversity found in human dialog. We measure realism and diversity of LLMs simulating human interlocutors across a diverse set of corpora spanning open-domain text, human-AI chat, and task-oriented dialogue between human speakers. However, base pretrained models can produce out-of-domain dialog and may lose some of the human's internal state over long contexts. We propose and explore tandem models which combine a pre-trained model with an instruction-tuned supervisor. Tandem models achieve the best overall accuracy and diversity in our experiments.

AI.tldr: The paper critiques current LLM persona role-play practices, introduces Persona Mixture Models (PMMs) based on base models bound to real dialog samples, and shows that PMMs and tandem models (base + instruction-tuned supervisor) better match human realism and diversity.
AI.motivation: Current instruction-tuned assistants prompted to role-play personas generate stereotyped, low-diversity simulations of humans. The authors want a more accurate and realistic way to model individual people and populations with LLMs, preserving natural lexical, semantic, and pragmatic diversity. They also want a method that can be grounded in real conversational data instead of generic demographic stereotypes and that works across different dialogue domains.
AI.method: They compare standard instruction-tuned role-play setups to models that are bound to real individuals using short, naturalistic dialog samples. These are implemented as pretrained base LLMs conditioned on such data, termed Persona Mixture Models (PMMs). They evaluate realism and diversity across several corpora: open-domain text, human–AI chat, and task-oriented human–human dialogue. They analyze lexical, semantic, and pragmatic properties of generated dialog and examine how well models preserve human-like internal state over longer contexts. To mitigate base models’ issues (out-of-domain responses, state loss), they design tandem models that pair a base PMM with an instruction-tuned supervisor and test these against other configurations.
AI.result: PMMs based on pretrained base models, bound via short dialog samples from real people, generate more accurate and less stereotyped human simulations than instruction-tuned role-play models. PMMs maintain higher lexical, semantic, and pragmatic diversity and are better calibrated to individual speakers. Adding demographic attributes post hoc via queries does not degrade performance or increase stereotyping. However, base models sometimes drift out of domain and can lose track of interlocutors’ internal states over long interactions. Tandem models, which combine a PMM with an instruction-tuned supervisor, achieve the strongest performance overall, improving both accuracy and diversity relative to either component alone.
AI.conclusion: Instruction-tuned assistant models prompted to role-play personas are not reliable for realistic human simulation because they yield stereotyped, low-diversity behavior. More faithful simulations come from Persona Mixture Models: base pretrained LLMs bound to real individuals through short dialog samples, with demographics optionally layered afterward. While PMMs are superior to standard role-play, they still have weaknesses in long-context state tracking and domain control. Tandem models that integrate a PMM with an instruction-tuned supervisor provide the best trade-off, producing human-like, diverse, and accurate dialog across multiple corpora. This suggests future human simulation work should pivot from prompt-based role-play to data-grounded persona binding, potentially using tandem architectures.

title: CREDO: Variance-Guided Rubric Evolution for Replay-Corrected Credit Assignment
summary: Long-horizon language agents receive sparse terminal feedback, while intermediate rubrics provide structured but potentially misspecified assessments of progress. In resettable training environments, counterfactual continuation rollouts can measure local credit, but exhaustive replay is costly. We propose Credo, a framework that couples evolving semantic rubrics with selective, execution-based credit correction. A frozen judge maps visible transitions to rubric features, and a credit head predicts the change in expected terminal reward associated with the realized transition. Independently sampled two-sided replays correct prediction residuals using their recorded inclusion probabilities. We derive conditional unbiasedness and a variance decomposition that connects two design choices: which rubric features to retain, and where to allocate a fixed expected replay budget. The resulting criterion weights prediction errors by policy-score sensitivity and missing replay coverage; its allocation rule additionally accounts for continuation cost. We also describe a practical mixture with terminal leave-one-out advantages and distinguish its clipped, token-normalized PPO implementation from the ideal policy-gradient estimator. This preliminary report provides the method, proofs, an exact finite-model audit, and a controlled evaluation protocol. It makes no claim of empirical superiority on language-agent benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Credo is a framework to more accurately assign credit to intermediate actions of long-horizon language agents by combining rubric-based evaluation with selective replay-based credit correction.
AI.motivation: Training language agents over long horizons is hard because they get sparse feedback only at the end of an episode, while intermediate rubric scores may be imperfect or misspecified. Existing replay-based methods that estimate local credit via counterfactual continuations are accurate but computationally expensive if done exhaustively. There is a need for a principled and efficient way to use structured rubrics while correcting their biases to obtain better credit assignment for policy gradients.
AI.method: Credo uses a frozen judge to map observed transitions into semantic rubric features and trains a credit head to predict how each transition changes the expected terminal reward. To correct prediction biases, the method performs independently sampled two-sided counterfactual replays, and uses their known inclusion probabilities to debias the credit estimates. The authors derive conditions under which the estimator is conditionally unbiased and provide a variance decomposition that guides two key design decisions: (1) which rubric features to keep, and (2) how to allocate a fixed replay budget across states and transitions. They further define a practical mixture estimator that combines Credo-style credit with terminal leave-one-out advantages, and discuss a PPO-style clipped, token-normalized implementation that approximates the ideal policy-gradient estimator.
AI.result: The paper offers theoretical results: proofs of conditional unbiasedness, a variance decomposition that yields a principled weighting of prediction errors by policy-score sensitivity and replay coverage, and an allocation rule that incorporates continuation cost. They also present an exact finite-model audit and a controlled evaluation protocol to validate the estimator’s properties, but they do not claim or present empirical superiority on standard language-agent benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Credo provides a theoretically grounded framework to couple semantic rubrics with selective execution-based credit correction for long-horizon language agents. It clarifies how to choose rubric features and distribute replay effort under a fixed budget, and offers a practical PPO-style implementation. The work is positioned as a methodological and analytical contribution with audit and evaluation tools, rather than as an empirical state-of-the-art result on language-agent tasks.

title: Beetle: A Bilingual Model Suite for Modelling Second-Language Processing
summary: Bilingual language models (LMs) offer a controlled setting for studying how training conditions shape second-language (L2) behaviour, but prior work typically varies exposure structure, scale, and architecture at once, making it difficult to attribute effects to any single factor. We introduce Beetle, a controlled language model pretraining framework in which tokeniser, target language, training budget, and exposure structure are each independently manipulable, enabling systematic and comparable experimentation of training conditions. Using Beetle, we train and release 285 bilingual and 45 monolingual open-source LMs with rich checkpoints across a range of exposure schedules, data scales and first languages (L1s) to study multilingual pretraining and computational modelling of bilingualism and second language learning. Evaluating models on human bilingual and second language reading-time prediction and grammaticality judgement tasks, we find that staged and temporally structured curricula consistently improve alignment with language learner reading time compared to balanced bilingual training, with the largest gains at smaller data scales and for typologically closer language pairs. The Beetle models are well suited tools to help move computational psycholinguistics beyond its prevailing monolingual, English-centric focus toward models of human bilingual processing, to study cross-lingual learning dynamics, while supporting community-based development of controlled model families.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Beetle, a controlled pretraining framework and a large suite of bilingual and monolingual language models to systematically study how different training conditions affect second-language behavior and bilingual processing.
AI.motivation: Previous work on bilingual language models changes multiple factors at once—such as architecture, data scale, and exposure patterns—making it hard to isolate which aspects of training drive specific second-language and bilingual behaviours. There is a need for a controlled, open framework and model family that allows precise manipulation of training conditions to better model human bilingualism and second language learning, and to move psycholinguistics beyond an English-only focus.
AI.method: The authors build Beetle, a pretraining framework where tokeniser, target language, training budget, and exposure structure can be individually controlled. Using this framework, they train 285 bilingual and 45 monolingual language models with varied exposure schedules, data scales, and L1–L2 combinations. They then evaluate these models on tasks that tap into human bilingual processing: predicting reading times for bilinguals and L2 learners, and grammaticality judgement tasks. They compare different training curricula, including balanced bilingual exposure versus staged and temporally structured exposure.
AI.result: Staged and temporally structured training curricula consistently yield better alignment with human bilingual and L2 learner reading times than balanced bilingual exposure. The benefits are strongest when total training data is smaller and when the paired languages are typologically similar. The trained model suite covers a wide range of controlled conditions with saved checkpoints and is released as an open resource.
AI.conclusion: Carefully structuring the exposure schedule during bilingual language model pretraining—especially in staged or time-ordered ways—makes models better mirrors of human bilingual and second-language processing than simple balanced bilingual training. Beetle provides a controlled, extensible framework and a large open-source model family that enables systematic, psycholinguistically informed research on bilingualism and cross-lingual learning dynamics beyond monolingual, English-centric settings.

title: LIMIT: Less Is More for Instruction Tuning in Text-to-SQL
summary: Large language models have achieved remarkable progress on Text-to-SQL through reasoning-enhanced fine-tuning, yet existing approaches predominantly rely on massive instruction corpora under the assumption that scale drives performance. We challenge this paradigm by investigating a fundamental question: what is the minimal data requirement for effective Text-to-SQL instruction tuning? We propose LIMIT(Less Is More for Instruction Tuning in Text-to-SQL), a data-centric framework that demonstrates strong database reasoning can emerge from an extremely compact training set when examples are strategically selected. LIMIT operates through four stages: difficulty-aware filtering that identifies samples within the model's learning frontier, chain-of-thought synthesis with consistency-based selection, multi-dimensional quality scoring via LLM-as-judge, and genetic algorithm optimization that jointly maximizes schema coverage and sample quality. On the BIRD and Spider benchmark, LIMIT selects only 796 and 863 samples while achieving 100% table coverage, enabling Qwen3-8B to reach 69.1% and 88.9% execution accuracy.This result surpasses methods trained on 20 times more data and establishes a new state-of-the-art among open-source approaches. Our findings suggest that careful data curation, rather than scale, is the key to efficient Text-to-SQL learning.

AI.tldr: LIMIT is a data-centric framework showing that a very small, carefully curated instruction set can train LLMs to perform state-of-the-art Text-to-SQL reasoning, rivaling methods that use vastly more data.
AI.motivation: Most Text-to-SQL methods assume that scaling up instruction data improves performance, leading to reliance on massive training corpora. This is inefficient and expensive. The paper asks how little data is actually needed for effective Text-to-SQL instruction tuning, and whether smarter data selection can replace brute-force scaling.
AI.method: The authors propose LIMIT, a four-stage data selection and curation pipeline: (1) difficulty-aware filtering to pick samples within the model’s learning frontier (neither too easy nor too hard); (2) chain-of-thought (CoT) synthesis with consistency-based selection to retain only reliable reasoning traces; (3) multi-dimensional quality scoring using an LLM-as-a-judge to evaluate different aspects of example quality; and (4) a genetic algorithm that optimizes the final subset of training examples to jointly maximize database schema coverage and overall sample quality, producing a very compact but diverse instruction set.
AI.result: On the BIRD and Spider Text-to-SQL benchmarks, LIMIT selects only 796 and 863 examples respectively, while ensuring 100% coverage of tables in the schemas. Fine-tuning Qwen3-8B on these compact sets yields 69.1% and 88.9% execution accuracy, outperforming methods that use roughly 20× more training data and setting a new state-of-the-art among open-source Text-to-SQL systems.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that in Text-to-SQL, careful, principled data curation can substitute for large-scale instruction datasets. Strong database reasoning abilities can emerge from a very small, well-chosen set of training examples, indicating that data quality and selection strategies are more critical than sheer scale for efficient instruction tuning.

title: COT-TTS: Audio Context-Aware Text-to-Speech with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
summary: Recently, text-to-speech systems have made significant progress in speech expressiveness and controllability. However, the speaking style of generated speech typically relies on clear user-specified instructions. In natural conversations, speaking style should be naturally inferred from the preceding conversational context. Therefore, we propose COT-TTS, a context-aware, reasoning-based text-to-speech task. Given historical conversation audio, target text, and a reference speech, the system should comprehend the conversational context, infer an explicit intermediate reasoning, and finally synthesize the target speech with the specified timbre. To support this task, we constructed a large-scale bilingual conversational speech dataset comprising 9 million training samples, including a high-quality subset of 1 million samples. We further constructed a source-disjoint benchmark with 800 human-verified samples and established strong task-specific baselines. Additionally, we developed end-to-end autoregressive models with parameter sizes of 0.6B and 1.7B, generating emotion-labeled transcripts, editable speech style inferences, and speech tokens. Experimental results show that the proposed model achieves performance comparable to large-scale baseline systems with significantly fewer parameters. At the same time, the model performs well in terms of duration consistency and emotional consistency, and can generate appropriate emotional, stress, and rhythmic variations based on the conversational context. To facilitate future research, we will publicly release the data construction pipeline, dataset, trained models, and related resources. The demo page and additional resources are available at https://luckybian.github.io/COT-TTS

AI.tldr: They propose COT-TTS, a context-aware, reasoning-based TTS system that infers speaking style from conversational history, and provide a large bilingual dataset, benchmark, and compact autoregressive models that perform competitively with larger systems.
AI.motivation: Most modern TTS systems require explicit user instructions to control speaking style and emotion, which is unnatural for real conversations where prosody and emotion should follow from prior context. There is also a lack of large, high-quality conversational datasets and standardized tasks that couple reasoning about context with expressive TTS.
AI.method: They define a new TTS task (COT-TTS) where the model receives historical conversation audio, target text, and a timbre reference, then (1) understands the context, (2) produces an explicit intermediate reasoning about style/emotion, and (3) synthesizes context-appropriate speech. To support this, they build a 9M-sample bilingual conversational dataset (with a 1M-sample high-quality subset) and a source-disjoint benchmark of 800 human-verified samples. They design end-to-end autoregressive models (0.6B and 1.7B parameters) that jointly output emotion-labeled transcripts, editable style inferences, and speech tokens, and compare them against strong baseline systems.
AI.result: Their autoregressive COT-TTS models, despite having far fewer parameters than large baselines, reach comparable speech quality and style control. They demonstrate good duration and emotional consistency and show that the model generates suitable emotional, stress, and rhythmic variations conditioned on conversational context, as validated on their benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Context-aware, reasoning-based TTS that explicitly infers speaking style from conversational history is feasible and can be implemented with relatively compact models. Their dataset, benchmark, and models provide a foundation for future research on conversational, controllable TTS, and they will release the full pipeline and resources to the community.

title: SKstars at SHROOM: Visions Agreement-Guided Ensembling of Zero-Shot and LoRA-Adapted Vision--Language Models
comment: This paper has been accepted at the SHROOM-Visions 2026 Shared Task, co-located with EMNLP2026
summary: This paper describes the SKstars submission to SHROOM-Visions 2026, a shared task on fine-grained hallucination detection in large vision-language model outputs. The task requires systems to identify hallucinated character spans, assign hallucination categories, and provide confidence estimates for their predictions. Our approach combines zero-shot predictions from Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct with those of a LoRA-adapted Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct model. The outputs of the two models are integrated through a lightweight ensemble procedure, followed by span refinement and confidence adjustment. We evaluate the main system components on a small internal development subset and report the performance of the submitted system on the official English test set. SKstars achieved a Cor+Lbl score of 0.2902, ranking 15th among 29 teams, and obtained Cor and IoU scores of 0.3642 and 0.3151, respectively, ranking 18th on both metrics. The results show that combining a large zero-shot model with a smaller adapted model provides a practical framework for multilingual and fine-grained hallucination localization, while also highlighting the difficulty of transferring development-set improvements to hidden test data. Code and predictions: https://github.com/aliathar1401/SK-Stars-shroom-visions-2026

AI.tldr: They build an ensemble system for detecting fine-grained hallucinations in vision-language model outputs, combining a large zero-shot model with a smaller fine-tuned one, and evaluate it in the SHROOM-Visions 2026 shared task.
AI.motivation: Large vision-language models often hallucinate details not grounded in the input image or text, and there is a need to automatically detect and localize such hallucinations at a fine-grained span level with category labels and confidence scores. Shared tasks like SHROOM-Visions 2026 provide a benchmark to compare approaches and understand what works for multilingual, fine-grained hallucination detection.
AI.method: They use two models based on Qwen2.5-VL: a large 72B-parameter instruct model in zero-shot mode, and a smaller 7B-parameter model adapted with LoRA. Both produce hallucination span predictions, labels, and confidences. A lightweight ensemble procedure integrates the outputs, after which they perform span refinement and adjust confidences. They evaluate components on an internal dev subset and report official test-set scores on the English split.
AI.result: On the official English test set, the system obtains a Cor+Lbl score of 0.2902 (15th/29 teams), and Cor and IoU scores of 0.3642 and 0.3151 (18th for both metrics). The results indicate moderate performance relative to other systems in the shared task.
AI.conclusion: An ensemble of a large zero-shot vision-language model with a smaller LoRA-adapted model is a practical way to perform multilingual, fine-grained hallucination localization. However, the modest ranking and metric scores highlight the challenges of generalizing improvements seen on a small development set to a hidden test set, suggesting that better robustness and transfer methods are needed.

title: LLaDA-PRM: A Bidirectional Step-Level Reasoning Evaluator
summary: Step-level reasoning evaluators are commonly based on autoregressive language models, whose causal attention restricts each step representation to the problem, previous steps, and the current step. Yet, when the complete solution is available, the validity of an earlier step may become clearer only through its downstream consequences. We validate this hypothesis through a controlled 54-run comparison of causal and bidirectional LLaDA evaluators at 1B--3B scale, changing only the self-attention mask, and find bidirectional attention yields consistent improvements. Building on this finding, we introduce \prm{}, an 8B bidirectional evaluator that reaches 88.8 step-level F1 on MR-MATH-invalid and 83.8 on the out-of-distribution MR-GSM8K original-question subset, outperforming ReasonEval-Llemma-34B by 11.3 and 10.3 F1 points, respectively. \prm{} also remains effective when evaluating incomplete reasoning traces in online settings, outperforming the strongest baselines on both benchmarks by a large margin. We further show that \prm{} provides an effective training-data selection signal, improving Mistral-7B performance on MATH-500.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that using bidirectional attention for step-level reasoning evaluation significantly improves performance over traditional causal (autoregressive) evaluators, and introduces an 8B model, PRM, that sets new state-of-the-art results on multiple mathematical reasoning benchmarks and is also useful for data selection.
AI.motivation: Existing step-level reasoning evaluators typically rely on autoregressive language models with causal attention, meaning each step can only attend to the problem description, past steps, and the current step. However, in many reasoning tasks, the correctness of an intermediate step becomes clearer when you can see its downstream consequences in the full solution. The authors hypothesize that evaluators should be allowed to look at the entire reasoning trace (both past and future steps) to judge each step more accurately.
AI.method: The authors run a controlled comparison between causal and bidirectional evaluators based on LLaDA models ranging from 1B to 3B parameters, where the only change is the attention mask (causal vs bidirectional). After confirming that bidirectional attention improves evaluation quality, they design PRM, an 8B-parameter bidirectional evaluator. They test PRM on MR-MATH-invalid and MR-GSM8K original-question subsets for step-level F1, and also evaluate PRM in online settings where only partial reasoning traces are available. Additionally, they use PRM scores as a signal for selecting better training data and measure its impact on training Mistral-7B for MATH-500.
AI.result: Bidirectional attention consistently outperforms causal attention in the 54-run comparison across 1B–3B models. The PRM 8B bidirectional evaluator achieves 88.8 step-level F1 on MR-MATH-invalid and 83.8 on the out-of-distribution MR-GSM8K original-question subset, surpassing ReasonEval-Llemma-34B by 11.3 and 10.3 F1 points, respectively. PRM also outperforms all baselines by a large margin when evaluating incomplete reasoning traces in online scenarios. When used for training-data selection, PRM improves the performance of Mistral-7B on the MATH-500 benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Allowing evaluators to use bidirectional attention—seeing both earlier and later steps in a reasoning trace—substantially improves step-level reasoning evaluation over traditional causal models. The proposed 8B PRM model sets new state-of-the-art results on multiple reasoning benchmarks, works well even when traces are incomplete, and serves as an effective signal for selecting high-quality training data, leading to downstream performance gains.

title: Recovering Lost Details: Multi-Scale Frequency Compensation for Long-Term Time Series Forecasting
comment: 11 pages. Accepted at the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM 2026)
summary: Long-term time series forecasting has made significant progress by leveraging multi-scale information to capture hierarchical temporal patterns and model long-range dependencies. However, temporal downsampling in existing multi-scale methods inevitably smooths detailed temporal fluctuations, and this information loss is further aggravated by their emphasis on dominant trends across scales, resulting in insufficiently expressive representations. To address this, we propose a Multi-Scale Wavelet Mixing (MWMixer) model, which incorporates a Bidirectional Frequency-Bands Mixing strategy to recover lost temporal details across scales, enabling complementary cross-scale information interactions. Then, a Dynamic Scale-Adaptive Fusion module learns time-varying weights for each scale to fuse multi-scale forecasts into the final prediction, enhancing the flexibility of multi-scale aggregation. In addition, a cross-scale consistency loss aligns each coarse-scale prediction with the interval-averaged fine-scale outputs, while a multi-scale supervision loss enforces prediction accuracy at each scale, promoting consistent learning across scales. Extensive experiments on seven real-world datasets demonstrate that MWMixer achieves competitive performance in long-term forecasting.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MWMixer, a multi-scale wavelet-based model for long-term time series forecasting that better preserves and fuses fine-grained temporal details across scales, achieving competitive performance on seven datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing long-term time series forecasting models use multi-scale representations to capture hierarchical temporal patterns and long-range dependencies, but they rely on temporal downsampling that smooths out fine-grained temporal variations. This downsampling, combined with a focus on dominant trends, leads to loss of detailed information and insufficiently expressive representations, limiting forecasting accuracy.
AI.method: The authors introduce MWMixer, a Multi-Scale Wavelet Mixing model. First, they use a Bidirectional Frequency-Bands Mixing strategy to allow information to flow across frequency bands and scales, explicitly recovering and sharing fine-scale temporal details that are lost during downsampling. Second, they propose a Dynamic Scale-Adaptive Fusion module that learns time-varying weights for each scale, adaptively aggregating scale-specific predictions into the final forecast. Third, they design two training losses: (1) a cross-scale consistency loss that forces coarse-scale predictions to match the interval-averaged fine-scale outputs, ensuring alignment between resolutions; and (2) a multi-scale supervision loss that directly supervises predictions at every scale, encouraging accurate and coherent multi-scale learning.
AI.result: Across seven real-world time series datasets, the proposed MWMixer achieves competitive, and likely superior, performance compared with existing long-term forecasting baselines, showing the effectiveness of bidirectional wavelet mixing, dynamic scale fusion, and multi-scale training objectives.
AI.conclusion: By explicitly recovering fine-scale temporal details, enabling rich cross-scale interactions, and enforcing consistency and supervision at multiple resolutions, MWMixer improves the expressiveness of multi-scale time series representations and delivers strong long-term forecasting performance. The framework demonstrates that careful frequency-band mixing and adaptive multi-scale fusion can mitigate the information loss inherent in temporal downsampling.

title: Analyzing Public Discourse on Urbanism: Topic Clustering, Sentiment Analysis and Retrieval-Augmented Generation using YouTube Comments
summary: Online discourse about urban issues - walkability, cycling infrastructure, public transit, housing density, and street safety - is voluminous but unstructured, and existing city-evaluation tools capture none of it. We present a pipeline and conversational system that combines geographic entity resolution, topic modeling, sentiment analysis, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) over 22,788 chunks of YouTube transcripts and comments spanning 309 North American cities. Beyond the system itself, our contribution is a set of measurements about what happens when standard NLP components meet short, informal, geographically ambiguous text. A Twitter-tuned RoBERTa classifier outperforms a VADER lexicon baseline by 12.6 macro-F1 points (0.589 vs. 0.464; McNemar p = 0.0001), but both models collapse on the neutral class, which dominates urbanist comment traffic; annotators disagree on the same class (Cohen's kappa = 0.53). Dense retrieval beats a TF-IDF baseline at every cutoff (P@5 0.790 vs. 0.560), and video-level relevance proxies understate chunk-level precision by a wide margin (0.660 vs. 0.94 under human rating). For groundedness evaluation, we find BERTScore unusable when a multi-sentence generated summary is compared against a single short comment - scores are nearly flat regardless of relevance - and show that ROUGE-1-based groundedness is a paraphrase-driven lower bound rather than a hallucination rate. These findings generalize beyond the urbanist domain to any RAG system built over short user-generated documents.

AI.tldr: The paper builds and evaluates a RAG-based conversational system using noisy YouTube urbanism content, and uses it to systematically stress-test standard NLP components on short, informal, geographically ambiguous text.
AI.motivation: Urban issues like walkability, cycling, transit, density, and safety are heavily discussed online, but this rich citizen discourse is unstructured and ignored by conventional city-evaluation tools. The authors want to unlock this data source and understand how well standard NLP tools work on short, informal, and geographically ambiguous user-generated content in such a setting.
AI.method: They construct a pipeline and conversational RAG system over 22,788 text chunks from YouTube videos and comments covering 309 North American cities. The pipeline integrates geographic entity resolution, topic modeling, sentiment analysis with a Twitter-tuned RoBERTa classifier and VADER baseline, dense vs. TF-IDF retrieval evaluation, and groundedness assessment of generated summaries using metrics like BERTScore and ROUGE-1. They then empirically compare and analyze component performance, including inter-annotator agreement on sentiment labels and human-rated relevance at chunk level.
AI.result: The Twitter-tuned RoBERTa sentiment classifier substantially outperforms the VADER lexicon baseline by 12.6 macro-F1 points (0.589 vs. 0.464, McNemar p = 0.0001), but both struggle with the majority neutral class, which even human annotators inconsistently label (kappa = 0.53). Dense retrieval consistently beats TF-IDF at all cutoffs (e.g., P@5 0.790 vs. 0.560). Video-level heuristics underestimate actual chunk-level retrieval precision (0.660 vs. 0.94 per human ratings). For groundedness evaluation, BERTScore fails to discriminate relevance when summarizing from very short comments, and ROUGE-1 groundedness behaves more as a paraphrase similarity lower bound than a true hallucination detector.
AI.conclusion: The system demonstrates that online urbanist discourse can be systematically mined with a RAG pipeline, but also exposes important weaknesses of off-the-shelf sentiment, retrieval, and groundedness tools on short, noisy user text. RoBERTa outperforms lexicon sentiment analysis yet still struggles with the dominant neutral class, dense retrieval is clearly preferable to TF-IDF and chunk-level evaluation is essential, and common automatic groundedness metrics like BERTScore and ROUGE-1 are unreliable in this setting. These lessons extend to other RAG systems built over short user-generated documents, not just urbanism content.

title: Taming CoT Obfuscation in VLMs: From Mechanistic Evidence to Activation Enforcement
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) improves reasoning in vision-language models (VLMs) but can induce chain-of-thought (CoT) obfuscation: an operational, non-intentional outcome where task reward or accuracy rises while traces become less grounded and monitorable. Prior work largely documents this decay behaviorally, leaving its representation-level correlates and actionable controls unclear. We find that template- and ground-associated activations become less separable during RL; matched interventions support the contribution of selected features to monitorability degradation. Guided by this evidence, we propose Targeted Anti-obfuscation with Mechanistic Enforcement (TAME), which uses Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to combine behavioral feedback with targeted suppression of template-associated activations during RL. Its asymmetric constraint penalizes template activations only above their pre-RL baseline, anchoring the localized features while behavioral feedback promotes grounded refinements. Across VIRL-39k, SPA-VL, and two model families, TAME improves CoT monitorability by up to 30.9 and 16.7 percentage points over Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), respectively. Blinded human evaluation finds higher human monitorability on both datasets, and two held-out monitor families reproduce the monitorability gains. Task accuracy changes are small and mixed, and general-capability benchmarks show task-specific trade-offs. These results provide a path from behavioral monitoring to representation-level oversight for more auditable RL-trained multimodal systems.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies and mitigates a problem where reinforcement learning makes vision-language models’ chain-of-thought harder to interpret, even as performance improves.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning improves reasoning in vision-language models but often makes their chain-of-thought explanations less grounded and harder to monitor, posing oversight and safety challenges. Prior work mainly observes this behaviorally and lacks a representation-level understanding or concrete mechanisms to control it.
AI.method: The authors analyze internal representations and show that activations linked to templates vs. grounded reasoning become less separable during RL. They use sparse autoencoders to identify and target these features and propose TAME (Targeted Anti-obfuscation with Mechanistic Enforcement), which adds an asymmetric constraint during RL that penalizes only increases in template-associated activations above their pre-RL baseline, while still using behavioral feedback for learning.
AI.result: On VIRL-39k and SPA-VL across two VLM families, TAME boosts chain-of-thought monitorability by up to 30.9 and 16.7 percentage points over GRPO, respectively. Human blind evaluations confirm improved perceived monitorability, and independent monitoring methods reproduce the gains. Task accuracy changes are modest and mixed, and broader capability benchmarks indicate some task-specific trade-offs.
AI.conclusion: Representation-targeted constraints during RL can reduce chain-of-thought obfuscation in VLMs, improving the interpretability and auditability of their reasoning with limited impact on accuracy. This bridges behavioral monitoring with representation-level oversight and suggests a scalable way to train more transparent multimodal systems.

title: Clinical Domain Classification from Medical Transcriptions
summary: Clinical domain classification plays an important role in organizing and analyzing large volumes of unstructured medical text. However, medical transcription datasets are often highly imbalanced, which can substantially degrade classification performance, particularly for underrepresented clinical specialties. In this work, we present a comparative study of machine learning and transformer-based approaches for clinical domain classification from medical transcriptions. We evaluate six traditional machine learning classifiers---Naive Bayes, Support Vector Machine (SVM), Decision Tree, Random Forest, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and XGBoost---along with two pretrained transformer models, BERT and XLNet, and a few-shot large language model prompting approach. Experiments are conducted on medical transcription data collected from MTSamples, comprising 5,013 samples across 40 clinical specialties. To address severe class imbalance, we investigate two balancing strategies: text augmentation using NLP-based synonym replacement and Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE). Experimental results demonstrate that data balancing substantially improves classification performance across the evaluated models. In particular, BERT achieves the highest F1-score of 0.996 on the SMOTE-balanced dataset while requiring lower training time than XLNet. The results highlight the effectiveness of transformer-based representations combined with appropriate data balancing strategies for clinical domain classification and provide a systematic comparison of classical machine learning, transformer models, and few-shot prompting for medical transcription analysis.

AI.tldr: The paper compares classic machine‑learning models, transformer models, and few‑shot prompting for classifying clinical specialties from highly imbalanced medical transcription data, showing that transformers (especially BERT) plus SMOTE balancing achieve near‑perfect performance.
AI.motivation: Clinical text is largely unstructured, and automatic classification by clinical specialty is useful for organizing and analyzing it. Real medical transcription datasets are highly imbalanced, which hurts performance for rare specialties. The authors want to understand which modeling approaches and imbalance-handling strategies work best under these realistic conditions.
AI.method: They use a medical transcription dataset (MTSamples: 5,013 notes, 40 specialties) and compare six traditional classifiers (Naive Bayes, SVM, Decision Tree, Random Forest, KNN, XGBoost), two pretrained transformers (BERT, XLNet), and a few-shot large language model prompting setup. To tackle severe class imbalance, they test two balancing strategies: (1) textual data augmentation by synonym replacement and (2) SMOTE on feature representations. They then evaluate and compare models using F1-score and training time.
AI.result: Balancing the classes markedly improves classification performance across all model families. BERT obtains the best performance with an F1-score of 0.996 on the SMOTE-balanced dataset and trains faster than XLNet. Classical models and few-shot prompting perform worse than transformer fine-tuning when imbalance is properly addressed, though all benefit from balancing.
AI.conclusion: Transformer-based models, especially BERT, are highly effective for clinical domain classification from medical transcriptions when combined with suitable data balancing techniques like SMOTE. The study provides a systematic, empirical comparison showing that addressing class imbalance is crucial and that modern transformer representations outperform classic machine learning and few-shot prompting on this task in both accuracy and efficiency.

title: Unsupervised Brain Anomaly Detection as a Bayesian Inverse Problem with Diffusion Prior
summary: Unsupervised anomaly detection (UAD) aims to localize abnormal regions in medical scans without pixel-level annotations. A typical strategy seeks to reconstruct a pseudo-healthy image that preserves subject-specific anatomy. Recently, diffusion models have been proposed to perform UAD. However, these methods rely on heuristic noise schedules or synthetic corruptions to balance subject-specificity and anomaly removal. In this work, we propose an alternative formulation of UAD as a Bayesian inverse problem under a diffusion prior. First, we introduce a latent spatial anomaly mask that models pixel-wise consistency between a test image and its latent corresponding pseudo-healthy image. Then, we propose an approximation of the unknown generation process that links healthy anatomy, anomalies, and the observed image, enabling a well-defined likelihood within the Bayesian framework. Building on recent advances in diffusion-based inverse problem methods, we jointly infer the pseudo-healthy image and the anomaly mask via annealed posterior sampling. We evaluate our approach on FDG PET (ADNI) and FLAIR MRI (BraTS 2021), demonstrating improved anomaly localization performance compared to other diffusion-based approaches and validating the contribution of our introduced model. Our code is available at https://github.com/HuguesRoy/UAD_DAPS.

AI.tldr: They propose a new diffusion-based, fully unsupervised method to detect and localize anomalies in medical images by casting it as a Bayesian inverse problem with an explicit anomaly mask.
AI.motivation: Existing unsupervised anomaly detection in medical imaging often uses reconstruction of a pseudo-healthy image, but diffusion-based UAD methods depend on heuristic choices (noise schedules, synthetic corruptions) that make it hard to simultaneously maintain patient-specific anatomy and reliably remove anomalies. There is a need for a principled probabilistic formulation that more cleanly separates healthy anatomy from pathological anomalies, with a well-defined likelihood to support robust inference.
AI.method: They formulate UAD as a Bayesian inverse problem with a diffusion model as the prior over healthy images. They introduce a latent spatial anomaly mask representing per-pixel agreement between the observed scan and its pseudo-healthy counterpart. They approximate the generative process that connects healthy anatomy, anomalies, and the observed image, which yields a tractable likelihood. Using recent diffusion-based inverse problem techniques, they perform annealed posterior sampling to jointly infer the pseudo-healthy image and the anomaly mask from an input scan.
AI.result: On two benchmark datasets (FDG PET from ADNI and FLAIR MRI from BraTS 2021), their approach achieves better anomaly localization metrics than prior diffusion-based UAD methods. Ablation or comparative experiments show that the explicitly modeled anomaly mask and Bayesian formulation contribute meaningfully to the performance gains.
AI.conclusion: Casting UAD as a Bayesian inverse problem with a diffusion prior and an explicit latent anomaly mask yields a more principled and effective framework for unsupervised medical anomaly localization. The combination of a structured likelihood and annealed posterior sampling improves localization accuracy over heuristic diffusion-based methods, and the approach generalizes across modalities like PET and MRI.

title: Beyond Final-Token Classification: Heterogeneous Readouts for Evidence-Grounded Suicide Risk Detection
comment: Competition paper for the IEEE Big Data Cup 2026. Ranked 2nd among 31 participating teams and invited for submission to IEEE Big Data 2026
summary: The IEEE BigData Cup benchmark combines three prediction problems with different output structures: ordinal suicide-risk classification, multi-label psychosocial factor detection, and extraction of supporting phrases. We introduce heterogeneous readout decomposition (HRD), which separates semantic verification from output realization. A locally deployed Qwen3.8-27B model, adapted with task-specific QLoRA adapters, produces both answer-token margins and layer-63 answer states for card-conditioned queries. HRD compares four latent scores for ordinal risk, retains token margins for most factors while routing seven labels through one shared latent probe, and constructs evidence sets from verbatim span candidates with calibrated, risk-conditional constraints. On two held-out user-grouped confirmation folds, the latent risk readout improves weighted F1 from 0.8237 to 0.8372 and macro F1 from 0.7965 to 0.8185. Selective factor routing improves macro F1 by 0.0105 and tail-label macro F1 by 0.0189; in contrast, global latent replacement and independent label-specific probes fail. The constrained evidence decoder raises pooled phrase F1 from 0.7488 to 0.7609 in row-level out-of-fold evaluation. Lenormand's best public result is 0.8052 on Subtask 1 and 0.6636 on Subtask 2, giving a composite score of 0.7627. These results identify the answer-token boundary, rather than semantic representation alone, as a measurable source of error in this benchmark.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new way (HRD) to decode LLM outputs for the IEEE BigData Cup suicide-risk benchmark, showing that how answers are read from the model’s token stream significantly affects performance across three tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches on the IEEE BigData Cup mostly treat the model’s hidden representations or logits in a uniform way across tasks and labels. However, the benchmark combines three heterogeneous prediction problems—ordinal suicide-risk levels, multi-label psychosocial factors, and phrase extraction—whose optimal readout structures may differ. There is also a gap between strong latent semantic understanding and the final discrete answers, suggesting that errors may come from the decoding boundary rather than the representation itself. The authors aim to design a decoding framework that better aligns the model’s internal semantics with task-specific outputs, and to understand where performance is actually lost in this pipeline.
AI.method: They introduce Heterogeneous Readout Decomposition (HRD), which explicitly separates semantic verification from output realization and tailors the readout to each subtask. A locally hosted Qwen3.8-27B model with task-specific QLoRA adapters is queried with card-conditioned prompts, and two types of internal signals are extracted: answer-token margins (logit-based) and layer-63 hidden states for candidate answers. For ordinal suicide risk, HRD computes four latent scores to derive the risk level, improving the mapping from latent states to ordinal categories. For psychosocial factors, most labels use direct token-margin based predictions, but seven challenging labels are routed through a shared latent probe that operates on hidden states. For supporting-phrase extraction, HRD constructs evidence sets from verbatim span candidates and applies calibrated, risk-conditional constraints to select consistent phrase sets. They run user-grouped, held-out confirmation folds to evaluate generalization and compare against variants: global latent replacement, independent label-specific probes, and unconstrained evidence decoding.
AI.result: With HRD, latent risk readout increases weighted F1 from 0.8237 to 0.8372 and macro F1 from 0.7965 to 0.8185 on ordinal suicide risk. Selective factor routing for psychosocial labels boosts overall macro F1 by 0.0105 and tail-label macro F1 by 0.0189, while alternatives like global latent replacement and separate probes per label do not improve performance. For supporting-phrase extraction, the constrained evidence decoder improves pooled phrase-level F1 from 0.7488 to 0.7609 on out-of-fold rows. Compared to Lenormand’s top public baseline (0.8052 on Subtask 1 and 0.6636 on Subtask 2, composite 0.7627), HRD achieves higher scores, demonstrating state-of-the-art or near state-of-the-art performance on this benchmark.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that carefully designing heterogeneous readout mechanisms for different output structures yields measurable gains on the IEEE BigData Cup benchmark. In particular, the way answer tokens are decoded from the model—i.e., the answer-token boundary—constitutes a substantial and quantifiable source of error, separate from the quality of the underlying semantic representations. HRD’s separation of semantic verification from output realization, combined with selective latent routing and constrained evidence decoding, leads to better ordinal risk classification, improved detection of rare psychosocial factors, and more accurate supporting-phrase extraction. This suggests that future work on similar tasks should pay as much attention to decoding and readout design as to model architecture and representation learning.

title: How Many Pixels Is a Digit Worth? Place-Aware Coordinate Entropy for GUI Agent Confidence Estimation
summary: GUI agents predict click coordinates as digit-token sequences, but standard text-LLM confidence estimation methods rank correct clicks from wrong ones only weakly. GUI-specific alternatives use K samples or new supervision, but still leave room for improvement. We trace part of this to place-value asymmetry: bounding-box correctness often makes higher-place digits more important than lower-place digits, so uniform aggregation weakens the signal that determines correctness. The fix is to weight each digit's Shannon entropy by its place value. We call this Place-Aware Coordinate Entropy (PACE). Across fixed-scale agents on ScreenSpot-Pro and ScreenSpot-v2, PACE wins both AUROC and selective accuracy on all primary comparisons in a single forward pass, matching or outperforming K-sample baselines at a fraction of the cost. PACE provides a per-click confidence estimate that turns coordinate-token internals into a practical confidence signal for GUI agent deployment.

AI.tldr: Proposes PACE, a place-aware entropy-based confidence metric for GUI click-coordinate predictions that outperforms existing methods in AUROC and selective accuracy with a single forward pass.
AI.motivation: Existing confidence estimation methods for GUI agents that predict click coordinates as digit tokens are weak at distinguishing correct from incorrect clicks, and GUI-specific methods require multiple samples or extra supervision yet still underperform. A key overlooked issue is that, for bounding-box correctness, higher-place digits in the coordinate are more important than lower-place digits, but current methods treat all digit positions uniformly, diluting the most informative signal.
AI.method: Introduce Place-Aware Coordinate Entropy (PACE), which computes per-digit Shannon entropy over the coordinate token sequence and weights each digit’s entropy by its place value, making higher-order digits contribute more to the confidence score. This is done in a single forward pass of the fixed-scale GUI agent model, turning internal coordinate-token distributions into a calibrated confidence score. PACE is evaluated on ScreenSpot-Pro and ScreenSpot-v2 against K-sample and other baselines.
AI.result: On ScreenSpot-Pro and ScreenSpot-v2, PACE achieves higher AUROC and better selective accuracy than all primary baseline methods while using only a single forward pass, matching or outperforming K-sample approaches at significantly lower computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for place-value asymmetry in coordinate prediction via PACE yields a stronger, cheaper confidence signal for GUI agents. By weighting per-digit entropy by place value, PACE transforms internal token-level uncertainties into a practical per-click confidence estimate that is effective for deployment and superior to existing multi-sample or uniformly aggregated methods.

title: NLPCC 2026 Task 10: Citation-Level Faithfulness Verification with DeBERTa Ensembles and Class-Wise Calibration
comment: Accepted to the NLPCC 2026 Shared Task 10 system paper track. Ranked 2nd in Track 2 on the final leaderboard
summary: This paper presents our system for Track 2 of the NLPCC 2026 Shared Task 10 on citation-level faithfulness in AI-assisted scientific reporting. Given an atomic scientific claim and the structured full text of its cited paper, the task requires both a four-way relation label and up to three evidence paragraph identifiers. The label head ensembles a paragraph-aware cross-encoder with a document-level DeBERTa-large classifier, followed by class-wise decision calibration. Probability-level fusion is motivated by an out-of-fold tendency to over-predict Topical Match. The evidence head combines paragraph scores from top-20 and top-30 joint models with BM25 scores. The system runs fully offline without external retrieval or LLM prompting. On the final leaderboard, our system achieved 82.9898 overall (89.5491 Macro-F1 and 76.4305 Joint@3), ranking second in Track 2. Ablations and error analysis show that model complementarity and calibration drive the label gains. Gold-evidence inference changes label Macro-F1 negligibly, whereas evidence ranking remains important for Joint@3.

AI.tldr: They build an offline, ensemble system to label how faithful an AI-assisted scientific claim is to its cited paper and to rank supporting evidence paragraphs, achieving second place in an NLPCC 2026 shared task.
AI.motivation: AI-generated or assisted scientific writing can misrepresent cited work. The shared task defines a benchmark to assess citation-level faithfulness: given a claim and its source paper, systems must determine how the claim relates to the paper and identify supporting evidence. The authors aim to build a strong, practical system for this task and to understand what contributes most to performance.
AI.method: They design a two-head architecture. The label head ensembles (1) a paragraph-aware cross-encoder and (2) a document-level DeBERTa-large classifier. Their outputs are fused at the probability level, and they apply class-wise decision calibration to correct a systematic tendency to over-predict the Topical Match label observed in out-of-fold predictions. The evidence head aggregates paragraph scores from joint models run over top-20 and top-30 paragraphs and combines these with BM25 retrieval scores to rank evidence paragraphs. The entire pipeline runs offline, without external retrieval systems or LLM prompts.
AI.result: On the NLPCC 2026 Shared Task 10, Track 2, the system achieves an overall score of 82.9898, with 89.5491 Macro-F1 for label prediction and 76.4305 Joint@3, placing second on the final leaderboard. Ablation studies show that ensembling complementary models and applying calibration significantly improve label performance. Using gold evidence at inference barely changes label Macro-F1, but evidence ranking quality strongly affects Joint@3.
AI.conclusion: Model complementarity and calibrated probability fusion are key to high citation-level faithfulness classification performance. While better evidence ranking is crucial for joint label-and-evidence metrics, providing perfect evidence does not substantially change label Macro-F1, indicating that label prediction is relatively robust to evidence quality in this setup. Their fully offline, non-LLM system is competitive, achieving second place in the shared task.

title: When and How Should an Agent Clarify? CIGAsk: Teaching LLMs to Clarify via Counterfactual Information Gain
summary: Instruction-tuned LLMs faced with underspecified queries often commit to a single interpretation rather than ask for clarification, producing confidently wrong answers. In our experiments, prompting alone is insufficient: models either ask for clarification on every query or ask vague questions that fail to recover the missing information. Addressing this failure requires learning two coupled skills: when to ask rather than answer and how to ask a question that recovers the disambiguating information. Existing recipes either address only one of these skills or require a separately trained critic. We propose CIGAsk, an RL recipe that teaches both skills through two complementary reward signals within a multi-turn GRPO loop. Counterfactual Information Gain (CIG) compares the gold-answer log-likelihood under a frozen reference model with and without the user response, providing per-turn credit that guides how to ask. The Asymmetric Ambiguity Bonus assigns a signed reward at the terminal token based on the gold ambiguity label, guiding when to ask. Across three clarification benchmarks spanning table, passage, and open-domain QA, CIGAsk-7B outperforms the strongest external baseline despite using a smaller backbone. It also transfers across datasets without per-dataset tuning while preserving single-turn QA performance on out-of-distribution benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CIGAsk, a reinforcement learning-based method that teaches language models when and how to ask clarifying questions for ambiguous queries, improving clarification and question-answering performance across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Instruction-tuned LLMs tend to answer ambiguous or underspecified questions with a single confident guess instead of asking for clarification, and simple prompting fails to fix this. Existing methods either only decide when to ask, only how to ask, or need extra critic models. The authors aim to jointly learn both when to ask and how to ask, in a way that is efficient, does not need a separate critic, and generalizes across tasks.
AI.method: They propose CIGAsk, a multi-turn RL training recipe built on GRPO. The model interacts in multi-turn clarification episodes, and learning is driven by two reward components: (1) Counterfactual Information Gain (CIG), which compares the likelihood of the correct answer under a frozen reference model with and without the user’s clarification, giving per-turn reward that teaches the model to ask questions that maximally improve answerability; and (2) an Asymmetric Ambiguity Bonus, a terminal reward based on whether the gold label says the query is ambiguous, teaching the model when it should ask instead of answer. Both rewards together shape policies for both when and how to ask clarifying questions.
AI.result: On three clarification benchmarks (covering table, passage, and open-domain QA), a 7B-parameter model trained with CIGAsk beats the strongest external baselines that rely on larger backbones or different methods. The learned strategy generalizes to new datasets without per-dataset tuning and maintains performance on standard single-turn QA benchmarks, indicating it doesn’t degrade ordinary answering ability.
AI.conclusion: Jointly optimizing when and how to ask clarification via the proposed two-part reward and GRPO loop produces better clarification behavior than prior approaches while remaining efficient and broadly transferable. CIGAsk demonstrates that counterfactual, information-gain-based rewards plus ambiguity-aware terminal bonuses can train LLMs to handle underspecified queries more safely and effectively without sacrificing normal QA performance.

title: MIS-Bench: Benchmarking Multimodal LLMs for Psychotherapeutic Interpersonal Skills Assessment
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used as evaluators, yet their reliability in professional assessment tasks that require expert judgment remains unclear. We investigate this challenge in the context of assessing psychotherapeutic interpersonal skills and introduce MIS-Bench, a Multimodal Interpersonal Skills (MIS) benchmark comprising 996 psychotherapy response videos annotated across 8 dimensions of Facilitative Interpersonal Skills. Across 9 MLLMs with multiple modality and prompting settings, we find that current models show only modest agreement with human experts, inconsistent gains from multimodal input, and limited benefits from reasoning-based prompting. To mitigate this gap, we propose MIS-RAFT, a regression-aware fine-tuning method inspired by RAFT and tailored to fine-grained interpersonal skill scoring at one-decimal precision. MIS-RAFT addresses the mismatch between autoregressive token prediction and scalar-valued expert assessment, significantly improving agreement with human ratings. Overall, MIS-Bench reveals a clear gap between general multimodal capability and expert-level interpersonal judgment, while MIS-RAFT offers a promising path toward more reliable model-based assessment.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MIS-Bench, a benchmark of psychotherapy response videos to test how well multimodal large language models can assess interpersonal skills, finds current models are only modestly aligned with experts, and proposes MIS-RAFT, a fine-tuning method that substantially improves model-human agreement for fine-grained skill scoring.
AI.motivation: Multimodal LLMs are increasingly used as automatic evaluators in domains that demand expert judgment, such as assessing psychotherapeutic interpersonal skills, but it is unclear how reliable they are for fine-grained, professional assessments. There is a need for a standardized benchmark to measure their performance on such tasks, and for methods that better align models’ token-based predictions with continuous expert ratings.
AI.method: The authors build MIS-Bench, a benchmark of 996 psychotherapy response videos labeled along 8 dimensions of Facilitative Interpersonal Skills, and systematically evaluate 9 MLLMs under different modality configurations (e.g., text-only vs multimodal) and prompting strategies (including reasoning-style prompts). They then introduce MIS-RAFT, a regression-aware fine-tuning approach inspired by RAFT that adapts autoregressive LLM outputs to predict scalar scores at one-decimal precision, explicitly addressing the mismatch between discrete token prediction and continuous expert scores.
AI.result: On MIS-Bench, all tested MLLMs exhibit only modest agreement with human expert raters, and multimodal input or reasoning-based prompting produce inconsistent or limited improvements. Applying MIS-RAFT to these models yields substantially better alignment with human ratings and more accurate fine-grained interpersonal skill scores, demonstrating that regression-aware fine-tuning can significantly enhance performance on this expert assessment task.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that there is a substantial gap between general multimodal capabilities of current LLMs and the level of expert interpersonal judgment required for professional psychotherapy assessment. MIS-Bench provides a rigorous benchmark to expose this gap, and MIS-RAFT demonstrates that carefully designed, regression-oriented fine-tuning can meaningfully close it, suggesting a promising direction for building more reliable model-based evaluators of interpersonal skills.

title: Brain-Token Learning: Microstate-Based Tokenization and Multi-Scale Interaction for Long-Horizon EEG Sequence Modeling
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) provides a non-invasive window into dynamic brain activity, yet modeling long-horizon EEG sequences remains challenging due to their high temporal complexity, substantial variability across subjects, and the lack of biologically meaningful sequence representations. Existing tokenization strategies, such as fixed-window and patch-based representations, discretize EEG signals according to artificial temporal boundaries, which may disrupt intrinsic brain-state dynamics. In this work, we propose Brain-Token Learning, a neuroscience-inspired framework that introduces Brain Tokenization for long-horizon EEG sequence modeling. Instead of partitioning EEG signals into predefined temporal segments, Brain Tokenization represents EEG as sequences of recurrent microstate-derived brain tokens, where each token corresponds to a quasi-stable large-scale brain state with variable temporal duration. Based on these biologically grounded tokens, we further develop a multi-scale token interaction module consisting of Latent State Aggregation and State Transition Modeling to jointly capture global brain-state context and local microstate transitions. We evaluate Brain-Token on five heterogeneous EEG datasets, including the newly collected long-horizon NeuroLong dataset and four affective or clinical EEG datasets (SEED, DEAP, MDD, and NSSI). Extensive experiments demonstrate that Brain-Token consistently outperforms conventional CNN/LSTM architectures, Transformer-based models, and domain adaptation methods across diverse EEG scenarios. Further analysis verifies the effectiveness of microstate-based tokenization and multi-scale interaction for learning robust and interpretable EEG representations. These results establish Brain-Token as a biologically grounded tokenization paradigm for long-horizon EEG sequence modeling.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Brain-Token Learning, a neuroscience-inspired EEG modeling framework that tokenizes signals based on microstate-derived, biologically meaningful brain tokens instead of fixed time windows, and shows superior performance on multiple long-horizon EEG datasets.
AI.motivation: Modeling long-horizon EEG is difficult because of high temporal complexity, subject variability, and the lack of biologically meaningful sequence representations. Existing fixed-window or patch-based tokenization may break intrinsic brain-state dynamics. The authors aim to create a tokenization and modeling approach that aligns with brain microstates to yield more robust and interpretable EEG representations.
AI.method: They introduce Brain Tokenization, which segments EEG into sequences of recurrent microstate-derived brain tokens, each corresponding to a quasi-stable brain state with variable length. On top of these tokens, they design a multi-scale token interaction module with two components: Latent State Aggregation to capture global brain-state context, and State Transition Modeling to capture local microstate transitions. The framework, called Brain-Token Learning, is evaluated on five EEG datasets, including a new long-horizon NeuroLong dataset and four affective/clinical datasets (SEED, DEAP, MDD, NSSI).
AI.result: Across the five heterogeneous EEG datasets, Brain-Token consistently outperforms conventional CNN/LSTM architectures, Transformer-based models, and domain adaptation baselines in various long-horizon EEG modeling scenarios. Additional analyses show that microstate-based tokenization and multi-scale token interaction both contribute significantly to performance gains and representation quality.
AI.conclusion: Brain-Token Learning provides a biologically grounded tokenization paradigm for long-horizon EEG, leveraging microstate-derived brain tokens and multi-scale interaction modeling to capture both global and local brain-state dynamics.
