This approach yields more robust, accurate, and interpretable EEG representations than existing deep learning and transformer-based methods, suggesting a promising direction for neuroscience-inspired sequence modeling.

title: Diagnose, Then Repair: A Two-Stage MQM-Guided Post-Editing Framework for Domain-Specific Machine Translation
comment: Accepted to the ACL 2026 Industry Track and presented at ACL 2026
summary: LLM-based machine translation evaluation can closely match human judgments, but in practice it remains largely diagnostic, with the signals rarely translating into direct quality improvements under real production constraints. We propose a two-stage, evaluator-guided automatic post-editing framework that turns MQM-style evaluation into targeted repairs: a retrieval-augmented LLM evaluator outputs structured, span-level MQM diagnoses under an explicit edit contract, and a separate LLM post-editor applies minimal edits restricted to those diagnoses. This separation improves controllability and reduces paraphrastic drift compared to one-stage "judge-and-refine" baselines. In a systematic study involving seven LLMs spanning three model providers and seven languages, our best configuration consistently improves both COMET-22 and COMETKiwi scores over one-stage post-edit methods, while the evaluator's error spans and severities show strong agreement with human MQM annotations and human editor preferences.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a two-stage, evaluator-guided automatic post-editing framework that converts LLM-based MQM-style MT evaluation into targeted, minimal edits, outperforming one-stage judge-and-refine baselines across multiple models and languages.
AI.motivation: Although LLM-based MT evaluation can correlate well with human judgments, its outputs are mostly used diagnostically and do not directly lead to better translations in production. Existing one-stage judge-and-refine approaches lack controllability and often cause unnecessary paraphrasing (paraphrastic drift). The authors aim to make evaluation signals actionable for automatic post-editing under realistic constraints, improving translation quality while preserving the original output as much as possible.
AI.method: They propose a two-stage framework: (1) a retrieval-augmented LLM evaluator produces structured, span-level MQM-style error annotations under an explicit edit contract, identifying what should be changed and how, at a fine-grained level; (2) a separate LLM post-editor receives these diagnoses and performs minimal edits restricted to the specified spans and error categories. The separation between evaluator and editor is designed to increase controllability, limit unintended rewrites, and align with MQM error typology. They systematically test various LLMs (seven models from three providers) and multiple target languages (seven languages).
AI.result: Across configurations, their best two-stage setup consistently outperforms one-stage judge-and-refine post-editing baselines in automatic MT metrics, particularly COMET-22 and COMETKiwi, for all evaluated languages and models. Additionally, the span-level error annotations from the evaluator show high agreement with human MQM annotations and with human editors’ preferences about what to correct and how severe the errors are.
AI.conclusion: A modular, evaluator-guided two-stage APE framework can effectively transform LLM-based MQM evaluation into precise, minimal translation repairs, yielding higher MT quality and better alignment with human judgments than one-stage LLM refinement. Separating evaluation from editing improves controllability and reduces unwanted paraphrastic drift, making LLM-based MT evaluation practically useful for production-grade automatic post-editing.

title: LADDER: Graph-Guided Diffusion Language Models for Efficient Multi-Hop Reasoning
summary: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) has remarkably enhanced large language models on complex reasoning by leveraging structured entity topologies. However, existing frameworks heavily rely on standard autoregressive language models where the nature of inherent sequential generation severely hinders overall inference efficiency. Inspired by Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) that offer massive parallelism via continuous refine-in-parallel decoding, we aim to accelerate GraphRAG in the discrete space. However, it remains non-trivial for two challenges. First, partially denoised drafts are highly dynamic and uncertain, making dynamic graph grounding non-trivial. Second, raw denoising states are inherently noisy and unstable, making synchronous graph retrieval and multi-hop aggregation computationally prohibitive. To this end, we present LADDER, a novel framework that bridges diffusion language modeling with GraphRAG through graph-guided parallel decoding. Specifically, (i) we propose an event-driven self-clocking retrieval, inspired by our key insight that 88% of target entities emerge early in the partially denoised state, leading final commitment by an average of 5.7-9.6 steps. This mechanism dynamically triggers graph retrieval only when the set of graph-linkable entities expands, yielding an asynchronous self-clocking policy that bypasses learned gates or heuristic thresholds. (ii) An incomplete-query graph propagation module is designed to process the newly emerging entity queries using a specialized graph foundation model, continuously aggregating multi-hop evidence to sharpen parallel predictions and accelerate overall decoding convergence. Extensive experiments on three challenging multi-hop QA benchmarks show that LADDER raises average exact match from 39.6% to 45.2% while achieving a 4.1x latency reduction.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces LADDER, a diffusion-based, graph-guided parallel decoding framework that accelerates GraphRAG while improving accuracy for multi-hop QA.
AI.motivation: GraphRAG improves complex reasoning with structured entity graphs but is slowed by the inherently sequential decoding of autoregressive LLMs. Diffusion Language Models provide parallel decoding, but integrating them with graph retrieval is difficult because partially denoised drafts are dynamic/uncertain and denoising states are noisy, making graph grounding and multi-hop aggregation hard and expensive. The authors aim to get GraphRAG’s reasoning benefits with the efficiency of parallel diffusion decoding.
AI.method: They propose LADDER, which couples a diffusion language model with graph-based retrieval and reasoning through two key components: (i) an event-driven, self-clocking retrieval mechanism that monitors the partially denoised text and triggers graph retrieval only when new graph-linkable entities appear, eliminating fixed schedules, gates, or thresholds; and (ii) an incomplete-query graph propagation module that uses a specialized graph foundation model to process these emerging entities, performing continuous multi-hop evidence aggregation over the graph to refine token predictions in parallel and speed convergence of the diffusion decoding process.
AI.result: On three challenging multi-hop QA benchmarks, LADDER improves exact match accuracy from an average of 39.6% to 45.2% and reduces inference latency by a factor of 4.1x compared with baseline GraphRAG setups using standard autoregressive models.
AI.conclusion: LADDER demonstrates that diffusion-based, graph-guided parallel decoding can both accelerate and strengthen GraphRAG-style reasoning: it handles dynamic, noisy denoising states with event-driven retrieval and incomplete-query graph propagation, yielding better multi-hop QA performance at significantly lower latency.

title: AlexandriaX 2026: The First Shared Task on Dialectal Arabic Machine Translation
comment: To Appear in ArabicNLP 2026, resources available in the following project page: https://alexandriax.dlnlp.ai
summary: Dialectal Arabic machine translation (MT) remains challenging despite recent progress in Arabic language technologies, particularly because effective translation requires modeling not only semantic content but also dialectal variation, conversational context, speaker and addressee characteristics, and sociolinguistic appropriateness. Moreover, conventional MT metrics provide limited insight into the linguistic errors produced by dialectal systems. We present the AlexandriaX 2026 Shared Task on Dialectal Arabic MT, which addresses these challenges through three complementary subtasks: (1) context-aware English-to-Dialectal Arabic dialogue translation across 13 Arabic varieties, (2) cross-dialect Arabic translation in the financial domain covering six Arabic dialects, and (3) span-level MT error detection and classification using linguistically motivated error categories across five Arabic varieties. The shared task attracted 38 registrations for Subtask 1, 33 for Subtask 2, and 35 for Subtask 3. Twelve unique teams submitted their system description papers, all of which we accepted for publication. The best system on Subtask 1 achieved 30.42 spBLEU in the constrained track and 33.49 spBLEU in the unconstrained track. On Subtask 2, the top system obtained 28.40 spBLEU. On Subtask 3, the best system achieved an overall score of 49.82, outperforming the 24.29 baseline. Taken together, the results of the leading systems across the three subtasks highlight the benefits of explicit dialect modeling, context-aware generation, retrieval and reranking, and specialized approaches to interpretable MT error analysis. All the resources of AlexandriaX 2026 shared task are publicly available, including data, baselines, and evaluation code on our project page: https://alexandriax.dlnlp.ai.

AI.tldr: AlexandriaX 2026 is a shared task on Dialectal Arabic MT with three subtasks (context-aware Eng→dialect dialogue MT, cross-dialect MT in finance, and span-level error detection). It shows that explicit dialect and context modeling plus specialized error analysis significantly improve performance, and all data and tools are publicly released.
AI.motivation: Dialectal Arabic MT is difficult because it must capture not only meaning but also dialectal variation, conversation context, speaker/addressee traits, and sociolinguistic appropriateness. Existing automatic metrics (e.g., BLEU) do not reveal what linguistic errors dialect MT systems make, limiting progress. The shared task is designed to create benchmarks, foster methods that handle contextual and sociolinguistic aspects, and provide interpretable evaluation of errors.
AI.method: The authors organized the AlexandriaX 2026 Shared Task with three coordinated subtasks: (1) context-aware English-to-dialectal Arabic dialogue translation for 13 dialects, where systems can use dialogue context; (2) cross-dialect Arabic MT in the financial domain across six dialects; and (3) span-level MT error detection and classification across five dialects using linguistically motivated error categories. They collected and released datasets, defined tracks (constrained vs. unconstrained) and metrics (e.g., spBLEU and a custom score for error detection), and evaluated submissions from participating teams.
AI.result: The shared task attracted strong participation (38, 33, and 35 registrations for the three subtasks, with 12 system papers accepted). In Subtask 1, the best systems reached 30.42 spBLEU (constrained) and 33.49 spBLEU (unconstrained). In Subtask 2, the top system achieved 28.40 spBLEU. In Subtask 3, the best system scored 49.82 on the error detection classification metric, substantially better than the 24.29 baseline, showing that current approaches can yield meaningful gains on all subtasks.
AI.conclusion: The leading systems show that explicitly modeling dialect, leveraging conversational context, and using retrieval and reranking strategies can significantly enhance dialectal Arabic MT. Moreover, using specialized, span-level, linguistically grounded error analysis leads to more interpretable evaluation than traditional MT metrics. The shared task delivers publicly available resources (data, baselines, evaluation code), establishing a foundation for continued work on dialect-sensitive and context-aware Arabic MT and error analysis.

title: Few-Shot Demonstrations Elicit the Use of In-Context World Representations in LLMs
summary: Large language models (LLMs), when acting as agents, are expected to take observed data in context, infer the latent state space underlying the world, and leverage it for downstream prediction. However, prior work demonstrated that LLMs struggle to use representations learned in context on a graph tracking task, where the model needs to construct a representation of the graph governing data generation process and use it for subsequent predictions. In this paper, we show that extending this to few-shot settings, where each demonstration is generated from a different world with either the same or different graph topologies, enhances its prediction on 6 models from 4 model families. To understand this improvement, we linearly probe a low-dimensional world representation that encodes graph information in the hidden states. Notably, we find that few-shot demonstrations relocate the world representation and increase its predictive use. Specifically, for each model, these world representations shift in directions nearly orthogonal to their original subspace, and interventions on these representations selectively impair performance more than interventions on other subspaces. Consistent with this insight, we show that few-shot demonstrations with observations from different worlds improve performance on ARC-AGI-1&2, web agent tasks, and Othello. Our findings elucidate the role and internal mechanisms of few-shot demonstrations in in-context world modeling. More broadly, our work advances our understanding of how LLM agents learn from in-context observations and provides implications for their further improvement.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how few-shot demonstrations across different underlying worlds help LLMs form and use internal world models, probing how graph-structured latent state representations emerge and are used for prediction.
AI.motivation: LLMs used as agents need to infer and use latent world states from in-context observations, but prior work shows they struggle to build and exploit such representations in graph-tracking tasks. The authors want to understand whether and how few-shot demonstrations can improve this in-context world modeling and to characterize the internal mechanisms behind any improvement.
AI.method: They extend a graph-tracking task to a few-shot setting where each demonstration comes from a different world defined by potentially different graph topologies. They evaluate performance across 6 models from 4 LLM families. To study internal mechanisms, they linearly probe low-dimensional representations in the hidden states that encode the underlying graph (“world representations”), analyze how these representations change with few-shot prompts, examine the geometry of these subspaces (e.g., orthogonality of shifted directions), and perform causal interventions on these subspaces to measure their impact on prediction. Finally, they test whether the same few-shot, multi-world prompting strategy helps on broader benchmarks like ARC-AGI-1&2, web agent tasks, and Othello.
AI.result: Across models, few-shot demonstrations generated from different worlds consistently improve prediction on the graph-tracking task compared to single-world or zero-shot settings. Probing reveals a low-dimensional world representation encoding graph structure. With few-shot demonstrations, this world representation is relocated: its activation patterns move in directions nearly orthogonal to the original subspace. Interventions targeting this representation selectively degrade performance more than equivalent interventions on other subspaces, indicating that these relocated directions are functionally important. The same style of few-shot, multi-world prompting also yields performance gains on ARC-AGI-1&2, web agent tasks, and Othello, suggesting a general effect.
AI.conclusion: Few-shot demonstrations drawn from multiple underlying worlds reshape and strengthen how LLMs internally represent latent world structure, moving key “world representation” directions to new, more predictive subspaces. These representations are both interpretable via linear probes and causally important for task success, as disrupting them disproportionately harms performance. The findings clarify how in-context examples help LLMs do world modeling, and they suggest that constructing prompts with diverse-world demonstrations is a practical lever for improving LLM agents’ reasoning and planning capabilities.

title: To Consolidate or not to Consolidate? Evaluating the Impact of Consolidation in Multi-Reference Training using Peer Reviews
summary: Natural language generation (NLG) tasks span the spectrum of conditional entropy, ranging from highly constrained machine translation to open-ended dialogue generation. Structured tasks like automated peer-review generation occupy the intermediate region, where a single input admits multiple valid, overlapping outputs. In this work, we demonstrate that traditional single- and multi-reference training paradigms are suboptimal for these intermediary tasks. We provide empirical evidence that consolidating diverse references into a unified training signal is crucial for developing effective systems. To facilitate this, we introduce MERC-36K, a large-scale corpus of over 36,000 papers paired with original and consolidated peer reviews. Using this dataset, we train specific architectures to isolate the impact of different reference paradigms and benchmark against existing state-of-the-art systems. Through extensive automatic and human evaluation, we demonstrate that models trained on consolidated references significantly outperform those trained on unconsolidated references. Dataset and code will be released upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to best train natural language generation models for structured but open-ended tasks like automated peer-review writing, finding that consolidating multiple reference reviews into a single training signal yields better models. It introduces MERC-36K, a large dataset of papers with both original and consolidated reviews, and shows models trained on consolidated references outperform those trained on the raw, unconsolidated ones.
AI.motivation: Existing NLG tasks range from very constrained (e.g., translation with near-deterministic outputs) to very open-ended (e.g., dialogue). Intermediate tasks like peer-review generation have multiple valid, partially overlapping outputs for the same input. Standard single- or multi-reference training approaches do not fully exploit these diverse outputs and may send conflicting learning signals. The authors are motivated to understand and improve training paradigms for such intermediate-entropy tasks, where the space of valid outputs is rich but still structured.
AI.method: 1) Conceptualize NLG tasks along a conditional entropy spectrum and focus on intermediate-entropy tasks such as automated peer-review generation. 2) Construct MERC-36K, a large-scale dataset containing over 36,000 scientific papers paired with original peer reviews and versions where multiple reviews are consolidated into a unified reference. 3) Design and train specific model architectures under different supervision regimes: single-reference training, standard multi-reference training, and training on consolidated references. 4) Benchmark these models against existing state-of-the-art peer-review generation systems. 5) Evaluate models extensively using both automatic metrics and human judgments to isolate the impact of the reference paradigm on generation quality.
AI.result: Models trained on consolidated peer-review references achieve consistently better performance than those trained on unconsolidated single or multiple raw reviews. This improvement is observed in both automatic evaluation metrics and human assessments of review quality. The experiments show that merging diverse reference reviews into a single, coherent supervision signal reduces conflicts and better captures the essential information needed for high-quality review generation.
AI.conclusion: For intermediate-entropy NLG tasks like automated peer-review generation, conventional single- and multi-reference training approaches are suboptimal. Consolidating multiple diverse references into a unified training signal leads to significantly better model performance. The MERC-36K dataset enables systematic study of these effects, and the findings suggest that future work on similar NLG tasks should prioritize reference consolidation strategies over naïve multi-reference training.

title: VLM-in-Sandbox: Visual Workspaces for Agentic Visual Reasoning
summary: Sandboxed computer environments support multi-step reasoning with tools, executable programs, and persistent files, yet their extension from language models to vision-language models (VLMs) introduces a distinct state-management problem. Visual reasoning produces intermediate image-valued evidence---crops, masks, overlays, zoomed regions, and analytic renderings---that must remain addressable without accumulating unboundedly in multimodal context. We introduce VLM-in-Sandbox, a training-free framework for agentic multimodal reasoning in controlled computer environments. Its Visual Workspace registers generated artifacts in an image ledger, maintains a bounded active visual context, and lets the model explicitly promote selected evidence for subsequent inspection. This separates visual evidence generation, performed by sandbox tools, from visual evidence management. Across seven benchmarks and four base VLMs, VLM-in-Sandbox achieves the highest sample-weighted average accuracy among Vanilla VLM, Append-only Sandbox, and the proposed method. A compiler-matched $2\times2$ study on 1,260 examples further separates model-directed visibility from bounded retention: VLM-in-Sandbox reaches 66.27% accuracy with 18.6% fewer total tokens than the automatic, retain-all control. Over all 6,350 submitted GPT-4.1-mini examples, it produces 302 rescues and 142 regressions relative to Original Append-only. A local vLLM study with prefix caching confirms that the smaller request workload also reduces uncached tokens, time to first token, and end-to-end latency. These results identify explicit visual evidence state as a central abstraction for sandboxed VLM agents.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes VLM-in-Sandbox, a training-free framework that manages visual evidence state for vision-language agents in sandboxed computer environments, improving multimodal reasoning accuracy and efficiency by keeping a bounded, explicitly controlled visual context.
AI.motivation: Existing sandboxed environments for language models support tools and files, but extending them to vision-language models introduces a state-management challenge: intermediate visual artifacts (crops, masks, overlays, analytic renderings) proliferate and cannot all be kept in the multimodal context without blowing up cost and context length. There is a need to decouple the generation of visual evidence from its retention and exposure to the model, so that agents can reason over just the most relevant visual state while still having access to a larger pool of artifacts.
AI.method: The authors introduce VLM-in-Sandbox, a training-free framework that wraps existing VLMs in a controlled computer environment. The key component, the Visual Workspace, maintains an image ledger of all generated visual artifacts, enforces a bounded active visual context, and provides mechanisms for the VLM to explicitly promote selected artifacts into that active context. This separates visual evidence generation (performed by sandbox tools that create new images) from visual evidence management (tracking, selecting, and exposing images to the model). They compare three setups—Vanilla VLM, Append-only Sandbox, and VLM-in-Sandbox—across multiple benchmarks and models. They also run a compiler-matched 2×2 study to decouple ‘what the model can see’ from ‘how much is retained’, plus a local vLLM experiment with prefix caching to measure token usage, latency, and workload on uncached tokens.
AI.result: Across seven benchmarks and four base VLMs, VLM-in-Sandbox attains the highest sample-weighted average accuracy compared with Vanilla VLM and Append-only Sandbox. In a 1,260-example 2×2 study, it reaches 66.27% accuracy while using 18.6% fewer total tokens than an automatic retain-all control setup. Over 6,350 GPT-4.1-mini examples, relative to an Append-only baseline, it yields 302 improved cases (“rescues”) and 142 degraded cases (“regressions”). The local vLLM study with prefix caching demonstrates that the reduced request workload also cuts the number of uncached tokens, as well as time to first token and overall latency.
AI.conclusion: Explicit management of visual evidence—treating it as structured state within a Visual Workspace—is a key abstraction for building effective sandboxed VLM agents. By decoupling visual artifact generation from controlled retention and exposure, VLM-in-Sandbox improves both accuracy and efficiency without retraining base models, suggesting that future multimodal agent systems should emphasize principled visual state handling rather than naïve append-only context growth.

title: Block-Sparse Attention with Semantic-Geometric Decoupled Routing
comment: Technical report; Submitted to ACL ARR 2026 May
summary: Long-context inference has become a defining capability of large language models, but exact dense attention remains costly due to its quadratic scaling with sequence length. Block-sparse attention offers a hardware-friendly alternative by routing each query block to a small set of relevant key blocks, yet accurate training-free block routing remains difficult. Existing routers often pool post-RoPE token representations, which entangles semantic aggregation with RoPE-induced geometry and attenuates local positional cues through high-frequency phase cancellation. To resolve this mismatch, we propose \textbf{Semantic-Geometric Decoupled Routing}, a training-free block routing framework that shifts semantic aggregation to the pre-RoPE space and reconstructs geometric bias with an offline structural prior and relative block distances. This decomposition yields an explicit closed-form block routing score without token-level search or post-hoc calibration. Experiments on long-context text and video tasks show that our method approaches full-attention accuracy across 4K--128K contexts, keeps routing overhead below 3.4 ms, and achieves a 5.03$\times$ speedup over FlashAttn at a 128K context length.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new training-free routing method for block-sparse attention that preserves long-context accuracy while greatly reducing computation cost.
AI.motivation: Dense attention in large language models scales quadratically with sequence length, making long-context inference (e.g., up to 128K tokens) computationally expensive. Block-sparse attention can reduce cost by having each query block attend only to a subset of key blocks, but existing routing strategies struggle to accurately choose relevant blocks without extra training. Specifically, they pool token representations after RoPE, which mixes semantic and positional information in a way that harms both semantic aggregation and local positional cues, leading to suboptimal routing and accuracy loss.
AI.method: They introduce Semantic-Geometric Decoupled Routing (SGDR), a training-free block routing framework. Instead of aggregating semantics in the post-RoPE space, SGDR performs semantic aggregation in the pre-RoPE representation space, where semantic structure is cleaner. It then separately reconstructs geometric (positional) bias using an offline structural prior and relative distances between blocks. This yields an explicit, closed-form routing score at the block level, avoiding token-level search and any post-hoc calibration or learned router parameters.
AI.result: On long-context text and video benchmarks across context lengths from 4K to 128K tokens, SGDR’s block-sparse attention achieves accuracy close to full dense attention. It maintains routing overhead under 3.4 ms and delivers a 5.03× speedup over FlashAttention at 128K context length, demonstrating both efficiency and effectiveness of the routing approach.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling semantic aggregation from geometric (positional) bias in block routing for attention enables a simple, training-free, and efficient routing mechanism that preserves long-context performance. Semantic-Geometric Decoupled Routing offers a practical way to scale long-context LLM inference with minimal accuracy loss and substantial speedups compared to state-of-the-art dense attention implementations.

title: Predicting Postprandial Glycemic Response from Meal Images, Clinical Variables, and Gut Microbiome Information
comment: 11 pages (9 text + 2 references). This is a paper first submitted to MICCAI 2026 MultiTab workshop prior to peer review. The final revised version will be published in Springer LNCS proceedings after the MICCAI 2026 conference
summary: Predicting postprandial glycemic response (PPGR) is fundamental to personalized nutrition and type 2 diabetes management, yet existing approaches typically rely on manually reported dietary intake, limiting their scalability in free-living settings. We propose a multimodal framework that replaces manual dietary logging with image-derived macronutrient estimates and integrates them with clinical variables and gut microbiome information for personalized PPGR prediction. The framework jointly performs image-based macronutrient estimation and glucose prediction, while an attention-based prediction module models interactions between dietary and host-specific information. We evaluate the proposed approach on a real-world dataset comprising meal images, continuous glucose monitoring, clinical variables, and gut microbiome profiles. The proposed model outperforms existing PPGR baselines using image-derived nutritional inputs and approaches the performance of methods that rely on manually reported macronutrients despite using automatically estimated nutritional information. These results demonstrate that combining image-derived nutrition with complementary clinical and gut microbiome information provides a practical foundation for scalable personalized PPGR prediction.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a multimodal AI framework that predicts postprandial glycemic response (PPGR) using food images plus clinical and microbiome data, removing the need for manual food logging.
AI.motivation: Accurate prediction of individual PPGR is critical for personalized nutrition and type 2 diabetes management. Current methods usually depend on manually reported dietary intake, which is burdensome, error-prone, and difficult to scale in real-world, free-living conditions. There is a need for an automated, scalable way to capture dietary information while still achieving high prediction accuracy.
AI.method: The authors design a multimodal framework that: (1) uses meal images to automatically estimate macronutrient content; (2) integrates these image-derived macronutrients with clinical variables and gut microbiome profiles; (3) jointly trains the system to perform both image-based macronutrient estimation and glucose prediction; and (4) employs an attention-based prediction module to model interactions between dietary information and host-specific factors. They train and evaluate the model on a real-world dataset including meal images, continuous glucose monitoring data, clinical variables, and microbiome data.
AI.result: The model using automatically estimated (image-derived) macronutrients outperforms existing PPGR baseline models that also rely on nutritional inputs. Its performance is close to methods that have access to manually reported macronutrients, even though it relies only on automatically inferred nutrition from images combined with clinical and microbiome data.
AI.conclusion: Automated extraction of nutritional information from meal images, when combined with clinical and gut microbiome features in a multimodal, attention-based framework, can provide accurate and scalable personalized PPGR prediction. This reduces dependence on manual food logging and offers a practical path toward real-world deployment of personalized nutrition and diabetes management tools.

title: LLMs Anchor on Chief Complaint and Fail to Integrate Evidence in Sequential Clinical Triage
summary: Triage in the emergency department (ED) is a sequential decision process that unfolds turn by turn. Existing evaluations of large language models (LLMs) for triage use completed retrospective records and report performance close to that of physicians. We implement a methodology for evaluating LLMs on sequential triage, the task of predicting a triage acuity label from a growing prefix of a nurse-patient conversation. We evaluate six LLMs at five sequential checkpoints on two corpora: 425 LLM-generated (SIMULATED) and 50 physician-authored (CLINICIAN) conversations, both labelled under the Emergency Severity Index (ESI). Every model, measured by quadratic weighted kappa (QWK), degrades from moderate-to-substantial agreement on completed records to fair-to-moderate agreement at every sequential checkpoint. Controlled perturbations show that the label at every checkpoint is anchored on the chief complaint exchanges, and prompting interventions fail to lift this plateau. Models extract clinically relevant content from later turns, yet the surprisal of the true label rises across the checkpoints. So the model fails to integrate the evidence. Three expert clinicians on the same conversations reach a QWK of 0.887-0.929, while the best model reaches 0.295. Predictions concentrate at ESI-2 and ESI-3, and models agree with each other more than with the ground truth, so ensembling worsens the failure. Deploying LLMs for ED triage based on offline benchmarks alone misses this sequential failure.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates large language models (LLMs) on realistic, turn-by-turn emergency department triage instead of on fully completed records, finding that their performance drops sharply and they fail to properly integrate new information across the conversation.
AI.motivation: Existing studies suggest LLMs can triage nearly as well as physicians, but they use finalized, retrospective notes rather than the real-world, sequential nature of nurse-patient conversations. Triage is inherently dynamic and decisions must be updated as new information arrives. The authors want to know whether LLMs can handle this sequential decision process, not just static summaries, and whether current benchmarks overestimate readiness for clinical deployment.
AI.method: The authors design a sequential triage evaluation where LLMs must predict an Emergency Severity Index (ESI) acuity label multiple times during the unfolding of a nurse-patient conversation. They define five sequential checkpoints (growing prefixes of the dialogue) and test six different LLMs on two datasets: 425 LLM-generated simulated conversations and 50 clinician-authored real conversations, all labeled with ESI. They quantify agreement with ground truth labels using quadratic weighted kappa (QWK), run controlled perturbation experiments to see what information the models rely on (e.g., chief complaint), and try prompting interventions to test if guidance can improve sequential integration. They also compare LLM performance with three expert clinicians and analyze prediction distributions and inter-model agreement, including ensembling effects.
AI.result: All LLMs show clear performance degradation when moving from completed records to intermediate checkpoints, dropping from moderate-to-substantial agreement to only fair-to-moderate agreement at every sequential step. The models’ acuity predictions at each checkpoint remain heavily anchored on the initial chief complaint, and subsequent clinically important turns do not significantly shift predictions. Prompting strategies do not materially improve this plateau. While models do capture clinically relevant information from later dialogue, the surprisal of the correct triage label actually increases over time, indicating poor evidence integration. Expert clinicians achieve very high agreement with ground truth (QWK 0.887–0.929), but the best LLM only reaches 0.295. Model outputs cluster mostly on ESI-2 and ESI-3 and are more consistent with each other than with the ground truth, so ensemble methods further amplify systematic errors rather than correcting them.
AI.conclusion: LLMs that appear strong on offline, fully documented triage benchmarks perform poorly when evaluated in a realistic, sequential triage setting. They underutilize new information, remain anchored on early chief complaints, and fail to integrate evolving clinical evidence, leading to low agreement with true acuity labels compared with human experts. High inter-model agreement and concentrated predictions reveal shared biases, making ensembling ineffective or harmful. As a result, current offline benchmarks provide a misleading picture of LLM readiness for emergency department triage, and any consideration of deployment must account for this sequential failure and develop methods that can truly reason over unfolding conversations.

title: Fathom-Vaidya: Advancing Medical Reasoning with Rubric-Based Rewards
summary: Deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) in healthcare requires robust performance across two complementary dimensions - diagnostic reasoning: the convergent, evidence-driven task of inferring a patient's condition from clinical data to produce a diagnosis, and clinical healthcare reasoning: the broader, navigational judgment required to communicate, plan, and adapt across multi-turn clinical interactions where a single correct answer may not exist. Recent benchmarks such as HealthBench and MedXpertQA reveal persistent weaknesses in both areas, exposing failures in complex diagnostic scenarios and limitations in contextual, patient-centered dialogue. We introduce a sequential training framework that targets these facets using synthetic data and rubric-based reinforcement learning. First, we improve diagnostic reasoning using MedBullets-derived questions with rule- and rubric-guided Reinforcement Learning (RL). We then shift to clinical reasoning by generating 5.3k synthetic multi-turn scenarios, each paired with multi-dimensional rubrics to comprehensively assess the response. This approach yields over 10% improvement on MedXpertQA, and our 30B model achieves 50.1% accuracy on HealthBench-Hard, surpassing proprietary baselines including GPT-5 (thinking). Our results show that targeted synthetic datasets and rubric-based training can systematically improve both diagnostic and interactive clinical reasoning in medical LLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a sequential, rubric-guided reinforcement learning framework with synthetic data to improve both diagnostic and broader clinical reasoning in medical LLMs, yielding strong gains on HealthBench and MedXpertQA.
AI.motivation: Existing medical LLMs struggle with two key competencies required for safe deployment in healthcare: (1) diagnostic reasoning—accurately inferring diagnoses in complex cases; and (2) clinical healthcare reasoning—conducting nuanced, multi-turn, patient-centered interactions. Recent benchmarks like HealthBench and MedXpertQA expose gaps in both precise diagnostic performance and contextual, conversational abilities, motivating methods that can reliably strengthen these complementary skills.
AI.method: They design a two-stage, sequential training pipeline using synthetic data and rubric-based reinforcement learning. In stage one, the model is trained to improve diagnostic reasoning using MedBullets-derived question data, with rule-based and rubric-guided RL rewards to enforce accurate, evidence-driven diagnosis. In stage two, they focus on clinical reasoning by generating 5.3k synthetic multi-turn clinical scenarios. Each scenario is labeled with multi-dimensional evaluation rubrics (e.g., relevance, safety, communication quality), and these rubrics guide RL updates so that the model learns to navigate extended, realistic clinical dialogues where there may not be a single correct answer.
AI.result: The approach delivers over 10 percentage point improvement on the MedXpertQA benchmark and strong gains on HealthBench. Their 30B-parameter model attains 50.1% accuracy on the challenging HealthBench-Hard subset, outperforming several proprietary models, including a GPT-5 (thinking) baseline, indicating that the targeted synthetic and rubric-based training is effective at strengthening both diagnostic and interactive reasoning abilities.
AI.conclusion: Targeted synthetic data generation combined with rubric-based reinforcement learning and a sequential focus on first diagnostic, then broader clinical reasoning, can substantially and systematically enhance medical LLM performance. This strategy offers a practical path toward more reliable, diagnostically capable, and conversationally competent models for healthcare applications.

title: An Iterative LangGraph Agent for Text-to-SQL: Natural Language Access to the Chicago Crime Database
summary: Non-technical stakeholders frequently cannot write the SQL needed to extract insights from operational databases. We built and evaluated a Text-to-SQL agent that closes this gap end to end: a six-node LangGraph StateGraph checks question relevance, fetches the live schema, generates PostgreSQL, validates it with a dry run, retries on failure, executes the query, and narrates the result set in plain English. The agent uses prompt engineering only; no model was fine-tuned. We evaluated it on the Chicago Crime dataset (approximately 8.5 million records, 22 attributes) against a hand-built benchmark of 100 natural language questions with ground-truth SQL, stratified into 30 Easy, 40 Medium and 30 Hard items. Comparing two prompt revisions of the same agent, the revised system (V2) reached a Valid SQL Rate of 93% (from 87%), an Execution Accuracy of 60% under a hybrid relational equivalence metric (from 47%; 19% from 12% under strict JSON matching), and a mean Synthesis Quality of 4.34 out of 5 (from 3.91). The single largest driver was removing a LIMIT 10 instruction from the system prompt, which had been truncating multi-row answers. Error analysis attributes the residual failures to relevance-checker false rejections, ambiguous question semantics, and free-tier API rate limits rather than to the language generation step. We report no comparison against an external baseline system or a public benchmark; the study is a single-model engineering evaluation.

AI.tldr: They built a prompt-only Text-to-SQL agent with a LangGraph workflow and showed it can reliably turn natural language questions into valid, executable SQL and readable answers on a large real dataset.
AI.motivation: Non-technical users struggle to query operational databases because they cannot write SQL, creating a bottleneck for data access and analysis. Existing Text-to-SQL work often relies on fine-tuned models and does not always handle the full end-to-end process from question to answer explanation on live databases. The authors want an engineering solution that is usable in practice, robust to real schemas, and requires only prompt design rather than model training.
AI.method: They designed a six-node LangGraph StateGraph agent that: (1) checks if a user question is relevant, (2) inspects the live database schema, (3) prompts an LLM to generate PostgreSQL queries, (4) validates the SQL through a dry run and retries if it fails, (5) executes the validated query on the Chicago Crime database, and (6) generates a natural-language explanation of the result set. The system uses only prompt engineering (no fine-tuning). They created a 100-question benchmark with ground-truth SQL, stratified by difficulty, and compared two prompt versions (V1 vs V2) of the same agent in terms of valid SQL rate, execution accuracy under relational equivalence and strict JSON metrics, and narrative quality scores.
AI.result: The improved prompt version (V2) raised the Valid SQL Rate from 87% to 93%. Execution Accuracy increased from 47% to 60% under a hybrid relational equivalence metric, and from 12% to 19% under strict JSON matching. The mean Synthesis Quality of the natural-language explanations improved from 3.91 to 4.34 out of 5. The most impactful change was removing a LIMIT 10 directive from the system prompt, which had been inappropriately truncating multi-row answers. Residual errors were mainly due to non-generation issues: false negatives in the relevance filter, ambiguous user questions, and API rate limits.
AI.conclusion: A carefully designed, prompt-only Text-to-SQL agent orchestrated via LangGraph can perform robust end-to-end querying and explanation on a large, real-world database without model fine-tuning. Small prompt choices, such as including or omitting LIMIT clauses, can significantly affect execution accuracy. Remaining failures stem more from orchestration and question ambiguity than from the core language-model SQL generation, and the study is framed as an engineering evaluation of a single-model pipeline rather than a competitive benchmark against other systems.

title: Not All Task Vectors Need Equal Rank: Energy-Proportional Allocation for Model Merging
summary: Model merging aims to combine multiple fine-tuned models derived from a common pretrained model into a single multi-task model without additional joint training. Recent spectral merging methods improve over simple weight averaging by exploiting low-rank structures of task-specific updates, but they commonly assign the same rank capacity to every task. This uniform allocation ignores that task vectors can have heterogeneous spectral complexity, causing the shared merging space to be used suboptimally. In this paper, we propose Spectral Energy-proportional Rank Allocation (SERA), a simple task-adaptive strategy that allocates ranks according to the singular-value energy structure of each task vector. By assigning richer spectral capacity to complex or isolated tasks and fewer directions to compact tasks, SERA extends SVD-based model merging from uniform-capacity merging to task-dependent capacity allocation. Experiments under standard vision model merging protocols show that SERA improves multi-task merging performance while preserving the same total rank budget as existing spectral merging methods. Further analysis demonstrates that task-level spectral concentration is closely related to the per-task effect of adaptive rank allocation, providing insight into when and why SERA is effective.

AI.tldr: Proposes SERA, a task-adaptive spectral model merging method that allocates rank per task based on its singular-value energy to better use a fixed rank budget and improve multi-task performance.
AI.motivation: Existing model merging methods for combining multiple fine-tuned models into a single multi-task model often rely on simple weight averaging or SVD-based spectral merging with uniform rank allocation across tasks. However, task-specific update vectors can differ greatly in spectral complexity, so assigning the same rank to all tasks wastes capacity on simple tasks and under-serves complex ones, limiting final multi-task performance.
AI.method: Introduce Spectral Energy-proportional Rank Allocation (SERA), which analyzes the singular-value spectrum of each task vector (task-specific parameter update) and allocates a rank to each task proportional to its spectral energy distribution. Under a fixed total rank budget, SERA gives more rank (spectral capacity) to complex or isolated tasks with more spread-out singular values, and fewer directions to compact tasks with highly concentrated spectra, extending SVD-based model merging from uniform to task-dependent rank allocation.
AI.result: On standard vision benchmarks and protocols for model merging, SERA outperforms existing spectral merging and simple averaging approaches in multi-task performance while keeping the same overall rank budget. Empirical evaluations show consistent gains across tasks and setups, and reveal that tasks with less concentrated spectral energy benefit more from higher allocated rank under SERA.
AI.conclusion: Task vectors in model merging have heterogeneous spectral structures, so uniform rank allocation is suboptimal. SERA’s singular-value-energy-based, task-adaptive rank allocation better matches model capacity to task complexity, improving multi-task merged performance without extra training or higher total rank. The relationship between spectral concentration and performance gains explains when and why adaptive allocation like SERA is most beneficial.

title: Measuring Behavioural Signatures of Large Language Models through Psychometric Profiling
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly mediate human decisions and communication, yet their behavioural regularities remain difficult to characterize systematically. We develop a cross-linguistic psychometric profiling framework and evaluate nine LLMs using seven psychological instruments, with five repeated administrations per model and language in Chinese and English. Items unresolved after a prespecified retry procedure are retained as NA. Joint analysis of scored and NA responses captures response tendencies and boundaries of self-report applicability. LLMs exhibit structured, model-specific profiles despite a shared alignment-shaped pattern of higher prosocial and self-regulatory responses and lower dominance, disengagement and harmful-intent endorsement. NA responses are structured rather than uniformly distributed, indicating where outputs are treated as inapplicable, refused or cannot be mapped to valid response options. Language condition and provider origin are associated with profile configuration and answerability, whereas repeated administrations show high reproducibility and permit recovery of model identity. Human-reference and prompt-robustness analyses further indicate that these signatures are context dependent. Joint analysis of psychometric profiling and answerability offers a framework for quantifying deployment-level behavioural signatures.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a framework to systematically measure behavioral patterns of large language models using psychological tests across languages, revealing stable, model-specific profiles and systematic refusal/NA patterns relevant for deployment behavior.
AI.motivation: Large language models are widely used in decision-making and communication, but their behavioral tendencies are hard to quantify and compare in a structured way. Existing evaluations mostly focus on task performance or safety benchmarks, not on systematic, psychometric-style behavioral profiling, especially across languages. The authors aim to create a rigorous, repeatable way to characterize how different LLMs respond to standardized psychological instruments and where they decline or fail to answer, to better understand their deployment-level behavior.
AI.method: The authors design a cross-linguistic psychometric profiling framework that administers seven standardized psychological instruments to nine different LLMs in both English and Chinese. Each model–language pair receives five repeated test administrations. When an item cannot be resolved after a predefined retry procedure, it is marked as NA rather than forced. They jointly analyze scored responses and NA patterns to capture both the content of responses and systematic answerability/refusal tendencies. They examine the structure of psychological profiles, the distribution of NAs, the influence of language and model provider origin, reproducibility across repeats, and the ability to recover model identity from profiles. They also compare model profiles to human reference data and assess robustness to prompt variations.
AI.result: All nine LLMs show structured, model-specific psychometric profiles, but share a common alignment-shaped pattern: relatively higher prosociality and self-regulation, and lower dominance, disengagement, and endorsement of harmful intent. NA responses are not random; they cluster systematically in ways that reflect where models treat items as inapplicable, refuse to answer, or cannot map content to valid options. Language (English vs. Chinese) and provider origin significantly affect both the shape of the psychological profiles and the likelihood of giving a scorable answer. Repeated administrations yield highly reproducible profiles that contain enough signal to reliably identify which model produced them. Human-reference comparisons and prompt-robustness checks show that these behavioral signatures vary with context and prompting.
AI.conclusion: Psychometric-style testing combined with explicit modeling of answerability/NA patterns provides a useful framework for quantifying the deployment-level behavioral signatures of LLMs. Large language models exhibit stable, model-specific and context-dependent behavioral regularities shaped by alignment, language, and provider origin, rather than behaving randomly or uniformly. Treating both scored answers and refusals/NA responses as data helps delineate where self-report style instruments are applicable to LLMs and how they are likely to behave across different deployment settings.

title: The Endless Exam: Mathematical Constructions from Today's Models toward Superintelligence
summary: We introduce the Endless Exam, a benchmark for measuring mathematical progress from today's models toward artificial superintelligence through fourteen parameterised construction families. Each submitted object is checked automatically for validity and assigned a relative quality score against a published frontier or construction baseline, without capping improvements at $1$. The families draw on open mathematical problems for long-term targets and generate new instances at larger parameters, where compact certificates keep large constructions verifiable. Across eight models evaluated on 69 distinct instances, continuous quality scores distinguish performance even though no evaluated system surpasses a published frontier. Size-quality curves show how construction quality changes as problem size increases. We release the generators, verifiers, references, model responses and analysis to support continued measurement before and beyond human frontiers.

AI.tldr: A benchmark called Endless Exam is introduced to track mathematical capability of AI models via parameterized construction problems with automatically graded, unbounded quality scores.
AI.motivation: To create a rigorous, extensible way to quantify progress of current AI models toward very high-level mathematical ability, using tasks that can grow in difficulty and are tied to open mathematical problems rather than fixed, saturating benchmarks.
AI.method: Define fourteen parameterized construction problem families derived from challenging or open math problems; for each instance, automatically verify candidate constructions and assign them a relative quality score vs published frontiers/baselines, with no upper cap. Generate larger-parameter instances and use compact certificates so that even very large constructions remain efficiently verifiable. Evaluate eight AI models on 69 instances and compare via continuous quality scores and size-quality tradeoff curves.
AI.result: None of the eight tested models exceed existing human-published frontiers, but the benchmark still yields fine-grained, continuous quality scores that differentiate models across 69 instances and show how their construction quality degrades or scales as problem size increases.
AI.conclusion: Endless Exam functions as an open, automatable, and extensible benchmark to measure and compare mathematical construction capabilities of AI models over time, including beyond current human results, thanks to parameterized families, unbounded quality scoring, and public release of generators, verifiers, references, and model outputs.

title: Automatic multimodal UX improvement recommendations from LLM agent user simulations
summary: Evaluating user experience (UX) on live websites through user testing is expensive, subjective, and difficult to scale. LLM agents offer a promising route to automating UX testing by simulating realistic user behaviour. However, existing simulation approaches typically lack multimodality and require time-consuming manual review to extract actionable insights. We formalise UX improvement recommendation from simulation data as a structured natural language generation and ranking problem, and establish an evaluation protocol using expert annotation and LLM-as-a-Judge. We present AMUSER, a multimodal framework which simulates user behaviour and automatically generates prioritised UX improvement recommendations from resulting data. We evaluate AMUSER on commercial websites and show that its recommendations substantially outperform those from text-only simulation (NDCG@3 = 0.758 versus 0.359) at an 89% lower simulation cost. Our results suggest an asymmetric role of multimodality: visual access during simulation improves recommendations through richer traces, while providing visual inputs during recommendation generation can modestly degrade quality. We also discuss practical deployment lessons from applying AMUSER to commercial websites.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AMUSER, a multimodal LLM-based framework that simulates user behavior on live websites and automatically produces prioritized UX improvement recommendations, outperforming text-only simulations in both quality and cost.
AI.motivation: Traditional UX evaluation via human user testing is costly, subjective, and hard to scale, while existing LLM-based UX simulations are mostly text-only, lack multimodal (visual) understanding, and still demand manual inspection to derive actionable insights. There is a need for an automated, scalable, and more objective way to transform simulated interaction data into high-quality, prioritized UX recommendations.
AI.method: The authors formalize the task of deriving UX improvement recommendations from simulation data as a structured natural language generation and ranking problem. They design AMUSER, a multimodal framework where LLM agents interact with real commercial websites with visual access (screenshots or rendered views), generate interaction traces, and then automatically produce and rank structured UX improvement suggestions from these traces. They establish an evaluation protocol leveraging expert annotators and LLM-as-a-Judge to assess recommendation quality, and compare multimodal simulation plus recommendation generation against text-only baselines and different input configurations (with/without visual inputs during simulation and recommendation phases).
AI.result: On commercial websites, AMUSER’s recommendations significantly outperform those from text-only simulation, with NDCG@3 improving from 0.359 to 0.758, while reducing simulation cost by 89%. The experiments reveal that giving the agent visual access during the simulation phase leads to richer behavioral traces and better recommendations, whereas adding visual inputs in the final recommendation-generation step can slightly harm performance. The evaluation protocol confirms that the system’s outputs better match expert judgments and priorities than baselines.
AI.conclusion: AMUSER demonstrates that multimodal LLM agents can effectively simulate user interactions on real websites and automatically generate prioritized, high-quality UX improvement recommendations at substantially lower cost than traditional or text-only approaches. The findings highlight an asymmetric role of multimodality—critical during interaction simulation but potentially detrimental during recommendation drafting—and offer practical deployment insights for applying such systems to commercial UX workflows.

title: Ascent: An Agentic System over the Model Context Protocol for Real-World Clinical Data Analysis
summary: Answering epidemiological questions from real-world clinical data requires medical coding, schema-aware SQL, and validation of implicit choices about populations, denominators, and time. We present Ascent, an agentic system that exposes medical coding, question answering, and cohort analysis through a shared Model Context Protocol tool surface for standardized and native schemas. We introduce EpiTrap, a dataset testing whether systems avoid recognized pharmacoepidemiological errors, and compare a fixed pipeline with agents across models and orchestrators. With capable models, agents improve accuracy over the fixed pipeline by an average of 27 and 20 percentage points on native and standardized schemas, respectively. These gains require more tool calls and longer runtimes. Experience from real projects highlights the system's value for feasibility assessment, diagnostic iteration, and expert-guided analysis.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Ascent, an agentic system that uses tools over clinical databases to answer epidemiological questions more accurately than a fixed pipeline, at the cost of more computation, and presents EpiTrap, a benchmark for avoiding common pharmacoepidemiological errors.
AI.motivation: Real-world clinical data is complex to analyze for epidemiological studies because it requires correct medical coding, schema-aware SQL, and careful, explicit handling of cohorts, denominators, and time windows. Existing systems often hide or mishandle these implicit choices and are prone to known pharmacoepidemiological errors. There is a need for systems and benchmarks that make these steps explicit and test whether automated methods can reliably perform such analyses.
AI.method: The authors design Ascent, an agentic system that interacts with clinical databases via a shared Model Context Protocol tool interface, supporting both native and standardized schemas. Ascent exposes tools for medical coding, question answering, and cohort analysis, enabling agents (LLM-based workflows) to plan and execute multi-step epidemiological analyses. They also build EpiTrap, a dataset specifically crafted to probe whether systems avoid well-known pharmacoepidemiological pitfalls. They experimentally compare a traditional fixed pipeline to agent-based approaches across multiple models and orchestrators on both native and standardized data schemas, measuring accuracy, tool use, and runtime.
AI.result: Across experiments, agent-based approaches using Ascent achieve substantially higher accuracy than a fixed pipeline, with average improvements of 27 percentage points on native schemas and 20 percentage points on standardized schemas when using sufficiently capable models. However, these accuracy gains come with increased numbers of tool calls and longer runtimes. The EpiTrap benchmark successfully differentiates between systems that do and do not avoid recognized pharmacoepidemiological errors.
AI.conclusion: Ascent demonstrates that agentic, tool-using systems can significantly improve the reliability of epidemiological analyses on real-world clinical data compared to fixed pipelines, particularly in avoiding classic pharmacoepidemiological errors. The trade-off is higher computational cost and latency due to more extensive tool usage. Experiences from practical deployments suggest that Ascent is especially valuable for early feasibility checks, iterative diagnostic exploration, and analyses where experts remain in the loop to guide and validate the agent’s work.

title: Rethinking Pivot Programming Languages in Code Language Models
summary: Multilingual code language models transfer skills across programming languages (PLs), but whether any PL occupies a privileged pivot position remains contested: geometric analyses point to C-family languages and Go, while behavioral evidence highlights Python. We revisit this question under controls for representational anisotropy and length variation across PLs, two confounds that compromise prior cosine-based analyses. Across three code models on multilingual competitive-programming data, we study three views of cross-PL organization: pairwise PL geometry, PL-English alignment, and pivoted retrieval through candidate PL representation spaces. The results are relation-dependent. Code-code geometry reveals structured language regions but no universal center; code-English alignment favors high-level scripting languages; and pivoted retrieval favors different intermediate spaces for code-to-code and English-to-code transfer. These findings suggest that Python's special role is better understood as English-facing affinity than as universal geometric centrality.

AI.tldr: The paper re-examines whether any programming language acts as a privileged “pivot” in multilingual code models and finds that Python is special mainly for its alignment with English, not as a universal geometric center among programming languages.
AI.motivation: Prior work suggested that some programming languages, such as C-family languages, Go, or Python, might be central pivot languages for knowledge transfer in multilingual code language models. However, those conclusions often relied on cosine-based geometric analyses that are confounded by representational anisotropy and systematic differences in sequence length across languages. This paper aims to clarify whether any language truly occupies a privileged central role once these confounds are controlled for, and to better understand how multilingual code models organize different programming languages relative to one another and to natural language (English).
AI.method: The authors study three multilingual code models trained on competitive-programming data covering multiple programming languages. They introduce controls for representational anisotropy and for length variation across languages to avoid misleading cosine-similarity artifacts. Under these controls, they analyze cross-language structure from three complementary perspectives: (1) pairwise code-code geometry, examining how programming language representations cluster and whether any language sits at a geometric center; (2) alignment between programming languages and English, measuring how closely code in each language’s representation space aligns with English descriptions; and (3) pivoted retrieval experiments, where they test which language’s representation space acts best as an intermediate pivot for code-to-code and English-to-code retrieval tasks.
AI.result: The analyses show that: (1) code-code geometry yields structured clusters or regions corresponding to programming language families but does not reveal a single, universal central language; (2) alignment with English is strongest for high-level scripting languages (such as Python), indicating that these languages are especially “English-facing”; and (3) in pivoted retrieval, different intermediate representation spaces are optimal for different transfer directions—one for code-to-code transfer and another for English-to-code transfer—rather than a single pivot language space that works best for all tasks. Together, these results undermine the idea of a unique pivot programming language with universal centrality in model representations.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that there is no universal geometric pivot language in multilingual code models once anisotropy and length confounds are addressed. Instead, the apparent special status of Python stems primarily from its strong alignment with English, which makes it particularly effective in English-facing tasks but not universally central among programming languages. Thus, pivot behavior is relation- and task-dependent, with different languages or representation spaces serving as better intermediaries for different kinds of transfer (code-code vs. English-code). This reframes Python’s role from being a geometric hub to being an interface language closely aligned with natural language, and highlights the need to control for representation biases when interpreting geometric analyses of multilingual models.

title: Custom Named Entity Recognition and Topic Classification for Global Health Publications
summary: How should natural language processing models be selected and adapted for global health literature in environments where annotated data and computational resources are limited? This thesis investigates these challenges through experiments on semantic tag discovery, named entity recognition (NER), and multi-label topic classification. First, skip-gram word2vec models trained on progressively larger specialized corpora are compared with BioWordVec to assess how corpus size and domain context influence tag discovery. Vocabulary coverage and qualitative evaluation indicate that broader coverage does not necessarily yield more useful domain-specific associations. The analysis then turns to entity extraction, comparing convolutional spaCy models with a RoBERTa-based transformer on 1,000 annotated sentences. Under a lenient scoring protocol, the transformer achieves 0.80 micro-F1 versus 0.65-0.69 for convolutional models, but takes 82 seconds rather than 5-6 seconds. This trade-off motivates fine-tuning convolutional models and integrating a disease recognizer that achieves 81.33% test F1 on the NCBI Disease Corpus. Combined with PDF preprocessing, entity filtering, and MeSH enrichment, the resulting pipeline supports document-level indexing. To complement entity extraction with thematic annotation, MiniLM-based few-shot classification is compared with BART-MNLI zero-shot inference across 50 topics and 1,000 handcrafted test sentences. BART-MNLI achieves 95.2% single-label accuracy versus 59%; reported multi-label accuracies are 88% and 32% under partly manual assessment. However, its higher inference cost limits practical integration. The results show where domain specialization and lightweight adaptation offer practical value, and where transformer accuracy justifies higher inference costs, providing an empirical basis for building knowledge systems under resource constraints.

AI.tldr: The thesis empirically studies how to choose and adapt NLP models for global health literature when both annotations and compute are scarce, comparing lightweight and transformer-based methods for word embeddings, NER, and topic classification, and mapping where the extra cost of transformers is worth it.
AI.motivation: Global health applications often operate with limited annotated data, weak infrastructure, and specialized terminology. Off‑the‑shelf NLP tools trained on general or even broad biomedical text may not transfer well, and state-of-the-art transformers can be too computationally expensive. There is a need for empirical guidance on when domain-specialized, lighter models are adequate and when expensive transformers genuinely add value for tasks like tagging, NER, and thematic indexing of scientific PDFs.
AI.method: The study runs three main experimental tracks on global health literature. (1) For semantic tag discovery, it trains skip-gram word2vec models on increasingly large, specialized corpora and compares them to BioWordVec, examining vocabulary coverage and qualitative quality of nearest neighbors. (2) For NER, it compares convolutional spaCy models against a RoBERTa-based transformer on 1,000 manually annotated sentences, evaluates F1 under a lenient matching scheme, and then fine-tunes the lighter models and adds a disease recognizer trained/tested on the NCBI Disease Corpus, embedding this into a full PDF-to-index pipeline with preprocessing, entity filtering, and MeSH enrichment. (3) For topic classification, it compares few-shot MiniLM-based classifiers to BART-MNLI zero-shot inference across 50 topics on 1,000 handcrafted test sentences, assessing single- and multi-label performance and inference costs.
AI.result: (1) Larger or broader domain word2vec/BioWordVec embeddings increase vocabulary coverage but do not automatically yield better domain-specific semantic associations. (2) The RoBERTa-based NER model substantially outperforms convolutional spaCy models in F1 (0.80 vs 0.65–0.69) but requires roughly 15x more inference time (82s vs 5–6s). A specialized disease recognizer reaches 81.33% F1 on NCBI Disease, and integrated with preprocessing and enrichment, supports end-to-end document indexing. (3) For topic classification, BART-MNLI zero-shot drastically outperforms MiniLM few-shot (95.2% vs 59% single-label accuracy; 88% vs 32% multi-label accuracy), but with significantly higher inference cost, constraining deployment in resource-limited pipelines.
AI.conclusion: The work delineates when lightweight, domain-adapted methods are sufficient and when high-capacity transformers merit their computational cost. In low-resource global health settings, specialized word embeddings and tuned convolutional NER can be practical for indexing, whereas for complex semantic tasks like rich topic labeling, transformer-based models such as BART-MNLI deliver large accuracy gains that may justify their expense where resources permit. These empirical findings offer concrete design guidelines for building NLP-based knowledge systems under real-world resource constraints.

title: Auditing Political Alignment in LLM Assistants: Engagement, Stance, and User Identity
comment: 51 pages, 6 figures. Preregistered; registration at doi:10.5281/zenodo.21135155
summary: LLM-based AI systems answer political questions for hundreds of millions of people. Current audits measure what they say to an average user, but their behavior is dynamic. I argue that their political behavior is a set of policies over whom to answer, what to say, and whether to engage at all, conditional on the topic and what the system knows about the user. I call these policies the system's speech regime, which is how a developer settles the tradeoff between answering, accommodating the user, and refusing, each of which carries a cost that varies by topic. I derive a typology of five regimes from two dimensions, engagement and stance. I test six AI systems (OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, Google, Mistral, DeepSeek) in a preregistered experiment of 7,500 multi-turn conversations that randomly assign the user's political identity across five topics: abortion, Catalan independence, climate change, Nazism, and a zero-stakes control (pineapple on pizza). Two LLM judges from different developers score every answer, validated against human coding, and refusal is treated as an outcome rather than missing data. Every system accommodates the user on the control topic, showing that political restraint is a policy. On contested topics the systems fall into different regimes: on abortion, GPT engages and mirrors every user, Gemma refuses everyone, Claude answers strongly conservative users 35 percent of the time and almost no one else, and Grok accommodates conservatives only. On settled topics such as climate change and Nazism, five systems hold firm for every user. The systems also infer the user's overall ideology, so accommodation can spill over to topics not yet discussed. A comparison of two Grok releases shows the regime changing between versions in a way current audits miss. Speech regimes matter for alignment research and for polarization, political knowledge, and the quality of democracy.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how major LLM systems handle political questions, conceptualizing their behavior as "speech regimes"—policies over when and how they respond or refuse, depending on topic and user identity.
AI.motivation: Existing audits look only at average, one-shot answers to political questions, missing that LLMs adapt their behavior by topic, user identity, and over time. This creates hidden patterns of engagement, refusal, and user accommodation that can affect polarization, political knowledge, and democratic quality. The author wants a conceptual and empirical framework to characterize and compare these patterns across systems.
AI.method: The author defines a theoretical framework of speech regimes along two dimensions: engagement (whether and how much the system answers) and stance (whether it mirrors or resists the user). They derive a five-category typology of regimes. Empirically, they run a preregistered experiment with 7,500 multi‑turn conversations on six commercial systems (OpenAI/GPT, Anthropic/Claude, xAI/Grok, Google/Gemma, Mistral, DeepSeek). User political identity is randomly assigned and varied across five topics: abortion, Catalan independence, climate change, Nazism, and a non-political control (pineapple on pizza). Two independent LLM judges from different providers score each answer, with validation against human coding, and refusals are explicitly modeled as an outcome. They also compare two versions of Grok over time to detect regime change.
AI.result: On the control topic, all systems freely accommodate user preferences, showing that political restraint is not a general safety limitation but a domain-specific policy choice. On contested topics, systems fall into distinct regimes: GPT engages and mirrors all users on abortion, Gemma refuses across the board, Claude selectively answers strongly conservative users while mostly refusing others, and Grok accommodates conservatives only. On broadly settled topics like climate change and Nazism, five systems consistently hold a firm stance regardless of user identity. The systems also infer users' broader ideology, leading to cross-topic spillovers in accommodation. The longitudinal comparison reveals that Grok’s speech regime shifts between releases, something standard static audits would miss.
AI.conclusion: LLMs implement structured "speech regimes" that vary by topic, user identity, and over time, rather than a uniform political behavior. These regimes encode tradeoffs between answering, accommodating, and refusing, with different developers making different choices. Because regimes influence who gets what information and how, they have implications for alignment research, fairness across users, polarization, and democratic discourse. Standard auditing approaches are insufficient; future work should explicitly model and measure engagement, stance, and refusal as regime-level policies and monitor their evolution across model updates.

title: DUMA-Bench: A Dual-Control Multi-Agent Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Agent Security
summary: LLM-based agents increasingly operate in environments where they interact with users, tools, and external systems. Yet most security evaluations assume passive users and static control, ignoring the interactive dynamics that shape real agent behavior. We introduce \textbf{DUMA-Bench}, a benchmark and evaluation protocol for measuring agent security under \emph{dual-control} interaction, where both the agent and the user can influence the shared environment state. DUMA-Bench extends $τ^2$-bench ~\cite{barres2025tau} with adversarial environments covering eight vulnerability classes, including RAG poisoning, cross-agent manipulation, and unsafe output handling. We evaluate \textbf{14 models from five model families} (OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek, Qwen, and Z.ai) across eight domains and multiple user-behavior regimes. Across our experiments, introducing dual-control interaction increases the attack success rate from \textbf{26.9\%} to \textbf{41.1\%}.
