These results show that agent security is not solely a property of the model but emerges from the interaction between the model, the user, and the environment. DUMA-Bench provides a missing evaluation layer for studying security in realistic agent deployments.

AI.tldr: DUMA-Bench is a benchmark to evaluate the security of LLM-based agents in interactive, dual-control environments where both user and agent influence the state.
AI.motivation: Existing security evaluations of LLM-based agents typically assume passive users and static environments, which fails to capture realistic, interactive settings where users, tools, and external systems all shape behavior. There is a need to understand how security emerges from these interactions, especially under adversarial conditions.
AI.method: The authors introduce DUMA-Bench, which extends τ^2-bench with adversarial environments designed around eight vulnerability classes (such as RAG poisoning, cross-agent manipulation, and unsafe output handling). They define a dual-control interaction setting where both user and agent can change the environment state, and evaluate 14 models from five major model families across eight domains and varying user-behavior regimes, measuring attack success rates under these conditions.
AI.result: Under traditional assumptions, the attack success rate is 26.9%, but when dual-control interaction is introduced, the attack success rate rises to 41.1%. This demonstrates that agents become significantly more vulnerable when realistic interactive dynamics are considered.
AI.conclusion: Security of LLM-based agents is an emergent property of the interplay between model, user, and environment, not just a static characteristic of the model itself. DUMA-Bench offers a needed evaluation layer for realistically assessing and comparing agent security in practical deployments.

title: Attributable Post-Rationalization in RAG Citations: A Controlled Reproduction and an RLVR Comparison
summary:
A RAG system can hand you the right answer and cite a source it did not actually use. Models output these unfaithful citations via post-rationalization: they write the answer first and then attach a citation to whatever passage looks close enough. Search agents are now trained with reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR), which pays them for getting the answer right. We asked whether that training also teaches them to cite honestly.
  Improving an existing methodology with a required control, we compared an instruction-tuned model against three RLVR agents trained from it, on four question-answering datasets, using only free-tier Kaggle GPUs. Post-rationalization is everywhere: on Wikipedia-based questions roughly one citation in seven is unfaithful. RLVR does not fix it. The agents post-rationalize at their base model's rate, and one lands slightly worse. Rewarding correct answers buys nothing in citation faithfulness, so faithfulness has to be trained and measured on its own terms.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR), which rewards correct answers, also reduces unfaithful citations in RAG systems, and finds that it does not: models still frequently attach citations to sources they did not use.
AI.motivation: RAG systems often provide citations as evidence, but models can "post-rationalize" by generating an answer first and then attaching plausible-looking but unfaithful citations. With the rise of RLVR-trained search agents optimized for correctness, it is important to know if such training also makes citations more honest, since users and downstream applications may trust citations as proof of grounding.
AI.method: The authors refine an existing evaluation methodology by adding a necessary control, then systematically compare an instruction-tuned base model with three RLVR-trained agents derived from it. They evaluate citation faithfulness across four QA datasets, including Wikipedia-based questions, using modest computing resources (free-tier Kaggle GPUs). They measure how often citations are unfaithful—i.e., the cited passages were not actually used to derive the answer, indicating post-rationalization.
AI.result: They find that post-rationalization is widespread: for Wikipedia-style questions, about one in seven citations is unfaithful. RLVR training focused on answer correctness does not reduce this behavior; the RLVR agents exhibit similar rates of unfaithful citations as the base model, and in one case perform slightly worse in citation faithfulness.
AI.conclusion: Optimizing models for answer correctness via RLVR does not inherently improve citation faithfulness in RAG systems. Since rewarding correct answers alone does not teach models to cite honestly, citation faithfulness must be explicitly targeted—both in training objectives and in evaluation—if we want reliable, truthful grounding and trustworthy citations.

title: Beyond Endpoint Performance: Process-Level Evaluation of Self-Evolving Agents
summary: Self-evolving agents convert interaction feedback into persistent artifacts, such as memories or skills, which in turn guide subsequent decisions. As these artifacts are iteratively updated throughout an experience stream, the capabilities they support may evolve. Consequently, endpoint performance alone offers an incomplete view of self-evolution. Process-level evaluation is therefore essential to identify when a target capability emerges and whether later updates strengthen, preserve, or weaken it. Motivated by this, we propose \textsc{EvoPathBench}, a benchmark that tracks individual capabilities during artifact-level self-evolution. EvoPathBench fixes the base model, tools, freezes evolving artifacts at successive checkpoints, and evaluates the target capability on held-out episodes. This benchmark evaluates agent self-evolution using public trading data and calibrated trajectories. It tests three capabilities: generalization to unseen tasks, retention after unrelated learning, and rule adaptation to new evidence. Experimental results show that gains on similar unseen tasks often weaken under distribution shift, retention losses are concentrated in a minority of evolution paths, and no method achieves reliable rule adaptation. Moreover, while self-evolution enables agents to generate candidate artifacts with substantial held-out gains, the selected updates consistently fall short of realizing this potential. Together, these findings establish capability-level process evaluation as a foundation for analyzing self-evolution, identifying candidate evaluation and selection as key targets for improvement.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces EvoPathBench, a benchmark for evaluating how specific capabilities of self-evolving agents change over time as their internal artifacts (memories, skills, rules) are updated.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of self-evolving agents mostly look at final performance, which hides when and how particular capabilities emerge, improve, or degrade during learning. Because self-evolution involves iterative updates to internal artifacts, there is a need for process-level evaluation that can track capability dynamics across these updates, especially to understand generalization, forgetting, and adaptation behaviors.
AI.method: The authors design EvoPathBench, a benchmark that: (1) fixes the underlying base model and tools; (2) lets only agent artifacts (e.g., memories, skills, rules) evolve; (3) freezes these artifacts at multiple checkpoints along an evolution path; and (4) evaluates a specific target capability at each checkpoint using held-out episodes constructed from public trading data and calibrated trajectories. They define three target capabilities to test—generalization to unseen but similar tasks, retention after unrelated learning, and adaptation of rules in response to new evidence—and compare different self-evolution methods along these dimensions.
AI.result: Experiments reveal several systematic patterns: performance gains on unseen tasks often fail to transfer under distribution shift and can even weaken; forgetting is not uniform but concentrated in a subset of evolution paths; none of the tested methods achieves consistently reliable rule adaptation; and, although self-evolution is able to propose candidate artifact updates that promise strong held-out gains, the actually chosen updates underperform these candidates.
AI.conclusion: Capability-level, process-oriented evaluation is crucial for understanding self-evolving agents. EvoPathBench provides a concrete framework for tracking how specific skills develop and degrade over time, highlighting significant gaps in current self-evolution methods—especially in robust generalization, selective retention, and rule adaptation—and pointing to evaluation and selection mechanisms for artifact updates as primary levers for future improvement.

title: Bridging Static and Agentic RAG for Taiwanese Historical Question Answering
summary: Agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enables language models to adapt retrieval based on previously retrieved evidence, but it remains unclear whether such adaptive orchestration consistently outperforms well-designed static pipelines. We conduct a controlled comparison of agentic and static RAG for Taiwanese historical question answering, sharing the same generator and hybrid retrieval backend. Despite similar aggregate performance, the two pipelines differ on 70.83% of questions, with their advantages largely canceling out when averaged. An oracle that selects the better response per question improves the composite score by 0.2417 over the better individual pipeline, revealing substantial headroom for question-level selection. We therefore introduce a post-hoc selector that compares the two responses and their cited evidence, significantly outperforming either individual pipeline and recovering 60.34% of the oracle headroom. These results show that aggregate comparisons can obscure meaningful question-level differences between retrieval strategies, suggesting that exploiting their complementarity may be more fruitful than seeking a universally superior pipeline.

AI.tldr: The paper compares adaptive (agentic) and static RAG pipelines for Taiwanese historical QA, finds they perform similarly on average but differ on most individual questions, and shows that a learned selector that chooses between them per question can significantly outperform either alone by exploiting their complementarity.
AI.motivation: While agentic RAG methods that adapt retrieval over multiple steps are popular, it is unclear whether they truly offer consistent gains over strong, carefully engineered static RAG pipelines. Aggregate metrics may hide nuanced, question-level differences between retrieval strategies, and there is untapped potential in exploiting these differences rather than betting on a single pipeline. The paper focuses on a concrete, challenging domain—Taiwanese historical question answering—to investigate this.
AI.method: The authors build two RAG pipelines that share the same language model generator and a hybrid retrieval backend (likely combining sparse and dense retrieval), differing only in how retrieval is orchestrated: one is an agentic/iterative retrieval pipeline that adapts based on previously retrieved evidence, and the other is a static, non-adaptive pipeline with a fixed retrieval strategy. They conduct a controlled evaluation on Taiwanese historical QA, compare question-level outcomes, define an oracle that picks the better of the two answers for each question, and then design a post-hoc selector model that, given the two candidate answers and their supporting evidence, predicts which answer is better. They evaluate how much of the oracle’s potential gain this selector can recover.
AI.result: The two RAG pipelines have similar overall/aggregate performance, but they produce different outcomes on 70.83% of questions, with neither clearly dominating the other; their strengths and weaknesses largely cancel out in the averages. An oracle that always chooses the better answer between the two per question improves the composite score by 0.2417 over the stronger individual pipeline, showing substantial room for question-level selection. The proposed post-hoc selector substantially outperforms both individual pipelines and recovers 60.34% of the oracle’s possible improvement.
AI.conclusion: Agentic RAG does not universally outperform a strong static RAG pipeline when judged by aggregate metrics, but the two approaches exhibit complementary strengths at the question level. Simple aggregate comparisons therefore understate the value of combining multiple retrieval strategies. A post-hoc selector that chooses between pipelines on a per-question basis can realize much of the latent performance headroom, suggesting that future work should focus less on finding a single best pipeline and more on methods that dynamically exploit the complementarity of diverse retrieval strategies.

title: TimeLitmus: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Cross-Modal Understanding and Explanation Faithfulness in Event-Conditioned Time-Series Prediction
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to make predictions from numerical time-series histories and textual events. Yet accuracy alone cannot reveal whether correct answers reflect effective integration of the two inputs or instead arise from event polarity, unimodal priors, or superficial cues. Likewise, plausible explanations may rationalize predictions without faithfully reflecting the evidence that drives model behavior. We introduce TimeLitmus, a diagnostic benchmark for cross-modal understanding and explanation faithfulness in event-conditioned time-series prediction. TimeLitmus contains 4,856 evaluation records across Finance and Traffic, combining natural prediction with controlled counterfactual and contrastive interventions, explanation-targeted faithfulness tests, and systematic shortcut controls. Across ten representative LLMs, standard prediction accuracy substantially overstates reliable cross-modal understanding: Hard Paired Contrast (HPC) pair correctness peaks at only 19.2% in Finance and 11.7% in Traffic, and all ten models show lower-than-expected consistency on Finance series-side controls. Models often recognize scenario relations explicitly yet fail to apply them during independent prediction. Explanation faithfulness shows a similar gap: in Traffic, most models cite the manipulated temporal factor in over 90% of cases, while behavioral support remains below 22%. Human annotators outperform LLMs on matched controlled and hard-pair diagnostics, confirming that these distinctions are recoverable from the inputs. Natural-only adaptation yields selective gains in evidence selection and input sensitivity, but not consistent gains in controlled or hard-pair behavior. The benchmark, evaluation suite, and supervised adaptation data will be released publicly.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces TimeLitmus, a diagnostic benchmark to test whether large language models truly integrate textual events and numerical time-series data, and whether their explanations faithfully reflect their decision process.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of LLMs on event-conditioned time-series tasks rely mainly on prediction accuracy, which cannot distinguish genuine cross-modal reasoning from shortcuts such as priors, superficial cues, or event polarity. Moreover, models can produce plausible natural-language explanations that do not faithfully track the evidence driving their predictions. The authors are motivated to build a benchmark that isolates and measures (1) true cross-modal understanding between text and time series, and (2) the faithfulness of explanations to underlying model behavior.
AI.method: They design TimeLitmus, a benchmark with 4,856 records across Finance and Traffic domains, combining several diagnostic components: (1) natural prediction tasks where models forecast time-series outcomes given textual events and numerical histories; (2) controlled counterfactual and contrastive interventions that alter specific aspects of the inputs to test whether models update predictions appropriately; (3) hard paired contrasts (HPC) that pair closely related scenarios where only deep cross-modal reasoning can distinguish the correct answer; (4) explanation-targeted faithfulness tests, where explanations are checked against whether the cited factors actually drive behavioral changes; and (5) systematic shortcut controls that probe reliance on unimodal or superficial cues. They evaluate ten representative LLMs on this suite, and also compare to human annotations on matched subsets. They explore natural-only supervised adaptation to see if fine-tuning on natural instances improves controlled and contrastive performance.
AI.result: Across ten LLMs, conventional prediction accuracy significantly overestimates genuine cross-modal understanding. On the hardest paired contrasts, correctness is very low (up to 19.2% in Finance and 11.7% in Traffic), and models show unexpectedly low consistency on Finance-side controls, suggesting reliance on shortcuts rather than principled integration of text and time series. Models can often verbally recognize relations in scenarios but fail to use them reliably in independent predictions. For explanation faithfulness, in the Traffic domain most models frequently mention the manipulated temporal factor in their explanations (>90% of cases), yet their actual behavioral changes aligned with that factor occur in less than 22% of cases. Human annotators clearly outperform LLMs on the controlled and hard-pair diagnostics, indicating the tasks are solvable and that the benchmark is not inherently ambiguous. Natural-only adaptation improves some aspects of evidence selection and sensitivity to inputs, but does not yield consistent improvements on the controlled diagnostics or hard-pair tasks.
AI.conclusion: TimeLitmus reveals a substantial gap between surface-level performance and genuine cross-modal reasoning and explanation faithfulness in LLMs for event-conditioned time-series prediction. Current models can appear competent and generate plausible explanations while actually relying on shortcuts and failing to apply scenario relations consistently. The benchmark and evaluation suite provide a more stringent diagnostic tool for measuring and improving cross-modal understanding and explanation faithfulness. The authors will release TimeLitmus and associated supervised adaptation data to support future research on more robust and interpretable LLM behavior in time-series prediction contexts.

title: From Concept Alignment to Causal Grounding: An Intervention Test of Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) can sound plausible yet be unfaithful to the model's underlying reasoning. Most prior work probes CoT faithfulness through input--output behavior or input attributions, leaving internal computation largely underexplored. We instead cast faithfulness as internal concept grounding: Does a large language model's (LLM) CoT reasoning engage the same internal concepts that support the LLM's direct prediction, and do the shared concepts causally drive its answer? Encoding a prediction pass and a CoT pass with a single shared sparse autoencoder (SAE), a reliable approximator of the latent concepts LLMs use, makes their internal concepts directly comparable. We introduce three correlational metrics of concept-level alignment and a causal metric, $Δp$, which ablates the shared concepts and measures the drop in answer probability. Across five LLMs and four datasets, concept alignment is generally high, as indicated by the correlational metrics; yet these only identify which concepts are shared, not how much they causally contribute. $Δp$ fills this gap: causal faithfulness varies substantially with model depth, peaking at mid-to-late layers rather than the final ones, and model scale reshapes the layer-wise profile. Moreover, causally important shared concepts are not always verbalized in the CoT. These dissociations suggest that faithfulness cannot be reliably assessed from surface-level or representational correspondence alone; assessing it requires causal tests of whether the internal concepts underlying a CoT actually drive the model's prediction.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how faithful chain-of-thought (CoT) explanations are to a language model’s true internal reasoning by comparing internal “concepts” used in direct prediction vs. CoT, using sparse autoencoders and new correlational and causal metrics.
AI.motivation: CoT explanations produced by large language models often look plausible but may not reflect the model’s actual reasoning process. Prior evaluations of faithfulness mostly look at input–output behavior or attribution over inputs, which miss how internal computations differ between direct answers and CoT answers. The authors aim to understand whether the same internal conceptual mechanisms drive both, and to move from surface-level alignment to causal tests of faithfulness.
AI.method: They treat faithfulness as internal concept grounding: CoT is faithful if it uses the same internal concepts that causally support the model’s direct prediction. They run the model in two modes, a direct prediction pass and a CoT generation pass, and jointly encode both with a single shared sparse autoencoder (SAE) trained as a reliable approximation of the model’s latent concepts. This allows direct comparison of concepts across passes. They then define three correlational metrics to quantify concept-level alignment between the two passes and introduce a causal metric, Δp, which is computed by ablating the shared concepts and measuring the resulting drop in the probability of the final answer. They evaluate these metrics across five LLMs and four datasets and analyze how alignment and causal faithfulness vary by layer depth and model scale, and whether causally important shared concepts are actually verbalized in the CoT.
AI.result: Correlational metrics show that internal concept alignment between direct prediction and CoT modes is generally high across models and datasets, meaning many concepts are shared at the representation level. However, correlational metrics alone cannot determine how much these shared concepts causally affect the final prediction. The causal metric Δp reveals that causal faithfulness is not uniform: it varies strongly across network depth, peaking at mid-to-late layers instead of the final layers, and differs systematically with model size. They also find that not all causally important shared concepts appear as explicit content in the CoT text, indicating a gap between internal drivers and verbalized reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Faithfulness of CoT explanations cannot be reliably inferred from surface behavior or representational overlap alone. Although CoT and direct prediction often share internal concepts, their causal roles differ across layers and scales, and key causal concepts may remain unspoken in the explanation. Reliable assessment of CoT faithfulness therefore requires causal interventions on internal representations—such as ablations of shared concepts—rather than only correlational or textual analyses.

title: World State Generator
summary: Language agents solve complex tasks through plans and actions. A single step the world refuses puts the goal out of reach, and what the agent does next decides the task. Prompted planners fail at exactly this point, rewriting the refused step in new words, meeting the same refusal, and burning the attempt budget without moving. They fail because the plan was never tied to the world, so a refusal has nothing in the plan to attach to. A world is where a task runs, and it has its own rules, its own admissible actions, and its own constraints. We build synthetic worlds across 7 domains and extract training data from them. A program enforces each world's rules and grades its goal, and every world is admitted only if its goal is reachable from its initial state. Agents run inside and leave verified failures paired with repairs that carried the run to a state the world certified, a record of about 226K trajectories. On this record we train the World State Generator, a model that writes a plan as checkable states of the world and keeps that plan aligned with the world it runs in. That alignment is what a plan written in language lacks, since the world it runs in has physical limits, logical dependencies, and required orders the language never states, and the plan encounters these rules only when a state fails. WSG takes that failure as the rule the world has stated and rewrites the remaining states to obey it, so the plan bends to the world as the run goes on. Across 7 public benchmarks, WSG raises end-to-end success for two open models near 30B parameters over prompting and brings to the level of proprietary model.

AI.tldr: They propose World State Generator (WSG), a planning model that represents and updates plans as explicit world states so that agents can recover from action refusals and stay aligned with environment constraints, significantly boosting success on multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Language-agent planners often fail when the environment or external tools refuse a single planned action. Current LLM-based planners typically respond by rephrasing the same infeasible step instead of adapting the whole plan, wasting attempts and never reaching the goal. This happens because plans are written purely in language, without a grounded connection to the environment’s admissible actions, constraints, and goal reachability. The authors want a planning mechanism that is explicitly tied to world dynamics so that failure signals can be used to systematically repair and realign the plan with what is actually possible.
AI.method: They construct synthetic, programmatically defined worlds across 7 domains, where each world has explicit rules, admissible actions, and a verifier for goal satisfaction. Worlds are only included if their goals are reachable from the initial state. Within these worlds, agents execute tasks and produce trajectories. When a run fails but can be repaired, they record pairs of verified failures and the corresponding repaired trajectories, accumulating about 226K trajectories. Using this dataset, they train the World State Generator (WSG), a model that represents a plan as a sequence of checkable world states rather than only natural-language steps. During execution, when a state or action is rejected by the world, WSG treats this as the world communicating a rule and rewrites the remaining future states so that they obey this rule, effectively repairing and realigning the plan on the fly.
AI.result: WSG substantially improves the robustness and effectiveness of language agents when interacting with constrained environments. On 7 public benchmarks, using two open-source models around 30B parameters, integrating WSG yields much higher end-to-end task success compared with standard prompting-based planners, and brings their performance close to that of strong proprietary systems.
AI.conclusion: Grounding plans in explicit, checkable world states and continuously updating those plans in response to environment feedback enables language agents to recover from refusals and adapt to the true constraints of the world. The World State Generator operationalizes this idea, leveraging a large corpus of failure–repair trajectories from synthetic domains. This world-aligned planning framework turns failure signals into structured constraints that reshape the remaining plan, closing a significant performance gap between open and proprietary models on complex, multi-step benchmarks.

title: Directing large language models to follow the letter or spirit of the law
summary: The distinction between the spirit and letter of the law is a central issue across research and everyday life, and a growing concern for building safe, intelligent machines. What is this distinction based on, and how can we develop machines that follow the intention behind a rule? We used targeted adaptation that made large language models prioritize the spirit or letter of the law. With minimal modifications, our method significantly changed LLM behavior across diverse measures, novel vignettes, real-world scenarios, and influential legal cases. An analysis of model internals revealed a low-dimensional space with three interpretable dimensions matching a formal pre-specified framework for the geometry of legal concepts. These findings show how legal thought in LLMs may be organized and directed.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to get large language models to follow the spirit vs. the letter of the law, and shows that small, targeted adaptations can reliably steer models along these dimensions, which appear to have a simple, interpretable internal representation.
AI.motivation: The spirit–letter distinction is crucial in law, ethics, and everyday rule-following, and it is especially important for making AI systems safe and aligned with human intentions, not just literal rules. However, we lack a clear understanding of how to systematically steer AI models toward respecting the underlying intent of rules. The authors aim to ground this distinction in model behavior and internal representations so we can better control how models reason about rules.
AI.method: The authors apply a targeted adaptation procedure to existing large language models that biases them to prioritize either the spirit or the letter of the law. They evaluate the impact of these minimal modifications on a range of tasks, including benchmark measures, new hypothetical vignettes, real-world situations, and key legal cases. They also analyze the models’ internal representations, using interpretability techniques to uncover a low-dimensional subspace associated with legal reasoning, and compare this subspace to a theoretically specified geometric framework for legal concepts.
AI.result: The adapted models show markedly different behaviors depending on whether they are tuned toward the spirit or the letter of the law, and this difference generalizes across multiple evaluation settings and novel scenarios. The internal representation analysis reveals that a small number of dimensions in the models’ latent space capture distinct, interpretable axes corresponding to the spirit–letter distinction and related legal concepts. These axes align well with a pre-defined formal framework for the geometry of legal notions.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that legal rule-following behavior in LLMs can be systematically steered toward either the spirit or the letter of the law using minimal, targeted adaptation, and that this behavior reflects a low-dimensional, interpretable structure in the models’ internal representations. This suggests that legal and normative reasoning in LLMs is organized in a way that can be understood and directed, offering a path toward building AI systems that more reliably follow human-intended meanings behind rules.

title: Epi-Logic: A Conceptual Framework for Epistemic Runtime Control, Schema Validity Checking, and Controlled Accommodation in Autonomous AI Agents
summary:
Autonomous AI agents are increasingly deployed in areas where wrong decisions are hard to reverse. This paper examines schema mismatch: the condition in which an agent operates within an interpretive frame that no longer applies to the current context. Outputs produced under such a mismatch can appear internally consistent, linguistically plausible, and largely factually correct; output-quality metrics alone therefore capture the underlying loss of validity only partially.
  The paper introduces Epi-Logic, a conceptual framework for epistemic runtime control. It couples the detection of schema dissonance, a graduated reduction of autonomy, and the auditable switch to a validated schema. A schema is formalised as a tuple of variable space, expectation model, validity conditions, axioms, and metadata. The Epi-Score aggregates seven graded dimensions of epistemic dissonance; the temporal validity dimension D8, violations of the validity conditions G, and axiom violations are carried as separate categorical paths that are not offset against the aggregate.
  The architecture rests on a checking asymmetry: formalised validity conditions can be checked at runtime, whereas the correctness of many actions is established only ex post. The paper separates two architectural properties, a conditional result from sequential changepoint detection, and an empirical remainder. Eight falsifiable propositions with named baselines describe the transition to empirical validation. All propositions are empirically testable hypotheses, not established results.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Epi-Logic, a framework to monitor and control autonomous AI agents when their internal interpretive schema no longer matches the real-world context, aiming to safely reduce autonomy and switch to validated schemas when epistemic problems are detected.
AI.motivation: Autonomous AI agents can make hard-to-reverse mistakes when they reason using outdated or mismatched interpretive schemas. Existing evaluation methods that focus on output quality (plausibility, fluency, surface-level factuality) fail to fully capture when an agent’s underlying assumptions and context model have become invalid. There is a need for runtime mechanisms that can detect such schema mismatches and adjust the agent’s autonomy and epistemic grounding before serious errors occur.
AI.method: The paper introduces Epi-Logic, a conceptual and architectural framework for epistemic runtime control of AI agents. It formalizes a schema as a tuple consisting of variable space, expectation model, validity conditions, axioms, and metadata. Epi-Logic defines an Epi-Score that aggregates seven graded dimensions of epistemic dissonance, while treating temporal validity (dimension D8), validity-condition violations (G), and axiom violations as separate categorical paths that cannot be compensated by high scores elsewhere. The architecture exploits a checking asymmetry: validity conditions and axioms can be evaluated online, whereas many action outcomes are only known ex post. The framework specifies how detecting schema dissonance triggers graduated reductions in autonomy and an auditable switch to a validated schema. It also distinguishes a conditional result derived from sequential changepoint detection theory from an empirical remainder, and formulates eight named, falsifiable propositions as baselines to guide empirical testing of the framework.
AI.result: The paper does not present empirical results; instead, it delivers a formal and conceptual architecture. It provides (1) a formalization of schemas as tuples with explicit validity conditions and axioms; (2) the definition of the Epi-Score and associated categorical dissonance paths; (3) an architectural design for detecting schema dissonance, reducing autonomy, and switching schemas in an auditable way; and (4) eight falsifiable, empirically testable propositions that serve as baselines for future validation. All of these are proposed contributions, not experimentally confirmed findings.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that managing schema mismatch in autonomous AI agents requires an explicit, runtime-checked epistemic control layer rather than relying solely on output quality metrics. Epi-Logic is proposed as such a framework: it leverages formal validity conditions, graded measures of epistemic dissonance, and principled autonomy reduction and schema-switching mechanisms. The work is positioned as a set of testable hypotheses and architectural blueprints, laying the groundwork for future empirical validation rather than claiming established performance gains.

title: OmniEdu: Open Foundation Models for Learning and Teaching
summary: Educational foundation models must solve problems, understand curriculum structure, diagnose learner difficulties, and provide appropriate instructional support. Existing educational language models often focus on either problem solving or tutoring, with training mixtures organized by source or task rather than capability. We present OmniEdu, an open family of foundation models for K-12 learning and teaching. Its instruction-tuning corpus combines over 100 educational resources and general instruction sources, organized around four capabilities: subject competence, curriculum grounding, diagnostic reasoning, and pedagogical action and scaffolding. Our pipeline integrates deterministic cleaning, semantic auditing and rewriting, task-specific quality scoring, token-budgeted diversity selection, and pedagogical instruction assignment. It yields 69,999 examples and 15.96M supervised response tokens, including 60,951 education-specific examples. We fine-tune 4B, 9B, and 27B models and evaluate curriculum grounding, K-12 problem solving, and pedagogical tutoring, alongside general capability. Education-oriented tuning consistently improves all three educational benchmark groups across model scales. OmniEdu-27B achieves 63.12% EM and 76.69% F1 on K12-Bench, 85.89% on MathFish, 86.95% on EDUMATH, and 78.74% in MathTutorBench's Scaffold setting. It also achieves the highest Teaching average on LongTutor among the evaluated models, at 3.02. These results demonstrate the value of curated, capability-balanced supervision for adapting general language models to educational tasks spanning problem solving, curriculum understanding, and instructional support.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces OmniEdu, a family of instruction-tuned foundation models for K-12 education, optimized across four core capabilities and showing strong performance on multiple educational benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing educational language models are typically optimized for a narrow slice of educational functionality (e.g., problem solving or tutoring alone) and are trained with mixtures organized by source or task rather than by the actual capabilities needed for effective educational support. There is a need for models that simultaneously handle problem solving, curriculum understanding, diagnostic reasoning about learner difficulties, and pedagogically appropriate instructional support, within a unified and systematically curated training framework.
AI.method: The authors build OmniEdu, a set of open models (4B, 9B, 27B parameters) instruction-tuned on a carefully constructed corpus. They aggregate data from over 100 educational and general instruction resources, then organize and label them according to four targeted capabilities: (1) subject competence, (2) curriculum grounding, (3) diagnostic reasoning, and (4) pedagogical action and scaffolding. The data pipeline applies deterministic cleaning, semantic auditing and rewriting, task-specific quality scoring, token-budgeted diversity selection, and assignment of pedagogical instructions. This yields about 70k instruction-response pairs with roughly 16M supervised tokens, most of which are education-focused. These are used to fine-tune base language models and produce the OmniEdu variants.
AI.result: Education-oriented, capability-balanced instruction tuning improves performance across model scales on three main groups of educational benchmarks: curriculum grounding, K-12 problem solving, and pedagogical tutoring. OmniEdu-27B attains 63.12% EM / 76.69% F1 on K12-Bench, 85.89% on MathFish, 86.95% on EDUMATH, and 78.74% on MathTutorBench (Scaffold setting). It also achieves the highest Teaching score on LongTutor among compared models, with an average of 3.02, indicating strong teaching quality as judged by that benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Curating a training corpus around explicit educational capabilities—rather than only tasks or sources—and applying a rigorous data pipeline produces general-purpose educational foundation models that perform well across diverse K-12 needs: solving problems, grounding responses in curricula, diagnosing student difficulties, and providing effective instructional scaffolding. OmniEdu demonstrates that capability-balanced supervision is an effective strategy for adapting general language models to broad educational applications.

title: Construting Reverse Thinking: Developing Large Language Models' Reverse Thingking Ability
summary: When facing complex problems, humans tend to try various ideas for different issues. Human thinking patterns exhibit remarkable flexibility in adapting to diverse scenarios. GPT-o1, GPT-o3, and DeepSeek-R1 adopt long chain-of-thought models to address complex problems by increasing reasoning depth, which default to a forward reasoning mode. We conducted statistical analysis on the accuracy of different mathematical problem datasets on models of different scales, and found five reasons for errors: Insufficient solution-space coverage, Computational mistakes, Unverified assumptions, Ignoring constraint conditions, Maximum response length limitation. To address the above issues, we proposed a backward reasoning pattern construction method aimed at enhancing the model's reverse thinking ability and dynamic adaptability. First, we constructed an easy-hard two-stage Math dataset for training large models and gradually improving their inference ability at different difficulty levels. The dataset contains forward reasoning paths as well as backward reasoning paths. And a two-stage supervised fine-tuning process is applied to progressively train the model's backward reasoning capability. Furthermore, a fine-grained reward mechanism is developed, employing smoothed reward signals to strengthen the model's ability to autonomously select thinking modes during the reasoning process, thereby avoiding reward hacking. A linear-decay balanced sampling strategy is designed to maintain a balance between forward and backward reasoning path samples during training, enabling the model to converge quickly and stably. Experimental results show that our method significantly improves reasoning efficiency and accuracy in tasks such as mathematical proofs, offering a flexible and efficient reasoning paradigm for solving complex problems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a backward reasoning framework for large language models to complement traditional forward chain-of-thought, using a specially designed math dataset, two-stage supervised training, a fine-grained reward scheme, and a balanced sampling strategy to improve reasoning accuracy and efficiency on complex mathematical tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing long chain-of-thought LLMs like GPT-o1, GPT-o3, and DeepSeek-R1 mainly rely on forward reasoning, which can struggle with complex problems due to limited solution-space exploration, calculation errors, unchecked assumptions, neglected constraints, and response-length limits. Human reasoning, in contrast, flexibly combines forward and backward thinking (e.g., working backward from a goal). The paper is motivated by the desire to equip models with similar reverse-thinking abilities and dynamic adaptability to address the identified error modes and improve performance on challenging mathematical reasoning tasks.
AI.method:
1) Error analysis: Perform a statistical study of model accuracy on multiple math datasets and model scales, identifying five key error sources.
2) Data construction: Build an easy–hard two-stage math dataset that contains both forward and backward reasoning paths, so models can learn how to reason from premises to conclusions and from goals back to given conditions.
3) Two-stage supervised fine-tuning: First train on easier data to establish basic backward reasoning, then on harder data to progressively enhance advanced backward inference.
4) Fine-grained reward mechanism: Design smoothed, fine-grained reward signals to guide the model in autonomously choosing between forward and backward reasoning modes during the reasoning process, while mitigating reward hacking.
5) Linear-decay balanced sampling: Introduce a sampling strategy that maintains a dynamically balanced proportion of forward vs. backward reasoning examples, using a linear decay schedule to ensure stable and fast convergence while preserving diversity of reasoning patterns.
AI.result: Experiments on mathematical tasks, particularly mathematical proofs, show that the proposed backward reasoning pattern and training framework significantly improve both reasoning accuracy and efficiency compared with baselines that rely primarily on forward chain-of-thought reasoning. The model demonstrates better handling of complex problems that previously suffered from insufficient solution coverage, computational slips, unverified assumptions, ignored constraints, or length limitations.
AI.conclusion: Augmenting LLMs with an explicit backward reasoning pattern, supported by a dedicated easy–hard math dataset, staged supervised training, fine-grained reward design, and balanced sampling between forward and backward paths, yields substantial gains in mathematical reasoning. The approach endows models with more flexible and human-like problem-solving capabilities, suggesting a promising and efficient paradigm for tackling complex reasoning tasks beyond pure forward chain-of-thought.

title: Chronologic: Measuring Language Models' Ability to Represent the Past
summary: Language models are appealing tools for research on the past. But to trust the evidence a model provides, researchers need to know whether its responses fit the period represented. Validation is challenging, because this is not a task living people ordinarily perform, and because many questions have multiple correct answers. We use historical texts to develop a benchmark for a model's representation of English-language contexts 1831-1930, relying on pairwise comparisons to multiple ground truths and strong distractors to score the hardest questions in an appropriately graduated way. We find that generative tasks are harder than discriminative ones; in fact, reasoning models can typically discern the weakness of their own generated answers. While models pretrained exclusively on historical text lead the pack when evaluated by answer likelihood, they cannot compete with commercial models in free generation. None of the models we tested represent historical contexts in a fully persuasive way yet, but progress toward that goal is evident.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how well language models represent 19th–early 20th century English contexts, finding that current models are improving but still fall short of fully convincing historical understanding.
AI.motivation: Researchers want to use language models to study historical periods, but they must know whether model outputs actually reflect the language and context of the target era. Standard validation is hard because humans do not regularly judge period-appropriateness, and many historically plausible answers can coexist. The paper aims to create a rigorous, realistically challenging way to test whether models truly capture historical English from 1831–1930.
AI.method: The authors build a benchmark based on authentic historical texts (1831–1930) and construct questions that compare model responses to multiple ground-truth options and strong distractors. They rely on pairwise comparisons to score models, especially on the most difficult items, and separately evaluate generative tasks (free text generation) and discriminative tasks (choosing among options). They also compare models pretrained solely on historical text with contemporary commercial models, and examine whether reasoning-focused models can judge the quality of their own generated answers.
AI.result: Generative tasks prove more difficult for models than discriminative ones. Reasoning-oriented models are often able to recognize flaws in their own generated responses when asked to evaluate them. Models trained only on historical text perform best when evaluation is based on answer likelihood (i.e., probability of correct answer), but they still lag behind major commercial models on open-ended generation quality. Across the board, no tested model yet provides fully convincing representations of historical contexts.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark reveals clear gaps in current language models’ ability to faithfully represent 1831–1930 English-language contexts, especially in free generation. Nevertheless, the observed performance, particularly from specialized historical models and advanced commercial systems, shows tangible progress. The work provides a more nuanced and graduated evaluation framework that can guide future model development toward more reliable use in historical research.

title: Convex AI Compositionality and the Governance of AI System Populations
summary: AI governance increasingly requires providers and public authorities to reason about multiple AI instantiations, alternative versions, and deployment configurations of multiple AI systems. Yet current regulation remains predominantly single-system-centric, acknowledging such multiplicity only sparsely without treating collections of related AI systems as governance objects. This creates an AI population governance problem: determining which instantiations can be meaningfully considered together and how their changing configurations can be represented and monitored. The first requirement has recently been addressed through trustworthiness-based accounts of AI identity. We address the second by introducing convex AI compositionality: a formal representation of the configurations generated by finite AI system populations that uses convex spaces. The core idea is that convex compositions of the operational states that a population of AI system instantiations may occupy over time are compatible with lifecycle reachability across the population and can preserve the formal identity relations between these systems. Well-known statistical and geometric constructions, such as weighted state distributions and convex hulls, become AI governance tools for distinguishing operational states, population weights, heterogeneity, and AI configuration change across different governance modes while remaining compatible, under stated conditions, with lifecycle reachability and AI identity. We illustrate our AI population governance framework through distributed healthcare deployments and controlled deployment of recruitment AI variants.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a formal framework, based on convex spaces, to represent and govern populations of related AI systems and their configurations over time, instead of regulating each system in isolation.
AI.motivation: Existing AI governance and regulation largely focus on single AI systems, but real-world governance must handle multiple instantiations, versions, and configurations of AI systems deployed in various contexts. This leads to an “AI population governance” problem: how to decide which AI instantiations belong together as a population and how to represent, track, and compare their changing configurations in a principled way. Prior work has mainly addressed AI identity (when different systems count as the same for trustworthiness), but not the dynamic configuration space of many systems.
AI.method: The paper introduces “convex AI compositionality,” a mathematical framework that models the set of possible configurations of a finite population of AI system instantiations as a convex space. It uses tools from convex geometry and statistics—such as weighted distributions over operational states and convex hulls—to represent mixtures and aggregations of states across a population. The framework is constructed so that these convex combinations remain compatible with lifecycle reachability (how systems can evolve over time) and with formal identity relations between systems drawn from existing trustworthiness-based accounts.
AI.result: The authors show that representing AI populations in convex spaces allows regulators and providers to distinguish and reason about operational states, population weights (how many systems in which state), heterogeneity, and configuration changes under different governance modes (e.g., centralized vs distributed deployments). They demonstrate that standard geometric/statistical constructs can serve as governance tools that preserve key properties like lifecycle reachability and identity under specified conditions. Case illustrations are given for distributed healthcare AI deployments and controlled experimentation with recruitment AI variants.
AI.conclusion: Convex AI compositionality provides a principled, mathematically grounded way to model and govern populations of related AI systems, rather than treating each AI system in isolation. By leveraging convex geometry and statistical representations, regulators and organizations can monitor changing configurations, compare governance regimes, and maintain consistency with lifecycle dynamics and formal identity notions. This framework aims to support more scalable and realistic AI governance, particularly in complex multi-system deployments such as healthcare and recruitment.

title: Low resource cross-modal alignment using HGNN to enhance speech representation
summary: Speech-text space alignment is a multimodal representation learning method consisting to map different speech and text into a shared representation space, leading to enrichment of the representation of each modality. Proposed architectures, such as SAMU-XLSR, typically follow a student/teacher framework, with the goal of fine-tuning an audio encoder to produce representations that closely match those of the text. In this way a speech representation is semantically enriched. However, such systems generally require large amounts of training data and considerable computational resource, making them difficult to apply to low resources languages under frugal constraints. The present work proposes a data-efficient space alignment method based on Heterogeneous Graph Neural Networks and link prediction. The core idea is to leverage message passing to explicitly transfer information from the text modality to the speech modality, thereby reducing the need for large training datasets and intrinsically enriching the acoustic representations, all in a more interpretable manner. Although thoroughly explored for high-resource languages, word-level tasks in speech remain relevant for certain low-resource languages. Therefore, we conducted experiments on speech-text alignment at the word level using the TIMIT (English) dataset and Yemba (a Cameroonian language). Our approach yields results comparable to those of SAMU-XLSR, a state-of-the-art method, and even surpasses it for the Yemba language in the task of word retrieval, while using far fewer resources, demonstrating its power, frugality, and efficiency.

AI.tldr: They propose a data-efficient method to align speech and text into a shared space using heterogeneous graph neural networks and link prediction, achieving SAMU-XLSR-level performance with far fewer resources, especially strong on a low-resource language.
AI.motivation: Existing speech-text alignment approaches like SAMU-XLSR rely on large datasets and heavy computation, which is impractical for low-resource languages and frugal settings. The authors want a method that can semantically enrich speech representations while being data- and resource-efficient and more interpretable.
AI.method: They model speech and text as a heterogeneous graph and use a heterogeneous Graph Neural Network with message passing and a link prediction objective. Information is explicitly propagated from text nodes to speech nodes, aligning them in a shared semantic space and intrinsically enriching acoustic representations while requiring less data than student-teacher architectures.
AI.result: On word-level speech-text alignment tasks using TIMIT (English) and Yemba, their method performs comparably to SAMU-XLSR overall and surpasses it on Yemba for word retrieval, despite using significantly fewer training resources.
AI.conclusion: Heterogeneous GNN-based speech-text space alignment with link prediction can achieve state-of-the-art or better performance for word-level tasks while being more data-efficient and computationally frugal, making it particularly suitable for low-resource languages and providing a more interpretable alignment mechanism.

title: GRUET: Quantifying Uncertainty of Agentic Reasoning-and-Acting Processes
summary: Agents have attracted considerably increasing attention due to the power of executing both Reasoning and Acting (ReAct) in open and dynamic environments. The ReAct process typically exhibits a multi-turn trajectory in which one drives Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate both reasoning chains and task-specific actions in an interleaved manner. However, agents often suffer from significant uncertainty, where identical tasks yield divergent trajectories; trajectories with higher uncertainty often produce incomprehensible behaviors, severely undermining agent credibility. This work conjectures that such trajectory-level uncertainty frequently stems from cumulative turn-level reasoning uncertainty induced by LLMs; the latter often exhibits a collection of branches of divergent reasoning chains and their resulting actions. Built upon this, we present the Graph-based Reasoning UncErtainty in Trajectories (GRUET) method for the uncertainty quantification of ReAct, comprising turn-level reasoning uncertainty quantification and trajectory-level uncertainty aggregation; the former precisely quantifies reasoning uncertainty via modeling the reasoning space spanned by potential reasoning branches as a graph and then approximating the reasoning space complexity with graph complexity, while the latter employs simple aggregation strategies for quantifying the overall trajectory credibility. Empirical evaluations across nine LLMs and five benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our proposed GRUET in terms of selective generation performance, measured by AUROC, AUPRC, and AUARC.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes GRUET, a graph-based method to quantify and aggregate reasoning uncertainty in multi-turn ReAct trajectories of LLM-based agents, improving reliability via better selective generation.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents that use ReAct exhibit high trajectory-level uncertainty: identical tasks can lead to very different reasoning-action paths, and high-uncertainty trajectories often result in bizarre or unreliable behaviors, harming trust and usability. Existing work lacks a precise way to quantify the uncertainty in the internal reasoning process and to connect it to overall trajectory credibility. The authors aim to understand and measure how turn-level reasoning uncertainty accumulates over multiple steps and to use that measurement to decide which trajectories or outputs are trustworthy.
AI.method: They introduce GRUET (Graph-based Reasoning UncErtainty in Trajectories), which treats the ReAct process as a sequence of reasoning steps where each step can branch into multiple possible reasoning chains and actions. For each turn, they model the space of potential reasoning branches as a graph, with nodes and edges representing alternative reasoning paths. They then define graph-complexity-based metrics to approximate how uncertain the reasoning is at that turn (e.g., via the richness and divergence of branches). To get a trajectory-level uncertainty score, they aggregate these per-turn uncertainty measures using simple aggregation strategies, producing a scalar that reflects the credibility of the whole ReAct trajectory. They test GRUET on multiple LLMs and benchmarks within a selective generation setup, where the system may abstain or prioritize low-uncertainty trajectories.
AI.result: Across nine different LLMs and five benchmarks, GRUET effectively distinguishes reliable from unreliable ReAct trajectories. In selective generation evaluations, it achieves strong performance as measured by AUROC, AUPRC, and AUARC, indicating that its uncertainty scores are well correlated with actual correctness or quality of trajectories. This shows that graph-based modeling of reasoning branches captures meaningful information about uncertainty in agent behavior.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that trajectory-level uncertainty in ReAct agents can be systematically explained by accumulated turn-level reasoning uncertainty, which can be captured by modeling the reasoning space as a graph. GRUET offers a practical, model-agnostic way to quantify this uncertainty and to estimate trajectory credibility, improving selective generation performance. This provides a foundation for building more trustworthy LLM agents whose behaviors can be assessed and filtered based on principled uncertainty estimates.

title: Enhancing speech representation learning with cross-modal knowledge transfer with HGNN under low resource settings: the case study of Yemba
summary: Acoustic representation learning is crucial for speech processing, yet low-resource languages (LRLs) face severe data scarcity, limiting the effectiveness of traditional and self-supervised methods. As a promising alternative, in this work, we propose to enhance acoustic representation trough a cross-modal transfer knowledge approach, based on heterogeneous graph neural networks (HGNNs), where acoustic and linguistic entities are modeled as distinct node types within a unified graph. Through message-passing mechanisms, linguistic nodes explicitly transfer knowledge to acoustic nodes, enabling structured and interpretable cross-modal information flow. To highlight this knowledge transfer and its benefits, we measured standard clustering metrics as an intrinsic evaluation of acoustic representation, and to emphasize applicability, we performed isolated-word recognition tasks using an English benchmark and a Cameroonian language dataset in low resources settings . Results demonstrate that acoustic representations consistently benefit from linguistic knowledge propagated through the graph. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of explicit cross-modal knowledge transfer for acoustic representation learning using HGNNs, highlighting a promising direction for speech representation in low-resource settings.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a heterogeneous graph neural network approach to transfer linguistic knowledge to acoustic nodes, improving acoustic representations for low-resource languages and demonstrating gains in clustering quality and word recognition tasks.
AI.motivation: Low-resource languages lack sufficient labeled and even unlabeled speech data, which undermines the performance of traditional and self-supervised acoustic representation learning methods. The authors are motivated to find a way to exploit richer linguistic information to enhance acoustic representations, especially in low-resource settings, in a structured and interpretable way.
AI.method: They build a heterogeneous graph neural network (HGNN) where acoustic entities (e.g., segments, words, or frames) and linguistic entities (e.g., phonemes, textual tokens, or lexical units) are modeled as different node types in a single graph. Using message passing, linguistic nodes explicitly pass information to acoustic nodes, realizing cross-modal knowledge transfer. They then evaluate the learned acoustic representations intrinsically through clustering metrics and extrinsically via isolated-word recognition tasks on an English benchmark and a low-resource Cameroonian language dataset.
AI.result: The HGNN-based cross-modal transfer method consistently improves the quality of acoustic representations, as shown by better clustering metrics. It also yields better performance on isolated-word recognition tasks in both English and a Cameroonian low-resource language compared to baselines without such linguistic knowledge transfer.
AI.conclusion: Explicit cross-modal knowledge transfer from linguistic to acoustic nodes via HGNNs is effective for improving acoustic representation learning, particularly in low-resource language scenarios. This appears to be the first use of HGNNs for such explicit cross-modal transfer in acoustic representation learning, and it points to a promising research direction for speech technology in low-resource settings.

title: MedRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement for Medical Agents via Clinically Aligned Self-Evolution
summary: Medical agents increasingly combine general reasoning models with specialized clinical tools, yet their capabilities remain largely fixed by what clinicians and engineers design before deployment. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a different paradigm in which agents learn from their own failures and autonomously expand their capabilities, but directly applying RSI to medicine introduces fundamental safety challenges. We introduce MedRSI, the first recursive self-improvement framework for medicine, which continuously transforms diagnostic failures into new clinical capabilities through tool composition and task-specific model training. Inspired by clinical practice, MedRSI introduces two mechanisms for clinically aligned self-evolution. Clinical-cost-aware failure prioritization directs improvement toward errors according to their potential clinical consequences rather than frequency alone. Fast discovery with slow registration separates rapid capability invention from conservative adoption, allowing new tools to enter the persistent agent only after demonstrating sustained benefit across subsequent patient cohorts. Across public glaucoma and heart disease benchmarks and two private clinical tasks, MedRSI progressively develops segmentation, measurement, prediction, multimodal reasoning, and generative capabilities, surpasses manually engineered medical agents, and autonomously discovers solutions to clinical problems not anticipated by its original designers. Our results show that medical agents need not remain constrained by capabilities specified before deployment: with clinically grounded mechanisms governing what to improve and what to retain, they can continuously construct, validate, and accumulate new capabilities from diagnostic experience. Code is available at https://github.com/ImprintLab/MedRSI.

AI.tldr: MedRSI is a framework that lets medical AI agents recursively improve themselves from their own diagnostic failures while enforcing clinically grounded safety controls.
AI.motivation: Current medical AI agents combine general models with fixed, predesigned tools. Once deployed, their capabilities are largely static and can only be extended through manual engineering. Recursive self-improvement promises agents that learn new capabilities autonomously from experience, but in medicine this raises serious safety concerns: naive RSI might prioritize frequent but clinically minor errors, or adopt unvetted tools that harm patients. The paper is motivated by the need for a principled way to let medical agents expand their capabilities over time while remaining aligned with clinical priorities and safety standards.
AI.method: The authors propose MedRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework specifically tailored for medicine. The system monitors diagnostic failures and turns them into opportunities for capability expansion through two key mechanisms: (1) clinical-cost-aware failure prioritization, which ranks errors by their potential clinical impact rather than by frequency alone; and (2) a fast-discovery / slow-registration process, where new tools and behaviors are rapidly invented and tested but only integrated into the agent’s persistent toolkit after they show consistent benefit on subsequent patient cohorts. MedRSI composes new tools and trains task-specific models to address identified failure modes, gradually enriching the agent’s diagnostic and reasoning capabilities.
AI.result: On public glaucoma and heart disease benchmarks and two proprietary clinical tasks, MedRSI progressively acquires new skills such as image segmentation, quantitative measurement, prediction, multimodal reasoning, and generative functions. It outperforms manually engineered medical agents and is able to autonomously discover effective solutions to clinical problems that its original designers did not anticipate. This demonstrates that the framework can safely and productively drive capability growth in real medical settings.
AI.conclusion: MedRSI shows that medical AI agents do not have to remain limited to static, pre-specified capabilities. With clinically grounded mechanisms for (a) deciding which failures to address and (b) cautiously deciding which new tools to retain, agents can recursively construct, validate, and accumulate new diagnostic capabilities from real-world experience. This offers a path toward continuously improving medical AI systems that remain aligned with clinical priorities and safety requirements.

title: Euston: Training Away Mathematical Sycophancy Without Losing the Mathematics
summary: Reasoning language models are trained to produce solutions, not to refuse them, and this bias persists when the problem they are handed is false. Asked to prove a corrupted theorem, a strong model will typically comply and produce a confident derivation of something untrue. We present Euston, an 8B mathematical claim-verification model trained to resist exactly this. Training data were generated with GraphSynth, a probabilistic factor-graph generator that couples attribute-level diversity to decode-time structural masking and span-synchronized verification, yielding 3{,}026 matched true/corrupted statement pairs (6,052 statements) drawn from arXiv papers spanning 2010--2025. We fine-tuned DeepSeek-R1-8B with GRPO under a rule-based, zero-API reward for 189 steps on four H100 GPUs. On a balanced 200-true/200-false held-out split, balanced accuracy rises from 29.50% to 63.75% and the discrimination gap---the difference between the rate of calling false statements false and the rate of calling true statements false moves from -0.5% (z=-0.1) to +27.5% (z=+6.0). Critically, the gain is not purchased with general mathematical ability: AIME 2026 accuracy under official semantics is 65.00% against a 69.17% base, a difference of -4.17% that is not statistically significant, whereas an earlier run of the same recipe on a smaller GraphSynth corpus collapsed to 40.00%. Median response length also falls from 19,217 to 18,296 tokens and the truncation rate from 25.8% to 8.3%, so the improvement does not come from thinking longer. We report the result together with the confounds that bound its interpretation, principally the all-false composition of the official evaluation sets and the low precision implied at realistic error prevalence.

AI.tldr: They fine-tune an 8B reasoning LLM to say “this theorem is wrong” instead of fabricating proofs, using a synthetic corpus of matched true/false math statements, and show it can detect false claims much better without noticeably hurting math ability.
AI.motivation: Current reasoning LLMs are optimized to produce solutions and tend to confidently “prove” false or corrupted mathematical statements instead of rejecting them. This makes them unreliable for tasks where verifying the truth of a claim is crucial. The authors want a model that can distinguish true from false mathematical claims and is explicitly trained to resist going along with incorrect premises, while preserving general problem‑solving performance.
AI.method: They build GraphSynth, a probabilistic factor‑graph based generator that samples diverse mathematical statements from arXiv math papers (2010–2025) and systematically creates paired true and corrupted versions (3,026 pairs). At decode time, they use structural masking and span‑synchronized verification to ensure both variants share structure but differ in truth. They then fine‑tune DeepSeek‑R1‑8B with GRPO (a reinforcement learning method) using a rule‑based, API‑free reward signal that incentivizes correct verdicts on these claims, training for 189 steps on four H100 GPUs. The resulting model, Euston, is evaluated on a balanced held‑out set and on AIME 2026 under official scoring.
AI.result: On a 200-true / 200-false held‑out verification set, balanced accuracy improves from 29.50% to 63.75%. The discrimination gap (true negative rate minus false negative rate) shifts from roughly zero (−0.5%, z=−0.1) to strongly positive (+27.5%, z=+6.0), indicating much better rejection of false statements. General mathematical capability, as measured on AIME 2026, declines only slightly from 69.17% to 65.00%, a difference not statistically significant, whereas an earlier run on a smaller GraphSynth dataset caused severe performance collapse to 40.00%. Response length decreases modestly (median from 19,217 to 18,296 tokens) and truncation rate drops from 25.8% to 8.3%, showing the gains are not due to longer reasoning. They also note important confounds such as the all‑false composition of some official benchmarks and the low precision the model would achieve when errors are rare in deployment.
AI.conclusion: It is possible to substantially increase a reasoning LLM’s ability to detect and reject false mathematical statements, via targeted RL fine‑tuning on carefully constructed true/false statement pairs, without significantly damaging its general problem‑solving skills or requiring longer chains of thought. However, evaluation nuances (e.g., benchmarks with only false items and realistic base error rates) limit how strongly the results can be generalized, and the authors emphasize these confounds when interpreting Euston’s performance.

title: Extracting Arguments, Not Just Classifying Them: Instruction-Tuned LLMs for Generative Component Detection
summary: Argumentative component detection (ACD) is a core subtask of Argument(ation) Mining (AM) and one of its most challenging aspects, as it requires jointly delimiting argumentative spans and classifying them into components such as claims and premises. While research on this subtask remains relatively limited compared to other AM tasks, most existing approaches formulate it as a simplified sequence labeling problem, component classification, or a pipeline of component segmentation followed by classification. In this paper, we propose ITFACD, a novel approach based on instruction-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) using compact instruction-based prompts, and reframe ACD as a language generation task, enabling arguments to be identified directly from plain text without relying on pre-segmented components. Experiments on standard benchmarks show that our approach achieves higher performance compared to state-of-the-art systems. To the best of our knowledge, this is one of the first attempts to fully model ACD as a generative task, highlighting the potential of instruction tuning for complex AM problems. Our code and the datasets used are openly available in the following GitHub repository.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ITFACD, an instruction-tuned LLM approach that treats argumentative component detection as a text generation task, achieving state-of-the-art results on benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Argumentative component detection is a key but difficult subtask in argument mining because it must both segment argument spans and label them (e.g., claims, premises). Existing work is limited and usually simplifies the problem via sequence labeling or pipeline setups that depend on pre-segmented components. There is a need for more flexible, powerful methods that can work directly from raw text and better capture the complexity of ACD.
AI.method: The authors propose ITFACD, which leverages instruction-tuned large language models with compact instruction prompts. Instead of treating ACD as sequence labeling or a pipeline of segmentation plus classification, they reframe it as a generative task where the LLM directly outputs detected argumentative components and their types from plain input text, without requiring prior segmentation.
AI.result: On standard ACD benchmarks, ITFACD outperforms state-of-the-art systems, demonstrating improved performance over prior sequence-labeling and pipeline-based approaches for argumentative component detection.
AI.conclusion: Modeling ACD as a generative task via instruction-tuned LLMs is effective and yields superior performance to existing methods. The work suggests that instruction tuning is a promising direction for tackling complex argument mining tasks and provides open-source code and data for further research.

title: ChemCLIR-Bench: Benchmarking Cross-Lingual Information Retrieval in Multilingual Chemical Patents
comment: Accepted to the EMNLP 2026 Industry Track. 22 pages including references and appendices; 7 pages of main text
summary:
Cross-lingual information retrieval (CLIR) is increasingly important in multi-national industries, where critical technical evidence may exist in a different language than the query. However, existing benchmarks do not adequately capture domain-specific cross-lingual retrieval or the retrieval-depth and recoverability failures that aggregate recall hides.
  In this work, we benchmark CLIR in the chemical domain, with a focus on patent data. We construct a multilingual dataset from Google Patents and the European Patent Office (EPO) data, spanning five languages (covering major Eastern and Western languages) and reflecting the diversity and complexity of real-world industrial documentation.
  Using this dataset, we systematically evaluate eight state-of-the-art embedding models for cross-lingual retrieval. Our results show a substantial performance gap between monolingual and cross-lingual settings: for the best-performing model, Recall@10 drops from 0.72 to 0.53 in cross-lingual setting. Retrieval depth also degrades significantly, with relevant documents ranked lower across languages in cross-lingual scenarios. Furthermore, some multilingual embedding models that perform strongly in monolingual settings exhibit sharp declines when queries and documents are in different languages, providing practical insights for model selection in cross-lingual use cases.
  These findings highlight critical limitations of current approaches and emphasize the need for more robust cross-lingual retrieval methods in domain-specific settings. Our benchmark provides actionable insights for model selection and establishes a controlled diagnostic evaluation framework for CLIR over industrial technical text. Data and code are publicly available at https://github.com/MohammadKhodadad/Multi-Lingual-QAC.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a multilingual patent benchmark in the chemical domain and shows that current multilingual embedding models suffer large performance drops in cross-lingual information retrieval compared to monolingual retrieval, especially in retrieval depth and ranking quality.
AI.motivation: Cross-lingual information retrieval is crucial in multinational industrial contexts (e.g., patents) where key technical documents are in different languages than the user’s query. Existing benchmarks focus on generic domains and mainly on aggregate recall metrics, which hide important failures in domain-specific settings, such as poor retrieval depth and limited recoverability of relevant documents. There is a need for realistic, domain-specific CLIR benchmarks and for understanding how well state-of-the-art multilingual embeddings actually work in such settings.
AI.method: The authors construct a multilingual chemical-domain patent dataset from Google Patents and European Patent Office data, covering five major Eastern and Western languages.
