They also perform mechanistic analysis of representational drift inside the models to link changes in internal representations to changes in reasoning ability and malicious semantic trajectory tracking.
AI.result: They find that efficiency methods appear to lower jailbreak success rates, but mainly because the model’s reasoning degrades, leading to attempted but unsuccessful malicious responses rather than truly aligned refusals. Mechanistic analysis shows a tight coupling between loss of reasoning capability and the model’s inability to follow and maintain malicious semantic trajectories in its internal representations. Among techniques, a combined strategy of quantization plus pruning yields the best trade-off between computational efficiency and robustness to jailbreaks.
AI.conclusion: Apparent robustness gains from efficiency methods like quantization and pruning often reflect capability-induced failure, not true safety alignment. Representational drift due to these methods weakens reasoning and disrupts malicious semantic trajectories, superficially lowering jailbreak success. Nonetheless, quantization combined with pruning emerges as a promising compromise between efficiency and robustness. The work emphasizes the need to distinguish genuine alignment from degraded capability when assessing the safety of LRMs and offers empirical guidance for their deployment.

title: Distill What You Trust: Reliability-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
summary: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation allows a student to learn from complementary specialists on its own trajectories. Domain-routed approaches, however, select one teacher per example and keep it fixed throughout the response. This design both depends on labels that mixed training corpora often lack and cannot adapt teacher selection when the expertise required changes within a trajectory. We propose \textbf{TrustMOPD}, which replaces example-level teacher selection with label-free, token-level supervision allocation. At each student-generated prefix, TrustMOPD uses each specialist's RL-induced displacement from a shared pre-RL reference as a proxy for local reliability, calibrates these scores across teachers, and constructs a weighted distillation target. Across mathematics, code, and instruction following, TrustMOPD outperforms the strongest label-free baseline, increasing the recovery ratio from $54.4\%$ to $91.5\%$ on \textsc{SingleCap} and from $54.5\%$ to $98.0\%$ on \textsc{MultiCap}, while approaching label-based MOPD on \textsc{SingleCap}. Randomizing token-level weights independently of the student-generated prefix performs no better than uniform weighting, supporting the importance of conditioning supervision on the evolving generation context.

AI.tldr: TrustMOPD is a token-level, label-free multi-teacher distillation method that dynamically weights specialist teachers based on their RL-induced deviations from a shared base model, yielding much higher expert recovery than existing label-free methods.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-teacher on-policy distillation methods route each example to a single teacher, requiring domain labels and assuming that the same expert is best for the whole trajectory. Mixed training corpora often lack reliable labels, and different parts of a single generated response may require different expertise. A more flexible, label-free method is needed that can adaptively select and combine teachers at a finer granularity than example-level routing.
AI.method: TrustMOPD introduces token-level teacher weighting without using domain labels. For each partial student-generated sequence (prefix), it compares each specialist teacher to a shared pre-RL reference model and measures the RL-induced displacement as a proxy for that teacher’s local reliability. These reliability scores are calibrated across teachers and converted into token-level weights, which define a weighted distillation target distribution over next tokens. The student is trained on its own on-policy trajectories using this dynamically mixed target rather than a single routed teacher.
AI.result: On benchmarks spanning mathematics, code, and instruction following, TrustMOPD significantly outperforms the strongest existing label-free multi-teacher baseline. It raises expert recovery ratio from 54.4% to 91.5% on the SingleCap setting and from 54.5% to 98.0% on MultiCap, and its performance on SingleCap approaches that of label-based multi-teacher on-policy distillation. An ablation where token-level weights are randomized independently of the prefix performs similarly to uniform weighting, indicating that the gains come from conditioning supervision on the actual evolving generation context.
AI.conclusion: Token-level, label-free supervision allocation enables more effective use of multiple specialist teachers than coarse, example-level domain routing. By leveraging RL-induced displacement from a shared reference as a trust signal, TrustMOPD can dynamically mix teachers along a trajectory, achieving near label-based performance while avoiding reliance on domain annotations. The importance of context-conditioned weighting is validated by ablations, suggesting that future distillation systems should focus on fine-grained, adaptive expertise combination rather than static routing.

title: Financial Language Models as Applied Artificial Intelligence Systems for News-Based Trading under Market Frictions
comment: 47 pages. Revise and resubmit at Engineering Applications of Artificial Intelligence
summary: Financial language models can transform unstructured firm-specific news into structured decision signals, but financial AI research lacks an integrated deployment framework for evaluating whether those signals remain useful in financial decision systems. Computer science research has developed strong methods for time-series forecasting, text classification, multimodal stock prediction, graph-based market modeling, and machine-learning operations, yet these streams do not provide a domain-specific protocol that jointly tests financial language-model outputs under event-time observability, probability calibration, execution timing, transaction costs, liquidity constraints, capacity limits, operational diagnostics, and statistical inference. We introduce MFAST, a Market-Friction-Aware Sentiment-to-Trading framework that converts timestamped financial text into auditable, reproducible, and market-feasible trading decisions. The application is news-based trading, where firm-specific text must be linked to securities before portfolio decisions can be evaluated. The framework links Refinitiv News Analytics to Center for Research in Security Prices (CRSP) equity data, restricts the primary out-of-sample evaluation to post-release news outside disclosed foundation-model data-freshness periods, and adds a public replication arm using open financial text and public price data. Results show that decoder-only language models outperform encoder baselines and dictionary sentiment in classification, calibration, return prediction, and net portfolio performance, while operational diagnostics reveal trade-offs among accuracy, latency, memory, throughput, and inference cost. The paper shows that credible evaluation of financial language models requires an end-to-end engineering approach combining language understanding, temporal discipline, market-friction-aware deployment, and reproducible validation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MFAST, a framework that converts timestamped financial news into realistic, auditable trading strategies and shows that decoder-only language models beat traditional methods in both prediction and trading performance.
AI.motivation: Although financial language models can extract signals from textual news, there is no unified, domain-specific framework to evaluate whether these signals remain useful when deployed in real trading environments with market frictions and operational constraints. Existing AI work focuses on isolated tasks (e.g., forecasting, text classification) and ignores key financial realities like event-time information flow, execution costs, liquidity, and capacity.
AI.method: The authors design MFAST (Market-Friction-Aware Sentiment-to-Trading), an end-to-end deployment and evaluation framework that: (1) transforms firm-specific, timestamped news into sentiment-based predictive signals; (2) links these signals to tradable securities using Refinitiv News Analytics and CRSP equity data; (3) enforces strict temporal discipline and excludes news within the pretraining data freshness windows of foundation models to preserve out-of-sample validity; (4) incorporates realistic trading constraints such as execution timing, transaction costs, liquidity, and capacity; (5) includes a public replication arm using open text and price data; and (6) benchmarks decoder-only language models against encoder-only models and dictionary sentiment on tasks such as classification, calibration, return prediction, and portfolio construction, while logging operational metrics (latency, memory, throughput, cost).
AI.result: Decoder-only language models systematically outperform encoder-based baselines and dictionary-based sentiment metrics across multiple dimensions: news classification accuracy, probability calibration quality, predictive power for returns, and realized net portfolio performance after market frictions. The framework also surfaces operational trade-offs, documenting how higher predictive performance interacts with latency, memory footprint, computational throughput, and inference costs.
AI.conclusion: Credible assessment of financial language models cannot rely on isolated prediction metrics; it requires an end-to-end, market-friction-aware engineering pipeline that respects temporal information flow and supports reproducibility. MFAST demonstrates how to integrate language understanding, realistic trading constraints, and rigorous validation, setting a domain-specific protocol for evaluating and deploying financial LMs in news-based trading applications.

title: STEVE: Stabilizing Textual Gradient-Based Prompt Optimization via Error-Driven Refinement and Regularized Verification
comment: Accepted to Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: AACL-IJCNLP 2026
summary: Textual-gradient methods automate prompt optimization through natural-language feedback, but their iterative updates can be unstable. We identify two sources of this instability: noisy gradients produced from already-correct examples and over-specialization to hard cases that degrades performance on simpler inputs. We introduce STEVE, a stabilization framework with two coupled mechanisms. Error-Driven Refinement generates gradients only from incorrectly handled examples, concentrating updates on informative failures. Regularized Verification treats every update as provisional and accepts it only when improvement on hard cases does not cause unacceptable regression on a preservation set. Across ten reasoning benchmarks, three evaluator/optimizer models, and established prompt-optimization baselines, STEVE reduces degradation and produces more robust prompts. Additional evaluations with gpt-5.4-mini/gpt-5.4 on symbolic reasoning, GSM8K-Platinum, and DS-1000 show that these gains persist with newer models and larger test sets. STEVE therefore provides a practical way to improve the stability and effectiveness of textual-gradient prompt optimization.

AI.tldr: STEVE stabilizes textual-gradient prompt optimization by updating only on incorrect cases and verifying that new prompts don’t harm performance on easier examples.
AI.motivation: Textual-gradient methods iteratively refine prompts via natural-language feedback, but their updates are often unstable: they can overfit to noisy signals from already-correct examples and overspecialize to hard cases, hurting performance on simpler inputs. The authors want a way to make these optimization procedures more reliable and robust across benchmarks and models.
AI.method: They propose STEVE, a stabilization framework with two key components. Error-Driven Refinement generates gradient-like feedback only from examples the model currently gets wrong, focusing learning signal on informative failures rather than all data. Regularized Verification then treats each candidate prompt update as tentative, accepting it only if it improves performance on hard examples without causing unacceptable regressions on a held-out preservation set that captures simpler or already-solved inputs. They evaluate STEVE across ten reasoning benchmarks, three different evaluator/optimizer models, and against existing prompt-optimization baselines.
AI.result: STEVE reduces degradation typically seen in textual-gradient prompt optimization and yields more robust prompts than baseline methods across ten reasoning benchmarks and three evaluator/optimizer models. Additional experiments on symbolic reasoning, GSM8K-Platinum, and DS-1000 with newer models (gpt-5.4-mini/gpt-5.4) and larger test sets show that the stability and performance gains generalize across settings and model generations.
AI.conclusion: By focusing updates on incorrect examples and verifying that new prompts do not harm performance on simpler or already-correct cases, STEVE offers a practical, model-agnostic way to stabilize textual-gradient prompt optimization. It consistently improves robustness and mitigates performance degradation, and its benefits persist with newer language models and more challenging benchmarks.

title: GRACE: Grounded Adversarial Reasoning over Canadian Law
summary: Large language models have shown strong performance across a range of legal tasks, but existing benchmarks rarely evaluate the ability to take and defend a legal position, reason under incomplete information, or synthesize multiple statutory provisions. This gap is particularly pronounced for Canadian law, which remains underrepresented in legal NLP. We introduce GRACE (Grounded Reasoning Adversarial Canadian LEgal examples), a dataset of 1,915 question-reasoning-answer instances grounded in Canadian federal legislation. GRACE covers three reasoning modes: adversarial advocacy, uncertainty, and applied reasoning. We develop a pipeline that partitions raw statutory text, generates scenario-based questions and reasoning, and filters examples through model-free citation verification and LLM-based quality auditing. As a proof of concept, we fine-tune CLeAR-4B (Canadian Legal Adversarial Reasoning), a lightweight model for grounded legal reasoning, and evaluate it against the unmodified Qwen3-4B base model in open- and closed-book settings. CLeAR-4B substantially improves agreement with teacher outputs and statutory citation behavior when the relevant act text is provided, while its grounding degrades sharply when the statute is withheld. These results suggest that GRACE can support the development of lightweight legal models that reason more effectively from supplied statutory text.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces GRACE, a new Canadian statute-grounded legal reasoning dataset, and shows that a small fine-tuned model (CLeAR-4B) can reason more accurately from provided legislation than a base model.
AI.motivation: Existing legal LLM benchmarks seldom test key lawyering skills such as taking/defending positions, reasoning with uncertainty, and synthesizing multiple statutory provisions, and Canadian law in particular is underrepresented in legal NLP resources. There is a need for a benchmark and models focused on grounded reasoning over Canadian federal statutes.
AI.method: The authors construct GRACE, a dataset of 1,915 question–reasoning–answer triplets rooted in Canadian federal legislation. They design a pipeline that: (1) partitions raw statutory text into manageable segments, (2) generates realistic scenario-based questions plus chain-of-thought style reasoning grounded in those statutes, and (3) filters and validates instances using model-free citation checks and LLM-based quality auditing. As a demonstration, they fine-tune a 4B-parameter base model on GRACE to create CLeAR-4B and evaluate it against the original Qwen3-4B model in both open-book (statute text provided) and closed-book (no statute text) settings.
AI.result: CLeAR-4B, the GRACE-tuned model, achieves substantially higher agreement with teacher model answers and exhibits more accurate and appropriate statutory citation behavior than the untuned Qwen3-4B when the relevant legislative text is available at inference time. However, its performance deteriorates markedly when statutes are not supplied, indicating a strong dependence on explicit grounding.
AI.conclusion: GRACE is an effective resource for training and evaluating lightweight legal LLMs on grounded reasoning with Canadian statutes. Fine-tuning on GRACE enables small models to reason more accurately and cite law more reliably when they are given the relevant legal text, supporting the development of practical, statute-grounded legal AI systems.

title: Constrained Decoding Eliminates Structural Failures in Small LLMs but Reveals a Scale-Dependent Semantic Gap
comment: 6 pages, ACL format Code and task suite: https://github.com/CruiseDevice/small-llm-structured-benchmark (tag v1.0)
summary: Small open-source large language models (LLMs) in the 0.6B-4B parameter range are increasingly deployed for structured output generation (JSON, function calling, data extraction), yet little is known about how constrained decoding (CD) interacts with model scale in this regime. We benchmark five models from three families across 14 structured-output tasks under three decoding conditions (native, Outlines, XGrammar). We introduce a two-axis evaluation that separates structural correctness (schema validity) from semantic correctness (content accuracy). We find that CD eliminates all structural failures across all models (schema validity: 78.6-92.9% to 100%), but content accuracy reveals a persistent semantic gap that is scale-dependent: type coercion failures are fully CD-rescuable, while instruction-semantic failures (e.g., multi-step function calling) remain CD-resistant. Schema conformance is necessary but not sufficient for semantic correctness; CD's reach ends exactly where schema conformance ends.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how constrained decoding affects small open-source LLMs’ ability to produce structured outputs, showing it fixes schema errors but not deeper semantic mistakes.
AI.motivation: Although small open-source LLMs are widely used for tasks like JSON generation and function calling, it is unclear how constrained decoding interacts with model size in the 0.6B–4B parameter range and what kinds of errors it can and cannot fix.
AI.method: The authors benchmark five models from three model families on 14 structured-output tasks under three decoding regimes (native decoding, Outlines, and XGrammar), and evaluate performance along two axes: structural correctness (schema validity) and semantic correctness (content accuracy).
AI.result: Constrained decoding raises schema validity from roughly 79–93% to 100% across all models, fully eliminating structural failures. However, many semantic errors persist, and these are dependent on model scale: type coercion errors can be resolved by constrained decoding, while instruction-semantic errors, such as those in multi-step function calling, largely cannot.
AI.conclusion: Constrained decoding guarantees schema-conformant outputs but cannot ensure semantic correctness; its benefits stop where schema enforcement stops, meaning that while structure can be fully controlled, deeper understanding and instruction following still depend on the model’s inherent capabilities and scale.

title: FLARE: A Full-Lifecycle Dense Supervision Paradigm for Long-Horizon Coding Agents via Generative Reward Model
summary: While test-time scaling enhances Large Language Model (LLM) agents in long-horizon software engineering (SWE), sparse binary rewards (Pass/Fail) create a severe credit assignment crisis and waste failed exploratory trajectories. Current trajectory optimization and scaling methods are costly and structurally limited, relying on heuristic state reuse without causal diagnosis or delayed scalar scoring without actionable online guidance. We propose FLARE (Full-Lifecycle Alignment and Reward Engine), a novel dense supervision paradigm driven by a lightweight Generative Reward Model (GRM). First, RADAR, an offline causal-aware diagnostic framework, extracts high-fidelity, hindsight-free supervision through causal-chain backtracking to distill a GRM providing real-time, step-level risk feedback. Second, FLARE uses this GRM to continuously optimize the agent across its entire lifecycle. During inference, FLARE acts as an Active Scaffold, autonomously intercepting high-risk generation steps for localized breakpoint re-execution, drastically reducing compute overhead. During post-training, the GRM's structured signals serve as process-supervised reranking scores for Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and step-level dense rewards for Reinforcement Learning (RL), mitigating policy collapse in sparse environments. Extensive evaluations show that FLARE establishes a new Pareto frontier across the agent lifecycle: FLARE (N=1) outperforms Global Rollout (N=5) with a 5x reduction in token consumption. Extending FLARE to training overcomes the sparse reward problem in long-horizon interactive tasks, delivering relative performance gains of 19.13% in SFT through process-aware data curation and a consistent 9.19% improvement in RL.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces FLARE, a framework that turns sparse pass/fail rewards in long-horizon software engineering tasks into dense, step-level feedback using a generative reward model, improving both inference-time efficiency and training-time performance of LLM agents.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agents for software engineering rely on test-time scaling and pass/fail signals, which leads to poor credit assignment, waste of failed trajectories, high compute costs, and limited guidance during generation. Current solutions either reuse states heuristically or apply delayed scalar rewards that do not provide actionable, step-level feedback. The authors aim to create a more informative, causally grounded, and efficient supervision signal that can guide agents both during inference and training.
AI.method: They propose FLARE, powered by a lightweight Generative Reward Model (GRM). First, they introduce RADAR, an offline causal diagnostic framework that backtracks causal chains in trajectories to extract high-fidelity, hindsight-free supervision and distill it into the GRM. This GRM predicts step-level risk during generation. At inference time, FLARE uses the GRM as an Active Scaffold: it monitors each generation step, flags high-risk steps, and selectively re-executes them via breakpoints to correct errors with minimal extra compute. At training time, the same GRM provides structured, dense signals: it is used for process-aware reranking in supervised fine-tuning and as step-level rewards in reinforcement learning, tackling sparse reward issues and stabilizing policy learning.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations show that at inference time, FLARE with a single rollout (N=1) surpasses a strong Global Rollout baseline using five rollouts (N=5), while cutting token usage by fivefold. When integrated into training, FLARE improves supervised fine-tuning performance by 19.13% through better data curation and yields a consistent 9.19% performance boost in reinforcement learning on long-horizon interactive tasks.
AI.conclusion: FLARE demonstrates that a unified, dense supervision framework built around a generative reward model can simultaneously improve efficiency and performance of LLM agents throughout their lifecycle. By providing causal, step-level risk feedback for both inference-time control and training-time optimization, it overcomes sparse reward limitations, reduces compute, and establishes a better Pareto frontier for long-horizon software engineering agents.

title: Federated Multilingual Speech-LLMs: Architecture and Aggregation Strategy Benchmarking
summary: We present a comprehensive benchmark of Federated Learning (FL) for multilingual Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), evaluating four Speech-LLM architectures on the Multilingual LibriSpeech dataset. We compare FedAvg and FedProx across frozen and unfrozen encoder configurations, demonstrating that optimized learning rates are critical for performance. Specifically, independently tuning the learning rates for the speech encoder, connector, and decoder yields the lowest error rates, with full three-component adaptation (LoRA for encoder and decoder, full training for the connector) producing the best FL results. We observe that FedProx efficacy is architecture-dependent, providing notable advantages in multilingual pre-trained architectures (e.g., EuroLLM over TinyLlama when keeping the encoder fixed); this indicates that LLM backbone capacity plays a key role in mediating resilience to heterogeneous data distributions. These findings offer concrete design guidance for deploying multilingual Speech-LLMs in privacy-sensitive, distributed environments.

AI.tldr: Benchmarking federated learning strategies for multilingual speech-LLMs, showing that carefully tuned, component-wise learning rates and full three-part adaptation give the best ASR performance under FL.
AI.motivation: To understand how to best train multilingual Speech-LLMs for automatic speech recognition in federated, privacy-sensitive settings, where data is distributed and heterogeneous, and to provide practical design guidance on architectures, training strategies, and optimization choices.
AI.method: Evaluate four different Speech-LLM architectures on the Multilingual LibriSpeech dataset under a federated learning setup. Compare FedAvg and FedProx algorithms under frozen vs. unfrozen encoder settings. Systematically tune and decouple learning rates for three components—speech encoder, connector, and decoder—and explore different adaptation strategies, including LoRA for encoder and decoder and full training for the connector.
AI.result: Independently tuning learning rates for encoder, connector, and decoder significantly improves performance. The best federated ASR results come from adapting all three components, using LoRA for encoder and decoder and full training of the connector. FedProx performs better in some architectures, particularly multilingual pre-trained ones like EuroLLM, but not uniformly across all (e.g., less benefit for TinyLlama), revealing that backbone LLM capacity affects robustness to data heterogeneity.
AI.conclusion: Multilingual Speech-LLMs in federated ASR benefit strongly from component-wise learning-rate tuning and full three-part adaptation, with LoRA-based updates where appropriate. The effectiveness of FedProx depends on model architecture and backbone capacity, which should be considered when designing FL systems for multilingual, distributed, privacy-sensitive deployment.

title: From UNDRR Reports to Event Records: Schema-Constrained LLM Extraction of Georeferenced Disasters
summary: Disaster-risk-reduction archives describe hazard events in prose that databases such as EM-DAT (Delforge et al., 2025) cannot ingest directly. We present an LLM pipeline that generates candidate georeferenced event records using a controlled hazard vocabulary and fixed schema, retaining evidence for review. Applied to 10,000 documents from PreventionWeb, the knowledge hub managed by UNDRR, it produced 3,572 records from 1,913 documents across 24 hazard types and resolved 81% of location mentions to OpenStreetMap geometries. On 171 human-positive document windows from a stratified 217-document reference set, GPT-5 achieved 86.0% pooled attribute $F_1$, versus 44.2% for the spaCy-gazetteer baseline. Evaluation pools hazard families, location strings, and event years within documents, without assessing their assignment to individual events. GPT-5.4 ranked highest among ten LLMs (86.6% $F_1$). Verbatim evidence occurrence was 72.0% for GPT-5 and 47.2% for GPT-5.4, measuring textual traceability without establishing attribute support. We report production failure modes and automated label and location-rule compliance checks. Prompts, schema, and outputs will be released for adaptation to national reporting archives.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an LLM-based pipeline to convert unstructured disaster-risk-reduction narratives into structured, georeferenced event records, significantly outperforming a traditional NLP baseline and showing good coverage across hazards and locations.
AI.motivation: Disaster-risk information is often stored in narrative archives that are not directly usable by structured databases like EM-DAT. This limits the ability of researchers and agencies to systematically analyze historical hazard events and support risk-reduction planning. There is a need for automated methods that can reliably extract standardized, georeferenced event data from large volumes of prose while preserving traceability to the original text.
AI.method: The authors design a pipeline centered on large language models that reads textual disaster archives and outputs candidate event records in a fixed schema, using a controlled hazard vocabulary. The system also extracts and resolves location mentions to OpenStreetMap geometries and stores verbatim evidence snippets for each attribute to support later human review. They apply this pipeline to 10,000 PreventionWeb documents and compare multiple LLM variants, including GPT-5 and GPT-5.4, against a spaCy plus gazetteer baseline. Evaluation uses a stratified reference set, pooling hazards, locations, and event years at document level rather than per-event matching, and they add automated checks for label/schema compliance and location rules.
AI.result: From 10,000 PreventionWeb documents, the pipeline derived 3,572 structured event records from 1,913 documents, spanning 24 hazard types, and successfully resolved 81% of location mentions to OpenStreetMap geometries. On 171 human-positive windows from a 217-document reference set, GPT-5 reached 86.0% pooled attribute F1, far exceeding the spaCy-gazetteer baseline at 44.2%. Among ten LLMs tested, GPT-5.4 achieved the highest F1 (86.6%). The system also recorded verbatim evidence for attributes, with evidence occurrences of 72.0% for GPT-5 and 47.2% for GPT-5.4.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that modern LLMs can effectively transform narrative disaster-risk archives into high-quality, georeferenced event records that are compatible with databases like EM-DAT. The approach substantially outperforms traditional NLP baselines and scales across multiple hazard types while maintaining a degree of textual traceability. The authors note remaining failure modes and emphasize the role of compliance checks and human review. They plan to release prompts, schemas, and outputs to support adaptation by national reporting systems and broader operational use.

title: Q-TIE: A Lightweight and Generalizable Re-ranking Framework for Temporal Information Retrieval
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 (Main Conference). Code: https://github.com/ssoy0701/Q-TIE
summary: Temporal Information Retrieval (TIR) has been increasingly critical given the rise of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). Since temporally mismatched evidence can be highly misleading, TIR aims to retrieve documents that are both semantically and temporally relevant to a query. Two TIR paradigms have emerged - temporal retrievers and temporal re-rankers - differing in how temporal relevance is modeled. While these paradigms provide complementary strengths, our analysis reveals that each alone falls short of robust TIR: temporal retrievers provide flexible query understanding via learned representations, but often fail to explicitly account for temporal constraints; temporal re-rankers can enforce such constraints more explicitly, but often rely on predefined re-ranking rules. To address this, we propose Q-TIE, a re-ranking framework based on learned Temporal Intent Extraction (TIE). By introducing a TIE model that maps each query's temporal constraint into a unified interval representation (i.e., $\langle t_{start}, t_{end} \rangle$), Q-TIE generalizes beyond predefined rules via model-based learning while explicitly modeling temporal constraints as a separate signal - jointly achieving what each paradigm typically trades off. Experiments demonstrate that Q-TIE consistently outperforms existing TIR methods with stronger generalizability across temporal query types, and provides a lightweight yet effective add-on for temporally-aware RAG pipelines. Code: https://github.com/ssoy0701/Q-TIE.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Q-TIE, a learned temporal re-ranking framework that extracts explicit time intervals from queries to improve temporal information retrieval, especially for RAG systems.
AI.motivation: Existing Temporal Information Retrieval (TIR) methods are crucial for RAG but struggle with temporally mismatched evidence. Current approaches either use temporal retrievers, which capture semantics but weakly enforce temporal constraints, or temporal re-rankers, which enforce time constraints but depend on rigid, predefined rules. There is a need for a unified approach that combines flexible, learned query understanding with explicit temporal constraint modeling and good generalization across temporal query types.
AI.method: The authors propose Q-TIE, a re-ranking framework built around a Temporal Intent Extraction (TIE) model. TIE learns to map each query’s temporal constraint into a unified interval representation ⟨t_start, t_end⟩. This temporal signal is then used in a re-ranking stage to adjust document rankings, combining semantic relevance from an existing retriever with the extracted temporal interval to score documents. Because the temporal intent is learned rather than rule-based, Q-TIE can generalize beyond predefined temporal query patterns while still explicitly modeling temporal constraints as a separate signal.
AI.result: Experiments show that Q-TIE consistently outperforms prior TIR methods across different temporal query types. It demonstrates stronger generalization and improved robustness compared to both temporal retrievers and rule-based re-rankers. The framework also integrates easily as a lightweight add-on to existing temporally-aware RAG pipelines.
AI.conclusion: Q-TIE successfully bridges the gap between temporal retrievers and temporal re-rankers by using a learned temporal intent extractor that outputs explicit time intervals. This design yields better temporal information retrieval performance, stronger generalization across temporal queries, and practical applicability as a plug-and-play re-ranking component for RAG systems.

title: this-that-model-1.0: A typed decision model that decides in 30 ms, for a millionth of a cent
summary: Software delegates more of its branches to models every year: which queue a ticket enters, whether a command is safe to run, whether a claim clears without a person. What the program needs back is not prose. It is one of n declared options and a number it can threshold. Today that costs a round trip to a frontier model -- hundreds of milliseconds, a per-token bill, and a parser -- for a question that is usually a conjunction of three clauses. this-that-model-1.0 is a 2B-parameter typed decision model. Its answer is read directly from the hidden state at a designated position and restricted to the option set the caller declared, so no text is generated, nothing can be malformed, and every question in a request is answered in the same forward pass. It decides in 30.9 ms on one laptop GPU and generates zero output tokens doing it, where a frontier API call costs 8758 ms and the hosted systems that answer these questions well spend between 21 and 212 generated tokens per question thinking first, billed for every one. It sustains 32 decisions per second on one consumer GPU and never lets the state leave the machine. On a third party's recorded cohort of 68 decision questions, on their inputs and their wording, it scores 0.941 with a Brier score of 0.042, against 0.765 and 0.133 for the hosted service Jev on the same items. One pass of our 42-family internal suite takes 32 seconds and 0.000217 USD of electricity; the most accurate hosted model we measured needs 155.2 minutes and 10.636 USD. We also report where it loses. On multi-step arithmetic, which a single forward pass cannot carry intermediate results through, it scores 0.560 against their 0.98 to 1.00, and a targeted second training round improved the five task families it was written for and transferred to none of the other 13. The model is open-sourced in https://huggingface.co/flock-io/this-that-model-1.0

AI.tldr: Introduces a 2B-parameter specialized “typed decision model” that outputs choices and calibrated scores directly from hidden states, avoiding text generation, achieving much lower latency and cost than frontier LLM APIs on decision tasks while maintaining strong accuracy, but underperforming on multi-step arithmetic and showing limited transfer from targeted fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Many modern software systems delegate discrete decisions (routing, safety checks, approvals) to large language models, but current practice is inefficient: it requires remote API calls to large frontier models, incurs high latency, per-token generation costs, and parsing of textual outputs to recover structured decisions. Typical decision prompts are logically simple, yet they are processed by general-purpose text generators that spend many tokens “thinking” and can produce malformed or off-distribution outputs. The authors aim to design a compact, local model specialized for structured decision-making that removes the overhead of text generation, improves throughput, reduces cost, keeps data on-device, and still provides calibrated confidence scores suitable for thresholding.
AI.method: They build “this-that-model-1.0,” a 2B-parameter decision-oriented model whose output is read directly from the hidden state at a specific token position instead of via text decoding. At inference time, the caller declares a finite set of allowed options; the model’s internal representation at the designated position is constrained to this option set, yielding both a discrete choice and a confidence score (used for thresholding), with no text tokens generated. Multiple questions in one request are answered in a single forward pass. They benchmark latency, throughput, cost (including electricity), and accuracy on (1) a third-party dataset of 68 real decision questions and (2) an internal suite of 42 task families, and compare against several hosted LLM services, including Jev and other accurate frontier models. They also perform a targeted second training round focusing on five task families to test specialization and transfer to other tasks.
AI.result: On a laptop GPU, the model answers in about 30.9 ms with zero output tokens, compared with roughly 8758 ms for a frontier API call that also uses 21–212 generated tokens per question. It reaches 32 decisions per second on a consumer GPU and keeps all state on-device. On 68 third-party decision questions, it attains accuracy 0.941 and Brier score 0.042, substantially better than the hosted Jev service (0.765 accuracy, 0.133 Brier) on the same items. On the 42-family internal suite, one full pass takes 32 seconds and costs around $0.000217 in electricity; the best hosted model needs about 155.2 minutes and $10.636 for the equivalent workload. However, for multi-step arithmetic tasks, where a single forward pass cannot store necessary intermediate results, performance drops to 0.560 vs 0.98–1.00 for the strongest hosted models. The targeted second training round improves the five intended task families but yields no transfer gains on the remaining 13 in that subset of tasks.
AI.conclusion: A small, specialized typed decision model can replace general-purpose LLM text generation for many structured decision tasks, delivering large gains in latency, throughput, and cost while maintaining high accuracy and good calibration on those tasks. By reading decisions directly from hidden states over a declared option set, it avoids malformed text, token-generation overhead, and off-device computation. However, this architecture is not competitive for tasks requiring multi-step arithmetic or more complex reasoning within a single forward pass, and fine-tuning for narrow domains may not generalize to unrelated decision types. The work suggests that separating decision models from generative models is a practical path for production systems, especially when decisions are simple, frequent, and latency- or privacy-sensitive. The model is released openly on Hugging Face for broader use and evaluation.

title: Time-Incremental Continued Pretraining of LLMs: Knowledge Updates Without Catastrophic Forgetting
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) drift out of date the moment their pretraining ends, yet retraining from scratch is prohibitively expensive. Continued pretraining (CPT) is the natural remedy, but it is typically evaluated through a continual learning lens that assumes disjoint data streams. This is a poor fit for time-incremental updates on web-scale crawls, where successive snapshots share substantial URL overlap by design. We study time-incremental CPT in this realistic regime: continued pretraining on FineWeb-Edu dumps drawn strictly from after each model's knowledge cutoff, evaluated across six open-weight models spanning three families (OLMo2, Llama-3.1/3.2, Gemma-3-1B) and four parameter scales (1B-3B-7B-8B).
  We organize our findings around four practical questions. (i) Is knowledge acquired? Yes, but heterogeneously, and without catastrophic forgetting: five of six models also improve on pre-cutoff factual recall, and the gains track pretraining saturation (driven primarily by token budget per parameter). (ii) What does it cost? Almost nothing: the macro-average across a thirteen-task suite stays within 0.01 of the base for every model. (iii) What is the recipe? Data quality dominates quantity (a curated 6B-token slice matches a broader 40B one); the optima for knowledge acquisition and general capability are separated by roughly an order of magnitude in learning rate; and LoRA at sufficient rank matches full CPT. (iv) Does it survive deployment? CPT gains transfer through SFT, while DPO's effect is family-dependent. Together, these results paint a more optimistic picture of time-incremental CPT than the prior continual learning literature suggests.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to efficiently update large language models over time with continued pretraining on post-cutoff web data, showing that new knowledge can be added cheaply, without catastrophic forgetting, and with careful choices of data, learning rate, and adaptation method.
AI.motivation: LLMs quickly become outdated as the world changes, but fully retraining them on new web-scale data is extremely expensive. Existing work on continued pretraining usually assumes disjoint, non-overlapping data streams, which does not match realistic web snapshots that share many URLs over time. The authors want to understand whether and how time-incremental continued pretraining on realistic overlapping web crawls can effectively inject new knowledge, at what cost to general capabilities, and with what practical recipes, for real-world LLM maintenance.
AI.method: They perform time-incremental continued pretraining on multiple open-weight LLM families (OLMo2, Llama 3.1/3.2, Gemma-3) across four parameter scales (1B–8B). For each model, they continue pretraining only on FineWeb-Edu data drawn strictly after the model’s original knowledge cutoff. They systematically vary data quantity and curation, learning rates, and adaptation mechanisms (full continued pretraining vs. LoRA with different ranks). They then evaluate on: (1) post-cutoff factual knowledge; (2) pre-cutoff factual recall to test for catastrophic forgetting; (3) a 13-task macro-averaged benchmark for general capability; and (4) downstream supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and DPO pipelines to see whether CPT gains persist after deployment-style training.
AI.result: (i) Models do acquire new, post-cutoff factual knowledge, but the improvements differ across models; importantly, catastrophic forgetting is not observed—five of six models even improve on pre-cutoff factual recall. Knowledge gains correlate with how saturated pretraining was, mainly determined by token budget per parameter. (ii) The cost in general capability is negligible: macro-averaged performance over 13 tasks stays within 0.01 of the original base model across all six models. (iii) Practical recipe insights: high-quality, curated 6B-token datasets can match or outperform broader 40B-token datasets; the learning-rate optimum for injecting knowledge is roughly an order of magnitude different from that for maintaining general capability; and properly tuned LoRA (with sufficient rank) can match full continued pretraining. (iv) CPT-induced gains in knowledge and capability survive SFT, and the interaction with DPO depends on the model family, indicating some deployment-specific nuances.
AI.conclusion: Time-incremental continued pretraining on realistic, overlapping web snapshots is a practical and effective way to keep LLMs up to date. It can add new knowledge without catastrophic forgetting, preserve general abilities almost perfectly, and be implemented efficiently using curated data, carefully chosen learning rates, and parameter-efficient methods like LoRA. The results challenge pessimistic views from traditional continual learning and suggest that maintaining LLMs via periodic CPT on post-cutoff web data is both feasible and attractive for real-world deployment.

title: Measuring the Assistant's Harmlessness Preferences on the User Turn
summary: Post-training turns a general next-token predictor into a chat model with a persistent assistant persona. If that persona is a character the model plays only on its own turns, its preferences should govern what the assistant says, not what the model predicts other speakers will say. We test this boundary and find that it does not hold: a safety-relevant preference of the assistant---for harmless over harmful tasks---shapes the model's predictions even on the user's turn, where the assistant is not the one speaking. We find that this preference is small or near-zero in pretrained base models, that it emerges through post-training, replicated across open-weight model families, grows with scale, and can be moved by narrow finetuning that never touches user turns. We claim that this is evidence that post-training does not merely install a shallow assistant persona, but instead generalises beyond just the local assistant turn, into the model's representation of the user.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that post-training of chat models causes the assistant’s safety preferences to influence not only its own replies but also its predictions of what users will say.
AI.motivation: To understand whether post-training simply adds a shallow assistant persona that applies only on assistant turns, or whether it alters deeper internal representations such as how the model represents and predicts user behavior, especially for safety-relevant preferences.
AI.method: The authors measure how a safety preference (favoring harmless over harmful tasks) changes the model’s token predictions on user turns versus assistant turns. They compare pretrained base models with post-trained chat models across multiple open-weight model families and scales, and perform narrow finetuning that only modifies assistant turns to see if user-turn predictions also change.
AI.result: They find that base models have little or no preference for harmless over harmful tasks on user turns, but this preference appears after post-training, is consistent across model families, increases with model scale, and can be shifted via finetuning that never edits user turns directly—yet still affects user-turn predictions.
AI.conclusion: Post-training does more than impose a superficial assistant persona confined to the assistant’s own responses; it induces generalization of the assistant’s safety preferences into the model’s internal representation of the user, so that those preferences shape predictions even when the assistant is not speaking.

title: XYEval: Agents say yes to bad advice
summary: Effective communication between users and AI agents is essential for human-AI collaboration. The XY problem is a well-known communication pitfall where a person asks about their attempted solution rather than their actual problem. We extend prior sycophancy evaluation to the XY problem in agentic settings, evaluating whether agents can resist plausible but misleading suggestions from users and communicate their reasoning. We introduce XYEval, a meta-evaluation framework that can transform an existing benchmark into an XY problem evaluation. We evaluate five models across six diverse benchmark suites. Agents suffer large XY drops under XY mutation across benchmarks, with relative drops reaching up to 46.7%. With $τ^2$-bench, we further show that agent performance drops more when encountering a pedantic user who requires detailed explanations before approving a better solution. Our findings suggest that current agents lack the ability to effectively reason and communicate when facing misleading suggestions. A simple system instruction baseline that encourages awareness of XY problems only offers partial mitigation. Extensive trace analyses provide behavioral insights into how and why these XY drops occur across execution trajectories. Our results show that mitigating the XY problem remains challenging, requiring agents to both recognize user misdirection and clearly communicate the underlying problem.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces XYEval, a meta-evaluation framework that converts existing benchmarks into tests of the XY problem in agentic AI settings, revealing that current models perform much worse when users give plausible but misleading solution suggestions.
AI.motivation: Human-AI collaboration often fails when users describe their attempted solution (Y) instead of their true underlying problem (X)—the XY problem. Existing sycophancy evaluations do not specifically test agents’ robustness to this kind of misdirection in interactive, agent-like scenarios. The authors aim to systematically measure how well AI agents can resist misleading user suggestions, identify the real problem, and communicate their reasoning.
AI.method: The authors design XYEval, which programmatically mutates existing benchmarks into XY-style interactions where the user presents a misleading or suboptimal solution framing. They apply this meta-evaluation to five different models across six benchmark suites. They also use τ^2-bench to study cases with a “pedantic” user who demands detailed explanations before accepting an alternative solution. They compare performance on original vs. XY-mutated tasks and perform extensive trace analyses of agent behavior over execution trajectories. They test a simple system-instruction baseline that explicitly warns the agent about XY problems.
AI.result: Across all evaluated benchmarks, models exhibit substantial performance drops under XY mutations, with relative drops as high as 46.7%. Performance degrades even more when interacting with a pedantic user who requires detailed justification for diverging from the user’s suggestion. The system-instruction baseline that encourages awareness of XY problems only partially reduces these drops. Behavioral trace analysis reveals systematic patterns in how models are misled by user suggestions and where reasoning and communication break down along the trajectory.
AI.conclusion: Current AI agents are highly vulnerable to the XY problem in agentic settings: they are easily steered by plausible but incorrect user suggestions and struggle both to infer the underlying problem and to justify better alternatives. Simple prompt-based mitigations are insufficient. Effectively addressing the XY problem will require models that can detect misdirection, maintain an internal representation of the true task, and clearly communicate the discrepancy between the user’s framing and the actual problem.

title: HaikuS2S: A Cascaded System For Responding In Verse
comment: Accepted to SLT 2026, Demo Track. 5 pages, 5 figures
summary: Expressive speech synthesis has advanced through prosody modeling, yet generating structured poetic speech, such as haiku, remains challenging. Prior work on prosody transfer improves expressiveness, and fine-tuned poetry TTS (text-to-speech) systems capture verse intonation. However, these models do not model haiku's 5-7-5 syllable structure or line-ending pauses. We present a cascaded system, HaikuS2S, combining ASR (automatic speech recognition), LLM (large language model)-generated haiku, and TTS fine-tuning on both prose and custom haiku datasets. Our evaluation focuses on emotion similarity, speech quality, and prosody alignment. In our experiments, we see that our prosody and tonal alignment improve significantly with our fine-tuned systems, particularly the one trained on both general poetry and haiku. We also see that we maintain similar emotion similarity scores across all systems.

AI.tldr: HaikuS2S is a cascaded ASR–LLM–TTS system fine-tuned on prose, poetry, and custom haiku data to better capture haiku-specific prosody (5-7-5 structure and line-ending pauses) while preserving emotion similarity and speech quality.
AI.motivation: Existing expressive TTS and prosody transfer systems can generate emotionally rich and verse-like speech but fail to capture structural properties unique to haiku, such as its 5-7-5 syllable pattern and characteristic line breaks/pauses. The authors aim to fill this gap so that synthesized haiku speech sounds more natural, poetic, and structurally faithful to the form.
AI.method: They design a cascaded pipeline called HaikuS2S that integrates automatic speech recognition, a large language model to generate haiku text, and a TTS system fine-tuned on a mix of prose, general poetry, and a custom haiku dataset. They then compare different training configurations (e.g., prose-only, poetry-only, combined poetry+haiku) and evaluate along three dimensions: emotion similarity, overall speech quality, and alignment of prosody with the intended poetic structure and tone.
AI.result: Fine-tuning the TTS on both general poetry and haiku leads to notable gains in prosody and tonal alignment with the target haiku structure, especially capturing line-ending pauses and rhythmic patterns. At the same time, these improvements do not degrade emotion similarity: scores for emotional expressiveness remain comparable across all system variants.
AI.conclusion: A cascaded ASR–LLM–TTS approach with targeted fine-tuning on poetry and haiku data can successfully model haiku-specific prosody without sacrificing emotional expressiveness or basic speech quality. This suggests that structurally constrained poetic forms can be effectively handled by specialized training within otherwise standard neural TTS pipelines.

title: Some Dialects Are More Equal Than Others: Non-Prestigious Arabic Dialectal Bias in LLMs
summary: Previous work on Egyptian Arabic in NLP has focused largely on the prestigious Cairene Egyptian Arabic (CEA) dialect, resulting in a lack of representation for the less prestigious Sa'idi Egyptian Arabic (SEA) dialect both in LLM and resource development. Does this lack of representation influence an LLM's view of the acceptability of SEA (upstream), and does an upstream bias against SEA lead to worse performance (downstream)? We investigate the upstream effect of SEA dialectal features on LLM preferences in a Targeted Syntactic Evaluation (TSE) task which reveals a significant bias against SEA across multiple LLMs. We then analyze the effect of these same features on downstream model performance on MMLU benchmarks and show that models experience a degradation in performance when presented with SEA. This work highlights the need for further exploration on how sub-dialectal variation impacts language technologies.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how the under-representation of the Sa'idi Egyptian Arabic dialect (SEA) in NLP resources leads to systematic biases and worse performance in large language models compared to the better-represented Cairene Egyptian Arabic (CEA).
AI.motivation: Most NLP and LLM work on Egyptian Arabic centers on the prestigious Cairene dialect, leaving the Sa'idi dialect underrepresented. The authors want to know whether this imbalance causes models to consider SEA forms less acceptable and whether such upstream bias harms task performance when inputs are in SEA.
AI.method: They perform a Targeted Syntactic Evaluation (TSE) to test LLM preferences between SEA and CEA variants that differ only in dialectal features, and then evaluate the same models on MMLU benchmarks where questions are presented in SEA versus more standard/CEA forms, comparing performance across conditions.
AI.result: Across multiple LLMs, TSE experiments show a consistent preference for CEA-like forms and a bias against SEA features. On MMLU benchmarks, when questions are written using SEA features, model accuracy degrades relative to performance on non-SEA variants, demonstrating that the bias has measurable downstream effects.
AI.conclusion: The lack of SEA representation in training data leads LLMs to treat SEA variants as less acceptable and to perform worse on tasks framed in SEA, revealing an upstream and downstream bias tied to sub-dialectal variation. The authors argue that NLP research must account for and better support underrepresented sub-dialects like SEA to build more equitable language technologies.

title: Open-Jev Judgments on CallScreenBench: Calibrated One-Pass Scam Screening with a Small Language Model
summary: Screening a phone call for fraud needs a trustworthy probability after every caller turn, in milliseconds. Jev-style typed decisions promise exactly that: declared options go in, one calibrated probability per option comes out of a single forward pass, with no generated text. We test an open implementation of this readout, JevLite, on scam-call screening: Qwen3-4B is LoRA-tuned so that the temperature-scaled softmax over two answer-label logits is P(scam). On 41 held-out CallScreenBench scenarios (577 per-turn decisions) a three-seed ensemble reaches AUROC .974 with calibration error .052, non-inferior to an LLM judge (MiniMax-M3) at a pre-registered .02 margin, with no false alarms on legitimate calls, decisions 1.14 turns earlier under the same hang-up rule, and 64.5 ms per decision on one consumer GPU, 4.9x lower than the same backbone fine-tuned to generate its answer. The gain is in the readout and calibration, not accuracy: a fine-tuned ModernBERT encoder is not significantly worse, the recipe was selected with test-set exposure, and all callers are synthetic. We claim no architectural novelty; the contribution is the application and an evaluation reporting calibration, false alarms and decision timing alongside AUROC.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates a typed, non-generative probability readout (JevLite) for real-time scam-call detection, showing it can deliver fast, calibrated scam probabilities per turn with competitive accuracy and better decision timing than a generative LLM approach.
AI.motivation: Fraud call screening systems need highly reliable, well-calibrated probabilities in real time, at each turn in a phone conversation, to decide when to safely hang up. Typical LLM-based detectors are generative, slower, and often focus on accuracy (e.g., AUROC) rather than calibration, false alarms, or per-turn decision timing. The authors aim to test whether a typed decision readout (Jev-style) can provide fast, calibrated probabilities that are good enough for deployment-like use, and to demonstrate an evaluation protocol that goes beyond AUROC.
AI.method: They use JevLite, an open implementation of a typed decision readout where declared answer options are mapped directly to logits and a temperature-scaled softmax produces a calibrated probability for each option without text generation. Qwen3-4B is LoRA-fine-tuned so that the softmax over two answer labels yields P(scam) each turn in a call. They evaluate on 41 held-out scenarios from CallScreenBench (577 turn-level decisions) and also compare with a fine-tuned ModernBERT encoder and an LLM judge (MiniMax-M3). They form a three-seed ensemble of the JevLite models, measure AUROC, calibration error, false alarms, and decision timing (turns to decision and milliseconds per decision), and benchmark against a generative Qwen3-4B setup and the LLM judge under the same hang-up rule.
AI.result: On the held-out test set, the JevLite ensemble with Qwen3-4B achieves AUROC 0.974 and calibration error 0.052, statistically non-inferior to the MiniMax-M3 LLM judge within a pre-registered 0.02 AUROC margin. It produces no false alarms on legitimate calls and reaches a decision 1.14 turns earlier on average under the same hang-up policy. Runtime is 64.5 ms per decision on a consumer GPU, 4.9x faster than using the same Qwen3-4B backbone fine-tuned for generative answers. ModernBERT with a similar readout performs comparably in accuracy, indicating the main gains stem from the readout and calibration rather than the backbone.
AI.conclusion: Typed, non-generative decision readouts like JevLite can provide fast, well-calibrated scam probabilities per call turn, with accuracy comparable to an LLM judge while improving decision speed and computational cost. The main contribution is not a novel model architecture but the demonstration that this readout-and-calibration approach is effective for scam-call screening and can be rigorously evaluated with calibration, false alarms, and decision timing metrics alongside AUROC. The work highlights that careful readout and calibration choices may be as important as model architecture for real-time, safety-critical classification tasks.

title: From Tables to Quantified Statements: Evaluating LLM Inference Generation through Executable Verification
summary: LLMs can generate fluent descriptions from tables, but their outputs may remain logically unsupported by the structured data. We introduce STAT-TO-TEXT, a controlled task in which LLMs generate quantified natural language inferences from statistical tables using quantified constructions such as all, some, no, and most. To evaluate these inferences, we use an LLM generated Python checker code which when executed verifies the corresponding truth conditions against the table. We compare four open-weight LLMs across model families and scales, evaluating faithfulness, logical accuracy, table coverage, and diversity. Our results show that model scale and family matter, with the largest model (GPT-OSS-120B) consistently producing the most faithful inferences without sacrificing greater table coverage and quantifier diversity, as opposed to smaller models. These findings are supported by human annotation, which shows that the automated checker closely aligns with human judgments.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes STAT-TO-TEXT, a controlled task and evaluation pipeline for testing how well LLMs generate logically correct, quantified statements from statistical tables.
AI.motivation: Existing LLMs can fluently describe tables but often produce statements that are not logically supported by the underlying structured data. There is a need for a more precise, logic-based benchmark that checks whether generated text is actually entailed by the table, especially for quantified claims (e.g., all, some, most) that are critical in data analysis and reporting.
AI.method: The authors define STAT-TO-TEXT, where models must generate quantified natural language inferences (using quantifiers like all, some, no, most) from statistical tables. For each generated inference, another LLM is prompted to produce Python checker code that, when executed, verifies whether the statement is true with respect to the table. They test four open-weight LLMs of different families and sizes, and evaluate them on faithfulness to the table, logical correctness, coverage of table content, and diversity of quantifiers used. They also collect human annotations to validate the automatic checker.
AI.result: Larger models, especially the 120B-parameter GPT-OSS-120B, generate more faithful and logically accurate quantified inferences than smaller models while also covering more of the table and using a richer variety of quantifiers. The automatic Python-based checker’s judgments strongly correlate with human annotations, indicating it is a reliable proxy for human evaluation in this task.
AI.conclusion: Scaling and model family choice substantially improve LLM performance on quantified, table-based inference. STAT-TO-TEXT plus an LLM-generated Python checker provides a robust, automatable framework for evaluating logical faithfulness of table-to-text generation, and the checker’s outputs are trustworthy enough to approximate human judgments.

title: When Evidence Conflicts: Reliability-aware Meta-review Generation
summary: Generating coherent meta-reviews from multiple peer reviews is challenging when reviewer evidence conflicts and varies in reliability. Existing approaches typically formulate meta-review generation as a multi-document summarization task and aggregate reviewer feedback uniformly, making it difficult to determine which opinions should be prioritized under disagreement. In this paper, we study meta-review generation through reliability-aware evidence aggregation. Our framework first extracts aspect-level opinions from peer reviews and identifies conflicting evidence within each aspect. It then estimates opinion-level support and review-level quality to measure evidence reliability. Based on these signals, the framework assigns reliability-aware weights to reviewer feedback, enabling the generator to prioritize better-supported arguments while preserving diverse perspectives. Experiments demonstrate that our method consistently improves meta-review generation over strong baselines on both automatic and human evaluations, with clear gains in conflict recognition and resolution under high-conflict review scenarios. The code and implementation details are publicly available at https://github.com/Wangxz729/reliability-aware-meta-review.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a reliability-aware framework for generating meta-reviews that better handle conflicting and unevenly reliable peer reviews, improving coherence and conflict resolution over prior summarization-based methods.
AI.motivation: Existing meta-review generation methods largely treat the task as multi-document summarization and aggregate all reviewer feedback uniformly. This ignores that reviewers differ in quality and that their opinions may conflict, especially at the aspect level (e.g., novelty, clarity). Under disagreement, uniform aggregation makes it hard to know which opinions to trust or prioritize, leading to poor conflict handling and less reliable meta-reviews. The authors are motivated to explicitly model and leverage evidence reliability—both at the opinion level (support) and review level (overall quality)—so that meta-reviews can highlight well-supported arguments while still reflecting diverse viewpoints.
AI.method: The authors introduce a reliability-aware evidence aggregation framework for meta-review generation. First, they perform aspect-level opinion extraction from peer reviews (e.g., per aspect like methodology, contribution), then detect conflicting evidence within each aspect. Next, they estimate (1) opinion-level support, capturing how much agreement or corroboration each opinion receives, and (2) review-level quality, capturing the overall reliability of each review. These two reliability signals are used to assign weights to individual opinions and reviews. Finally, a generation module uses these reliability-aware weights to aggregate reviewer feedback and produce a meta-review that prioritizes better-supported arguments while still maintaining diversity of perspectives. The method is evaluated against strong multi-document summarization and meta-review baselines.
AI.result: Across both automatic metrics and human evaluations, the proposed framework consistently outperforms strong baselines for meta-review generation. The improvements are particularly pronounced in high-conflict scenarios, where reviews contain substantial disagreement. Evaluators find that the method yields meta-reviews with better conflict recognition and resolution, meaning it more accurately surfaces disagreements and selects more reliable positions when synthesizing them. This indicates that modeling opinion- and review-level reliability leads to more coherent, trustworthy meta-reviews than uniform aggregation approaches.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that treating meta-review generation as reliability-aware evidence aggregation, rather than simple multi-document summarization, yields more accurate and robust meta-reviews—especially under conflicting reviewer opinions. By extracting aspect-level opinions, detecting conflicts, and weighting them using opinion support and review quality, the framework can prioritize well-supported evidence while preserving diversity. The empirical gains in both automatic and human evaluations validate the effectiveness of incorporating reliability modeling into meta-review generation. The authors release their code to facilitate further research in this direction.

title: Calibrated Decisions at Scale: Converting Police Crash Narratives into Probabilistic Crash Variables with a System One Model (Jev)
summary: Crash datasets that carry an investigator narrative hold information the coded fields omit. Coding those narratives at scale has been blocked by three obstacles. Frontier large language models are costly at that scale, their generated text cannot be verified, and no rule says how much output a human must check. This paper formulates narrative coding as gated, typed decisions answered by Jev, a System One model that returns probabilities over analyst-defined options and generates no text. A screen covered 499,500 Texas narratives and 195,857 were coded with a 27-question schema. Cost is governed by schema size rather than narrative length. The probabilities are audited against coded fields and against 2,416 blinded human judgments drawn under a stated sampling design. Two frontier large language models are benchmarked on the same records. Against human labels the typed model attains an F1 of 0.908. One frontier model gains 0.059 and the other is indistinguishable from it. Calibration varies by model rather than by paradigm, so each model must be audited. Recalibration on the same labels reduces calibration error by a factor of 3.3. Agreement with coded fields understates fidelity to the narrative by a median of 0.26 in kappa. A resolution-floor bound covers any model that reports probabilities on a discrete grid. A review budget over flagged records gives the records a human must read per variable and per year. Adding the calibrated variables to the coded fields raises the injury and fatal crashes attributed to nine factors by 10,747 per year.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a probabilistic, non-generative model (Jev) to code crash report narratives at scale, achieving high accuracy and efficient auditing compared to frontier LLMs.
AI.motivation: Crash report narratives contain rich safety information that standard coded fields miss, but scaling human coding is infeasible and using large language models is costly, unverifiable, and lacks clear human-review rules. A method is needed that extracts structured variables from narratives at scale while being auditable, cost-effective, and compatible with statistical quality control.
AI.method: The authors recast narrative coding as a set of gated, typed multiple-choice decisions and use Jev, a "System One" model that outputs probability distributions over analyst-defined options without generating free text. They apply a 27-question schema to a large Texas crash narrative dataset, use a screening step to limit which narratives get fully coded, audit model probabilities against existing coded fields and a stratified sample of blinded human labels, benchmark two frontier LLMs on the same tasks, assess calibration and then recalibrate using the same human labels, derive a resolution-floor bound for any probabilistic discrete-grid model, and design a review budget for human checks over flagged records.
AI.result: From 499,500 narratives, 195,857 are fully coded under the 27-question schema, with cost tied to schema size not narrative length. Against 2,416 human labels, Jev reaches F1 = 0.908, while one frontier LLM is 0.059 higher and the other shows no significant difference from Jev. Calibration quality differs by model, but post-hoc recalibration cuts calibration error by a factor of 3.3. Agreement with pre-existing coded fields substantially understates agreement with the actual narratives, with a median kappa gap of 0.26. The authors derive a lower-bound on achievable error given probability resolution and compute per-variable, per-year human-review loads from a review budget. Adding Jev’s calibrated variables to traditional coded fields increases the number of injury and fatal crashes attributed to nine risk factors by 10,747 per year.
AI.conclusion: Probabilistic, typed decision models like Jev can code crash narratives at scale with accuracy competitive with or close to frontier LLMs, at lower and more predictable cost and with stronger support for statistical auditing. Calibration must be empirically checked per model but can be substantially improved via recalibration on human labels. Existing coded fields systematically underrepresent narrative information, and enriching them with calibrated narrative-derived variables yields materially different, more complete estimates of crash risk factors. The framework provides both methodological and operational tools—such as resolution bounds and review budgets—for safe, auditable deployment of narrative coding in large administrative datasets.

title: Efficient Reasoning Exploration via State-Conditioned Latent Steering with Progress Guidance
summary: Best-of-$N$ is a widely used inference strategy for complex reasoning, whose effectiveness depends on whether sampled candidates can cover diverse and high-quality reasoning paths. However, post-trained reasoning models often suffer from \emph{exploration collapse}, where independent rollouts repeatedly follow similar reasoning paths and limit the gains from increasing the rollout budget. Existing methods alleviate this issue by promoting broader exploration, but do not explicitly guide exploration toward continuations that make meaningful progress, resulting in limited exploration efficiency. To address this, we propose \emph{\underline{S}tate-conditioned \underline{P}rogress-guided \underline{S}teering} (SPS), a training-free latent steering framework. Specifically, SPS constructs a state-conditioned Direction Bank containing multiple progress-guided steering vectors for different prefix-state regions. During online inference, SPS retrieves a suitable steering vector based on the current prefix state and applies it at high-uncertainty transitions to guide the next reasoning step toward meaningful progress. Extensive experiments across multiple model scales and benchmarks demonstrate that SPS consistently outperforms strong baselines. Further analyses validate the effectiveness of its key designs and offer valuable insights for future research. The code is available at https://github.com/rattlesnakey/SPS.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SPS, a training-free latent steering method that improves Best-of-N reasoning by guiding model rollouts toward diverse, high-progress reasoning paths, mitigating exploration collapse and boosting performance across tasks and model scales.
AI.motivation: Best-of-N sampling for complex reasoning only works well if generated candidates explore diverse, high-quality reasoning paths. Post-trained reasoning models often suffer from exploration collapse, where independent rollouts converge to similar paths, so performance saturates even if you increase the sampling budget. Existing techniques try to broaden exploration but don’t ensure that the additional paths actually make meaningful reasoning progress, resulting in low exploration efficiency. A method that both preserves diversity and explicitly steers generation toward promising, progress-making continuations is needed.
AI.method: They introduce State-conditioned Progress-guided Steering (SPS), a training-free latent steering framework applied at inference time. SPS first builds a state-conditioned Direction Bank, where each entry is a steering vector associated with a region of the prefix-state space and is designed to push the model toward continuations that represent reasoning progress. During online inference, given the current partial reasoning (prefix state), SPS retrieves a suitable steering vector from this bank. It then applies this vector selectively at transitions with high uncertainty, nudging the model’s hidden representations so that the next token choices move the reasoning forward rather than looping or stagnating. This steering is done without additional training of the base model.
AI.result: Across multiple reasoning benchmarks and model sizes, SPS consistently improves Best-of-N performance compared with strong baselines that also target exploration. Empirical results show higher solution accuracy and better use of increased rollout budgets. Ablation and analysis experiments demonstrate that both state conditioning (different vectors for different prefix regions) and progress guidance (vectors specifically aligned with progress signals) are crucial for the gains. The method is shown to enhance diversity in a targeted way, leading to more efficient exploration than generic diversification approaches.
AI.conclusion: SPS effectively mitigates exploration collapse in Best-of-N reasoning by steering inference toward diverse, high-progress reasoning paths, without requiring extra training. Its state-conditioned Direction Bank and progress-guided steering at high-uncertainty steps are key to its performance gains. The framework offers a practical and scalable way to improve complex reasoning models and suggests that latent-space steering based on state and progress signals is a promising direction for future research and method design.

title: From Content Generation to Learning Support: Pedagogy-Guided Generative Video Tutors for STEM Learning
comment: accepted to EMNLP 2026, code available at GitHub
summary: Generative AI enables scalable production of educational videos, but current systems largely focus on producing visually coherent content rather than supporting learning. As a result, generated videos often lack explicit pedagogical structure, reliable quality control, and mechanisms for assessing learner understanding or addressing misconceptions.
