In this work, we introduce PIVOT (Pedagogy-guided Instructional VideO Tutoring), a generative video tutoring framework for STEM learning via learning-centered instructional support.1 Inspired by conventional teaching workflows, our framework integrates pedagogy into the full generation pipeline: it first uses instructional principles to guide storyboard generation, then produces verified multimodal videos through code-centric generation and a pedagogical verification harness, and finally connects videos with assessment and misconception-aware remediation. Experiments and expert evaluations across four STEM domains show that our framework produces educational videos with pedagogically aligned content, clear and engaging presentation, coherent instructional flow, and perceived effectiveness for learning. These findings suggest a human-centered perspective on educational content generation: generative systems should be evaluated and designed not only by what they produce, but also by how they support teaching practices, learner understanding, and corrective feedback.

AI.tldr: The paper presents PIVOT, a pedagogy-guided generative AI framework that creates STEM video tutorials with built-in instructional structure, quality checks, and assessment/remediation links.
AI.motivation: Existing generative AI for educational videos prioritizes visual coherence over learning effectiveness, lacking explicit pedagogy, systematic quality control, and ways to assess and respond to learner understanding or misconceptions.
AI.method: PIVOT integrates pedagogical principles throughout a three-stage pipeline: (1) generate storyboards driven by instructional design principles, (2) create and verify multimodal videos via code-centric generation plus a pedagogical verification harness, and (3) link each video to assessments and misconception-aware remediation activities.
AI.result: Across four STEM domains, experiments and expert reviews show that PIVOT’s videos are more pedagogically aligned, clearer, more engaging, and exhibit better instructional flow and perceived learning effectiveness than standard generative approaches.
AI.conclusion: Effective educational content generation should be human- and learning-centered: systems like PIVOT must be evaluated and designed not just by output appearance, but by how well they embody teaching practices, support learner understanding, and provide corrective feedback.

title: You Can Tell Who's Asking: What the Web's Questions Are Made Of, and Where They Come From
comment: Accepted to the 13th Web as Corpus Workshop (WaC-13) at EMNLP 2026. 14 pages, 4 figures. Code and data: https://github.com/bodhiumlabs/tell-whos-asking
summary: Questions scraped from the web are used across academia and industry as a proxy for what people want to know. Across QA training data, retrieval benchmarks, and content strategy, questions on a page are assumed to reflect human intent. We test this assumption at scale by extracting 13.4B question occurrences across 110 FineWeb snapshots (2013-2025), and report three findings. First, you can tell who is asking: provenance (the host/page of questions) leaves a signal in question form, and a logistic model can separate genuine user questions from templated/manufactured ones at AUC 0.725 via length and surrounding context rather than question type, though only 0.554 against commerce FAQ writing. Second, question frequency does not measure demand: the most-frequent questions are boilerplate/templated (over 70% of the top thousand), so occurrence counts measure how often a string was published and not how often it was asked. Third, over twelve years the genuine share of occurrences fell by 79% (42-56% after controlling for crawl composition), with question length and context decreasing. We present the first diachronic, occurrence-level measurement of web question provenance, and find the crawlable web's questions have shifted from being asked by humans toward manufactured for machines to read.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that many web questions used in QA research aren’t genuine user queries but manufactured or templated content, and that this problem has worsened over time.
AI.motivation: Many NLP and IR systems rely on web-scraped questions (for training, evaluation, and content strategy) under the assumption that these questions reflect real human information needs. The authors are motivated to test whether this assumption is valid, how reliably we can distinguish genuine user questions from templated or manufactured ones, and how the nature of web questions has changed over time.
AI.method: They extract 13.4 billion question occurrences from 110 temporal snapshots of the FineWeb crawl spanning 2013–2025. Using features like question length and surrounding context (rather than question type), they train a logistic classifier to distinguish genuine user questions from templated/manufactured questions and evaluate it via AUC. They then analyze question frequency distributions and temporal trends in provenance, length, and context, controlling for crawl composition, to measure how the share and characteristics of genuine questions evolve over time.
AI.result: 1) Provenance strongly affects question form: a simple logistic model can separate genuine user questions from templated ones with an AUC of 0.725, although performance drops to 0.554 when distinguishing from commerce FAQ-style writing. 2) Frequency of question strings is a poor proxy for user demand because over 70% of the top 1,000 most frequent questions are boilerplate or templated, indicating that counts reflect how often content is published, not how often humans ask it. 3) From 2013 to 2025, the share of genuine questions among web question occurrences falls by 79% (42–56% decline after controlling for crawl composition), accompanied by shorter questions and less informative surrounding context.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that a large and growing portion of web questions are not genuine user queries but manufactured artifacts, often optimized for machines (e.g., SEO, FAQs) rather than reflecting real human intent. Question occurrence frequency on the web is therefore an unreliable measure of information demand, and assumptions underlying many QA datasets, retrieval benchmarks, and content strategies need to be revisited. The authors provide the first large-scale, diachronic, occurrence-level analysis of web question provenance and show a systematic shift from human-asked to machine-targeted questions on the crawlable web.

title: Re:CAP - Auditing Retrieval Coverage in Production RAG Pipelines
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is hard to monitor in production: exhaustive relevance labels do not exist for non-stationary multi-million-passage corpora that re-index in real time. As a result, retrieval quality is generally understudied and often deprioritised in favour of generation-oriented metrics. In this work, we propose auditing retrieval coverage by probing for evidence of missing documents rather than enumerating every relevant one. Our method Re:CAP (REtrieval Coverage Audit by iterative Probing) is a reference-free audit loop applied to a deployed RAG pipeline's initial answer and retrieved context: it identifies the topics already covered, generates probing questions for plausibly missing topics, retrieves candidate documents, and applies an LLM-as-judge to retain only those that introduce previously-unretrieved information. On four public benchmarks, Re:CAP recovers 9-29% of gold labels that flat BM25 top-500 cannot reach, rising to 48% on TREC-COVID. On MuSiQue Re:CAP beats flat hybrid top-500 by +12.9 pp on recall at less than half the document budget. An ensemble BM25, dense, and hybrid baseline (top-500 each) still leaves out 21.2% of gold docs on TREC-COVID that Re:CAP recovers; human annotators judge that 78.9% of those structurally distinct documents add new information to the baseline answer (Fleiss $κ$ = 0.79, n = 123), and 73.9% on live production traffic (n = 180). End-to-end recall is reproducible to within $\pm$1% across three independent runs, making Re:CAP a stable instrument for periodic retrieval audits.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Re:CAP, a method to audit retrieval coverage in RAG systems by probing for missing information instead of exhaustively labeling all relevant documents.
AI.motivation: In production RAG systems with huge, constantly changing corpora, it is infeasible to obtain exhaustive relevance labels, so retrieval quality is poorly monitored and often ignored in favor of generation metrics. The authors want a practical way to assess and improve how much relevant information retrieval actually surfaces, without needing full ground truth.
AI.method: Re:CAP is a reference-free audit loop that operates on a deployed RAG pipeline. Starting from the system’s initial answer and retrieved context, it: (1) infers what topics are already covered; (2) generates probing questions for potentially missing topics; (3) retrieves candidate documents for these probes; and (4) uses an LLM-as-judge to keep only documents that introduce information not present in the original retrieved set. This process estimates and improves retrieval coverage without enumerating all relevant docs.
AI.result: On four public benchmarks, Re:CAP surfaces many relevant documents missed by strong baselines. It recovers 9–29% of gold labels that a flat BM25 top-500 baseline cannot, and up to 48% on TREC-COVID. On MuSiQue, it outperforms a flat hybrid top-500 baseline by +12.9 percentage points in recall while using less than half the document budget. Even when compared to an ensemble of BM25, dense, and hybrid retrievers (top-500 each), Re:CAP still finds 21.2% more gold documents on TREC-COVID. Human annotators confirm that most of these additional documents add genuinely new information, and the audit’s recall is stable across runs (within ±1%).
AI.conclusion: Re:CAP provides a practical, stable, and reference-free way to audit retrieval coverage in RAG pipelines by actively probing for missing information. It significantly increases recall over strong retrieval baselines while maintaining a reasonable document budget, and human studies validate that the extra documents usually contribute new, useful content. This makes Re:CAP suitable as a periodic auditing tool for monitoring and improving retrieval components in production RAG systems.

title: TAC-Time: Texts as Channels For Multimodal Time Series Forecasting
summary: Most existing time series forecasting methods rely solely on numerical observations, overlooking rich contextual information from auxiliary texts. Recent multimodal approaches attempt to incorporate textual signals, but they often treat text as static features or use large language models as forecasting backbones, limiting their ability to capture temporal dynamics and increasing computational cost. To address these challenges, we propose TAC-Time, a unified framework that transforms textual information into additional temporal channels. By modeling text features jointly with numerical sequences in a shared temporal backbone, TAC-Time preserves temporal continuity and periodic structures while remaining efficient and scalable. This formulation also enables systematic interpretability analyses. We show strong cross-modal dependencies through attention and frequency-domain analyses, and identify predictive textual signals whose correlation-aware alignment yields partial forecasting improvements. Extensive experiments on real-world multimodal benchmarks demonstrate that TAC-Time outperforms prior methods.

AI.tldr: TAC-Time is a multimodal time series forecasting framework that converts text into temporal channels and models them jointly with numerical series to improve accuracy and interpretability efficiently.
AI.motivation: Existing time series forecasting models largely ignore auxiliary textual context or treat it as static features. Recent multimodal methods either bolt on text features without temporal structure or use large language models as forecasting backbones, which struggle to capture temporal dynamics properly and are computationally expensive. There is a need for an efficient, scalable way to integrate time-varying textual information into forecasting while respecting temporal continuity and enabling interpretability.
AI.method: TAC-Time transforms text associated with each time step into temporal feature channels, aligning them with numerical time series. Both modalities are fed into a shared temporal backbone that explicitly models temporal continuity and periodic patterns. The design allows standard temporal architectures to jointly process numeric and textual signals. The framework supports interpretability via attention analysis and frequency-domain analysis to examine cross-modal dependencies and identify predictive text patterns.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world multimodal forecasting benchmarks show that TAC-Time consistently outperforms existing unimodal and multimodal baselines. Analyses reveal strong cross-modal dependencies between textual and numerical channels. By aligning and leveraging predictive textual cues in a correlation-aware way, TAC-Time yields measurable improvements in forecasting accuracy over prior approaches.
AI.conclusion: TAC-Time offers an efficient, unified, and interpretable framework for multimodal time series forecasting that incorporates text as a sequence of temporal channels rather than static features or heavy language-model backbones. This approach better preserves temporal structure, reveals meaningful cross-modal relationships, and achieves superior performance on real-world datasets while remaining scalable.

title: Efficient LLM Distillation for Bangladesh Legal Context: A Smartphone-Compatible Retrieval-Augmented Generation Model
summary: Legal information in Bangladesh is inaccessible to most citizens. Statutory text is English-only, trained lawyers are concentrated in urban centres, and cloud-dependent AI fails where mobile connectivity is unreliable, a setting in which hallucinated legal text causes direct harm. The system addresses statutory interpretation only; queries that require judicial precedent or case-law reasoning fall outside its scope. We target the statutory access gap by compressing a 9-billion-parameter Gemma-2 teacher into a 2-billion-parameter student through two-phase progressive knowledge distillation. Phase 1 performs supervised fine-tuning on 9,429 quality-gated legal question-answer pairs (65% acceptance from 14,514 generated queries); Phase 2 minimises sparse Kullback-Leibler divergence against the teacher's top-50 per-token logits at temperature tau = 4.0, implemented via QLoRA (4-bit NF4, rank-32 LoRA adapters). Prior legal language models target general legal English; this system specialises in Bangladeshi statutory law. Every response is grounded through hybrid retrieval combining dense semantic search (60%) and BM25 (40%) across 36,029 statutory passages from the Bangladesh Constitution and national legislation. On a 50-query English benchmark, the distilled model reaches ROUGE-L 0.4715 and BERTScore F1 0.5679, a 103% ROUGE-L and 143% BERTScore gain over the retrieval-augmented undistilled baseline (ROUGE-L 0.2323, BERTScore 0.2340). The adapter quantises to 1.6 GB (GGUF Q4_K_M) and runs at 4-8 tokens per second on a Pixel 6 with no network access. Cross-lingual evaluation on 50 Bangla queries yields ROUGE-L 0.4083 and BERTScore 0.8133, showing effective retrieval from Bangla input against an English-only corpus. In a single-evaluator pilot, a practising lawyer rated 50 responses at a weighted mean of 4.16/5 (90% rated 4 or 5), supporting utility beyond text-overlap metrics.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a small, offline legal-qa model for Bangladeshi statutory law by distilling a large model, paired with hybrid retrieval, to reliably answer statute-based questions on edge devices.
AI.motivation: Most Bangladeshi citizens lack practical access to statutory law: the laws are only in English, lawyers are concentrated in cities, and typical large AI systems need the cloud and may hallucinate, which is dangerous in legal settings. There is also a gap in models specialized specifically for Bangladeshi statutes rather than generic legal English. The authors want a compact, offline, and safer system focused on statutory interpretation that ordinary users can access via mobile devices, even with poor connectivity.
AI.method: They perform progressive knowledge distillation from a 9B-parameter Gemma-2 teacher to a 2B-parameter student. Phase 1 is supervised fine-tuning on 9,429 curated legal QA pairs generated then quality-filtered from an initial pool of 14,514 questions. Phase 2 is distillation via minimizing a sparse KL-divergence between the student’s predictions and the teacher’s top-50 logits per token at temperature 4.0, implemented with QLoRA (4-bit NF4, rank-32 LoRA adapters). The model is coupled with a hybrid retrieval system over 36,029 English statutory passages from the Bangladesh Constitution and national laws, using a weighted combination of dense semantic search (60%) and BM25 (40%). The final system is quantized to a small GGUF Q4_K_M adapter that can run on-device (e.g., a Pixel 6) without network access.
AI.result: On a 50-query English benchmark, the distilled model achieves ROUGE-L 0.4715 and BERTScore F1 0.5679, which is a 103% ROUGE-L and 143% BERTScore improvement over a retrieval-augmented but undistilled baseline (ROUGE-L 0.2323, BERTScore 0.2340). For 50 Bangla queries against the same English-only corpus, the system attains ROUGE-L 0.4083 and BERTScore 0.8133, indicating strong cross-lingual retrieval and answer quality. A single practising lawyer evaluated 50 answers and gave a weighted mean rating of 4.16/5, with 90% of responses scoring 4 or 5, suggesting practical usefulness beyond automatic text-overlap metrics. The model runs at 4–8 tokens per second on a Pixel 6 with a 1.6GB quantized adapter and no internet.
AI.conclusion: A compact, edge-deployable legal QA model tailored to Bangladeshi statutory law can be obtained via two-phase distillation from a larger teacher model, combined with hybrid retrieval, while remaining accurate and practically useful. The approach substantially outperforms an undistilled baseline, works cross-lingually from Bangla queries to an English corpus, and runs fully offline on consumer hardware, offering a promising way to close statutory access gaps in low-connectivity environments.

title: When Residualization Helps an Audit: Format Effects, Slice Gains, and Their Limits
summary: Evaluation scores used around LLM systems -- including reward models, rerankers, and LLM judges -- can track surface form instead of the quality they claim to measure. When presented with a terse correct solution and a commented buggy solution for the same MBPP problem, a public preference reward model selects the correct one no better than a coin flip (0.507). Subtracting the predictable surface component from such scores is increasingly common, but removal alone does not yield a more valid measurement: the removed component may carry construct-relevant signal, and residualization cannot tell which is which. Under designed interventions -- unit-test labels with comment-only edits -- residualization attenuates the reward model's format effects by about 0.12 on both correct and buggy code, while the correct-versus-buggy margins move by less than 0.01. In observational NLI and QA settings, we freeze a held-out replication before scoring and re-evaluate it using labels from disjoint annotators; this supports only a narrower conclusion: better agreement with the construct labels on a pre-declared slice where a surface-only predictor errs, not a repaired score. Full-population agreement falls in every observational setting with a reported positive slice gain, and within-question ranking falls in every such QA setting. When construct and surface features are entangled, residualization can decorrelate a score while degrading construct alignment, and, in a controlled model, configurations just as damaging to construct alignment pass every pre-adjustment check, so no committed gate is a guarantee. We assemble these distinctions into a reporting protocol whose outcomes, refusal included, state what an adjusted score may be claimed to show: an audit-time diagnostic reported beside the construct-alignment cost it incurs, never a replacement for the raw score.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that common techniques for removing superficial format biases from LLM-based evaluation scores (like reward models and LLM judges) often fail to improve and can even harm alignment with the true quality they are supposed to measure.
AI.motivation: LLM-centered systems rely heavily on learned evaluation scores (reward models, rerankers, LLM judges) to guide training, selection, and deployment. However, these scores can be sensitive to superficial surface features (like verbosity, comments, or formatting) instead of the underlying construct (e.g., correctness, reasoning quality). A growing practice is to "residualize" scores—subtracting out predictable surface components—to debias them. The authors are motivated by the concern that this is treated as a fix without sufficient evidence that it actually improves construct validity, and may instead discard useful signal or even degrade true alignment while only decorrelating from surface proxies.
AI.method: 1) Construct an experimental setting using MBPP code problems where they contrast terse correct solutions with commented buggy solutions and measure how a public preference reward model ranks them. 2) Apply designed interventions by editing comments only while holding unit-test labels fixed, to isolate superficial format effects from true correctness. 3) Perform residualization on reward model scores to remove predictable variance due to surface features, and then analyze how this affects (a) sensitivity to format and (b) separation between correct and buggy code. 4) In observational NLI and QA datasets, compute scores on an initial label set, freeze a held-out replication, and later rescore using independently annotated labels to check whether residualized scores better align with construct labels, especially on pre-declared slices where a surface-only predictor fails. 5) Analyze how residualization influences overall agreement with construct labels, within-question ranking quality, and correlations with surface predictors, including via a controlled model that allows them to explore configurations where surface and construct features are entangled.
AI.result: 1) In MBPP, the preference reward model distinguishes terse correct from commented buggy solutions at about chance (0.507), showing high susceptibility to surface cues. 2) Designed comment-only interventions show that residualization reduces format effects by about 0.12 on both correct and buggy code, but does not meaningfully improve correct-versus-buggy separation (margins shift by <0.01). 3) In observational NLI and QA settings, residualization yields only narrow benefits: it improves agreement with construct labels on pre-declared slices where a surface-only predictor errs, but does not produce a reliably better global score. 4) Whenever a positive slice gain is reported, overall agreement with labels over the full population decreases, and within-question ranking performance in QA also consistently falls. 5) In a controlled model where construct and surface features are entangled, they show that residualization can decorrelate scores from surface proxies while simultaneously harming alignment with the construct, and that even configurations with severe construct damage can pass all pre-adjustment checks used to justify residualization.
AI.conclusion: Residualization of LLM evaluation scores—subtracting off predictable surface components—cannot be treated as a generic, safe fix for format or style biases. Because construct-relevant and surface features are entangled, residualization may remove useful signal, reduce agreement with true quality labels, and degrade within-task ranking, even when diagnostic checks suggest success. The authors recommend that adjusted scores be framed only as audit-time diagnostics, always accompanied by an explicit accounting of the construct-alignment cost, and never presented as a full replacement for raw scores. They propose a reporting protocol that makes these distinctions clear and encourages explicit refusal to treat adjusted scores as repaired measures when evidence is insufficient.

title: LoopCD: Loop-wise Contrastive Decoding for Improving Reasoning in Looped Language Models
summary: Looped Language Models (LoopLMs) perform "latent reasoning" by recursively refining internal latent representations with shared weights, offering a more effective alternative to explicit verbal reasoning. Despite their effectiveness, we find that LoopLMs remain prone to loop instability: unstable refinement across iterations can produce localized uncertain "hard" tokens associated with reasoning errors. To address this, we propose LoopCD, loop-wise contrastive decoding that enhances the reasoning performance of LoopLMs by intervening on these tokens at inference time. Specifically, we exploit the internal dynamics of LoopLMs and contrast the logits from earlier iterations with logits from the last refined iteration to form the final sampling distribution. We find that this strategy is highly efficient, introducing only negligible inference overhead and requiring no additional training, while effectively improving reasoning performance by naturally refining reasoning-critical hard tokens. Extensive experiments show that our method improves the performance of recent representative LoopLMs across various reasoning tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces LoopCD, a contrastive decoding method for Looped Language Models that stabilizes their iterative latent reasoning and improves performance without extra training.
AI.motivation: Looped Language Models refine latent representations over multiple iterations and can outperform explicit chain-of-thought reasoning, but they suffer from loop instability. This instability manifests as localized uncertain “hard” tokens that correlate with reasoning errors. There is a need for an inference-time method that leverages the internal loop dynamics to correct these unstable tokens without retraining the model.
AI.method: The authors propose LoopCD (loop-wise contrastive decoding). During inference, they run the LoopLM for multiple refinement iterations. They then identify and intervene on reasoning-critical hard tokens by contrasting the token logits from earlier iterations with those from the final refined iteration. By forming a new sampling distribution that combines or contrasts these logits across iterations, LoopCD downweights unstable, error-prone predictions and refines the final output. The method is purely an inference-time modification, requires no additional training, and adds minimal computational overhead.
AI.result: LoopCD significantly improves reasoning performance of various recent LoopLMs on multiple reasoning benchmarks. It effectively stabilizes loop dynamics and reduces errors associated with hard tokens, with only negligible additional inference cost and without modifying model weights.
AI.conclusion: LoopCD is an efficient, training-free decoding strategy that exploits the iterative internal dynamics of LoopLMs to mitigate loop instability. By contrastively combining logits across iterations, it naturally refines uncertain, reasoning-critical tokens, leading to consistent gains in reasoning tasks for modern LoopLMs with minimal overhead.

title: Vimarsha: Faithful ASR Evaluation for Indian Languages with Demographic Diversity, In-the-Wild Audio and Spelling Variations
summary: Evaluation benchmarks for Indian language automatic speech recognition (ASR) suffer from two systematic biases: optimistic scores from clean, controlled audio conditions, and pessimistic scores from overly rigid transcription standards that penalize valid linguistic variations. We introduce Vimarsha, a 100-hour benchmark spanning all 22 scheduled Indian languages, designed to address both distortions. Vimarsha combines demographically diverse on-field recordings with carefully mined in-the-wild audio selected for acoustic difficulty, alongside a lattice of variations framework that encodes multiple valid transcriptions per utterance. Evaluations of 10 state-of-the-art ASR models reveal substantial shifts in model rankings under realistic conditions, geographic and demographic performance disparities, and systematic failure modes across speaking rates and acoustic environments.

AI.tldr: The paper presents Vimarsha, a 100-hour, 22-language benchmark for Indian language ASR that uses realistic, diverse audio and flexible transcription matching to give fairer, more informative evaluations.
AI.motivation: Existing Indian language ASR benchmarks are biased: they overestimate performance by using clean, controlled recordings, and underestimate it by enforcing rigid transcriptions that treat valid linguistic variants as errors. This misrepresents true ASR capabilities and obscures practical limitations, especially across different regions and demographics.
AI.method: The authors construct Vimarsha, a benchmark covering all 22 scheduled Indian languages, by (1) collecting demographically diverse field recordings, (2) mining challenging in-the-wild audio specifically chosen for acoustic difficulty, and (3) introducing a "lattice of variations" framework that encodes multiple acceptable transcriptions per utterance to account for legitimate linguistic variation. They then evaluate 10 state-of-the-art ASR systems on this benchmark.
AI.result: When tested on Vimarsha, 10 leading ASR models show large changes in their relative rankings compared to standard, cleaner benchmarks. The results reveal significant geographic and demographic disparities in performance, as well as consistent failure modes related to speaking rate and acoustic conditions.
AI.conclusion: More realistic, variation-aware benchmarks like Vimarsha provide a more accurate picture of ASR performance for Indian languages, uncovering biases and weaknesses that cleaner, rigid benchmarks hide. This benchmark can guide fairer evaluation, better model development, and targeted improvements for diverse speakers and challenging acoustic environments.

title: From Articles to Publishers: Aggregating Language Model Predictions for News Source Reliability Inference
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Computational Social Systems (TCSS)
summary: Traditionally, the reliability of news publishers is assessed by expert organisations that evaluate editorial practices, transparency and factual standards at source. When this process is translated into a computational approach, the problem is often formulated at the level of individual articles, with models being trained on a set of pre-labelled articles and their performance being evaluated in a test phase. In this work, we investigate news source reliability inference as a source-level prediction problem. We propose a two-stage framework in which transformer-based language models first estimate the reliability of individual articles and subsequently aggregate article-level predictions to infer the reliability of previously unseen publishers. To approximate realistic deployment conditions, we enforce a strict publisher-disjoint evaluation protocol, ensuring that no publisher appears in both training and test sets. Experiments on 19,476 political news articles from 439 English-language publishers labeled with NewsGuard reliability ratings show that aggregation substantially improves robustness and performance, increasing accuracy from approximately 0.60 at the article level to 0.69 at the publisher level. Finally, we analyze how prediction errors vary across political orientations, revealing statistically significant associations between political leaning and misclassification patterns. Overall, our findings show that publisher reliability can be inferred from aggregated textual signals alone, supporting scalable and content-based approaches to automated news source assessment.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and evaluates a two-stage, source-level framework to infer news publisher reliability by aggregating transformer-based article predictions under publisher-disjoint evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing reliability assessments rely on expert organizations and manual source-level judgments, while computational work often focuses on classifying individual articles. This mismatch leads to models that may not generalize well to unseen publishers and ignores that reliability is fundamentally a property of sources, not just articles. The authors aim to design a method and evaluation setup that better reflect real-world deployment, where one wants automated, scalable, content-based reliability assessments for publishers that have not been previously labeled.
AI.method: They conceptualize reliability prediction as a source-level task and introduce a two-stage framework. First, transformer-based language models are trained to estimate the reliability of individual news articles using labels derived from NewsGuard’s publisher ratings. Second, these article-level predictions are aggregated (e.g., via averaging or similar schemes) to generate a reliability estimate for each publisher, including previously unseen ones. To simulate realistic deployment, they impose a strict publisher-disjoint split between training and test data, so no publisher’s articles appear in both sets. They then run experiments on 19,476 English-language political news articles from 439 publishers, comparing article-level vs. aggregated publisher-level performance, and analyze misclassification patterns by political orientation.
AI.result: On the NewsGuard-labeled dataset, article-level reliability prediction achieves about 0.60 accuracy. When article predictions are aggregated at the publisher level, accuracy increases to about 0.69, showing that source-level aggregation boosts robustness and performance. The evaluation protocol confirms that the model can generalize to unseen publishers under publisher-disjoint splits. Further analysis reveals that prediction errors are not uniform across the political spectrum: there are statistically significant associations between a publisher’s political leaning and the model’s misclassification behavior.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that publisher reliability can be inferred reasonably well from textual content alone by aggregating article-level transformer predictions, without direct access to editorial metadata or manual source-level reviews. This supports scalable, automated, content-based approaches to assessing news source reliability and highlights the importance of modeling reliability at the source level under publisher-disjoint evaluation. The observed dependence of errors on political orientation suggests that future work should explicitly address and mitigate such biases when deploying automated reliability systems.

title: Memory vs. Context? Influential Factors of Factual Recall in Language Models
comment: Accepted to the BlackboxNLP 2026 Reproducibility Challenge (Special Track), EMNLP 2026
summary: We reproduce and stress-test the work of Yu et al. (2023), who characterize how language models (LMs) arbitrate between memorized knowledge and contradictory in-context statements. We replicate their world-capitals experiments on 31 models spanning Pythia, GPT-2, Qwen3, and Ministral families, including base and post-trained variants, and extend evaluations to five additional knowledge relation types from the ParaConflict dataset. We empirically confirm most of their original findings: larger models and higher-frequency entities tend to favor memorized answers, with substantial family-level variance. However, several conclusions do not generalize cleanly: entity-frequency effects disappear on Qwen3-14B and 32B; post-training shifts the memory-context trade-off inconsistently across families; question phrasing alone can change a model's reliance on memorized knowledge by up to 80 percentage points; and semantically unrelated prose can mimic coherent supporting context. Our results clarify where Yu et al.'s claims hold and to what extent they generalize to other prompts.

AI.tldr: The paper stress-tests and extends Yu et al. (2023) on how language models choose between memorized knowledge and conflicting in-context information, showing which findings generalize and which break under broader models, relations, and prompt variations.
AI.motivation: Yu et al. (2023) suggested systematic patterns in how LMs arbitrate between their parametric memory and contradictory context, but their evidence was limited to specific models, a narrow task (world capitals), and one kind of knowledge relation. Given rapid model evolution and the importance of understanding LM reliability under conflicting information, there is a need to test whether those patterns are robust across model families, sizes, post-training regimes, and more diverse knowledge types and prompts.
AI.method: The authors replicate Yu et al.’s world-capitals setup on 31 language models from Pythia, GPT-2, Qwen3, and Ministral, covering both base and post-trained versions. They then extend the evaluations to five other types of factual relations drawn from the ParaConflict dataset. Across these conditions, they systematically vary entity frequency, model size, post-training status, and prompt phrasing, and also test the effect of inserting semantically unrelated yet coherent prose that superficially resembles supporting context. They compare models’ tendencies to output memorized answers vs. in-context contradictory statements.
AI.result: They largely confirm the original observations that bigger models and higher-frequency entities are more likely to stick with memorized facts and that these patterns differ substantially across model families. However, they also uncover several non-robust aspects: for Qwen3-14B and 32B, the relation between entity frequency and preference for memorized knowledge vanishes; post-training alters the memory vs. context trade-off in inconsistent, family-dependent ways; variations in question wording alone can swing reliance on memorized knowledge by up to 80 percentage points; and even semantically unrelated but well-formed prose can be misinterpreted as supportive context, shifting the model’s answers.
AI.conclusion: The paper shows that while some of Yu et al.’s findings about memory vs. context arbitration are reproducible, many do not generalize across modern model families, relation types, and prompt styles. Model behavior is highly sensitive to architecture, training and post-training procedures, and subtle prompt changes. This calls for caution when extrapolating from narrow experimental setups and suggests that reliable characterization of LM memory-context trade-offs must account for family-specific effects, prompt dependence, and vulnerability to spurious contextual cues.

title: Taramandal-GPT: Enhancing Astrodynamics Problem-Solving with Knowledge Retrieval and Structured Thinking
comment: Proceedings of All India Hindi Technical Conference, 05-06 February 2026
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable progress in natural language understanding, yet their effectiveness in specialized fields like astronomy and astrodynamics remains limited due to challenges in multi-step reasoning, symbolic manipulation, and domain-specific terminology. To address this, we present Taramandal-GPT (Constellation-GPT), a domain-adapted framework built on the Qwen3-8b backbone, enhanced with a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline and a fallback mechanism for improved contextual precision. We evaluate it on the Astrodynamics Problems Benchmark (APBench), a dataset of 299 questions covering foundational to advanced levels of space science. Using a dual evaluation method - numeric margin-based scoring and semantic similarity assessment - Taramandal-GPT achieves competitive performance against state-of-the-art open- and closed-source models, with notable strength in thinking-intensive tasks. These results highlight the value of specialized LLMs for domains demanding accuracy and interpretability, positioning Taramandal-GPT as a step toward reliable Artificial Intelligence (AI) assistants for astrophysics, spacecraft engineering, and space exploration.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Taramandal-GPT, an astronomy- and astrodynamics-focused large language model that combines domain adaptation with retrieval-augmented generation and a fallback mechanism, achieving competitive performance on a dedicated astrodynamics benchmark.
AI.motivation: General-purpose LLMs struggle with multi-step reasoning, symbolic manipulation, and domain-specific terminology in specialized fields like astronomy and astrodynamics. There is a need for more accurate and interpretable AI tools that can handle complex, technical tasks in these domains, such as astrophysics research, spacecraft engineering, and mission design.
AI.method: The authors build Taramandal-GPT on top of the Qwen3-8b model and adapt it to the astronomy/astrodynamics domain. They integrate a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline so the model can consult external, domain-relevant knowledge, and add a fallback mechanism to improve contextual precision when primary reasoning is uncertain. They evaluate the system on the Astrodynamics Problems Benchmark (APBench), containing 299 questions from basic to advanced levels, and use two evaluation strategies: (1) numeric margin-based scoring for quantitative answers and (2) semantic similarity assessment for more open-ended responses.
AI.result: On APBench, Taramandal-GPT performs competitively with state-of-the-art open- and closed-source LLMs. It shows particular strength on tasks that require intensive reasoning, indicating that the combination of domain adaptation and RAG improves the model’s ability to handle complex astrodynamics and astronomy problems.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that specialized LLMs, when combined with retrieval and careful evaluation, can significantly improve performance in technical, high-precision domains. Taramandal-GPT is positioned as a promising step toward reliable AI assistants for astrophysics, spacecraft engineering, and space exploration, emphasizing the importance of domain-focused adaptation for accuracy and interpretability.

title: Canonical Procedural Actions: An Auditable Annotation Protocol for Tool-Use Agent Traces
comment: 23 pages, 5 figures, 9 tables. Includes ancillary files for reproducing the reported analyses
summary: Tool-use agent traces identify messages and API calls, but procedural analyses also need explicit units of action and inspectable links to their evidence. We present Canonical Procedural Actions (CPAs), an annotation protocol that records a procedural function, its first agent-event anchor, the agent events that realize it, and separate contextual evidence. Multiple actions may share a message anchor without an inferred within-message order. A retail case study produces a versioned 24-entry codebook through open induction, recorded consolidation, and successive application audits. Two isolated LLM contexts annotate 32 trajectories disjoint from development at the trajectory level, producing 499 and 491 occurrences with anchor-label overlap A=0.982. Requiring identical context-event references reduces overlap to 0.798. These are structural repeatability measures, not semantic accuracy: 16 of 26 task IDs also occur in development, and historical tool payloads were truncated to 110 characters. Retrospective controls show that collapsing all labels raises overlap to 0.986, while simple endpoint rules reproduce the tool-anchored portion with 0.997 overlap. Assistant-message actions have 0.971 overlap, with a per-label minimum of 0.816. Applying the frozen codebook to 244 further trajectories yields 4,058 records, including eight diagnostic outcomes. The contribution is an explicit, auditable annotation instrument and a case study of its construction and measurement limits; human-reference validity and downstream utility remain to be established.

AI.tldr: Introduces Canonical Procedural Actions (CPAs), an annotation protocol to structurally capture and reliably repeat how tool-using agents perform procedural actions, and reports a retail case study showing high structural repeatability but leaving semantic validity for future work.
AI.motivation: Existing tool-use agent traces log messages and API calls but are insufficient for procedural analysis, which needs finer-grained, explicit units of action and traceable links to their supporting evidence. There is a lack of a standardized, auditable way to annotate these procedural actions so they can be analyzed, compared, and measured for reliability across annotators or models.
AI.method: The authors design Canonical Procedural Actions (CPAs), an annotation scheme that encodes each action with: (1) a procedural function label, (2) its first agent-event anchor, (3) the set of agent events that realize it, and (4) separate contextual evidence. They perform a retail-domain case study, developing a 24-entry action codebook via open induction, consolidation, and iterative audits. Two independent LLM-based annotators, operating in isolated contexts and on trajectories unseen during development, annotate 32 trajectories, generating ~500 CPA occurrences each. They then compute overlap metrics between the two CPA sets at different strictness levels (shared anchor labels, identical context-event references, and various control baselines). They finally freeze the codebook and apply it to 244 additional trajectories to test scalability and generate diagnostic outcome categories.
AI.result: In the main reliability experiment, the two independent annotation runs yield 499 and 491 CPA instances, with an anchor-label agreement (A) of 0.982, indicating very high structural consistency in assigning labels to anchors. When requiring identical context-event references as well, agreement drops to 0.798, showing that more detailed structural alignment is harder. Controls show that trivial labeling baselines can achieve very high apparent overlap (0.986 when all labels are collapsed; 0.997 for tool-anchored actions with simple endpoint rules), highlighting that overlap is primarily a structural repeatability metric rather than a semantic one. Assistant-message actions show 0.971 overlap overall, with the weakest individual label still at 0.816. Applying the finalized 24-label codebook to 244 new trajectories produces 4,058 CPA records and eight categories of diagnostic outcomes, indicating the procedure scales and exposes where the scheme struggles.
AI.conclusion: The study delivers an explicit, auditable annotation protocol for procedural actions in tool-use traces and demonstrates that LLM-based annotators can apply it with high structural repeatability in a retail case study. However, the reported metrics primarily capture structural agreement, not semantic correctness or human-grounded validity. The authors emphasize that establishing human-reference validity, understanding semantic accuracy, and assessing the downstream utility of CPA-based annotations for system evaluation or control remain open work.

title: Structure Before Sampling: Community-Aware Core-Set Selection for Data-Efficient Text-to-Speech
summary: Text-to-speech (TTS) corpora are costly to record, yet many utterances add little new phonetic information. Core-set selection reduces this cost by choosing a small training subset under a fixed audio-duration budget. We represent a corpus as a phonotactic graph that links each utterance to its most phonemically similar ones, and we first test whether this graph has structure. In Bangla and English corpora, its clustering is 199 and 56 times that of a size-matched random graph, and its modularity is more than twice that of a degree-preserving random graph. We then propose Community Representative, a selector that samples across graph communities and spreads its choices within each one, starting from utterances rich in rare phonemes. At every budget and in both languages, it covers more rare phoneme bigrams than random and entropy-based selection, and this lead holds on held-out utterances. TTS models trained on its 20% core-sets have a significantly lower character error rate (CER) than models trained on equal-duration random or entropy-based subsets in both languages. When all models train for the same number of epochs, the Bangla core-set model also outperforms full-corpus training (3.93% vs. 4.47% CER) with 4.5x less training time.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a graph-based core-set selection method for TTS corpora that greatly reduces data collection and training cost while improving or matching model performance.
AI.motivation: Recording large, high-quality TTS corpora is expensive, yet many recorded utterances are redundant and add little new phonetic information. Existing subset selection approaches (e.g., random or entropy-based) do not explicitly exploit the phonotactic structure of the corpus or focus on rare phonetic events, leading to inefficient use of recording and training budgets. The authors aim to formalize and exploit the inherent structure in TTS corpora to select smaller but more informative subsets that preserve phonetic diversity, especially rare phoneme combinations, and thus reduce cost without sacrificing (or even improving) TTS model quality.
AI.method: The authors first model TTS corpora (Bangla and English) as phonotactic graphs, where nodes are utterances and edges connect phonemically similar utterances. They quantify the structural properties of these graphs using clustering coefficients and modularity, comparing them to random and degree-preserving random graphs to show non-trivial structure. Building on this, they propose a core-set selection algorithm called Community Representative. This method identifies communities in the phonotactic graph, then selects utterances by (1) prioritizing those rich in rare phonemes and (2) sampling across communities and spreading selections within each community. They compare this method with random and entropy-based selection, under fixed audio-duration budgets, evaluating coverage of rare phoneme bigrams and downstream TTS model performance (character error rate) on held-out data.
AI.result: The phonotactic graphs for both Bangla and English corpora show strong structure: clustering coefficients are 199x (Bangla) and 56x (English) higher than size-matched random graphs, and modularity is more than double that of degree-preserving random graphs. The proposed Community Representative selector consistently covers more rare phoneme bigrams than random or entropy-based methods at all budget levels and in both languages, including on held-out utterances. TTS models trained on 20% core-sets selected by Community Representative achieve significantly lower character error rates than models trained on equal-duration random or entropy-based subsets in both languages. In Bangla, when all models are trained for the same number of epochs, the core-set model even outperforms a model trained on the full corpus (3.93% vs. 4.47% CER) while requiring 4.5x less training time.
AI.conclusion: TTS corpora exhibit strong phonotactic structure that can be exploited for efficient subset selection. By modeling the corpus as a phonotactic graph and selecting community-representative utterances that emphasize rare phonemes, it is possible to build much smaller core-sets that retain or enhance phonetic coverage. The proposed Community Representative method consistently improves coverage of rare phoneme bigrams and yields better or comparable TTS model performance relative to larger or naively selected datasets, delivering significant savings in recording and training time. This suggests that structured, graph-based core-set selection is a practical and effective way to reduce TTS data and compute costs while improving quality.

title: Mitigating Entity Type Confusion in Cross-Domain NER via Multidimensional Quantification and Reasoning Enhancement
summary: Cross-domain Named Entity Recognition (CD-NER) aims to transfer the rich knowledge in the source domain to the target domain. Recent studies adopting decomposition or generation paradigms have achieved significant performance improvements, demonstrating high accuracy in entity span detection. However, during entity type classification, models severely suffer from entity type confusion, the erroneous tendency that models classify entities of one type in the text as another similar but incorrect type. To address this issue, we first propose a Multidimensional Confusion Quantification Model (MCQM) that quantifies a model's confusion extent between entity types from three dimensions: source-target hierarchy analysis, semantic similarity analysis, and explicit data evaluation. Moreover, we propose the Progressive Bidirectional Reasoning Chain (PBRC). PBRC leverages the source-target hierarchy and confusion analysis from the MCQM to prompt the LLM to generate two-stage reasoning information. The two-stage reasoning information is utilized to augment the knowledge of the model, significantly mitigating entity type confusion and improving the model's generalization performance. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves new state-of-the-art results on all domains of the CrossNER dataset.

AI.tldr: They propose a method to reduce entity type confusion in cross-domain NER by quantifying confusion and guiding an LLM with structured reasoning, achieving SOTA on CrossNER.
AI.motivation: In cross-domain NER, even when models can accurately detect entity spans, they frequently misclassify the entity types (e.g., confusing similar labels). Existing decomposition/generation methods improve span detection but do not adequately address this type confusion, which harms generalization to new domains. The authors aim to explicitly characterize and reduce this entity type confusion to improve cross-domain transfer.
AI.method: 1) They design a Multidimensional Confusion Quantification Model (MCQM) that measures how much a model confuses each pair of entity types using three perspectives: (a) source–target hierarchy analysis of the label spaces, (b) semantic similarity between types, and (c) explicit evaluation on data to observe empirical confusions. 2) Based on MCQM, they introduce a Progressive Bidirectional Reasoning Chain (PBRC) for large language models. PBRC uses the hierarchy and confusion statistics to prompt the LLM to perform two-stage reasoning: progressively reasoning from source to target and reverse, generating intermediate reasoning information that clarifies type distinctions. This reasoning output is then used to augment the model’s knowledge during classification, reducing confusion when assigning entity types.
AI.result: On the CrossNER benchmark across all its domains, their approach achieves new state-of-the-art performance. The key improvement is a substantial reduction in entity type confusion, resulting in better overall CD-NER accuracy and stronger generalization than prior decomposition or generation-based baselines.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling and quantifying entity type confusion, then using that analysis to guide structured, bidirectional reasoning in an LLM, is an effective way to improve cross-domain NER. Their MCQM+PBRC framework not only mitigates confusion between similar entity types but also enhances generalization across domains, setting new SOTA results on CrossNER and suggesting that reasoning-guided knowledge augmentation is a promising direction for CD-NER.

title: URA-NER: A Unified Retrieval-Augmented Framework with Retrieval Alignment and Uncertainty Reduction for Low-Resource NER
comment: 8 pages,3 figures, accepted at IJCNN 2026, conference WCCI 2026
summary: In-context learning (ICL) based on large language models (LLMs) has shown promising potential in alleviating performance bottlenecks caused by the limited availability of annotated data in Named Entity Recognition (NER). However, existing methods still face issues of retrieval misalignment and generation uncertainty, making their performance heavily dependent on the LLM's capabilities. As the parameter scale of LLMs decreases, their performance in few-shot settings deteriorates significantly. In this paper, we propose a novel unified retrieval-augmented framework, URA-NER, including three key components: Progressive Granularity Retrieval (PGR), Model-aware Representation Enhancement (MaRE), and Reason-aware Knowledge Verification. PGR is a two-stage retrieval mechanism that achieves stage alignment. It first retrieves demonstrations for span detection based on the query's global semantics, and then for type classification based on the specific entity context, providing fine-grained local information. Moreover, MaRE employs entity pre-recognition to guide the construction of representations, ensuring the query and demonstrations are aligned within the LLM's semantic space and attention pattern. In addition, to mitigate generation uncertainty, we propose RaKV, a closed-loop "generation-retrieval-verification" process. It explicates the LLM's reasoning paths, leverages them for the retrieval of external knowledge, and reorganizes the knowledge into verification evidence aligned with the original reasoning paths. We conduct extensive experiments on multiple low-resource NER datasets. Results demonstrate that URA-NER significantly enhances the performance of LLMs under low-resource settings, with particularly pronounced gains for smaller LLMs, achieving new state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes URA-NER, a unified retrieval-augmented framework that improves low-resource NER performance of large language models, especially smaller ones, via better retrieval alignment, representation enhancement, and reasoning-based knowledge verification.
AI.motivation: In-context learning with LLMs can reduce dependence on annotated data for NER, but current ICL-based NER methods suffer from retrieval misalignment and generation uncertainty, causing performance to rely heavily on very large models and degrade sharply for smaller LLMs in few-shot settings. The paper aims to make retrieval-augmented ICL more robust and effective, particularly for smaller models and low-resource NER scenarios.
AI.method: The authors introduce URA-NER, comprising three main components: (1) Progressive Granularity Retrieval (PGR), a two-stage retrieval mechanism that first retrieves demonstrations for span detection using global semantics of the query, then retrieves demonstrations for entity type classification using local entity context; (2) Model-aware Representation Enhancement (MaRE), which uses entity pre-recognition to shape query and demonstration representations so they are well aligned in the LLM’s semantic space and attention patterns; and (3) Reason-aware Knowledge Verification (RaKV), a closed-loop generation–retrieval–verification process that extracts the LLM’s reasoning paths, retrieves external knowledge conditioned on these paths, and reorganizes the knowledge into verification evidence that is consistent with the original reasoning, thereby reducing generation uncertainty.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple low-resource NER datasets show that URA-NER significantly improves LLM performance in low-resource settings, with especially large gains for smaller LLMs. The method achieves new state-of-the-art results on several NER benchmarks in few-shot or low-resource regimes.
AI.conclusion: The proposed URA-NER framework effectively addresses retrieval misalignment and generation uncertainty in ICL-based NER. By combining progressive retrieval, model-aware representation enhancement, and reasoning-based knowledge verification, it makes retrieval-augmented NER more robust and performant, particularly for smaller LLMs and low-resource scenarios, establishing new state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks.

title: End-to-end Jordanian dialect speech-to-text self-supervised learning framework
summary: Speech-to-text engines are extremely needed nowadays for different applications, representing an essential enabler in human-robot interaction. Still, some languages suffer from the lack of labeled speech data, especially in the Arabic dialects or any low-resource languages. The need for a self-supervised training process and self-training using noisy training is proven to be one of the up-and-coming feasible solutions. This article proposes an end-to-end, transformers-based model with a framework for low-resource languages. In addition, the framework incorporates customized audio-to-text processing algorithms to achieve a highly efficient Jordanian Arabic dialect speech-to-text system. The proposed framework enables ingesting data from many sources, making the ground truth from external sources possible by speeding up the manual annotation process. The framework allows the training process using noisy student training and self-supervised learning to utilize the unlabeled data in both pre- and post-training stages and incorporate multiple types of data augmentation. The proposed self-training approach outperforms the fine-tuned Wav2Vec model by 5% in terms of word error rate reduction. The outcome of this work provides the research community with a Jordanian-spoken data set along with an end-to-end approach to deal with low-resource languages. This is done by utilizing the power of the pretraining, post-training, and injecting noisy labeled and augmented data with minimal human intervention. It enables the development of new applications in the field of Arabic language speech-to-text area like the question-answering systems and intelligent control systems, and it will add human-like perception and hearing sensors to intelligent robots.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an end-to-end transformer-based speech-to-text framework tailored for low-resource languages, demonstrated on Jordanian Arabic, that uses self-supervised and noisy student training plus data augmentation to leverage unlabeled and noisy data and surpasses a fine-tuned Wav2Vec baseline.
AI.motivation: Many languages, especially Arabic dialects and other low-resource languages, lack sufficient labeled speech data for training accurate speech-to-text systems. Manual annotation is expensive and slow, which hinders building robust ASR for applications like human-robot interaction and intelligent control. There is a need for approaches that can leverage large amounts of unlabeled or weakly labeled audio and minimize human intervention.
AI.method: The authors design an end-to-end transformer-based ASR model and a surrounding training framework for low-resource settings. The framework ingests speech from multiple sources, generates or accelerates ground-truth labels using external resources, and applies customized audio-to-text processing. It employs self-supervised learning for pretraining and noisy student training for self-training, allowing the use of unlabeled and noisily labeled data in both pre- and post-training stages. Multiple data augmentation techniques are integrated to further improve robustness. The system is instantiated for the Jordanian Arabic dialect.
AI.result: The proposed self-training approach yields a 5% relative reduction in word error rate compared with a fine-tuned Wav2Vec model baseline. It also produces and releases a Jordanian Arabic spoken dataset and demonstrates that the combined use of pretraining, post-training, noisy labels, and augmentation can effectively improve ASR performance in low-resource conditions with limited manual labeling.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that integrating transformer-based end-to-end modeling with self-supervised pretraining, noisy student self-training, and data augmentation is an effective strategy for low-resource ASR. The framework can efficiently exploit unlabeled and weakly labeled data while reducing human annotation effort, and it successfully delivers a high-performance Jordanian Arabic speech-to-text system. This enables new applications such as Arabic question-answering and intelligent control systems, and provides a generalizable approach for other low-resource languages and dialects.

title: LLJ Cards: Best practices for the Use of LLMs as Judges
summary: In recent years, large language models (LLMs) have emerged as a popular alternative for evaluation. Often referred to as LLMs as judges (LLJs), these systems have been widely adopted by researchers and practitioners across a broad range of measurement tasks, driven by their strong performance, scalability, and cost-effectiveness relative to human judgment. However, a growing body of work has shown that the use of LLJs raise concerns about their validity and reliability as evaluators. Existing efforts to address these challenges have largely focused on developing bias-mitigation techniques and refining prompting strategies. While these approaches represent an important step forward, they primarily offer technical fixes and leave a more fundamental challenge unaddressed: the lack of standardized, transparent, and reproducible evaluation practices. In this paper, we introduce LLJ Cards, a framework that synthesizes best practices from measurement theory, natural language generation, and machine learning literature into practical guidelines for LLJ-based evaluations. While LLJs offer a promising path toward scalable evaluation, their effective use requires grounding in rigorous evaluation principles to ensure validity, reliability, and reproducibility. LLJ Cards addresses this need by providing a structured framework for applying these principles in the design and reporting of automated evaluations.

AI.tldr: The paper critiques current use of large language models as evaluators (LLMs-as-judges) and proposes LLJ Cards, a standardized framework to make such evaluations more valid, reliable, and reproducible.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as automatic judges for many evaluation tasks because they are scalable and cheap compared to humans. However, growing evidence shows that these LLM judges can be biased, inconsistent, and opaque, and existing fixes (bias reduction, better prompts) do not solve the deeper problem: there is no shared, transparent, and standardized way to design, document, and report LLM-based evaluations. This undermines validity, reliability, and comparability of results across studies.
AI.method: The authors synthesize best practices from measurement theory, natural language generation evaluation, and machine learning methodology to create a practical guideline framework called LLJ Cards. This framework structures how researchers should plan, conduct, and document evaluations that rely on LLMs as judges, specifying key choices, assumptions, and procedures that must be made explicit to support rigorous evaluation.
AI.result: The main result is a conceptual and procedural framework (LLJ Cards) that organizes principles for using LLMs as judges into a set of standardized documentation and design guidelines. While the abstract does not report empirical experiments, it positions LLJ Cards as a tool to improve the rigor, transparency, and reproducibility of automated evaluations.
AI.conclusion: LLMs-as-judges are powerful but risky evaluation tools whose benefits can only be realized if their use is grounded in established evaluation principles. LLJ Cards offers a structured way to apply these principles, promoting validity, reliability, and reproducibility in LLJ-based evaluations by standardizing how such evaluations are designed and reported.

title: QLoRA Fine-Tuning of Ministral LLM for Sequence-to-Function Protein Annotation
summary: Functional annotation of newly sequenced proteins remains a bottleneck in molecular biology: the number of sequences in public repositories grows far faster than the capacity for manual curation. Most computational approaches consider annotation as multi-label classification over a fixed ontology, which constrains predictions to a predefined label set. In this work we study the the protein annotation as a sequence-to-text generation problem. We fine-tune the 3B-parameter Ministral 3 base model with QLoRA (4-bit NF4 quantization with low-rank adapters) on sequence annotation pairs. We assess predictions with an LLM-as-expert protocol: a GPT model prompted as a senior molecular-biology curator scores organism identification as binary and function annotation quality. We conclude that QLoRA-fine-tuned compact LLMs can generate curator-style annotations with genuine biological value for a substantial subset of proteins. We also discuss future directions in data quality, model scaling, and evidence grounding that are needed to make the approach sufficiently reliable for practical use.

AI.tldr: They fine-tune a small 3B-parameter LLM with QLoRA to generate free-text biological function annotations from protein sequences, evaluated by an LLM-based expert protocol, and show it can produce curator-like, biologically meaningful annotations for many proteins.
AI.motivation: Protein sequence databases are growing much faster than human curation capacity, making functional annotation a key bottleneck. Standard automated methods treat the task as multi-label classification over a fixed ontology, which restricts outputs to predefined labels and may miss nuanced or novel functions. The authors aim to explore a more flexible, generative framing that could yield richer, curator-style descriptions without being bound to a rigid label set.
AI.method: They reframe protein functional annotation as a sequence-to-text problem and fine-tune a 3B-parameter Ministral 3 base language model using QLoRA, employing 4-bit NF4 quantization with low-rank adapters to keep training efficient. The model is trained on protein-sequence / annotation text pairs. For evaluation, they use an LLM-as-expert setup, prompting a GPT model as if it were a senior molecular-biology curator to judge binary organism-identification correctness and to rate the quality of function descriptions produced by the fine-tuned model.
AI.result: The QLoRA-fine-tuned 3B LLM is able to generate free-text annotations that a GPT-based expert judge considers curator-like and biologically meaningful for a substantial portion of tested proteins, both in terms of organism identification and functional description quality. This indicates that even relatively compact LLMs, when specialized with low-rank adaptation on domain data, can capture useful biological semantics beyond fixed-label classification.
AI.conclusion: Treating protein annotation as sequence-to-text generation with compact, QLoRA-fine-tuned LLMs is a promising alternative to conventional multi-label ontology classification, capable of yielding curator-style, biologically informative descriptions for many proteins. However, to reach reliability sufficient for real-world deployment, the authors emphasize the need for improvements in training data quality, scaling models or training regimes, and better grounding of generated statements in explicit evidence and supporting information.

title: Toward a Unified Mathematics of Concepts
summary: Concepts are commonly defined as abstract, compact representations of knowledge and treated as basic units of intelligent behavior. Yet, cognition, psychology, and AI lack a shared mathematical language for them. Modern systems represent concepts as vectors, distributions, symbols, graphs, and other structures, but these formalisms are typically treated as competing rather than as solutions to a common problem. We propose an operation-based view that evaluates mathematical frameworks by the conceptual operations they support, identifying thirteen operations (including similarity, composition, generalization, and grounding) that recur across cognition, psychology, and AI. We show that ten frameworks embody distinct commitments to concepts as self-contained content, relational structure, or evolving process, and that these commitments determine which operations each supports naturally. For example, vector-based models facilitate graded similarity and generalization but struggle with explicit composition, whereas symbolic models support composition but offer but generalize poorly. No single framework we examined naturally supports all operations without extension. We test this account empirically using categorization as a case study, operationalizing nine theories on the same items against human judgments. Despite addressing the same conceptual question, the theories produce different procedures and results, demonstrating that mathematical commitment shapes what a theory can explain. We call for hybrid formalisms that treat content, relation, and process as jointly primary.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an operation-based framework to compare different mathematical representations of concepts across cognition, psychology, and AI, showing that each formalism supports a different subset of key conceptual operations and arguing for hybrid models that combine their strengths.
AI.motivation: There is no shared mathematical language for concepts across cognition, psychology, and AI. Existing formalisms—vectors, probability distributions, symbolic structures, graphs, etc.—are typically viewed as competing approaches rather than alternative solutions to the same underlying problem. This makes it hard to systematically compare theories, understand their limitations, or integrate insights across fields. The authors aim to provide a principled way to evaluate and relate these frameworks by the operations on concepts they enable.
AI.method: The authors adopt an operation-based perspective: instead of starting from representational formats, they identify thirteen core conceptual operations (such as similarity, composition, generalization, grounding) that recur across cognition, psychology, and AI. They then analyze ten major mathematical frameworks for representing concepts, characterizing each in terms of its underlying commitments: concepts as self-contained content, relational structure, or evolving process. They determine which operations each framework supports naturally or only with extensions. Empirically, they use categorization as a case study, implementing nine existing theoretical models on the same set of items and comparing their predictions to human categorization judgments, exposing how representational commitments lead to different procedures and outcomes.
AI.result: The theoretical analysis shows that the ten examined frameworks cluster around three commitments—content, relation, and process—and that each commitment confers strengths for some operations while limiting others. For instance, vector-space models naturally support graded similarity and smooth generalization but are weak at explicit symbolic composition; symbolic models excel at composition and discrete structure but generalize poorly and struggle with graded similarity. No single framework natively supports all thirteen operations; every one would require nontrivial extensions to cover the full set. The empirical categorization study reveals that nine operationalized theories, though all ostensibly about the same conceptual phenomenon, yield different computational procedures and divergent predictions on the same stimuli, each aligning with human data in different ways.
AI.conclusion: Mathematical choices about how to represent concepts are not neutral: they embody specific commitments that determine which conceptual operations are naturally expressible, what phenomena can be captured, and where each theory will succeed or fail. Treating different frameworks as simple competitors obscures their complementary strengths. The authors argue that future work on concepts should adopt an operation-based lens and pursue hybrid formalisms that treat content, relational structure, and dynamic process as co-equal, thereby enabling a broader and more flexible set of conceptual operations. This, they claim, is necessary for a unified, cross-disciplinary theory of concepts in cognition, psychology, and AI.

title: Evaluating Decision Models for Text Annotation in Computational Social Science
summary: Computational social science increasingly relies on large language models for text annotation, and the validity of published findings now rests on the labels generated by such models. Decision models, a new model class built for categorical question answering, answer typed questions with a choice, a probability distribution over the label set, and a confidence score rather than free text, at a small fraction of frontier inference prices. Whether their answers are accurate, and whether that stated confidence can be trusted on social science constructs, are unknown. Here, we mirror the evaluation of Ziems et al. (2024) on 18 computational social science classification tasks (7,977 items), comparing the first commercial decision model and two open-weight counterparts against 19 frontier and open-weight language models under the same zero-shot protocol. The decision model trails the per-task best LLM on 14 of 15 evaluation tasks, with a median deficit of 11.6 macro-F1 points, at a median 44 times lower measured cost. Its confidence is better calibrated than the verbalized confidence of 16 of the 19 LLMs, yet three frontier models show lower median calibration error (0.157 against 0.066). While items above 0.9 confidence are typically labeled accurately (median accuracy 0.815), on one task, empathy in peer-support dialogues, the model reports high confidence while performing near chance. Nonetheless, our results suggest that decision models are useful as a first step in the annotation pipeline: routing low-confidence items to an LLM matches or exceeds the LLM alone at a quarter to half of its cost.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates new decision models for categorical text annotation against traditional large language models (LLMs) on computational social science tasks, finding they are cheaper, somewhat less accurate, but often better calibrated and useful in hybrid pipelines.
AI.motivation: Computational social science now heavily depends on LLMs for labeling text data, but these models are expensive and their label confidence is often poorly calibrated, threatening the validity and cost-efficiency of large-scale studies. Decision models offer structured outputs and lower cost, yet their accuracy and reliability on nuanced social science constructs had not been systematically evaluated.
AI.method: The authors replicate the Ziems et al. (2024) evaluation protocol across 18 computational social science classification tasks (7,977 items). They compare one commercial decision model and two open-weight decision models against 19 frontier and open-weight LLMs under a uniform zero-shot setup. They assess macro-F1 performance, cost, and calibration of confidence scores, and examine a hybrid pipeline where low-confidence items from the decision model are routed to a stronger LLM.
