AI.result: The best decision model underperforms the per-task best LLM on 14 of 15 evaluation tasks, with a median deficit of 11.6 macro-F1 points, but operates at a median 44× lower cost. Its confidence estimates are better calibrated than verbalized confidence from 16 of 19 LLMs, though three frontier LLMs still achieve lower median calibration error (0.157 vs. 0.066). High-confidence predictions (>0.9) are usually accurate (median accuracy 0.815), but there are failures such as empathy detection where the model is confidently wrong. The hybrid pipeline that routes low-confidence items to an LLM matches or beats LLM-only performance at roughly 25–50% of the LLM cost.
AI.conclusion: Decision models are not yet as accurate as the best LLMs on computational social science labeling tasks, but they are far cheaper and often better calibrated, making them promising front-end annotators. Used in a routing pipeline that escalates uncertain items to stronger LLMs, they can replicate or surpass LLM-only labeling quality at substantially reduced cost, though care is needed on tasks where they can be confidently wrong, such as complex empathy judgments.

title: Written as a Record, Read as an Address: What a Forward Pass Leaves in an Operation's KV Cache
summary: When a language model reads an operation such as "Swap the contents of Box F and Box B", its forward pass writes keys and values for those tokens into the KV cache. Prior work on entity tracking establishes what models use: bindings are resolved at query time rather than stored as explicit latent state. We ask what they write at the operation span and how it is accessed. We split a forward pass into a frozen writer and a reader: the writer's cache is recomputed without gradients, while the reader sees only the instruction and operation tokens, with all state descriptions hidden, and is trained in isolation. Anything the reader recovers was therefore already present in the unmodified cache. On a synthetic boxes task, a base reader recovers $\leq 0.06$ of queried bindings against $0.75$--$1.00$ after training, and recoverability tracks the operation's read/write footprint. We find two modes of access. Across Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B, operation-span transplants causally redirect which visible state is read even when the two worlds hold identical values, revealing a routing record. Isolation training preserves routing and adds direct access to the payload, the value the operation read, from the single operand-name token in a narrow mid-depth band (layers 12--15 of 32 in Llama-3.1-8B, 14--17 in Mistral-7B) --- the same site that holds the routing record. The same recipe extends to further operations, ToMi and GSM8K, but is bounded by training coverage and costs open-book accuracy. Operation tokens thus leave localized, causally recoverable records that support both routing and direct payload access, though the model that writes them reads mainly the address they carry and not the value.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates what information transformer language models store in the KV cache at the span of symbolic operations (like swapping items in boxes), showing that operation tokens leave localized, causally recoverable records used primarily for routing (which address to read) rather than storing payload values, and that a separate trained reader can be taught to access payloads from these records.
AI.motivation: While prior work shows that language models resolve entity bindings at query time instead of maintaining explicit latent state, it remains unclear what exactly is written into the KV cache at the location of operations (e.g., swap, move) and how this information is accessed. Understanding this is key for mechanistic interpretability of how models track state and perform algorithmic tasks, and for explaining why models succeed or fail at symbolic reasoning and tracking entities through operations.
AI.method: The authors conceptually split a single forward pass into a frozen writer and a trainable reader. The writer is the original language model whose KV cache is computed without gradients on full inputs. The reader is another model (or head) that only sees the instruction and operation tokens, while all explicit state descriptions are hidden; it consumes the writer’s frozen KV cache. They evaluate how much information about bindings and state can be recovered by this reader, comparing a base (untrained) reader to a trained one, and analyze how recoverability correlates with the read/write footprint of operations. They use a synthetic boxes task and extend the approach to other tasks (ToMi, GSM8K), employ cache transplantation experiments to test causal effects, and localize information to specific layer ranges in Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B.
AI.result: On the synthetic boxes task, a base reader recovers at most 0.06 of queried bindings, whereas a trained reader recovers 0.75–1.00, with recoverability closely tracking where operations read and write in the model. Cache transplant experiments across Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B show that operation-span representations causally redirect which visible state is read even when underlying values are identical, indicating a stored routing record. After isolation training, the reader can directly access the payload (the value read by the operation) from a single operand-name token, within a narrow mid-depth layer band (layers 12–15 of 32 in Llama-3.1-8B, 14–17 in Mistral-7B), which coincides with the routing record’s location. Extending to ToMi and GSM8K shows similar patterns but performance is limited by coverage of training and reduces open-book accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Operation tokens in transformer LMs write localized, causally meaningful records into the KV cache that serve two roles: (1) routing, by encoding which addresses or visible states should be read, and (2) potential direct access to payload values when an appropriate reader is trained. However, the original model that writes these records mainly uses them as address information rather than as stored values. This clarifies how models implement algorithmic state updates: they do not primarily cache explicit latent states but instead store compact routing metadata at operation spans, which can nonetheless be leveraged by suitably trained readers to reconstruct more detailed state information.

title: Assessing Readability with LLMs: The Role of Reasoning and Few-Shot Prompting
summary: Readability assessment is essential for tailoring texts to intended audiences across educational, healthcare, and information retrieval domains. However, traditional readability formulas struggle to generalize across genres and languages, while supervised machine learning models rely on scarce, domain-specific annotated corpora, limiting their applicability--particularly for less-resourced languages. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a highly scalable, multilingual alternative that requires no task-specific training, yet the impact of advanced prompting strategies on their performance remains underexplored. In this paper, we conduct a systematic benchmark of diverse open-source LLMs for multilingual readability assessment, focusing on the prediction of discrete readability levels required by educational frameworks. In addition to English, we evaluate our approach on a less-resourced language, Slovenian, to establish whether LLMs remain effective in low-resource settings. Specifically, we investigate the influence of explicit reasoning, demonstrating that Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting and reasoning-oriented models yield significant improvements over direct answering. Furthermore, our exploration of few-shot in-context learning reveals that providing just one labelled example per category (1-shot) substantially enhances prediction quality compared to zero-shot settings, with additional examples offering diminishing returns. By comprehensively comparing these approaches against traditional unsupervised metrics and state-of-the-art supervised baselines, we establish the viability of out-of-the-box LLMs as robust, cross-lingual readability assessors.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks open-source LLMs for multilingual readability assessment, showing that explicit reasoning (CoT) and minimal few-shot examples make LLMs strong cross-lingual readability predictors, even in low-resource languages like Slovenian.
AI.motivation: Traditional readability formulas fail to generalize well across genres and languages, and supervised ML models depend on scarce, domain-specific labeled data, which is especially problematic for low-resource languages. With the rise of LLMs that can work zero-shot or few-shot and support many languages, there is a need to understand how well they can assess readability, which prompting strategies work best, and whether they can replace or complement existing methods.
AI.method: The authors systematically benchmark multiple open-source LLMs on the task of predicting discrete readability levels aligned with educational frameworks. They evaluate performance in English and a low-resource language (Slovenian). They compare prompting strategies: direct answering vs. explicit reasoning via Chain-of-Thought and reasoning-centric models, and explore few-shot in-context learning with varying numbers of labeled examples per category (from zero-shot to 1-shot and more). Results are contrasted with traditional unsupervised readability metrics and supervised state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.result: Explicit reasoning via Chain-of-Thought prompting and use of reasoning-optimized models significantly improves readability level prediction compared to direct answers. Few-shot in-context learning further boosts performance, with a single labeled example per category (1-shot) giving a large gain over zero-shot, while adding more examples produces diminishing returns. The LLM-based approaches perform competitively with or better than traditional unsupervised formulas and supervised baselines, for both English and Slovenian.
AI.conclusion: Out-of-the-box, open-source LLMs can serve as strong, multilingual readability assessors without task-specific training. Their effectiveness extends to low-resource languages like Slovenian. Advanced prompting strategies—particularly explicit reasoning (CoT) and minimal few-shot examples—are key to unlocking this performance, establishing LLMs as practical, cross-lingual alternatives or complements to traditional readability measures and supervised models.

title: Adapting Tree-Structured Speculative Decoding to DeepSeek-V4 for Efficient Inference
summary: Repeated execution of the target model during autoregressive decoding is a major source of LLM inference latency. Unlike linear speculation, which follows a single candidate chain, tree-structured speculation retains multiple branches from shared prefixes; under the same budget, this broader coverage can improve acceptance and efficiency. Adapting it to DeepSeek-V4 is nontrivial: its CSA/HCA online compressed attention concentrates the difficulty on the target-verify side, where branches diverging from a shared prefix compress into different states, breaking cross-branch state consistency. We integrate tree-structured speculative decoding into the DeepSeek-V4-Flash pipeline via branch-aware causal verification, temporary state isolation, and accepted-path state refresh, keeping verification and compressed-state updates consistent across branches. Across budgets D=5 to D=8, batch sizes 1 to 64, and three datasets (GSM8K, MBPP, ShareGPT), tree speculation achieves a higher accepted length than the matched linear configurations in all settings (e.g., at D=8 about 2.83--3.41 versus 2.39--2.84) and improves throughput in nearly all configurations---marginal only at the smallest budget---by up to about 18.5%. More importantly, the gains follow stable, transferable regularities: the relative gain grows with the budget and is most pronounced for less predictable workloads at small-to-medium batch sizes, while beyond a certain budget throughput plateaus and decouples from the still-rising accepted length. These results show that retaining multiple candidate paths under the same budget can effectively improve DeepSeek-V4 decoding efficiency, and offer experience for adapting speculative decoding to future models with compressed, sparse, or structured context representations.

AI.tldr: They adapt tree-structured speculative decoding to the DeepSeek-V4 model, resolving consistency issues caused by its compressed attention, and demonstrate higher accepted token lengths and up to ~18.5% throughput gains versus linear speculation under the same compute budget.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive decoding in large language models is slow because it repeatedly runs the target model step-by-step. Linear speculative decoding speeds this up but explores only a single candidate prefix, limiting acceptance and efficiency, especially under higher budgets or unpredictable workloads. DeepSeek-V4 uses compressed attention (CSA/HCA), complicating speculative decoding because branches that share prefixes compress into incompatible states, breaking cross-branch consistency. There is a need to exploit tree-structured speculation’s broader search while maintaining correct compressed states and realizing real throughput gains in such modern architectures.
AI.method: They design a tree-structured speculative decoding scheme for the DeepSeek-V4-Flash pipeline. Technically, they introduce: (1) branch-aware causal verification so each branch is validated correctly against the target model, (2) temporary state isolation so divergent branches can maintain their own compressed attention states without corrupting others, and (3) accepted-path state refresh to reconcile and update the compressed states once a branch is accepted. This ensures both verification and compressed state updates stay consistent across branches despite CSA/HCA’s online compression. They evaluate across speculation budgets D=5–8, batch sizes 1–64, and three benchmarks (GSM8K, MBPP, ShareGPT).
AI.result: Tree-structured speculation consistently achieves higher accepted sequence lengths than parameter-matched linear speculation in all tested settings. For example, at budget D=8 they obtain accepted lengths of about 2.83–3.41 tokens versus 2.39–2.84 for linear speculation. Throughput improves in nearly all configurations, with marginal gains only at the smallest budget, and peaks at about 18.5% improvement. They observe regular patterns: relative throughput gain increases with speculation budget and is strongest for less predictable tasks and small-to-medium batch sizes. However, beyond a certain budget, throughput saturates even though accepted length continues to rise, indicating diminishing returns in actual speed.
AI.conclusion: Tree-structured speculative decoding can be successfully adapted to models with compressed, structured context representations like DeepSeek-V4. By carefully managing branch-aware verification and compressed-state consistency, it delivers reliably higher acceptance rates and notable throughput gains over linear speculation under the same compute budget. The observed scaling regularities (with budget, workload predictability, and batch size) suggest practical guidelines and provide a template for extending speculative decoding to future LLM architectures that use compressed, sparse, or otherwise structured attention states.

title: When Quantization Preserves Accuracy but Not Evidence: Explanation-Aware Post-Training Quantization for Medical LLMs
summary:
Post-training quantization (PTQ) enables efficient deployment of large language models, and PTQ methods are usually optimized and evaluated with generic reconstruction, perplexity, or answer accuracy. But in explanation-critical domains, preserving only the final answer may be insufficient, since users may also inspect generated rationales to judge whether a prediction is trustworthy. We study this issue in medical multiple-choice question answering, where rationales should provide evidence that supports the selected answer.
  We propose an explanation-aware objective for transformation-based PTQ. Our method builds an offline faithfulness cache from full-precision teacher rationales and uses it during optimization to preserve answer-supporting evidence tokens and evidence-conditioned answer behavior. We instantiate it on OSTQuant under W4A4KV4 quantization and evaluate four 7B--8B medical and instruction-tuned LLMs on MedExQA, MedExpQA, and ChallengeClinicalQA. While a same-calibration OSTQuant baseline preserves task accuracy, it can substantially weaken answer-supporting rationales. Our objective is to preserve the full-precision model's answer-supporting behavior rather than improve gold-label accuracy, and our method better preserves the full-precision model's answer behavior and rationale-to-answer support. These results suggest that PTQ for explanation-critical settings should evaluate preservation of answer-supporting evidence, not only answer accuracy. Code and evaluation scripts are available at https://github.com/dut0817/EAQuant.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an explanation-aware post-training quantization method that preserves not just answer accuracy but also the answer-supporting rationales of medical LLMs.
AI.motivation: Standard PTQ methods focus on preserving model accuracy or perplexity, but in explanation-critical domains like medical QA, users rely on rationales to assess trustworthiness. Existing PTQ can keep answer accuracy while degrading the quality and faithfulness of rationales, which is problematic for safety and reliability.
AI.method: They design an explanation-aware objective for transformation-based PTQ (instantiated on OSTQuant with W4A4KV4 quantization). The method constructs an offline faithfulness cache using full-precision teacher rationales, then uses this cache during quantization optimization to explicitly preserve tokens that provide answer-supporting evidence and the answer behavior conditioned on that evidence. The optimization thus constrains the quantized model to behave similarly to the full-precision model in terms of rationale-to-answer support, not just final predictions.
AI.result: On MedExQA, MedExpQA, and ChallengeClinicalQA using four 7B–8B medical and instruction-tuned LLMs, the explanation-aware PTQ maintains task accuracy comparable to a standard OSTQuant baseline with the same calibration. However, unlike the baseline—which can significantly degrade answer-supporting rationales—the proposed method better preserves the full-precision model’s answer behavior and the faithfulness of rationales to answers.
AI.conclusion: For explanation-critical applications such as medical QA, PTQ should be evaluated and optimized not only for answer accuracy but also for preservation of answer-supporting evidence in model rationales. The proposed explanation-aware PTQ objective effectively maintains the full-precision model’s rationale-to-answer support under aggressive quantization, highlighting the need for explanation-aware metrics and objectives in model compression.

title: MSI-Bench: Evaluating Multi-Speaker Voice Interaction for Collaborative AI Agents
comment: 23 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables. Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/M2cha4l1124/MSI-Bench ; Code: https://github.com/boson-ai/MSI-Bench
summary: Voice provides a natural and immediate interface for AI agents. Many settings in which voice agents could be useful, including meetings, households, and collaborative work, are inherently multi-speaker. Supporting these settings introduces challenges that are largely absent from one-on-one interaction. We introduce the Multi-Speaker Interaction Benchmark (MSI-Bench) for evaluating multi-speaker voice interaction. Each test case is a short multi-party multi-turn audio scene with participant context, expected tool calls, and atomic rubrics. The benchmark targets three capability families: multi-speaker memory, multi-speaker instruction following, and multi-speaker reasoning. It comprises 1,152 test cases, evenly split between Mandarin Chinese and English (576 each). The strongest configuration on each split passes all rubrics on only 66.8% of English and 54.5% of Mandarin cases, and the strongest open-weight configuration on 34.0% and 19.3%. Failure analysis separates perception from reasoning: open-weight models are bottlenecked by the multi-speaker audio front-end, while frontier systems still fail speaker-scoped decision making on clean transcripts---and models across the board often respond when no one has addressed them. These results identify speaker-grounded perception, speaker-scoped decision making, and conversational restraint as concrete targets for future voice agents.

AI.tldr: Introduces MSI-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating AI voice agents in multi-speaker scenarios using 1,152 Mandarin and English audio test cases across memory, instruction following, and reasoning.
AI.motivation: Voice agents are naturally suited for many real-world scenarios like meetings and collaborative work, which are inherently multi-speaker. Existing evaluations focus mostly on one-on-one interactions, missing the unique difficulties of multi-speaker environments such as tracking who said what, following speaker-specific instructions, and making contextually appropriate decisions. The paper is motivated by the need for a systematic way to measure and improve these multi-speaker interaction capabilities.
AI.method: The authors construct the Multi-Speaker Interaction Benchmark (MSI-Bench), where each test case is a short, multi-party, multi-turn audio scene accompanied by participant context, expected tool calls, and fine-grained (atomic) rubrics for evaluation. The benchmark covers three capability families—multi-speaker memory, multi-speaker instruction following, and multi-speaker reasoning—and contains 1,152 test cases evenly divided between Mandarin Chinese and English. They evaluate various systems (including frontier and open-weight models) and analyze failure modes by separating perception (audio understanding, diarization) from reasoning (decision making given clean transcripts).
AI.result: On MSI-Bench, the strongest evaluated configuration passes all rubrics on 66.8% of English and 54.5% of Mandarin test cases, while the strongest open-weight configuration achieves only 34.0% and 19.3%, respectively. Failure analysis shows that open-weight models are mainly limited by the multi-speaker audio front-end (perception layer), whereas even the best proprietary systems still fail at speaker-scoped decision making when provided with perfect transcripts. Additionally, models frequently respond even when no speaker has explicitly addressed them.
AI.conclusion: Current voice agents struggle significantly in realistic multi-speaker settings, with substantial gaps in both perception (speaker-grounded understanding of audio) and reasoning (speaker-scoped decision making and conversational restraint). MSI-Bench provides a structured way to diagnose and quantify these weaknesses. The paper concludes that improving speaker-grounded perception, speaker-specific decision policies, and the ability to withhold responses unless appropriately addressed are key directions for the next generation of voice agents.

title: The Answer-Basin Representation Hypothesis: We Are Not Probing or Steering Concepts
summary: The Linear Representation Hypothesis associates high-level concepts with directions in language models, but it remains unclear how these concept-related linear structures are organized within the model. We propose the Answer-Basin Representation Hypothesis: the probability measure induced over answers by the model's continuation distribution organizes these linear structures, with its statistics represented along linear directions shared across questions. All continuations yielding the same answer form an answer basin, whose mass is their total probability. These basin masses define the pushforward probability measure over answers. We posit that concept-related linear structure emerges from differences in the answer measure rather than being determined by changes in concept labels. Experiments across models and tasks link concept-consistent effects and their reversals in probing and steering to the alignment between concept labels and the answer measure.

AI.tldr: They propose that concept directions in language models are organized by how the model distributes probability over answers, not just by label changes, and validate this via probing and steering experiments.
AI.motivation: Existing linear representation views say concepts correspond to directions in activation space, but we lack an account of how these directions are globally organized and why concept effects sometimes reverse across prompts, tasks, or models.
AI.method: They introduce the Answer-Basin Representation Hypothesis: group all continuations that correspond to the same answer into an “answer basin,” measure the total probability mass of each basin as a pushforward answer distribution, and analyze linear directions that encode statistics of this answer measure across questions. They then run probing and steering experiments on multiple models and tasks, comparing concept labels to the answer-basin-induced measure and studying when concept-consistent directions appear or flip.
AI.result: They find that linear directions associated with concepts track changes in the answer probability measure; concept-consistent probe features and steering directions emerge when concept labels align with the answer-basin structure, and reversals occur when this alignment breaks.
AI.conclusion: Concept-related linear structure in LMs is better explained by differences in the probability measure over answers (answer basins) than by labels alone, providing a unifying account of when and why concept directions appear or invert in probing and steering experiments.

title: Decomposing Error and Style in Automated Clinical Coding
summary: In automated clinical coding, where the label space spans tens of thousands of diagnosis and procedure codes, models are currently evaluated against a single gold annotation, treating any deviation as error. But we find when two teams code the same 110 ACI-Bench encounters, they agree on only 73% of codes (Jaccard similarity) for the same note; even after an independent clinical audit removes erroneous codes, agreement rises only to 77%. Is that gap error or something systematic? We model the systematic component as coding style $ψ$, a coder- or site-specific policy over what to code and how much to document, and recast coding as $p(\mathrm{code}\mid\mathrm{note},ψ)$, estimating $ψ$ with a 10-dimension rubric. If style were noise, conditioning on it would do nothing. Instead, across five datasets a model conditioned with a data-matching style raises ICD F1 by up to 26 points and an extreme mismatched one lowers it by up to 21. Four prompt based coding methods spanning 39-49 F1 converge to 52-56 once style is supplied (All p<0.05). Much of what single-gold evaluation charges to model error is recoverable, unmodeled style.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that a large portion of errors in automated clinical coding evaluations actually comes from unmodeled differences in human coding style, not just model mistakes.
AI.motivation: Automated clinical coding systems are typically evaluated against a single gold-standard set of codes, assuming any difference from that set is an error. However, human coders themselves disagree substantially even after expert auditing, suggesting that some of what is labeled as model error may instead stem from systematic differences in coding style across coders or institutions. The authors aim to quantify and model this style variation and see how it affects model performance and evaluation.
AI.method: The authors analyze coder agreement on 110 ACI-Bench clinical encounters coded independently by two teams, before and after an independent clinical audit, using Jaccard similarity. They introduce the notion of coding style ψ, defined as a coder- or site-specific policy over what to code and how thoroughly to document. They formally recast coding as a conditional distribution p(code | note, ψ). They then construct a 10-dimensional rubric to estimate ψ for different datasets or coders. Using this style representation, they condition automated coding models on different styles and measure ICD code prediction F1 across five datasets, comparing data-matched styles against mismatched or extreme styles. They also evaluate several prompt-based coding methods with and without style conditioning.
AI.result: Two independent coding teams show only 73% Jaccard agreement on codes for the same notes, which rises to only 77% even after removing clearly erroneous codes via an independent clinical audit. Conditioning automated coding models on a data-matched style ψ increases ICD F1 by up to 26 points, while conditioning on an extremely mismatched style reduces F1 by up to 21 points across five datasets. Multiple prompt-based coding methods that originally span a performance range of 39-49 F1 converge to a narrower, higher band of 52-56 F1 once style is incorporated, with all improvements statistically significant (p<0.05).
AI.conclusion: Human clinical coders exhibit substantial, systematic variation in coding style that persists even after error correction. Much of what standard single-gold evaluations classify as model error is actually due to unmodeled differences in coding style. By explicitly modeling and conditioning on a learned style representation, automated clinical coding systems can achieve markedly higher and more consistent performance, indicating that evaluation frameworks should account for style rather than treating all deviations from a single gold annotation as mistakes.

title: The Copy Ceiling: An Input-Exposure Control for Ontology-Grounded Generation over Curated Corpora
summary: When a language model answers from a curated corpus via graph-based retrieval, a large grounding uplift does not establish reasoning over the retrieved structure: the context may already expose the gold answers. We propose exposure accounting, which classifies each gold item by whether the shown context exposes it and whether the answer recovers it. Its scalar reference is the copy ceiling, the recall a verbatim copy of the context achieves; signed gain over copy measures the model's recall relative to this deterministic, judge-free baseline. Across ten models, unaided recall averages 0.26 and grounded recall 0.92, yet gain over copy is uniformly negative (-0.067 to -0.022). Of 11,360 gold-item observations, representing 1,136 target instances evaluated under ten models, only three unexposed items receive lexical credit. A stratified model-judged audit of 423 observations, with a symmetric quotation-verification policy, estimates that 97.1% of credited items assert the requested relation; all three unexposed credits fail relational adjudication. On targets the scaffold does not expose, lexical recovery falls from 0.121 unaided to 0.004 grounded; adjudication validates 71 of the 92 unaided credits and none of the three grounded credits, without establishing full-frame relational recovery rates. Rephrasing questions outside the graph's title vocabulary reduces exposure from 0.964 to 0.328, while an absence-triggered fallback activates on only 2 of 506 questions. A paired production study improves judged quality by +0.27 pooled, but negative controls do not establish content specificity beyond a well-formed on-corpus block. These results support exposure accounting as a standing control for corpus-derived evaluations. The accounting distinguishes exposed-item omissions from beyond-exposure recoveries; it does not determine whether reasoning occurred.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that when language models answer questions using graph-based retrieval from a curated corpus, their apparent gains from grounding mostly come from copying exposed answers, not from reasoning over the graph. It proposes “exposure accounting” to separate what is already visible in the context from what the model truly recovers beyond exposure, and finds almost no evidence of beyond-exposure recovery.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of grounded language models often report high performance when models are given structured, graph-based retrieval contexts from curated corpora. However, these results may conflate simple copying of already-exposed facts with genuine reasoning over the retrieved structure. There is a need for a systematic way to measure how much of a model’s success is just copying exposed information versus inferring or reasoning about information that is not trivially exposed in the context.
AI.method: The authors introduce “exposure accounting,” which, for each gold (target) item, classifies whether the retrieval context explicitly exposes that item and whether the model’s answer recovers it. They define the “copy ceiling” as the recall that a deterministic verbatim-copy system could achieve by copying from the context, and define “gain over copy” as the model’s recall minus this baseline. They then evaluate ten language models across 1,136 target instances (11,360 gold-item observations), comparing unaided versus grounded settings. They perform a stratified human audit of 423 observations under a symmetric quotation-verification policy to check if credited items truly assert the requested relation. They also manipulate question phrasing to reduce exposure and examine fallback behavior, plus a paired production study and negative controls to assess judged answer quality and content specificity.
AI.result: Unaided model recall averages 0.26, while grounded recall reaches 0.92, suggesting a large apparent benefit from grounding. However, gain over copy is uniformly negative across models (-0.067 to -0.022), indicating models perform worse than the simple copy baseline when controlling for exposure. Out of 11,360 gold-item observations, only three unexposed items receive lexical credit, and all three fail relational adjudication under human judgment. For targets not exposed by the scaffold, lexical recovery drops from 0.121 unaided to 0.004 grounded; adjudication confirms 71 of 92 unaided credits and none of the three grounded credits. Rephrasing questions outside the graph title’s vocabulary sharply reduces exposure (from 0.964 to 0.328), and an absence-triggered fallback is almost never used (2/506 questions). A paired production study shows a +0.27 pooled improvement in judged answer quality with grounding, but negative controls indicate this may reflect general on-corpus fluency rather than content-specific reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Exposure accounting provides a necessary control for evaluations where answers are derived from a corpus via structured retrieval. It separates omissions of already-exposed items from genuine beyond-exposure recoveries and shows that most apparent gains from graph-based grounding in this setting are due to copying exposed facts, not reasoning over the retrieved structure. However, exposure accounting itself cannot determine whether reasoning occurred; it only bounds what could be achieved by copying and highlights where true reasoning would need to manifest (in beyond-exposure recoveries).

title: OSWorld-Pro: Process-based Evaluation for Computer Use Agents
summary: Evaluation of Computer-Use Agents (CUAs) is often limited to the final deliverables they create (at the end of hundreds of steps) and assessed with functional verifiers, as seen in OSWorld. However, such evaluation of end-state performance lacks transparency into how and why agents fail in various tasks, obfuscating critical insight for subsequent improvement. For instance, agents that err during keyboard inputs would require a different mitigation strategy from those that fail to precisely provide click-based inputs on the graphical UI. We introduce OSWorld-Pro: a set of over 300 tasks containing over 2800 subgoals to enable the procedural evaluation of CUAs grounded in over 67,000 human annotations. We use robust human-aligned LLM-Judges to evaluate the fulfillment of OSWorld-Pro subgoals and thereby reveal the progress that models make throughout a series of sequentially dependent subgoals. Our findings reveal that OSWorld-Pro is challenging even for state-of-the-art LLMs, with top performers like Claude Opus 5 achieving only 75.7% vs. 83.4% on OSWorld. Furthermore, we identify critical process-focused failure modes of various models (e.g. subgoal-irrelevant actions and click-based mistakes) to provide insights to improve performance and efficiency of CUAs.

AI.tldr: OSWorld-Pro is a new benchmark that evaluates computer-use agents procedurally at the subgoal level rather than only on final task success, revealing detailed failure modes.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of computer-use agents focus on final task completion using functional verifiers, which hides how and where agents fail during long multi-step interactions. This lack of process transparency makes it hard to design targeted improvements, since errors in different interaction modalities (e.g., keyboard vs. mouse-click) require different mitigation strategies.
AI.method: The authors construct OSWorld-Pro, a benchmark of 300+ tasks decomposed into 2800+ sequentially dependent subgoals, supported by over 67,000 human annotations. They use robust, human-aligned LLM-based judges to automatically assess whether each subgoal is completed, enabling procedural tracking of an agent’s progress through the task. They run various state-of-the-art LLM-based CUAs on OSWorld-Pro and analyze detailed process-level behaviors and failure patterns, such as irrelevant subgoal actions or click-based mistakes.
AI.result: State-of-the-art models perform significantly worse on OSWorld-Pro than on standard OSWorld end-state evaluation; for instance, Claude Opus 5 achieves 75.7% on OSWorld-Pro versus 83.4% on OSWorld. The subgoal-level evaluation exposes concrete failure categories like subgoal-irrelevant actions and systematic click errors, varying across models.
AI.conclusion: OSWorld-Pro is a more challenging and diagnostic benchmark for CUAs than traditional end-state evaluations. Its fine-grained, subgoal-level judgments provide richer insight into agents’ process-level weaknesses, enabling more targeted methods to improve both performance and efficiency of computer-use agents.

title: Human-LLM Deliberation as Interactive Proof: Conditions for Verifiability Without Transparency
summary: When an LLM supplies an argument that a user could not readily construct, how can the user decide whether to accept its claim? Inspired by interactive proofs, we model human-LLM deliberation as an interaction between a prover with unrestricted internal search and a resource-bounded human verifier. The verifier requests and checks supporting details without access to the LLM's internal state. Passed checks accumulate evidence toward an acceptance threshold. We prove anytime-valid soundness against adaptive provers: the probability of ever accepting a false claim is at most a chosen error level, provided the task supplies bounds on false passes and human checking errors that remain valid after every relevant history. A finite-horizon completeness bound additionally requires bounds on the adequacy of honest responses and sufficient diagnostic progress. Further checks can strengthen the evidence for acceptance, but each requires another adequate response and reliable human effort. Whether this tradeoff permits certification depends on the verifier's effort budget, cognitive load, expertise, and fatigue. We identify conditions under which the supplied bounds certify a specified sequence of local checks but not a specified global check under the same resource budgets.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes human-LLM interaction as an interactive proof-like process, giving conditions under which a human can statistically control the chance of ever accepting a wrong LLM claim through sequential checking.
AI.motivation: Users often rely on LLMs for arguments or reasoning they cannot easily generate or check themselves. This creates a trust problem: how can a resource-limited human decide whether to accept an LLM’s nontrivial claim without access to its internal reasoning process? Existing approaches either assume idealized users, ignore human error and fatigue, or lack formal guarantees on the risk of accepting incorrect claims. The paper aims to provide a principled framework with explicit probabilistic guarantees for human acceptance decisions in these asymmetric settings.
AI.method: The authors model the human-LLM interaction as an interactive proof system: the LLM is a prover with powerful (in principle unbounded) internal computation, and the human is a resource-bounded verifier who can only request and check local pieces of evidence. They define a protocol in which the human issues queries for supporting details and then evaluates each response using bounded cognitive resources. Each passed check contributes evidence toward an overall acceptance threshold. They introduce formal assumptions about (i) bounds on the probability that a false claim passes any given local check, (ii) bounds on human checking errors, and (iii) conditions ensuring these bounds remain valid after any interaction history, including adaptive prover strategies. Using probability and martingale-style arguments, they derive anytime-valid soundness guarantees—bounds on the probability of ever accepting a false claim—as well as finite-horizon completeness bounds that incorporate assumptions about honest prover behavior and diagnostic progress over time.
AI.result: They prove that for any chosen error level (e.g., 1%), there exists a deliberation protocol such that, as long as the supplied per-check error bounds and human reliability assumptions hold uniformly over the interaction history, the probability that the human ever accepts a false claim is at most that target error level. These guarantees are anytime-valid: they hold no matter how many checks are performed or when the human decides to stop. They also derive conditions under which, given a finite number of interaction rounds and assumptions on the informativeness of honest answers, the protocol is likely to accept true claims (a completeness bound). Additionally, they show that while a given set of bounds may certify a sequence of specified local checks, they may fail to certify a more ambitious global check pattern under the same resource constraints, clarifying limits on what can be safely verified with bounded human effort.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that human-LLM deliberation can be placed on a rigorous footing similar to interactive proofs, yielding formal, anytime-valid guarantees about the risk of accepting incorrect LLM claims, provided we can bound false positive rates of local checks and human checking errors in a history-robust way. However, achieving certification in practice depends critically on human factors—effort budget, cognitive load, expertise, and fatigue—as each additional check both increases evidential strength and consumes limited human resources. The framework highlights a fundamental tradeoff: stronger guarantees require more reliable and informative checks, which may not be feasible for all tasks or users, and some desired global verification strategies may be unattainable even when local checks are certifiable under the same constraints.

title: Jev for Scientific Decisions: Evaluating Semantic Choices and Their Consequences
comment: 11 pages, 1 figure, 5 tables. Includes references and appendices
summary: Scientific workflows often require choosing among known relations before a deterministic calculation can proceed. Whether observations share a culture, treatment or reference standard can change the scientific meaning of the resulting count or comparison. We evaluate Jev as a semantic decision component using a harness that follows its documented guidance and assigns arithmetic to code. The study compares twelve model configurations on twenty source-grounded Choices across ten scientific cases, each repeated five times. We measure semantic selections, downstream outputs and final claim labels separately. Jev matched five other configurations at complete semantic correctness and achieved the lowest observed median latency among successful responses. Across three comparison models, seven wrong selections on one culture-history question changed downstream counts while preserving the correct final label. These results identify a useful role for Jev in prepared scientific decision tasks and show why evaluating that role requires checking the relations and quantities that a workflow will reuse.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates Jev, a semantic decision component, on scientific workflow choices and finds it can select correct semantic relations efficiently with low latency.
AI.motivation: In scientific workflows, the meaning of counts and comparisons depends on correctly selecting the underlying relations (e.g., culture, treatment, reference standard) before deterministic calculations. Existing systems may get final labels right while making wrong intermediate semantic choices, which risks misinterpreting reused quantities. The authors want to rigorously test Jev as a component that makes these semantic choices and to show why evaluating such tools must look beyond just final answers.
AI.method: The authors implement a test harness that follows Jev’s documented usage guidance and maps semantic decisions to arithmetic code in workflows. They design 20 source-grounded Choice tasks across 10 scientific cases, each run 5 times, and compare 12 model configurations, including Jev and several baselines. They separately measure (1) semantic decision correctness, (2) downstream numerical outputs, and (3) final claim labels, enabling them to see where wrong semantic choices may still yield apparently correct final answers.
AI.result: Jev achieves complete semantic correctness, matching five other configurations on that metric, but also delivers the lowest observed median latency among all successful configurations. In a focused analysis of three comparison models, they find seven incorrect semantic selections on a culture-history question that altered intermediate counts while leaving the final claim label unchanged, exposing a hidden class of errors invisible to label-only evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Jev is effective and efficient as a semantic decision component for prepared scientific decision tasks. However, the study shows that evaluating such components only on final labels can miss important semantic and quantitative errors. Proper assessment must explicitly examine the correctness of selected relations and the resulting quantities that workflows will reuse, underscoring the need for relation- and quantity-aware evaluation in scientific automation.

title: ToneCL: Contrastive Learning for Few-Shot Syllable-Level Tone Classification
summary: Tone languages constitute over 50-70% of the world's languages, but the vast majority are low-resource, lacking the large transcribed corpora needed for automatic tone classification. Existing datasets are typically collected at the sentence level, whereas field linguists require fine-grained syllable-level annotations. We propose ToneCL, a lightweight contrastive learning framework for few-shot syllable-level tone classification. We simulate low-resource conditions on Mandarin and Vietnamese, limiting labeled data to tens of examples per tone class. ToneCL is pretrained on unlabeled speech with augmentations that preserve tonal identity, then fine-tuned on few-shot examples. Experiments show our method consistently outperforms baselines, achieving 91.6% on six-speaker Mandarin at 10 shots. Cross-lingual transfer is also effective: pretraining on Vietnamese and fine-tuning on Mandarin reaches 91.0\% accuracy at 10 shots. Ablation confirms that frequency band rejection is the most critical augmentation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ToneCL, a contrastive learning framework that enables accurate syllable-level tone classification for low-resource tone languages using only a few labeled examples per tone class.
AI.motivation: Most of the world’s tone languages are low-resource and lack large, transcribed corpora, especially at the fine-grained syllable level needed by field linguists. Existing datasets are usually sentence-level, and current tone classification methods rely on large labeled datasets, making them unsuitable for documenting under-resourced tone languages.
AI.method: The authors design ToneCL, a lightweight contrastive learning framework. It is first pretrained on unlabeled speech using augmentations that preserve tonal identity (with a focus on frequency band rejection) to learn tone-relevant representations. Then it is fine-tuned in a few-shot setting, with only tens of labeled examples per tone class. They simulate low-resource conditions on Mandarin and Vietnamese to evaluate the approach, including cross-lingual transfer where pretraining and fine-tuning are done on different languages.
AI.result: ToneCL consistently outperforms baseline methods for syllable-level tone classification in few-shot scenarios. On a six-speaker Mandarin dataset with 10 labeled examples (shots) per tone class, it achieves 91.6% accuracy. When pretrained on Vietnamese and fine-tuned on Mandarin with 10 shots, it still attains 91.0% accuracy, demonstrating effective cross-lingual transfer. Ablation studies show that frequency band rejection is the most crucial augmentation for performance.
AI.conclusion: Contrastive pretraining with tone-preserving augmentations allows robust syllable-level tone classification with very few labeled examples, making it promising for low-resource tone languages. The effectiveness on both within-language and cross-lingual settings, and the critical role of frequency band rejection, suggest that ToneCL can help bridge the gap between practical field linguistics needs and current data-hungry tone classification methods.

title: DolphinBench: Mapping the Pareto Frontier of Agent Memory
summary:
Agents today often take real-world actions that depend on long-term memory and context recall over time. However, most current memory benchmarks are built for a conversational question-answer format, where the question itself signals that some fact must be retrieved, and often which one. Moreover, benchmarks rarely require anything beyond accuracy from submissions, allowing memory systems to make unreasonable cost/time tradeoffs to achieve higher scores.
  We present DolphinBench, a benchmark that evaluates memory directly through an agent's task completion. DolphinBench includes three knowledge-work personas with roughly 500k tokens of user messages per persona and evaluates agents on tasks that depend on information from that history. We verify all 200 tasks per persona by running an agent with and without the relevant history, requiring success with it and failure without it.
  Finally, we require all evaluations to report total cost and latency alongside accuracy, which enables us to evaluate agent memory systems holistically. No existing memory benchmark combines all three. The dataset and evaluation code are available at https://dolphinbench.ai.

AI.tldr: DolphinBench is a benchmark that tests how well AI agents use long-term memory to complete tasks over extended histories, measuring not just accuracy but also cost and latency.
AI.motivation: Existing memory benchmarks mostly use short conversational QA setups where the question itself clearly indicates which fact to retrieve. They also focus purely on accuracy, allowing systems to use impractical amounts of compute or time to get higher scores. This does not reflect real-world agent settings where memory must support long, realistic workflows and where efficiency matters.
AI.method: The authors build DolphinBench, a benchmark centered on agent task completion rather than isolated QA. They design three realistic knowledge-work personas, each with about 500k tokens of accumulated user messages. For each persona, they create 200 tasks whose successful completion crucially depends on information somewhere in that long history. They validate each task by running an agent twice: once with access to the relevant history and once without. A task is retained only if the agent succeeds with the history and fails without it, confirming that the task truly depends on long-term memory. The benchmark further requires that all evaluations report total cost and latency in addition to accuracy.
AI.result: DolphinBench provides a validated collection of tasks across three personas where success is demonstrably dependent on long-term memory access to large histories. It offers a standardized way to measure not only whether an agent can recall needed information to complete tasks, but also the associated cost and latency. No previous benchmark simultaneously evaluated long-context task performance, memory dependence, and resource efficiency in this way.
AI.conclusion: DolphinBench fills a gap in evaluating agent memory systems by tying evaluation to realistic task completion over very long histories and by incorporating cost and latency into the benchmark. It enables more holistic and practical assessment of long-term memory mechanisms, encouraging methods that are both accurate and efficient, and provides a public dataset and codebase for the research community.

title: SocioVerse2: A Longitudinal Dynamic Social Simulation Framework under a Human-AI Co-evolutionary Paradigm
summary: Social simulation offers the social sciences an experimental instrument that the real world cannot supply, and generative agents have transformed it by acting as silicon samples that unite agent-based modeling with real behavioral data. Existing platforms verify collective behavior, align simulated populations with real societies in cross-sections, and employ autonomous agents for the research process. However, two social science requirements remain without systematic support: intervention in the content of a simulation and the researcher's control over the process that produces it. We present SocioVerse2, which extends SocioVerse 1.0 into a human-AI co-evolutionary paradigm built from two loops and one infrastructure. The longitudinal simulation loop simulates the target population with evolving environments and forks counterfactual branches via interventions. The controllable research loop takes the study itself as an editable state and updates state versions via controllable editing. The social science agentic infrastructure carries both loops through composable skills with researcher checkpoints, a population service over five persona pools, and an environment service over 21 real-world signal sources with point-in-time guarantees. We validate SocioVerse2 across three case families and seven case studies, from reproducing canonical agent-based models to modeling policy processes on real records and nowcasting macro-economic indices beyond the response model's knowledge cutoff. With the human-AI co-evolutionary paradigm, these cases go beyond system demonstrations to become substantive studies that investigate frontier questions in their respective disciplines. Code, data services, and a workbench are released as open-source resources.

AI.tldr: SocioVerse2 is a human-AI co-evolutionary social simulation platform that lets researchers both intervene in simulations and control the research process, using generative agents, rich real-world signals, and composable skills, validated across multiple social science case studies.
AI.motivation: While generative-agent-based social simulations can reproduce collective behaviors and align with real-world data, social scientists still lack systematic support for (1) intervening in the content of ongoing simulations (e.g., counterfactual scenarios, policy changes) and (2) tightly controlling and editing the research process itself as it unfolds. Existing systems mostly demonstrate capabilities rather than enabling substantive, controlled social-science studies over time. There is a need for an infrastructure that turns these simulations into rigorous, manipulable experimental instruments co-steered by humans and AI.
AI.method: The authors design SocioVerse2 as a human-AI co-evolutionary framework composed of two main loops plus a shared infrastructure. The longitudinal simulation loop runs evolving simulations of target populations, with dynamic environments and explicit forking into counterfactual branches produced by interventions. The controllable research loop treats the study design and process as an editable state, allowing researchers to version, modify, and steer it via controllable editing. Underneath, a social science agentic infrastructure provides: (a) composable agent skills with researcher checkpoints, (b) a population service drawing from five persona pools, and (c) an environment service integrating 21 real-world signal sources with point-in-time guarantees. The platform is implemented and then exercised on diverse tasks to show generality and fidelity.
AI.result: SocioVerse2 is validated across three case families and seven concrete case studies: reproducing classic agent-based models, modeling policy processes grounded in real documentary records, and nowcasting macro-economic indices that extend beyond the knowledge cutoff of the underlying response models. In these cases, the system can both conduct realistic, data-grounded simulations and support researcher interventions and process control. The platform and its components (code, data services, and a workbench) are made available as open-source resources.
AI.conclusion: SocioVerse2 operationalizes a human-AI co-evolutionary paradigm for social simulation, where both the simulated society and the research workflow are explicitly steerable and editable. This enables moving from mere system demos toward substantive, frontier social-science studies that leverage generative agents, rich real-world signals, and structured researcher control. The open-source release is intended to make this new style of controlled, intervention-ready social simulation broadly accessible to social scientists.

title: Linguistic Features for Interpretable Textual Entailment
summary: Despite the success of neural models in natural language processing, their black-box nature limits interpretability and conceals the linguistic phenomena underlying their predictions. We present SLITE, an explainable hybrid model for Recognizing Textual Entailment that integrates two complementary layers of semantic analysis: a structural-relational layer, based on semantic compatibility and incompatibility between compositional entities, and a distributional-informational layer, based on structured patterns of information change between embedding-based representations of the premise and the hypothesis. We propose 17 features that combine entity-level semantic relations, polarity-sensitive lexical matching, and alignment measures over semantic sub-representations of the similarity matrix, including measures based on entropy and transfer entropy. A logistic regression trained on these features achieves an accuracy of 83% on three-class SICK and 96% on SICK-CE, outperforming IsoLex by 4 percentage points and falling within 2 percentage points of RoBERTa with a fraction of its computational complexity. Ablation studies and SHAP analysis confirm that structural-relational features are the primary drivers of classification, while distributional-informational features provide essential complementary contributions, particularly for detecting neutrality and contradiction. Our results demonstrate that further exploration of hybrid approaches is a viable and scientifically productive alternative to massive neural architectures, and we hope they will strengthen the dialogue between linguistic theory and computational modeling of inference

AI.tldr: SLITE is an interpretable hybrid model for textual entailment that combines symbolic semantic relations with information-theoretic features over embeddings, achieving near–state-of-the-art accuracy with far lower complexity.
AI.motivation: Neural NLP models achieve strong performance but act as black boxes, making it hard to understand what linguistic phenomena drive their predictions. The authors want an RTE model that is both accurate and interpretable, and that explicitly connects linguistic theory with computational inference, as an alternative to opaque, massive neural architectures.
AI.method: They design SLITE, a hybrid explainable model for Recognizing Textual Entailment, with two semantic layers: (1) a structural-relational layer that encodes semantic compatibility/incompatibility between compositional entities (including entity-level relations and polarity-sensitive lexical matches); and (2) a distributional-informational layer that models structured patterns of information change between premise and hypothesis embeddings. From these they engineer 17 features—covering semantic relations, polarity-sensitive matches, and alignment metrics over sub-parts of the similarity matrix, including entropy and transfer-entropy-based measures—and train a logistic regression classifier on these features. They then perform ablation and SHAP analyses to assess feature contributions.
AI.result: The logistic regression model using the 17 hybrid features attains 83% accuracy on the three-class SICK dataset and 96% on SICK-CE, outperforming the IsoLex baseline by 4 percentage points and coming within 2 percentage points of RoBERTa’s performance, while using much less computation. Analyses show that structural-relational features account for most of the predictive power, while the distributional-informational features are especially helpful for correctly classifying neutrality and contradiction.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid models that combine explicit structural semantics with distributional and information-theoretic features can yield highly competitive performance in textual entailment while remaining transparent and computationally lightweight. Structural-relational features are central, but distributional-informational signals add important nuance. This supports the view that interpretable, linguistically grounded methods are a viable, scientifically valuable alternative to large black-box neural architectures and can foster stronger connections between linguistic theory and computational models of inference.

title: onPanda: Efficient Annotation of On-Policy Alignment Data for LLMs and Agents via Token-Level Correction
summary: We present onPanda, an interactive tool for efficiently annotating LLM alignment data and agent trajectories. onPanda adopts token-level correction as its core interaction: while reading a model response, the annotator locates the first inappropriate token and either picks a substitute from the model's candidate tokens or types the correct text via free-form editing. The system then truncates everything after that position and continues generation from the corrected prefix, repeating this locate-correct-continue loop until a satisfactory response is obtained. This mechanism lets annotators precisely steer model outputs at low cost: a small controlled study suggests that onPanda reduces median annotation time by 52% over manual post-editing. Since the vast majority of tokens in the final response are generated by the model itself, the resulting data largely preserves the model's sampling distribution and is well suited for constructing on-policy SFT and preference data. Furthermore, the token-level corrections recorded during annotation provide fine-grained supervision with precise positions and naturally paired positive--negative samples. onPanda also connects to external tools and harnesses, enabling interactive trajectory annotation in realistic environments. In addition, we release Panda-CVL, a dataset annotated with onPanda, together with a benchmark for token-level correction.

AI.tldr: onPanda is an interactive token-level correction tool that speeds up creating alignment and agent-trajectory data for LLMs while keeping data close to the model’s own distribution.
AI.motivation: Collecting high-quality alignment and trajectory data is slow and costly when humans must manually post-edit or fully rewrite model outputs; existing methods also struggle to keep data on-policy with the model’s sampling distribution and rarely capture fine-grained, token-level supervision signals.
AI.method: Introduce onPanda, an annotation interface centered on token-level correction. Annotators read a model response, identify the first inappropriate token, replace it either by choosing from model-suggested alternatives or via free-form editing, after which the system truncates subsequent text and regenerates from the corrected prefix. This locate-correct-continue loop repeats until the response is satisfactory. The tool logs all token-level edits and can connect to external tools and harnesses for annotating interactive trajectories.
AI.result: In a small controlled study, onPanda cuts median annotation time by 52% compared with manual post-editing. Most tokens in final outputs remain model-generated (preserving the model’s sampling distribution). The authors also release Panda-CVL, an alignment dataset created with onPanda, and a benchmark specifically for token-level correction.
AI.conclusion: Token-level correction as a core interaction paradigm enables faster, cheaper, and more precise construction of LLM alignment and trajectory datasets while staying close to the model’s own distribution; the logged corrections provide rich, fine-grained supervision, and the released Panda-CVL dataset and benchmark support further research on such correction-based methods.
